Marcus rested his chin in his palm, eyes dragging across the printed newspaper column. "...an absolute travesty to modern cuisine..." the critic had written. Marcus blinked slowly, his gaze drifting from the black ink to a tiny, grey spider spinning a web in the corner of the office ceiling. The spider was making a lot of progress. Marcus traced the edge of his desk with his thumbnail, scraping off a tiny fleck of dried varnish. He looked back at the paper. "...a culinary disaster..." He let out a long, slow exhale that ruffled the top edge of the page. The ticking of the wall clock seemed unusually loud today. He tapped his index finger against his cheek in a slow, steady rhythm, wondering if it was too early to start boiling the potatoes, or if he should just watch the spider finish its web first.

The famous blogger shoved his phone into my face, his finger jabbing furiously at the screen. "One star!" he yelled, veins popping in his forehead. "I told my two million followers your risotto tastes like wet cardboard!" I watched his mouth move. He had a piece of spinach stuck between his front teeth. It was a fascinating shade of forest green. "Are you even listening to me?" he demanded, slamming his hand on the pass. I rested my weight against the counter, tracing circles on the stainless steel with a damp rag. "Wet cardboard," I repeated. "Right." My eyes wandered to the ceiling fan spinning lazy, endless circles above us. "Did you want a to-go box for the rest of it, or should I just toss it?" I asked, suppressing a yawn that threatened to stretch my jaw.

"He says the duck was a rubbery insult to poultry," the sous-chef read aloud, pacing the kitchen with the magazine in hand. Chef Lin sat on an overturned milk crate, methodically popping the bubbles on a sheet of leftover bubble wrap. Pop. Pop. Pop. "An insult," Lin echoed, her tone devoid of inflection. She stared out the back window at the empty alleyway. A stray cat walked past a dumpster. Lin watched it until it disappeared around the corner. "He says our sauce lacks depth!" the sous-chef continued, his voice shrill with panic. Lin grabbed another section of the plastic wrap. Pop. Pop. "Depth," she murmured, resting her cheek against the cold cinderblock wall. She checked her watch, realized it was only two o'clock, and let out a heavy sigh. "Let me know when he gets to the dessert section," she said, closing her eyes.

I scrolled through the three-page email from the Times food critic, my chin propped heavily on my fist. Abysmal. Catastrophic. Inedible. The words blurred together into a grey block of text. I clicked my ballpoint pen. Click-clack. Click-clack. I minimized the email window and opened a tab for a solitaire game, dragging a black eight onto a red nine. The critic had devoted an entire paragraph to hating the garnish on my scallops. I leaned back in my squeaky leather chair, staring at a water stain on the ceiling tiles that looked vaguely like a map of Italy. I clicked back to the email, scrolled to the very bottom to see if there was a signature, and then opened another tab to look up the weather forecast for the weekend. Partly cloudy. I dragged a red seven onto the black eight.

Elias watched the YouTube review on his tablet, his chin resting flat on the kitchen prep table. On screen, the local food critic was dramatically gagging into a napkin, declaring Elias’s signature bouillabaisse an offense to the ocean. Elias blinked once. He picked up a stray piece of raw macaroni from the counter and rolled it back and forth under his index finger. Forward, backward. Forward, backward. The critic in the video was now shouting about the texture of the clams. Elias slowly turned his head to watch a drop of water gather at the tip of the sink faucet, swell to its breaking point, and fall. Plink. He looked back at the tablet, grabbed a Sharpie, and started drawing tiny mustaches on the faces of the health inspectors pictured in the mandatory poster on the wall.

"This steak is an absolute atrocity!" the critic bellowed, throwing his napkin onto the linen tablecloth. The entire dining room went silent. I stood at the end of his table, arms crossed, my weight shifted onto my left leg. I stared at the way his double chin jiggled when he shouted. "I will ruin this establishment!" he sputtered. I let my eyes wander to the ornate chandelier above him, mentally counting the glass crystals. Forty-two, forty-three, forty-four. "Did you hear me, Chef?" he snapped. I shifted my weight to my right leg and let out a slow, long breath through my nose. "I heard you," I said, keeping my voice entirely flat. "Atrocity." I glanced at the wall clock. Still another three hours until closing. I picked at a piece of lint on my apron strings. "Can I take the plate, then?"

Chef Moreau held the handwritten letter from the Parisian critic loosely in one hand. 'A disaster of flavor profiling,' the cursive looped aggressively. Moreau sat at his desk, his eyes drifting away from the paper to stare out the window. A single cloud moved across the pale blue sky. It looked a bit like a shoe. He brought his attention back to the letter, reading the next line about his truffles being wasted on a peasant palate. He yawned, stretching his arms high above his head until his shoulders popped, then slumped back down into his chair. He picked up a paperclip and began bending it out of shape, carefully straightening the metal wire until it was completely flat. Once it was straight, he stared at it for a moment, then tossed it into the trash can. He picked up another paperclip.

The kitchen was in total chaos over the scathing article in the morning gazette. Julian was pacing, Maria was crying, and the dishwasher had started praying. I sat on a flour bucket in the dry storage room, resting my chin in my hands. The critic had called my duck confit a culinary tragedy. I tapped my foot against the concrete floor, watching a line of ants march systematically toward a spilled grain of sugar. One ant picked it up and turned around. The others followed. I traced the grout lines in the cinderblock wall with my eyes. Down, across, up, across. Julian burst through the door, waving the newspaper frantically. "What are we going to do?!" he shrieked. I slowly blinked at him, then looked back at the ants. "I suppose we should sweep the floor," I murmured, staring at the empty wall.

The television in the breakroom blared the harsh words of the city's top food critic. "Chef Aris has lost his touch, his menu is a wasteland!" the man on the screen declared. Aris sat slumped on the vinyl couch, his eyelids heavy. He was busy peeling the label off his water bottle. He managed to get a long, continuous strip going, his focus entirely on not breaking the paper. The critic listed every flaw in the roasted lamb. Aris successfully removed the label, balled it up, and flicked it toward the recycling bin. It missed. He didn't move to pick it up. He let his head fall back against the wall, staring at the flickering fluorescent light tube above him. It buzzed a low, steady B-flat. He closed his eyes, listening to the buzz rather than the television, waiting for the hour to pass.

I scrolled past the giant, bolded 'F MINUS' at the top of the blog post. The critic had spent three thousand words tearing apart my tasting menu. I propped my feet up on my desk and stared at the ceiling. I tapped my fingers against my thigh in a slow, one-two-three rhythm. I swiped down on the screen again. He hated the caviar. He hated the foam. I let out a long breath that puffed my bangs up off my forehead. I swiped over to my home screen, opened a puzzle app, and started sorting digital colored balls into matching tubes. The critic had promised this review would end my career. I dragged a blue ball into a tube with two other blue balls. Level complete. I stared at the 'Next Level' button, resting my heavy head entirely in my left hand, and clicked it.

"He called your pastry a dense brick of despair," the restaurant manager panicked, reading the magazine article from behind his desk. Chef Clara stood by the doorway, leaning heavily against the frame. She examined her fingernails, noticing a slight chip in the clear polish on her thumb. She scraped at it with her index finger. "Clara, this is the Michelin inspector!" the manager yelled. Clara let out a slow, breathy sigh and shifted her gaze to the potted ficus in the corner of the room. The leaves were dusty. She wondered how long it would take to wipe down each individual leaf. "A brick," she repeated, her voice lacking any inflection. She checked her watch, watching the second hand sweep its slow circle around the dial. "Is there anything else?" she asked, her eyes already wandering to the patterns in the carpet.

I sat alone in the empty dining room, the critic’s printed review sitting on the table in front of me. The headline read, The Death of Fine Dining. I dragged my finger through a ring of condensation left by a water glass, connecting the droplets into a puddle. I read the part where he called my venison aggressively chewy, then looked away to stare at the shadows stretching across the wooden floorboards. The hum of the refrigerator in the back kitchen droned on, a steady, endless vibration. I rested my cheek on the cool surface of the table. I picked up a leftover breadstick and started breaking it into perfectly equal, half-inch pieces, lining them up in a neat row next to the devastating article. When I ran out of breadstick, I just sat there, listening to the hum of the fridge.

I watched Miller’s face fall as I delivered the news, but my eyes drifted to the scuff mark on the gym floor. It looked a bit like a squashed map of Italy. Miller started rambling about his dedication, his extra hours in the weight room, and how much the varsity squad meant to his father. I nodded slowly, resting my chin on my palm. My foot traced the outline of the scuff mark. I mentally mapped out my grocery list, realizing I was nodding at the wrong intervals. Miller’s voice droned on, blending into the hum of the fluorescent lights above. I tapped my pen against the clipboard, counting the seconds between each tap, waiting for the inevitable moment he would finally pack his duffel bag and walk out the door.

Coach Henderson leaned forward, giving his speech about character and hard choices to the teenage point guard sitting across the desk. From the corner chair, assistant coach Dave stared at a fly buzzing erratically against the windowpane. It bumped the glass, backed up, and bumped it again. Dave rested his chin on his fist. The kid started crying. Henderson offered a tissue, his voice dipping into a low, somber register. Dave sighed, peeling a fleck of dried glue off his clipboard. He wondered if they were having meatloaf for dinner at the cafeteria tonight. The crying stretched on, punctuated by heavy sniffles. Dave slowly crossed his left leg over his right, watching the second hand on the wall clock make its slow, agonizing crawl toward three-thirty. The fly finally found the open crack in the window and escaped.

"It comes down to roster size," Coach Martinez said, steepling her fingers on the metal desk. I watched a drop of condensation slide down the side of her iced coffee cup. It hit the napkin, blooming into a dark wet circle. She was talking about my footwork, about how I needed another year of development in the recreational league. I let out a long breath, my eyes tracing the acoustic tiles on the ceiling. One, two, three, four tiles across. Eight down. Thirty-two tiles total. "Are you hearing me, Sarah?" she asked, leaning in. I nodded, scratching an itch on my knee. "Yeah. Roster size." I checked the clock above her head. If she wrapped this up in the next two minutes, I could still catch the 4:15 bus and make it home in time to watch TV before my brother hogged the remote.

Marcus delivered the bad news to the backup goalie with the exact same script he had used for the last five cuts. "You have heart, Kevin, but we need speed." As Kevin launched into a pleading monologue about his summer training regimen, Marcus stared blankly at the wall chart behind the boy’s head. He began counting the number of red thumbtacks. Fourteen. He moved on to the blue ones. Twenty-two. Kevin’s voice was a steady, rhythmic buzz, like a lawnmower two streets over. Marcus rested his chin in his hand, letting his eyelids droop to half-mast. He shifted his weight, the leather chair squeaking loudly in the small office. He wondered if he should get tacos or a burger for lunch. Kevin paused, waiting for a response. Marcus offered a practiced, empty smile, pointing his pen toward the door.

The head coach paced the locker room, detailing the difficult decisions the coaching staff had to make this season. Sitting on the bench, Leo picked at a loose thread on his athletic shorts. He pulled it, watching the fabric pucker, then smoothed it out, only to pull it again. "We just don't have a spot for you on the offensive line," the coach said heavily. Leo let out a slow exhale, staring at the scuffed toe of his right cleat. He tried balancing a spare whistle on his index finger. It wobbled and fell onto the rubber floor. He didn't bother picking it up. The coach kept talking about future opportunities and intramural leagues. Leo suppressed a yawn, resting his head back against the cold metal lockers. He mentally calculated how many levels of his video game he could beat with all this newly freed-up afternoon time.

I sat behind my desk while Jenkins readied himself for the verdict. I’d made up my mind on Tuesday, and by Friday afternoon, the whole routine felt like chewing old gum. "I'm releasing you from the squad," I said. Jenkins gasped, gripping the armrests of his chair. I leaned back, my eyes drifting to the window. Two pigeons were fighting over a piece of bread on the sidewalk below. I watched them peck and flutter, entirely engrossed in the crumbs. Jenkins started asking what he could do to change my mind. I tapped my fingers on my thigh—tap, tap, tap—waiting for his oxygen to run out. I checked my wristwatch. 3:42 PM. The traffic on I-95 would be backing up soon. "It's final," I said softly, grabbing a paperclip and bending it back and forth until the metal snapped in my fingers.

I sat on the bleachers waiting for my turn, watching Coach Miller cut Thompson on the far side of the gymnasium. Thompson was waving his arms, pacing back and forth in front of the clipboard. I rested my chin on my hands, my eyes tracking the slow, circular sweep of the janitor's floor buffer down the hall. Whirrrr. Swoosh. Whirrrr. I pulled my phone from my pocket, illuminated the screen, saw no new messages, and turned it off. Thirty seconds later, I did it again. Coach Miller was still talking. Thompson was still pacing. I picked up a stray piece of athletic tape from the bleacher wood, rolling it into a tiny, perfect sphere between my thumb and forefinger. I tossed it onto the lower step. It bounced twice. I grabbed another piece of tape, hoping this one would bounce three times before Thompson finally left.

Elena sat in the dugout, delivering the final roster decisions to the girls who hadn't made the cut. Chloe was the fourth one. "Your swing just isn't there yet," Elena said, her voice flat. Chloe’s eyes welled up with tears. Elena rested her cheek on her fist, her gaze fixed on the chain-link fence. She watched a plastic grocery bag caught in the wire mesh, flapping rhythmically in the wind. Flap. Flap. Flap. Chloe asked if she could stay on as a manager. Elena drew a series of interconnected triangles on the margin of her roster sheet, filling each one in with dark blue ink. She shaded outside the lines on the third triangle. "No managerial spots left," Elena murmured, not looking up. She capped her pen, uncapped it, and capped it again, waiting for the girl's shadow to finally move out of the dugout doorway.

Coach Reynolds looked like he was delivering a eulogy instead of cutting me from the tennis team. He had his hands clasped together on his desk, his brow furrowed in deep, exaggerated concern. I stared at his tie. It had a pattern of tiny, repeating sailboats. I started counting them. Three on the knot, twelve visible on the chest. Reynolds paused, expecting me to react to the news that my backhand was a liability. "Right," I said, my voice entirely flat. I slumped lower in my chair, stretching my legs out in front of me. I looked at the ceiling fan, tracking one specific wooden blade as it spun in endless circles. Thwack, thwack, thwack went the motor. I let out a long, heavy breath through my nose, wondering if the cafeteria was serving those square pizzas for lunch today, or if it was just sloppy joes again.

I stood against the cinderblock wall of the locker room while Coach Harris told the final three walk-ons they were done. Harris loves the sound of his own voice. He was five minutes into a speech about resilience. I stared at the peeling gray paint near the baseboard, chipping a loose flake off with the toe of my sneaker. I kicked it. It slid two inches. I kicked it again. Harris raised his voice, emphasizing the word sacrifice. I let my head fall back against the cold wall, staring up at the flickering fluorescent tube. It hummed a steady, monotonous B-flat. I mentally recited the alphabet backwards. Z, Y, X, W... V. When I looked back down, Harris was still making dramatic hand gestures. I pulled out my keys, silently tracing the jagged edges of my house key with my thumb, waiting for the endless monologue to conclude.

"It's a numbers game," Coach Bradley said, reciting the phrase for the seventh time that morning. The young gymnast sat across from him, her face crumpling into quiet sobs. Bradley leaned his elbows on the desk, his eyes drifting past her to the clock on the wall. 10:14 AM. He picked up a pencil and began tapping the eraser silently against his legal pad. He noticed the faint outline of a coffee stain on his desk and began scratching at it with his thumbnail. The girl hiccuped, wiping her eyes with the back of her hand. Bradley offered a slow, automatic nod. He wondered if it was too early to eat the sandwich he had packed. Probably. He went back to scratching the stain, hoping she would run out of tears before 10:20 so he could finally go get a cup of decent coffee from the breakroom.

The e-sports coach was pacing the small room, explaining why he was dropping Alex from the starting roster. Alex slouched deep into his gaming chair, spinning slowly from side to side. He stared at the blank monitor in front of him, watching his own distorted reflection warp and stretch with every spin. "Your reaction times just aren't matching the new meta," the coach said earnestly. Alex let out a long sigh, picking up a stray pen from the desk. He began taking it apart, unscrewing the cap, removing the ink cartridge, and popping out the tiny spring. He lined the pieces up on his mousepad in order of size. The coach kept talking about team synergy. Alex reassembled the pen, clicked it three times, and started unscrewing it again. He stared at the wall behind the coach, counting the little perforated holes in the acoustic paneling.

I watched Sarah’s hand hover over the open leather notebook on my desk. She froze as I walked in, her eyes wide with a terror I supposed she felt was justified. "I can explain," she stammered, dropping my diary like it burned her. I leaned against the doorframe, letting out a slow, long breath that ruffled my bangs. "Okay," I said, my voice entirely flat. I traced a scuff mark on the linoleum with the toe of my sneaker. She launched into a frantic monologue about trust and curiosity, waving her arms. I watched a fly buzz around the overhead light fixture, tracing its lazy, looping path. "Are you even listening?" she shrilled. I blinked slowly, shifting my weight to the other leg. "You read it. Cool. Can you just close the window? There's a draft." I dropped my backpack, already thinking about whether I had enough clean socks for tomorrow.

Mark lay on his back, tossing a tennis ball at the ceiling and catching it with a rhythmic thwack. Across the cramped dorm room, David sat completely paralyzed, Mark’s private journal splayed open on his lap. "Mark, I swear, the wind blew it open," David squeaked, his face flushed a deep, blotchy red. Thwack. Mark caught the ball, his expression entirely slack. He stared at the water stain above his bed, noting it vaguely resembled a lopsided duck. "The wind," Mark repeated, his tone perfectly monotone. He tossed the ball again. Thwack. "Listen, I just saw the part about Emily—" David began, his voice trembling. Mark let his arm drop over the side of the bed, the ball rolling away under a pile of dirty laundry. He rested his cheek against the rough fabric of his pillow. "Don't care," Mark murmured, closing his eyes to the afternoon sun. "Just put it back."

My journal was resting on Clara’s bed, the pink ribbon bookmark dangling in a way I never left it. Clara was crying, apologizing profusely for invading my innermost thoughts. I sat heavily at my desk, resting my chin in my palm, and stared past her at the brick wall outside our window. It was gray. Very, very gray. She sobbed something about boundaries. I picked at a chipped piece of polish on my thumbnail, peeling it off in one satisfying strip. "I’m a monster," she wailed, burying her face in her hands. I let out a heavy puff of air, watching a dust mote drift slowly downward in the beam of sunlight. "It’s mostly just grocery lists and complaining about bio class anyway," I mumbled, resting my forehead against the cool wood of the desk. "If you're done, I need a nap before dinner."

The realization that Greg was reading his diary elicited absolutely nothing from Julian. He stood in the doorway, a half-empty bag of chips in his hand, chewing slowly as Greg scrambled backward, knocking over a desk lamp. The crash echoed loudly in the quiet room. Julian didn't flinch. He chewed another chip, the crunching sound loud and methodical. "Julian, man, I'm sorry!" Greg pleaded, holding his hands up defensively. Julian swallowed, shifting his gaze from the spilled pages to the digital clock on the microwave. 4:12 PM. Still two hours until the dining hall opened. He dragged his feet across the carpet, grabbed the remote, and collapsed onto the futon. He turned on a documentary about sea sponges, letting the drone of the narrator wash over the room. "Can you move?" Julian asked, his voice devoid of inflection. "You're blocking the TV."

Finding my roommate deeply engrossed in my dream journal should have sparked outrage. Instead, I stood in the doorway, staring at the back of her head, listening to the rhythmic ticking of our wall clock. Tick. Tick. Tick. "The part where I turn into a giant pigeon is on page forty," I said, my voice barely carrying over the hum of the mini-fridge. Maya jumped, spinning around with a gasp, the book clattering to the floor. She started speaking a mile a minute, stringing together apologies and excuses. I slouched against the closet door, letting my eyes glaze over as her mouth moved. I mentally counted the ceiling tiles. Twelve by twelve. One hundred and forty-four. "Did you hear me?" Maya asked, looking panicked. I gave a slow, noncommittal shrug, kicking off my shoes with a dull thud. "Yeah. Pigeon. Page forty. I'm going to take a shower."

Chloe watched as Jenna frantically tried to shove the leather-bound diary back under the mattress. Jenna’s face was the picture of pure guilt, her eyes darting everywhere but Chloe’s face. Chloe leaned heavily on the door handle, letting out a prolonged, rattling sigh. She let her gaze wander to the wilting fern in the corner, thinking she should probably water it eventually. Maybe tomorrow. Or next week. "I only read a page!" Jenna blurted out, her voice cracking. Chloe blinked lazily. She walked over to her desk, her slippers shuffling softly against the floorboards, and sat down. She propped her elbows on the surface, resting her face in her hands, squishing her cheeks upward. "Did you find the part where I review all the dining hall soups?" Chloe asked, her tone entirely flat. Jenna shook her head dumbly. Chloe closed her eyes. "Shame."

I caught him red-handed, his fingers tracing the ink of my private notebook. Liam looked up, paralyzed, waiting for the explosion. I just stood there, the strap of my messenger bag digging into my shoulder, feeling an overwhelming heaviness in my limbs. I let the bag slide to the floor with a soft thwump. "I was looking for a pen," Liam lied, his voice shaking. I stared at the blank wall behind his head. The paint was chipping near the molding. I needed to put in a maintenance request. I let out a breath that felt like it carried the weight of a thousand useless hours. "The pens are in the mug," I said, my voice a monotonous drone. I dragged myself over to my bed, collapsing face-first onto the mattress. "Close the book before you leave," I mumbled into the duvet, already drifting away.

Elias sat cross-legged on the floor, flipping through pages of handwritten poetry, oblivious to the fact that Arthur had entered the room. Arthur leaned against the doorjamb, crossing his arms, and watched Elias read. He watched a spider slowly weave a web in the corner of the ceiling, fascinated by the precise, repetitive movements. Finally, Elias turned a page, saw Arthur, and shrieked, dropping the book. "Arthur! I—" Arthur held up a single, limp hand, silencing him. He walked to the window, staring out at the empty campus quad. A single plastic bag tumbled across the grass in the breeze. "It's fine," Arthur said, his voice entirely devoid of color. He dragged his fingertips lazily across the dusty windowsill, inspecting the gray residue left on his skin. "Just don't bend the pages when you put it back."

My secret thoughts were spread wide open on the kitchen counter, and my roommate was desperately trying to smooth down the pages as I walked in. "I knocked it over," she babbled, her hands shaking. I leaned against the refrigerator, feeling the cool metal through my t-shirt. I watched a drop of water slowly gather at the lip of the kitchen faucet, swell, and finally fall into the sink with a tiny plink. Plink. Plink. The rhythm was hypnotic. "I swear I didn't read anything about your ex," she continued, breathless. I let my head roll back against the fridge with a soft thud, staring at the fluorescent light buzzing overhead. "Cool," I muttered, my jaw feeling heavy. I opened the fridge, staring blankly at a jar of pickles and a half-empty carton of milk, entirely forgetting what I had originally come into the kitchen to find.

When Sam realized Taylor was reading his journal, he didn't shout. He didn't snatch it away. He simply stood in the center of the room, his shoulders slumped, arms hanging loosely at his sides. Taylor began a frantic, panicked explanation, the words tumbling over each other in a rush of desperate anxiety. Sam let his eyes wander. He noticed the scuff marks on Taylor's sneakers. He noticed the way the blind on the window was slightly crooked. He let out a long, slow exhale that fluttered his lips. "Taylor," Sam interrupted, his voice a low, unchanging hum. Taylor snapped his mouth shut. Sam dragged himself to his desk chair and slumped into it, spinning around once, slowly. He stared at the ceiling, tapping a perfectly steady, unhurried rhythm on his thigh with one finger. "Can you just order the pizza now? I want pepperoni."

She was holding my locked diary, a bent bobby pin in her other hand. A cliché, really. I leaned against the frame of our dorm door, feeling my eyelids droop. "It's not what it looks like," she whispered, her eyes wide with fear. I let out a prolonged breath through my nose. I stared at the poster of a rock band on her wall, tracing the letters of the logo with my eyes over and over again. "You picked the lock," I stated, my voice completely devoid of melody. She nodded frantically, tears welling up. I felt an overwhelming urge to just lie down. I dragged my feet across the rug, picking up a lint roller from my desk. I sat on the edge of my bed, methodically rolling it back and forth over my jeans, watching the white sheet turn gray with fuzz. "Whatever," I sighed.

The journal was completely open, resting on the coffee table, and Max was hunched over it. Leo walked into the apartment, keys jingling, and stopped. Max froze, caught in the act. Leo’s face remained a perfectly blank canvas. He walked slowly to the sofa and dropped onto the cushions, his body sinking deeply into the upholstery. Max started rambling about accidentally finding it under the couch cushions. Leo stared at a tiny hole in the knee of his jeans, picking at a loose white thread. He pulled it, watching the fabric pucker slightly. He let out a heavy, rattling sigh that seemed to deflate his entire chest. "Did you read the entry from Tuesday?" Leo asked, his tone flat and unhurried. Max nodded, swallowing hard. Leo rested his chin in his hand, his eyes glazed. "Told you the cafeteria tacos were a mistake."

Aunt Clara stood up from the Thanksgiving table, tapped her spoon against her wine glass, and declared she had officially initiated into an eclectic Wiccan coven. My mother gasped, dropping her fork with a clatter. Uncle Bob went red in the face, sputtering about family tradition. I rested my chin in my palm, watching a lone housefly bump repeatedly against the windowpane. It flew away, circled the chandelier, and smacked the glass again. Buzz, thud. Buzz, thud. Clara was explaining the rule of three and the phases of the moon. I slowly dragged my fork through the remaining mashed potatoes on my plate, carving out a little trench and watching the gravy pool inside it. 'Did you hear me, David?' Clara asked, her voice cracking with emotion. 'Yeah,' I mumbled, not looking up. 'Wiccan. Pass the salt?'

The living room erupted into chaos the moment Sarah announced she was converting to Buddhism. Their father paced the worn carpet, waving his arms as he quoted Bible verses, while their mother wept softly into a floral handkerchief. Marcus sat on the sofa, methodically folding a foil gum wrapper into a tiny accordion. He pressed it flat against his knee, then pulled it apart again, watching the silver ridges catch the lamplight. Sarah’s voice rose, defending the Eightfold Path, but Marcus had moved on to trying to balance the wrapper on his index finger. He stared at the dusty grandfather clock in the corner. The pendulum swung left, then right. Left, then right. It was only 2:15 PM. He sighed heavily, sinking deeper into the cushions, wondering if the grocery store still had those jalapeño chips in stock.

The family Zoom call was supposed to be a quick check-in, but Cousin Leo had commandeered the screen to announce his conversion to Islam. He was speaking passionately about his recent pilgrimage and the peace he had finally found. I kept myself on mute, nodding my head at exactly four-second intervals while my eyes tracked the cursor on my second monitor. I scrolled past three pages of discounted running shoes, adding a gray pair to my cart before clicking a new tab for vacuum cleaner reviews. Leo was crying now, thanking everyone for their open hearts. 'Alhamdulillah,' he said, pressing a hand to his chest. I leaned back in my desk chair, spinning a ballpoint pen around my thumb. It slipped and clattered to the floor. I left it there, staring at the loading bar of a YouTube video about lawn care.

Grandma gripped the edge of the dining table, her knuckles white, as she proudly proclaimed she had discovered the truth through Scientology. The rest of the family sat frozen in a stunned silence. Elena kept her head down, tracing the intricate whorls of the oak wood grain with her thumbnail. She followed a dark brown line until it looped into a knot, then started on a new line. Grandma began passing out heavy, hardbound books, talking rapidly about thetans and clear states. Elena accepted her copy, placing it flat on the table. She stared at the dust motes dancing in the shaft of sunlight filtering through the blinds. She counted them. One, two, three, four... She tapped her foot a slow, steady rhythm against the chair leg. 'What do you think, Elena?' Grandma beamed. Elena blinked. 'Cool book cover.'

My older brother stood in the kitchen, explaining why he was adopting Orthodox Judaism and how our mother’s kitchen needed to be kashered. He went into intense detail about separate plates for meat and dairy. I leaned against the refrigerator, slowly peeling a sticker off an apple. I got the top corner up, rolling the waxy paper between my thumb and forefinger, trying to pull the whole thing off in one continuous piece. It ripped halfway down. I exhaled loudly, flicking the torn scrap into the sink. 'You’ll need entirely new sponges,' he emphasized, gesturing wildly. I shifted my weight to my left leg, looking up at the ceiling fan. It wobbled slightly on its highest setting. Click-whir, click-whir. I checked the screen of my phone. No new notifications. I locked the screen and went back to the apple sticker.

When Eleanor sat her husband down to tell him she was joining a charismatic Pentecostal church, she held his hands and looked deeply into his eyes. She spoke of speaking in tongues and feeling the fire of the spirit. Arthur let his hands rest limply in hers. His gaze drifted past her shoulder, fixing on a gray squirrel outside the bay window. The squirrel was navigating the intricate baffle Arthur had installed on the bird feeder last week. Arthur watched it stretch its paws, calculating the jump. Eleanor’s voice grew louder, praising her new congregation’s vibrant worship. The squirrel leaped, missed the edge of the feeder, and tumbled into the bushes below. Arthur let out a long, slow breath, slumping his shoulders. He pulled one hand free to scratch the back of his neck, his eyes scanning the yard for the squirrel's return.

Uncle David called a special family meeting in the living room to announce his newfound devotion to Hinduism. He was draped in a simple tunic, holding a string of prayer beads, and speaking softly about karma and the cycle of rebirth. I sat cross-legged on the rug, counting the tassels fringing the edge. Fourteen, fifteen, sixteen. The patterned rug had a recurring geometric diamond shape. I traced one with my index finger, then moved to the next. David was explaining the significance of Lord Ganesha now. I rested my chin heavily on my hand, feeling my eyelids droop. I forced them open, shifting my focus to the bookshelf. I began alphabetizing the spines in my head. Atonement, Beloved, Catch-22... 'This changes everything,' David whispered, his eyes shining with unshed tears. 'Yep,' I replied, picking a piece of lint off my sock.

Chloe stood at the head of the dinner table, announcing to her parents that she had officially converted to Shintoism after her semester abroad in Japan. She pulled out a small wooden amulet, explaining the concept of kami and the importance of nature spirits. Her mother, Linda, rested her elbow on the table, letting her cheek fall into her palm. Linda stared blankly at the half-eaten chicken breast on her plate, using her fork to push a single green pea back and forth across the porcelain. Left, right. Left, right. Chloe was detailing the purification rituals she now practiced every morning. Linda let out a heavy puff of air that rustled her bangs. She pulled her phone from her pocket, unlocked it under the table, and began swiping aimlessly through a match-three puzzle game, ignoring the flashing combos.

Dad gathered us around the patio fire pit to declare he had been baptized into the Mormon church. He talked about his spiritual awakening with the missionaries and the profound truth of the golden plates. I sat in the Adirondack chair, poking the glowing embers with a long iron stick. A spark floated up into the night air, and I watched it fade to black. I poked the log again. Another spark. Dad was testifying about eternal families, his voice thick with emotion. I pulled my phone out, staring at the home screen. I swiped left to the app library, then swiped right. Left, right, left. I locked it, slid it back into my pocket, and went back to jabbing the charred wood. 'Are you listening, buddy?' Dad asked. I didn't look up from the ashes. 'Yeah. Golden plates. Got it.'

Grandpa parked his wheelchair in the center of the living room, proudly declaring that he had found his true home with the Jehovah’s Witnesses. He held up a colorful pamphlet, eager to explain why they didn't celebrate birthdays anymore. Ten-year-old Toby sat on the floor nearby, entirely focused on his own reflection in the side of a brass floor lamp. He stretched his mouth wide, watching his face distort in the curved metal. He puffed out his cheeks, then sucked them in. Grandpa started reading a passage about the impending earthly paradise. Toby rolled onto his back, staring at the popcorn ceiling. He found a bump that looked vaguely like a cloud, then another that looked like a shoe. He let out a loud, drawn-out sigh, stretching his arms above his head until his joints popped, before rolling over to inspect the carpet fibers closely.

My twin sister, Mia, sat me down on my bed to tell me she was converting to Jainism. She was incredibly animated, explaining the absolute vow of non-violence and how she would no longer eat root vegetables. I sat next to her, staring at my shoelaces. I untied the left one, pulled it tight, and carefully tied a double knot. Then I untied the right one and did the same. Mia was talking about the microscopic organisms in the soil. I leaned back against the headboard, tapping a slow, rhythmic beat against the wall with my knuckles. One, two, three, tap. One, two, three, tap. 'You're not taking this seriously,' Mia said, crossing her arms. I looked at the digital clock on my nightstand. It flashed 4:12. I watched it wait to turn to 4:13. 'I am,' I said flatly. 'No potatoes.'

At the neighborhood barbecue, Aunt Patricia cleared her throat loudly to announce she had found profound meaning in Christian Science. She was talking eagerly about the illusory nature of the material world and the power of spiritual healing. From a lawn chair nearby, Greg watched a single bead of condensation slide slowly down the side of his plastic cup. It joined another droplet, merging into a larger stream that hit the table. He used his index finger to smear the water puddle into a perfect circle. Patricia raised her hands, testifying about overcoming a recent cold through sheer prayer. Greg leaned his head back, staring up into the canopy of the oak tree. He began counting the leaves on the lowest branch. When he lost his place, he simply started over from one, his face completely devoid of expression.

Uncle Arthur’s voice droned on, a flat hum blending with the refrigerator's buzz. He held up Grandfather’s gold pocket watch, lecturing about current scrap metal prices and potential auction reserves. I rested my chin heavily on my palm, my eyes drifting from his moving mouth to the floral wallpaper behind him. There were exactly forty-two blue daisies in the vertical strip next to the door. I traced them mentally, top to bottom, then bottom to top. “Are you even listening?” Arthur demanded, tapping the crystal face. “You could get a thousand for this.” I let out a long breath, watching a dust mote float through a sunbeam. “Yeah, a thousand,” I murmured, shifting my weight on the hard wooden chair and starting my count of the yellow daisies.

Elise picked at a stray thread on the hem of her jeans while her sister paced the living room. Sarah was delivering another impassioned presentation about why their great-grandmother’s patchwork quilt belonged in a high-end textile auction rather than a cedar chest. Elise slouched deeper into the sofa cushions, tilting her head back to study the popcorn ceiling. She found a patch that vaguely resembled a continent and imagined how long it would take to walk across it. Sarah whipped out a printed graph showing historical auction trends for Americana. Elise let out a heavy exhale, idly spinning her phone on the glass coffee table until it clattered to a stop. “Mmhmm,” Elise offered when Sarah paused for breath, already returning her gaze to the ceiling’s bumpy white terrain.

Mom held the tarnished silver teapot aloft, rattling off a list of antique dealers she planned to visit on Tuesday. I sat across the kitchen island, meticulously lining up a row of breadcrumbs I’d gathered from my empty plate. I pushed them into a perfect square, then rearranged them into a triangle. “The craftsmanship alone will fetch a premium,” she insisted, polishing a spot with her thumb. I rested my forehead against the cool granite countertop, listening to the rhythmic ticking of the wall clock. Tick. Tick. Tick. It was only two in the afternoon. I scraped the breadcrumbs into a tiny pile and flattened them with my index finger. “Right,” I said, closing my eyes and wondering if the paint in the hallway was finally dry enough to touch.

Marcus leaned his chair onto its back two legs, balancing precariously as his cousin detailed the lucrative antique market. The subject was the mahogany grandfather clock standing in the hallway, an heirloom Julian desperately wanted to liquidate. Marcus stared past Julian’s shoulder, utterly fixated on a housefly repeatedly headbutting the windowpane. Thwack. Buzz. Thwack. Julian produced a folder of appraisal documents, pointing out highlighted numbers with a dramatic flourish. Marcus let the chair drop forward with a dull thud, resting his cheek flat against the dining table. He traced the natural rings in the oak surface with a fingernail, counting them outward from the center. “Did you see this valuation?” Julian asked. Marcus didn't look up, just continued dragging his nail along the groove. "Saw it," he mumbled.

My brother paced the length of the garage, holding our great-grandfather’s cavalry sword. He was midway through his third explanation of how the proceeds from a private collector could fund his startup. I sat on an overturned bucket, peeling a sticker off a rusty toolbox in microscopic flakes. The adhesive stuck to my thumb, and I spent a solid minute rolling it into a tiny grey ball. “It’s just gathering dust here,” Leo argued, swinging the blade in a lazy arc. “We have to be practical.” I tossed the sticky ball onto the concrete floor and squashed it with my sneaker. I checked my phone screen—no notifications. I locked it, waited three seconds, and unlocked it again. “Totally practical,” I echoed, swiping left and right through my home screens without opening a single app.

Aunt Helen’s manicured finger tapped aggressively against the velvet jewelry box containing the family’s ruby pendant. She outlined a comprehensive plan to consign the piece, citing taxes, insurance costs, and split inheritances. Clara sat opposite her, systematically tearing a paper coaster into increasingly smaller triangles. When the triangles became too tiny to rip, Clara arranged them into a geometric mosaic on the café table. Helen’s voice became a continuous background hum, much like the espresso machine whirring behind the counter. Clara rested her chin in her hands, her eyes glazing over as she watched a barista wipe the same spot on the counter five times. “Clara, are you with me on this?” Helen pressed. Clara blinked slowly, sweeping the paper shreds into her palm. “Sell it, keep it, whatever you think is best.”

Dad threw open the barn doors to reveal the ‘68 Mustang, launching into his rehearsed speech about Kelly Blue Book values and classic car auctions. I leaned against the doorframe, crossing my arms and staring at a spider web swaying gently in the rafters. The spider was completely motionless, and I felt a deep kinship with it. Dad opened the hood, pointing out original engine components while I repeatedly clicked the end of my ballpoint pen. Click-clack. Click-clack. Dad shot me a warning glare, so I slipped the pen into my pocket, switching to tapping my toe against the dirt floor in a steady four-four rhythm. “This engine is pristine,” he declared, wiping a smudge of grease. “Yep. Very pristine,” I replied, checking my watch and realizing only four minutes had passed.

Grandma held her late mother’s diamond ring to the light, explaining how selling it could comfortably finance her luxury cruise to the Bahamas. Dennis slouched in the armchair opposite her, his legs stretched out entirely rigid. He stared blankly at the television, which had been muted for the last half hour, watching an infomercial for a vegetable chopper. The presenter enthusiastically diced onions in absolute silence. Dennis began to count the number of diced pieces that fell into the plastic container, losing track around fifty and starting over. Grandma was talking about ocean-view cabins and unlimited buffet packages now. Dennis let out a prolonged, heavy sigh, sinking further down until his neck rested uncomfortably on the chair’s back edge. “A cruise sounds great,” he droned, eyes still glued to the silent slicing of a tomato.

My sister slapped the appraisal sheet onto the Steinway grand piano, determined to convince me that keeping the generational instrument was financial suicide. I sat on the piano bench, pressing middle C with my index finger. Plink. I waited for the sound to die completely, then pressed it again. Plink. She talked about the space it took up, the cost of tuning, and the climate control required to preserve the wood. I leaned over, examining a minor scratch on the mahogany leg, then started picking at a hangnail on my thumb. "We could split fifty thousand dollars," she emphasized, tapping the paper. I blew a stray lock of hair out of my eyes, watching it flutter and settle back down. “Fifty grand,” I repeated flatly, pressing the D key this time just to mix things up.

Uncle Gregory marched around the antique writing desk, passionately detailing its Victorian provenance and the eager buyer waiting in London. Sam sat on the edge of the rug, completely absorbed in pulling loose threads from the carpet's fringe. He wound a red string tightly around his index finger, watching the fingertip turn a dark, throbbing purple, then unwound it to let the blood rush back. Gregory slammed a hand onto the desk to emphasize a point about shipping logistics. Sam didn't flinch. He just laid flat on his back, staring up at the slowly rotating ceiling fan. One, two, three, four blades chasing each other endlessly in a circle. “We need a decision today,” Gregory insisted loudly. Sam rolled his head to the side, letting his eyes droop half-shut. “Go for it,” he whispered.

Aunt Beatrice lined up the heirloom porcelain dolls on the dining table, categorizing them by their mint condition and potential market value. I sat across from the creepy ceramic faces, resting my heavy head in both hands. I stared at a drop of condensation sliding slowly down the outside of my water glass. I made a silent bet with myself about whether it would reach the bottom before Beatrice finished explaining the rare bisque firing technique of 1890. The drop hit the tablecloth. I lost. She moved on to discussing the original silk dresses. I took a sip of the lukewarm water, swishing it around my cheeks, inflating and deflating my mouth like a pufferfish. "This one is worth a fortune," she beamed. I popped my cheeks. "Cool," I said, gazing out the window.

Mr. Henderson held the generational oil painting of the family farmhouse, debating aloud the pros and cons of listing it at a local gallery versus a national auction house. His son, Leo, sat at the kitchen island, meticulously building a complex tower out of sugar packets. He stacked them two by two, holding his breath as he placed the final packet on the fourth tier. Mr. Henderson paced back and forth, his slippers scuffing the linoleum, creating a rhythmic, grating sound. Leo knocked the sugar tower down with a flick of his wrist, watching the pink and white packets scatter across the counter. He immediately began sorting them back into separate color piles. "What do you think, Leo? Local or national?" his father asked. Leo swept the packets into a heap. "Whichever is faster."

Arthur dragged the utility knife across the taped cardboard, the ripping sound the only thing breaking the afternoon silence. He peeled back the flaps to reveal a mountain of vintage photographs and ribbon-tied letters. Resting his chin heavily in his palm, he picked up the nearest envelope, glancing at the faded cursive. "Dearest Eleanor," he read aloud, his voice flat in the dusty air. He let the paper slip from his fingers back into the box. He shifted his weight, tracing a crack in the floorboards with the toe of his sneaker. Pulling his phone from his pocket, he swiped through a blank home screen three times, locked it, and shoved it back. He stared at the remaining six boxes the previous owners had left behind, letting out a long, slow exhale that ruffled the dust motes dancing in the singular beam of sunlight.

I pushed open the attic hatch, halfway hoping a bat would fly out just to give me a reason to move faster. Instead, I found a plastic bin shoved into the corner by whoever lived here before me. I kicked the lid off with my heel. Inside sat a pristine, motorized train set. I pulled out the locomotive and set it on the dusty floorboards. Pushing the little switch, I watched the wheels spin in place with a weak, mechanical whine. I rested my head against a wooden beam, watching the tiny plastic wheels turn. And turn. And turn. I picked at a loose thread on my sweater, pulling it until it snagged. "Choo choo," I muttered to the empty room, not bothering to change my pitch. I stopped the train, dropped it into the plastic bin, and slowly went back downstairs to stare into the open refrigerator.

Maya sat cross-legged under the eaves, systematically pulling records from the milk crate left behind by the sellers. Pull, glance, stack. Pull, glance, stack. Jazz, classical, polka. She didn't own a record player, nor did she plan to buy one. She leaned her head back against the drywall, letting her eyes unfocus until the exposed insulation above blurred into pink cotton candy. A fly buzzed slowly near her ear, and she didn't bother to swat it away. She checked the digital clock on her wrist—2:14 PM. It felt like it had been 2:14 for an hour. She dragged another cardboard sleeve from the crate, not even reading the title, just tossing it onto the growing pile beside her knee. The thump of cardboard against wood echoed in the stagnant air. She exhaled a breath that ruffled her bangs and slumped sideways onto the floorboards.

The velvet trunk in the attic was heavy, but opening it only revealed a collection of moth-eaten Victorian clothing. I pulled out a feathered hat that looked like a squashed crow, placing it on my head. I walked over to the cracked vanity mirror propped against the chimney brick. My reflection stared back, the absurd plumage drooping over my left eye. I didn't smile or laugh. I just stood there, listening to the rhythmic dripping of the bathroom faucet two floors below. Drip. Pause. Drip. I counted the drops up to fifty before taking the hat off and dropping it into the trunk. I sat on the edge of the trunk, swinging my legs. My heels tapped a slow, steady rhythm against the brass lock. I pulled my phone out, saw zero new notifications, and let my hand drop heavily back into my lap.

Liam lined up the brass trophies the previous owners had abandoned in the rafters. First by height, from the tallest bowler to the smallest soccer player. Then he rearranged them by date, squinting at the tarnished plaques. 1984, 1985, 1988. He rested his chin in his hands, staring at the metallic congregation. He tapped his index finger against his lips, the tempo matching the ticking of his wristwatch. He knocked the tallest trophy over with his knuckle. It hit the floorboards with a dull clank. He left it there. Rolling onto his back, Liam stared up at the exposed nails poking through the roof sheathing. He began to count them. One, two, three. When he reached forty-seven, he lost track, closed his heavy eyelids, and blew a puff of air out of his mouth, letting his arms splay wide across the dusty floor.

I untied the twine holding the stack of leather-bound diaries together. The real estate agent said the old man who lived here was a sailor, so I sat on a crate, expecting tales of storms and sea monsters. I cracked open the first book. August 4th: Ate porridge. Painted the fence. August 5th: Rain. I rested my forehead against the heel of my hand. I flipped ahead fifty pages. November 12th: Bought new socks. I let the journal fall shut, dust billowing into a gray cloud. I didn't sneeze. I just watched the particles slowly settle back onto the cover. I slumped against the sloping ceiling, listening to the distant drone of a lawnmower down the street. I peeled a flake of dry paint off the wall, rolled it into a tiny ball between my fingers, and softly flicked it across the empty room.

The cardboard box was marked "XMAS" in thick black marker. Julian sat cross-legged on the attic floor, pulling out tangled strings of lights. He plugged them into the single working outlet. Half the bulbs remained dark. He stared at the weak, blinking red and green lights, his face completely expressionless. He picked up a plastic reindeer with a missing antler and spun it slowly on its side. It made a scraping sound against the wood. He spun it again. And again. He let out a long, shuddering sigh and let his head drop backward until it bumped lightly against the wall. A spider crawled across a rafter a few feet away. Julian watched its slow progress for a solid ten minutes, charting its path down the wood grain, wishing the spider would do something unexpected, like fall or suddenly sprint. It just kept crawling. Slowly.

The previous owner left a velvet-lined display case filled with labeled rocks tucked behind the water heater. I popped the rusty latches and dragged it into the weak light of the dormer window. Quartz. Feldspar. Obsidian. I picked up a gray lump labeled Limestone. I weighed it in my palm. It felt exactly like a rock. I set it back down. I picked up a piece of granite. Also a rock. I propped my elbows on my knees, resting my face in my hands, squishing my cheeks together so my lips puckered. I blew air through my lips, making a sputtering sound. The noise died instantly in the heavy attic insulation. I checked my watch. Only three minutes had passed since the last time I looked. I slowly pushed the lid down on the rocks and rested my cheek against the cool glass surface.

Chloe dragged her feet as she walked across the attic, kicking a stray crumpled paper out of her path. She stopped in front of a plastic storage bin overflowing with college textbooks on microeconomics left by the last tenants. She picked up a thick, gray volume, flipping through pages of bar graphs and equations. Her eyelids drooped. She let the heavy book slide from her hands, landing with a muffled thud on a stack of spiral notebooks. Slumping down next to the bin, she pulled a blade of dry grass from her shoe and began splitting it down the middle with her thumbnail. Once it was shredded, she tossed the pieces aside and let her head loll back. She stared at a water stain on the ceiling, tracing its uneven borders with her eyes, wondering how many hours she would have to wait until dinnertime.

I found a battered copy of a property board game hidden beneath an old tarp. I unfolded the board on the floorboards, setting up the banker’s tray. I chose the metal thimble. I rolled the dice. Six. I moved the thimble six spaces. I rolled for an imaginary opponent. Four. I moved the wheelbarrow. I propped my chin in my hand, staring unblinking at the paper money. I rolled again. Double twos. I didn't bother moving the pieces. I just kept rolling the dice, listening to the plastic clatter against the cardboard. Clatter. Clatter. Clatter. I stacked the tiny green houses into a wobbly tower, watching them lean, until I casually swiped my hand through them, scattering the plastic across the floor. I left them there, lay back against the dusty wood, crossed my arms, and stared up at the shadows in the rafters.

A towering stack of copper pots stood in the shadowy corner of the attic, abandoned by whoever sold the house. Marcus sat cross-legged in front of them with two wooden spoons he had brought upstairs. He tapped the smallest pot. Tink. He tapped the largest pot. Tonk. He tapped the floor. Thwack. His face was completely expressionless, his eyes half-closed. Tink, tonk, thwack. Tink, tonk, thwack. The rhythm was slow, steady, and metronomic. He switched to just tapping the large pot, his wrist moving while his arm remained limp. He let out a loud, groaning yawn that stretched his jaw until it popped. He dropped the spoons. They clattered against the copper. Marcus slid down until he was lying flat on his back, staring at a cobweb swaying gently in the drafts near the ceiling vent, waiting for the afternoon to finally be over.

The carousel of the slide projector clicked loudly, throwing a faded image onto the attic wall. It was a picture of a station wagon. Click. Another station wagon. Click. A blurry thumb over a lens. The family who lived here before clearly weren't photographers. I rested my forehead against the plastic casing, my finger resting heavily on the advance button. Click. Click. Click. I didn't even look at the pictures anymore, just watched the square of light flash against the drywall. I dragged a fingernail slowly back and forth across the dusty floorboards, tracing the same groove over and over until my finger turned gray. I let out a heavy breath, fogging up the projector's lens. The square of light turned fuzzy. I didn't wipe it off. I just laid my head on my arms and listened to the machine's steady, unending mechanical hum.

Detective Miller held up the grisly photographs of the basement, detailing the gruesome events of 1994. Arthur rested his chin in his palm, his eyes tracing a long, jagged crack in the plaster above the detective's head. "So," Arthur said, his voice a flat, steady drawl, "does that mean the floorboards down there are going to settle unevenly? Because I have a contractor coming Thursday." Miller blinked, lowering the photos in shock. Arthur stifled a massive yawn with the back of his hand and leaned heavily against the doorframe. The day had dragged on endlessly since noon, just a loop of sitcom reruns and counting the cars passing on the street outside. Finding out his living room once hosted a cartel shootout was just another piece of information floating in the stagnant afternoon air. He checked his watch. Still two hours until dinner.

I clicked my pen. In, out. In, out. The historian’s email sat open on my monitor, detailing the triple homicide that took place exactly where my dining table currently sits. I dragged the cursor in slow, lazy circles around the attached photos. The blood spatter roughly matched the outdated wallpaper I’d spent all morning peeling off. I leaned back in my rolling chair, spinning halfway around, staring up at the blank ceiling. A fly buzzed near the windowpane, bumping against the glass in a rhythmic, endless thud. I spun back to the screen. Someone had died here. I rested my cheek on the desk, letting out a heavy exhale. Maybe I should vacuum. Or maybe I’ll just watch the dust motes drift through the shaft of sunlight for another hour. The afternoon stretched out ahead, entirely empty.

Mrs. Gable leaned entirely over the picket fence, her eyes wide as she whispered the neighborhood's darkest secret. "The police dug up three bodies right under your rosebushes," she hissed. Clara paused her rhythmic raking. She watched a single brown leaf flutter from the oak tree to the grass. She dragged the rake across the lawn, the metal tines making a hollow scraping sound. "Is that so," Clara murmured, her face perfectly slack. She piled the new leaf onto the mound. She had been raking since nine in the morning. It was now three. The pile hadn't seemed to grow at all. Mrs. Gable waited for a gasp, a scream, anything. Clara just leaned her weight onto the wooden handle, staring blankly at the suburban street where nothing ever happened, wondering if it was too early to go inside and stare at the television screen.

The crowbar slipped from my hand with a heavy clatter. Beneath the warped floorboard of the guest room, a rusted hunting knife lay nestled beside a stained scrap of fabric. A cold case right in my hands. I stared at the weapon. My phone vibrated with a notification from a mobile game I hadn't opened in months. I picked up the device, swiped away the alert, and scrolled mindlessly through the menu. I let out a heavy breath, letting my head loll back against the wall. The silence of the empty house pressed in on my ears. I picked up the rusted blade, turning it over to inspect the dried crimson flakes. I supposed I had to call the police now. That meant sitting on hold, waiting around. I dropped the knife back into the hole, pulling a loose thread from my sweatpants, watching it unravel slowly.

The true-crime podcast host’s voice reached a dramatic crescendo, naming the exact address of the infamous Blackwood stranglings. Marcus sat on his living room sofa, his legs draped over the armrest. He looked at the podcast playing on his phone. It was his address. He blinked slowly. The host described the horrific scene that had unfolded in the very spot Marcus’s feet currently dangled over. Marcus let his arm drop off the edge of the cushions, his knuckles brushing the carpet. He stared at a faint water stain on the ceiling, tracing its irregular borders with his eyes. The host's voice droned on about forensic evidence and missing clues. Marcus reached for the remote, mindlessly clicking through seventy channels of daytime infomercials, his expression flat. The revelation changed nothing about the agonizingly slow crawl of the clock ticking on the mantelpiece.

I tossed the yellowed police report back into the dusty cardboard box. It detailed a gruesome poisoning in the very kitchen where my slow cooker was currently making entirely too much noise. I sat cross-legged on the attic floor, resting my chin in my hands. A spider crawled slowly across the wooden beam a few feet away. I tracked its agonizingly slow progress for a full five minutes. The report said the previous owner collapsed clutching his throat, right next to the refrigerator. I let out a long, loud puff of air, blowing a stray lock of hair out of my eyes. The rain drummed against the roof in a steady, repetitive rhythm. I picked up a stray packing peanut and squished it between my fingers, waiting for the washing machine cycle to finish downstairs so I would have a reason to stand up.

"I have a legal obligation to tell you," the real estate agent stammered, wringing her hands in the foyer. "This property was the site of an unsolved kidnapping." Julian stood by the doorway, gently tapping his car keys against his thigh. Tap. Tap. Tap. He looked past her, out the front window, at a neighbor slowly pushing a lawnmower in straight, repetitive lines. "Uh-huh," Julian said, his voice completely devoid of inflection. He shifted his weight to his other leg. The agent wiped sweat from her brow, clearly expecting him to demand his money back. Julian stared at the beige walls. He had three empty rooms to paint and absolutely no desire to start. "Do you know if the kidnapper took the original brass doorknobs?" Julian asked, stifling a yawn with the back of his wrist. "Because these cheap aluminum ones are driving me crazy."

Deep in the crawlspace, my flashlight beam hit a clump of faded yellow police tape snagged on a rusted pipe. CRIME SCENE DO NOT CROSS. I slumped against the concrete wall, letting the flashlight dangle from my limp wrist. The beam swept back and forth across the dirt floor like a pendulum. I picked at a piece of loose dried mud on my jeans, flicking the dust away into the shadows. The previous tenants had run a counterfeit ring down here and shot a guy over a bad deal. I stared at the yellow tape, my eyes half-closed. I had been down in this damp basement for hours, moving identical cardboard boxes from the left wall to the right wall. The tape didn't make the task any faster. I let my head thump softly back against the concrete, waiting for six o'clock to finally arrive.

The contractor peeled away the drywall, exposing the original studs. Splintered holes riddled the wooden beams. "Looks like a shotgun blast," the worker whistled. "Happened right here in your master bedroom. See the trajectory?" Evelyn sat in an oversized armchair, her posture slumped, rhythmically clicking the top of her ballpoint pen. She gazed lazily at the bullet holes, her expression blank. Her morning had consisted of watching paint dry in the hallway and waiting for the plumber to fix a dripping sink. The sink had dripped exactly twenty-two times a minute. She knew, because she had counted. "Fix the drywall," Evelyn murmured, resting her cheek against her palm. She watched a dust mote drift slowly through a shaft of afternoon sunlight, completely unbothered by the violence etched into the framework of her home. The hours stretched endlessly before her, devoid of any real momentum.

A local news reporter shoved a microphone in my face the second I opened the front door. "How does it feel to live in the infamous Butcher's den?" he demanded, a cameraman hovering over his shoulder. I leaned heavily against the doorframe, my eyes heavy. I looked at the microphone, then at the reporter’s aggressively bright tie. "The Butcher," I repeated flatly. "Yes! He dismembered victims in your bathtub!" I let out a long sigh, staring at the grey clouds rolling sluggishly across the sky. I had spent the last two hours trying to organize my sock drawer by color, giving up halfway through. The prospect of an interview sounded like just another chore. "Can you tell him to stop filming?" I said, rubbing my temples. "I'm just waiting for the mail carrier to drop off a package. It was supposed to be here yesterday."

The documentary narrator spoke in a hushed baritone, panning across the unmistakable exterior of Leo’s house. A brutal robbery gone wrong had left a family trapped in the cellar. Leo lay entirely flat on his back on the rug, his arms spread out like a starfish. He rolled his head to the side to look at the screen. The reenactment showed a masked man breaking through the identical kitchen window Leo had just washed. Leo let out a slow, rumbling groan, staring up at the popcorn ceiling. He began counting the little textured bumps above the ceiling fan. One, two, three. The documentary blared dramatic string music, promising horrifying revelations after the commercial break. Leo slowly reached out a foot, trying to hook the television remote with his big toe to change the channel to a cooking show, just to hear a different voice.

I smoothed out the crumbling blueprint I’d pried from behind the baseboard. Red X's marked spots across the property, labeled with victim numbers from a notorious serial killer case I vaguely recognized from a late-night wiki spiral. I sat down heavily on the bare mattress, my shoulders sagging. I stared at the paper. Then I stared at the beige wall opposite the bed. I tapped my foot against the floorboards. Tap. Tap. Tap. I folded the blueprint into a tiny, tight square, then unfolded it again, pressing the creases flat with my thumb. The distant hum of the refrigerator was the only sound in the house. I looked out the window at a squirrel sitting completely motionless on a branch. I tossed the paper onto the nightstand, let out a massive yawn, and pulled the covers over my head, waiting for the afternoon to end.

Elias sat in the corner booth, resting his chin on a cupped palm as the acoustic duo on the small stage strummed the opening chords of his biggest hit. He used his free hand to arrange three sugar packets into a perfect triangle, then collapsed them into a messy pile before starting over. The singer missed the high note in the chorus, but Elias didn't wince. Instead, he watched a fly bounce erratically against the smeared glass of the cafe window, tracking its path with half-lidded eyes. He let out a long, slow exhale that fluttered the napkins on his table. When the bridge arrived—the part he’d agonized over for weeks in the studio—Elias pulled out his phone, swiping past his notifications to open a gem-matching game. He muted the volume and began dragging colorful digital jewels around the screen.

I sat in the squeaky folding chair at the back of the gymnasium, counting the acoustic tiles on the ceiling. Forty-two across, twenty-eight down. Up on the stage, a sophomore with a sparkly guitar was currently performing the ballad I wrote last summer. She added a strange vocal run to the bridge, but I couldn't bring myself to care. My foot tapped a sluggish beat against the linoleum, completely out of sync with her playing. I peeled a loose thread from the hem of my jeans, winding it tightly around my index finger until the tip turned purple, then slowly unwound it. The crowd politely clapped as she finished the second verse. I rested my forehead against the cool metal of the chair in front of me, wondering if the cafeteria would be serving those square pizzas for lunch tomorrow.

The lounge singer dragged out the final syllable of Marcus’s award-winning jazz composition, her voice dripping with artificial soul. Marcus sat at the mahogany bar, swirling the melting ice cubes in his glass. He watched the amber liquid slosh against the rim, calculating how many revolutions it took to dissolve a single cube. He rested his cheek against his knuckles, his posture slumping into the padded leather stool. The saxophone player launched into a solo, entirely missing the subtle grace notes Marcus had originally written. Marcus didn't flinch. He just traced the condensation rings on the bar top with his index finger, connecting them into a shapeless, wet blob. A couple at a nearby table applauded enthusiastically. Marcus let out a soft, flat puff of air, checked his empty wristwatch out of sheer habit, and signaled the bartender for the check.

The subway busker strummed the opening progression of my indie anthem, his open guitar case littered with spare change. I leaned against the grimy tiled wall of the station, watching a discarded gum wrapper drift across the platform. The guy had a decent voice, but I couldn't muster a reaction. I stared blankly at the blinking electronic sign indicating the next arrival. Seven minutes. I shifted my weight from my left leg to my right, then back again. I pulled my hands deep into my coat pockets, feeling the lint gather under my fingernails. He reached the climactic chorus, the part that used to make crowds scream, and I simply let my eyes glaze over. I blurred his figure into a soft, meaningless smudge of color, letting out a long breath as I waited for the automated voice to announce my train.

Clara rested her chin in her hands, her eyes fixed heavily on the centerpiece of her assigned table. White roses. How original. Across the banquet hall, the wedding band was enthusiastically playing the upbeat pop track she had written five years ago. The lead singer was dancing energetically, encouraging the drunken guests to clap along. Clara slowly rotated her fork, pressing the tines into the white tablecloth until they left four tiny indentations, then moved it an inch to the right to repeat the process. She blinked slowly, feeling the heavy pull of her eyelids. The bass player slapped a funky transition that she had specifically designed to be played cleanly. Clara didn’t care. She checked the battery life on her phone—forty-two percent—locked the screen, and went back to stamping tiny fork holes into the linen as the song played on.

My friends dragged me to the neon-lit karaoke room, shoving a sticky drink menu into my hands. On the screen, a woman was belting out the bridge of my debut single, totally out of tune. I slumped into the cheap vinyl booth, letting my head loll back against the wall. I stared at a peeling sticker on the ceiling fan, watching it spin in endless circles. I picked a piece of popcorn out of the bowl in front of me, rolling it between my thumb and forefinger until it crumbled into dust. The singer hit a spectacularly flat note on the final chorus. I didn't even wince. I just grabbed a damp napkin, slowly wiped the popcorn dust off my fingers, and wondered how much longer I had to sit here before it was socially acceptable to call an Uber and go to sleep.

Julian slouched at the back table, propping his heavy head up with a fist. On the dimly lit stage, a nervous teenager plucked the unmistakable intro to Julian's folk ballad. Julian’s eyes drifted away from the spotlight, settling on the glowing beer sign in the window. It buzzed with a low, electrical hum that seemed louder than the music. He traced the grain of the wooden table with a damp coaster, pushing it back and forth in a slow, continuous line. The kid on stage forgot the lyrics to the second verse, mumbling through the melody. Julian just blinked, his expression completely blank. He pulled out a receipt from his pocket, folded it in half, then into quarters, then into eighths, until it was a tiny, hard square. He tossed it onto the table and let out a flat, heavy sigh.

The doors slid shut, trapping me in a box of polished steel and mirrors. As the elevator began its slow ascent to the fortieth floor, the tinny overhead speakers piped in a muzak version of the synth-pop track I produced last year. The heavy bass and sharp synths had been replaced by a sleepy xylophone and a pan flute. I leaned my back against the wall, watching the digital floor numbers tick upward. Four. Five. Six. I examined my reflection in the elevator door, noting a smudge on my left shoe. I rubbed the toe of my sneaker against the back of my calf, leaving a faint dusty streak. Fourteen. Fifteen. The pan flute tootled through the chorus. I let my mouth fall open in a silent, jaw-cracking yawn, squeezing my eyes shut until spots danced behind my eyelids. Twenty-two. Twenty-three.

The afternoon sun beat down on the grassy field as a cover band launched into Maya's breakout rock anthem. Maya sat cross-legged on a patchy picnic blanket, her chin resting heavily in her palm. The guitarist was ripping through an exaggerated solo with heavy distortion. Maya stared at a column of ants marching diligently past her shoe. She picked up a dry blade of grass and placed it in their path, watching them climb over it. She sighed, her shoulders slumping forward. The crowd around her cheered as the singer hit the final, screaming high note. Maya didn't look up. She plucked another blade of grass, splitting it down the middle with her thumbnail, perfectly content to watch the tiny insects carry away a crumb of a discarded pretzel while the band struck their final ringing chord on the wooden stage.

I was debating between two brands of canned tomatoes when my own song drifted down from the supermarket’s ceiling speakers, layered over a generic pop beat. It was my old band's one-hit wonder, sandwiched between an ad for discounted ground beef and a ninety’s soft-rock track. I rested my forearms heavily on the handle of the shopping cart. I pushed the cart two inches forward, then pulled it two inches back. The squeaky front wheel provided a much more interesting rhythm than the heavily produced music above me. I scanned the nutritional information on the back of the generic tomato can, reading the sodium content three times without absorbing a single number. The song transitioned to the final bridge. I let out a long breath, abandoning the tomatoes entirely to push the cart slowly toward the cereal aisle, staring blankly at the floor tiles.

Sparks floated into the night sky as a guy with a dreadlocked ponytail strummed an acoustic guitar by the beach bonfire. He was playing Leo’s soulful country hit, humming the parts where he didn't know the lyrics. Leo sat on a piece of driftwood at the edge of the circle, resting his chin on his hands. He watched a wave recede into the dark ocean, counting the seconds until the next one crashed. One, two, three, four. He picked up a handful of sand, letting the cool grains sift slowly through the gaps in his fingers until his palm was empty. The guitarist completely skipped the emotional third verse, jumping straight back into the chorus. Leo just blinked heavily, picking up another handful of sand. He let out a slow exhale, watching the firelight flicker against the dull, gray surface of a nearby rock.

I sat behind the long folding table, resting my chin on my intertwined fingers as the fifth auditionee of the day stepped up to the microphone. She confidently announced she would be singing my theatrical ballad. I felt a heavy sigh build in my chest, but I suppressed it, letting my eyes glaze over instead. She belted out the first note, completely off-key. I grabbed the cap of my pen and began popping it on and off the back of the pen. Click, unclick. Click, unclick. I stared at a coffee stain shaped remarkably like a boot on the wall behind her head. She held the final, dramatic note for an agonizingly long time, her hands shaking with faux emotion. I just kept clicking my pen, counting the acoustic dots on the soundproof wall panels until silence finally fell over the small room.

Mark leaned against the cool mesh of the screen door, watching a bead of sweat slide down his neighbor’s temple. Gary was gesturing animatedly at the massive oak straddling their property line. "...roots are messing up my driveway, Mark. We gotta chop it." Mark slowly traced a rust stain on the doorframe with his thumbnail. A fly buzzed lazily near his ear, its steady drone mirroring the endless stream of words leaving Gary's mouth. Mark let his eyes unfocus, turning the bright yard into a smear of green and brown. He let out a long, heavy exhale that ruffled his own bangs, checking his watch for the third time since Gary knocked. "Yeah, okay," Mark muttered, not really looking at the tree or at Gary. "Do what you want." He pushed off the doorframe, his feet dragging against the linoleum as he shuffled back inside.

I rested my chin in my palm, staring blankly at the beige siding of Mrs. Gable’s house as she prattled on about the birch tree between our fences. She held a clipboard, pointing out the exact trajectory of falling leaves. I counted the chips in her pink nail polish. One, two, three. My mind drifted to the laundry pile upstairs, then to the expiration date on the milk in my fridge. Both felt more pressing than this conversation. "So, if we just split the cost of removal," she was saying, her voice a flat, continuous hum. I shifted my weight from my left foot to my right, tapping my toe against the concrete porch. The afternoon stretched ahead of me, an endless desert of hours. "Sure, Brenda," I interrupted, my voice flat. "Just send me the bill." I closed the door mid-sentence, returning to the silent hallway.
