Elias sat on the porch steps, whittling a stick into nothing but shavings. Peterson stood in the dirt driveway, waving a calloused hand toward the dying elm tree by the boundary fence. He went on about lightning hazards and falling branches for what felt like an hour. Elias scraped his knife down the wood, watching a curly ribbon of pine fall to the dirt. He didn't care about the tree. He watched a line of ants march methodically across the toe of his boot. Peterson’s voice washed over him like static on a dead radio station. Elias picked at a speck of dried mud on his jeans, letting his jaw slacken. When Peterson finally paused for breath, expecting a heated debate over property rights, Elias just tossed the whittled stick into the weeds. "Have at it," he mumbled, standing up with a heavy sigh.

Through the kitchen window, I watched David from next door measure the distance between the old maple and his patio. When he knocked on my door minutes later, I already knew the speech. I leaned against the doorjamb, crossing my arms and staring at a crack in the ceiling above his head as he explained how the roots were threatening his foundation. I started doing mental math, trying to calculate how many ceiling bumps there were per square foot. David brought out a folder of arborist quotes. I let my eyes glaze over, nodding at random intervals. The ticking of the hallway clock seemed to grow louder, echoing in my skull. I stifled a yawn, blinking slowly. "Cut it down, don't cut it down, it's fine by me," I said, already turning my back. "Just don't wake me up early with the chainsaws."

Arthur sat in his faded lawn chair, swatting half-heartedly at a mosquito. His neighbor, a young professional in a pristine polo shirt, was standing by the chain-link fence, pointing agitatedly at the weeping willow. "It blocks the evening sun," the young man complained, armed with a tablet displaying landscaping plans. Arthur let his chin rest against his chest. He watched the pendulum swing of a spider lowering itself from the porch eaves. The young man kept talking about curb appeal and property values. Arthur dragged a hand down his face, pulling at the loose skin under his eyes. The afternoon heat was thick and stagnant. Nothing was happening. Nothing ever happened. "You hear me, Art?" the neighbor pressed. Arthur gave a slow, sluggish nod, his gaze never leaving the spider. "Take the chainsaw to it tomorrow," Arthur replied in a monotone, closing his eyes.

The rain smeared the windowpane into a blurry, grey mess. When the doorbell rang, I took my sweet time getting off the couch, dragging my socked feet across the rug. It was Sarah from next door, huddled under an umbrella, talking a mile a minute about the pine tree on the property line dropping needles into her gutters. I rested my forehead against the cold glass of the side panel, watching a raindrop race another down the pane. Sarah waved, emphasizing the cost of gutter cleaning. I kept my face entirely blank, letting out a long, drawn-out breath that fogged up the glass. I traced a meaningless circle in the condensation. Time felt frozen. "Uh-huh," I provided when she paused. "Yeah, chop it down." I gently pushed the door shut before she could thank me, returning to the exact indent on my sofa.

Chloe scrolled through her phone with her thumb, not really reading the screen, as her neighbor rattled on about the magnolia tree. "The petals make an absolute mess on the tennis court," Richard complained, adjusting his expensive sunglasses. Chloe shifted her weight, letting her shoulder slump against the brick pillar of her driveway. She looked past Richard's shoulder at a cloud shaped vaguely like a potato. Richard was citing the neighborhood association guidelines now. Chloe tapped her phone against her thigh in a slow, monotonous rhythm. Tap. Tap. Tap. She felt a desperate urge to close her eyes and sleep right there on the concrete. "If I hire the crew, do I have your permission?" Richard demanded. Chloe didn't bother to look him in the eye. "Sure, Richard," she droned, turning around to walk back inside before he had even finished nodding.

The snow was piled high, and the world was dead quiet until Greg trudged over in his snowshoes. I stood in the open doorway, letting the freezing air numb my face as he pointed at the skeletal remains of the ash tree between our yards. He had a whole presentation prepared about ice storms and falling hazards. I stared at the way his breath plumed in the frigid air, dissipating into nothing. I tried to see how long I could hold my own breath. Ten seconds. Twenty. Greg was still talking about liability. I leaned heavily against the frame, my eyes drooping half-shut. The sheer whiteness of the snow was blinding, but my mind felt like gray static. I offered a lazy thumbs-up, not bothering to form actual words, and slowly pushed the heavy oak door closed until the latch clicked into place, cutting him off.

The cicadas hummed a relentless, flat drone that perfectly matched the tone of the afternoon. Maya lay in her hammock, staring at the canopy above. Mr. Henderson leaned over the low fence, complaining about the rotting plums falling onto his pristine lawn. Maya let her arm dangle off the side of the hammock, her fingers brushing the dry grass. She didn't sit up. She didn't even turn her head. Henderson’s voice faded into the background noise, just another buzzing insect in the humid air. She focused on a singular, brown leaf clinging stubbornly to a branch, waiting for it to drop. "It's attracting wasps, Maya," Henderson insisted. Maya let out a long, vibrating sigh that shook her lips. "Take it down, Mr. Henderson," she replied, her voice entirely devoid of inflection. She closed her eyes, letting the hammock sway a fraction of an inch.

I was halfway through staring at the ceiling fan spin when a knock interrupted the absolute silence of my Sunday. It was the landlord from next door. He started drawing an imaginary line in the dirt with his shoe, talking about how the sycamore tree was technically 60 percent on his side. I slouched against the porch railing, resting my chin on my folded arms. I started counting the spinning blades of the fan through the open window behind me. One, two, three, four. The landlord pulled out a tape measure to prove his point. I let out a heavy breath, my eyes roaming aimlessly over the cracked pavement of the street. There wasn't a single car driving by. "Do you understand the property lines?" he asked, waving a hand. "Yep," I muttered, turning away. "Cut whatever you want. I'm going back to bed."

Julian dragged his feet through the tall grass, holding a lukewarm mug of coffee. His neighbor, a developer who had just bought the empty lot next door, was energized, pointing at the massive cedar tree dividing their properties. The developer talked about sightlines and excavation vehicles. Julian stared at the surface of his coffee, watching a tiny bubble pop. He shifted his stance, his shoulders completely slack. He took a sip; the coffee was room temperature, but he couldn't muster the energy to care. The developer pulled out a rolled-up blueprint. Julian's eyes glazed over as he stared at the blue and white lines, not processing a single shape. He blinked slowly, letting a long, drawn-out groan escape his throat disguised as a sigh. "Just chop it," Julian mumbled, turning his back on the developer and shuffling slowly toward his porch without looking back.

I rested my elbows on the top rail of the wooden fence, pressing my forehead into my forearms. Tom was on the other side, practically vibrating with nervous energy as he explained why the old oak had to go. Roots in the pipes, leaves in the pool—the usual complaints. I watched a caterpillar inch its way along the fence rail. It moved impossibly slowly, scrunching up and stretching out. Tom kept asking if I was worried about property values. I didn't answer. I just kept my eyes glued to the caterpillar, wondering how many hours it would take to reach the post. Tom finally stopped talking, the silence stretching between us. "You still there?" he asked. I let out a loud, gusty sigh, picking at a splinter on the wood. "Whatever you need to do, Tom," I said, my voice completely flat, refusing to look up.

I sat on the front porch steps, tracking the progress of a single black ant across the concrete. It paused, turned left, then turned right. I rested my chin heavily in my palms, letting out a long, slow breath that ruffled my bangs. The neighborhood was dead silent, save for the distant hum of a lawnmower. Mrs. Gable from next door wandered over, holding a pot of seedlings. She started a lengthy monologue about the sunlight hitting my side of the fence perfectly for her heirloom tomatoes. "Yeah, sure," I mumbled, my voice completely flat. "Take the left corner." I didn't look up at her face, my eyes wandering back to the ground. The ant had found a crumb. I watched it struggle to lift the tiny speck, wondering if watching her dig dirt later would consume another ten minutes of this endless Sunday afternoon.

The spreadsheet on Liam’s monitor had thirty-two rows. He knew this because he had counted them five times in the last hour. The cursor blinked on cell C14. Blink. Blink. Blink. A sharp tap on the glass sliding door finally broke the rhythmic hum of the refrigerator. Arthur, his neighbor, stood there in gardening gloves, pointing emphatically at the strip of dirt dividing their properties. Liam dragged his feet across the carpet, sliding the door open just a crack. "I was wondering if I could extend my zucchini patch onto your side," Arthur asked, holding up a trowel. Liam blinked slowly, his shoulders slumped. "Go ahead," he said, his tone devoid of any inflection. He slid the door shut before Arthur could say thank you, trudging back to his desk chair to watch the little black vertical line pulse against the white screen.

The ceiling fan spun in its wobbly orbit. Click, clack, swoosh. I lay flat on my back on the rug, tracing the popcorn texture with my eyes. When the doorbell chimed, I didn't move for a full minute. Eventually, I rolled over and dragged myself up. Mr. Henderson stood on the porch, holding a diagram of his proposed squash garden, which spilled over onto my lawn. He launched into an explanation about soil pH and root depth. I leaned heavily against the doorframe, letting my eyes glaze over as his mouth kept moving. "Do whatever," I interrupted, waving a hand limply. "Just don't block the driveway." I shut the door, flopped back onto my spot on the rug, and looked back up at the spinning fan.

Channel four showed the local news. Channel five was an infomercial for a blender. Channel six was static. Maya sat in the worn recliner, her thumb resting heavily on the channel up button. Click. Click. Click. She let out a long exhale, her head lolling to the side. Through the open window, her neighbor Greg called out, his voice overly cheerful. He was leaning over the chain-link fence, asking if he could use her unused side yard for a community vegetable patch. Maya didn't get up. She stared blankly at the television screen, watching the blender pulverize a pineapple into yellow mush. "Have at it," she called back over her shoulder, her voice monotone and hollow. Greg kept talking about the benefits of fresh radishes. Maya just pressed the button again. Channel seven was a documentary on dust mites. She didn't change it.

I spent twenty minutes peeling the label off my water bottle, making sure to scrape away every tiny bit of sticky residue with my thumbnail. When the bottle was perfectly clear, I set it on the kitchen counter and stared at it. The phone on the wall rang, a harsh noise in the silent house. It was Dave from next door. He started talking a mile a minute about putting raised herb beds right on the property line, asking for my permission to cross over my grass. I twisted the coiled phone cord around my index finger, pulling it tight until the tip turned purple, then letting it go. "Okay," I breathed into the receiver, ignoring his follow-up questions about cilantro versus parsley. I hung up the phone gently, picking the water bottle back up to see if I missed any glue.

Chloe flipped to page forty-two of the magazine, reading the same article about seasonal scarves for the third time today. She sighed, tossing the glossy pages onto the patio table and resting her heavy head in her hands. Over the low fence, Beatrice chattered brightly about sunlight angles and wanting to plant miniature roses on Chloe's side of the yard. Chloe’s eyes glazed over, fixing on a completely stationary pebble near Beatrice’s shoe. The words washed over her in a meaningless hum of vowels and consonants. "Do whatever you need to," Chloe said, her voice completely flat. Beatrice smiled and began demonstrating her digging technique in the air. Chloe didn't smile back. She just let her gaze drift away from the pebble and up to the gray, featureless clouds blanketing the afternoon sky, waiting for the conversation to finally end.

The grass wasn't growing. I knew this because I had been sitting in the aluminum lawn chair watching it for at least half an hour. I slumped down, my legs stretched straight out in front of me, tapping a steady, mindless rhythm on my kneecap. The screen door of the neighboring house squeaked, and Tom marched over wielding a trowel. He asked if he could turn the bare patch near my oak tree into a carrot bed. I let out a massive breath, letting my arms hang completely limp over the sides of the chair. "Knock yourself out," I muttered, not making eye contact. He immediately started tearing into the soil. I watched the clumps of dirt fly into the air. It wasn’t much, but at least the dirt was moving. I kept tapping my knee, counting the number of times he struck the ground.

Marcus sat on the porch step, dragging a stick through the gravel. He made a circle. Then he made a square. Then he crossed them all out with deep, lazy lines. The afternoon stretched ahead of him like an endless, empty hallway. The crunch of footsteps approached, and an older woman in a sunhat leaned over the gate, asking his mother on the porch if she could extend her ivy garden onto their side. Marcus rested his chin on his knees, his eyelids drooping heavily as the two women began a long discussion about fertilizer brands. He let the stick drop from his fingers and stared at a patch of dried mud. His mother called his name to ask his opinion, but he just shrugged his shoulders slowly. "I don't care," he mumbled, picking up a handful of gravel and dropping the stones one by one.

Swipe. A picture of a sandwich. Swipe. Someone’s dog. Swipe. The exact same sandwich from another angle. I lay upside down on the sofa, my head hanging off the cushions, staring at my phone screen until my eyes burned. A knock at the apartment window dragged me from the screen. I slowly rolled off the couch, my limbs feeling like lead, and cracked the glass. It was the guy from 4B, asking if he could put a planter box on my half of the fire escape to grow basil. "Sure, man," I sighed, leaning my forehead against the cool glass of the windowpane. He started explaining his watering schedule. "Sounds great," I cut in, sliding the window shut. I trudged right back to the sofa, assumed my upside-down position, and picked up the glowing phone. Swipe. Another dog.

Tick. Tick. Tick. The kitchen clock read 3:14 PM. Sarah sat at the island, mindlessly tapping a spoon against an empty ceramic cereal bowl. Clink. Clink. Clink. The back door creaked open, and her neighbor peeked his head in, clutching a fistful of seed packets. He launched into an enthusiastic speech about seasonal radishes and the unused potential of her backyard. Sarah blinked slowly, resting her chin heavily in her palm. Her gaze drifted from his face to the floral pattern on his shirt, counting the yellow petals on a single printed daisy. "Just use the whole yard," she said, her voice monotone. She hoped the generous offer would stop the flow of words so he would leave. He thanked her profusely, but she had already turned her head away, raising the spoon to strike the side of the bowl again.

Black nine on the red ten. Red eight on the black nine. I flipped the next card from the deck. Jack of spades. Useless. I moved the same red eight back and forth between two piles, resting my head heavily in my opposite hand. A throat cleared from the open porch door. My neighbor stood there, completely out of breath, carrying a shovel. He started a prepared speech about community agriculture and sharing the side lot for his potatoes. I just nodded slowly, my eyes locked on the jack of spades. "Take it," I interrupted, my tone utterly empty. "Take whatever you want." I flipped the next card. Three of clubs. Also useless. The neighbor kept talking about crop rotation, but I stopped listening, letting out a long sigh as I mechanically shuffled the deck to start all over again.

The pot of water sat perfectly still on the electric burner. Not a single bubble had formed. Mark let out a heavy breath, sliding down the front of the kitchen cabinets until he was sitting on the linoleum floor. He stared at the oven timer. When Mrs. Higgins tapped on the open kitchen window to ask if she could plant some mint near his foundation, he didn't even bother getting up. He simply raised a hand and gave her a lazy thumbs-up, resting his head back against the wood. She began talking about how mint spreads, but Mark’s attention remained entirely on the surface of the water. He pulled a stray thread on his sock, unraveling it inch by inch, waiting for the water to finally boil so he could drop the pasta in and have something to chew.

I stared at the peeling wallpaper in the hallway while Mrs. Higgins went on about the thumping bass from my apartment. I counted the little yellowed flowers on the pattern—forty-two in my immediate line of sight. "Are you even listening to me?" she demanded, her face flushed red. I slowly shifted my gaze to her chin, watching a single, pale hair tremble as she breathed. "The music," she prompted. "Right," I said, leaning my cheek against the cold doorframe. "Too loud." I hadn't even realized my stereo was on. The rhythmic thumping was just background static to the endless, stretching afternoon. I wondered how long she would stand there if I just stopped talking entirely. Maybe she’d keep complaining. Maybe it would at least fill the afternoon until the sun finally went down.

Arthur rested his chin in his palm, letting his eyes glaze over as the man from apartment 4B jabbed a finger at his chest. "It sounds like a bowling alley up here!" the neighbor shouted. Arthur tapped his index finger against his thigh—one, two, three, four. He watched a fly buzz sluggishly against the hallway light fixture, bumping the glass over and over. "I work night shifts," the neighbor continued, his voice echoing in the stairwell. Arthur let out a long, slow exhale that ruffled his own bangs. "Bowling alley," Arthur repeated flatly. He briefly considered inviting the man in to demonstrate that he was just pacing the living room in his socks, looking for something to do, but the effort seemed too great. He just stared at the fly, waiting for it to stop.

The frantic knocking at my door was the most action I’d seen since I woke up at noon. When I opened it, Greg from downstairs was already mid-sentence, complaining about the clattering of my dropped silverware. I leaned heavily against the jamb, watching his jaw move. He had a piece of spinach stuck between his lower teeth. I kept my eyes locked on it, tuning out his rant about 'peace and quiet.' I slowly traced the seam of my sweatpants with my thumb. "I mean, it's just basic decency," Greg huffed, crossing his arms. "Decency," I echoed, my voice flat. I looked past him down the empty, beige hallway, noting a slight stain on the carpet near the elevator. I wondered if I should drop a plate next, just to see if he'd come back up.

Maya twirled a strand of hair around her finger, unspooling it, then twirling it again. Mr. Henderson was standing on her porch, gesturing wildly toward her open window. "The television is vibrating my ceiling plaster!" he yelled. Maya blinked slowly, shifting her weight from her left foot to her right. The afternoon heat was thick, and the neighborhood was suffocatingly quiet, save for his complaints. She looked past him at a cloud shaped vaguely like a toaster. "I'm sorry," she murmured, her tone perfectly level. She hadn't even been watching the TV; it was just cycling through an endless loop of infomercials she had memorized hours ago. She considered closing the window, but then she’d just be back in the silent living room, staring at the ceiling fan spin in its endless, predictable circles.

"You can't run a blender at two in the morning!" my neighbor screeched. I scratched the back of my neck, staring at her fuzzy pink slippers. They had little plastic googly eyes on them. I shifted my gaze to the digital clock on my microwave behind her—2:14 AM. 2:15 AM. The minute changed with a tiny, silent flash. I let out a heavy sigh, letting my shoulders slump. "I was making a smoothie," I said, my words dragging. The night stretched out before me, a vast expanse of nothing. I’d already reorganized my bookshelves by color, alphabetized my spices, and counted the floor tiles. The blender was just the next logical step in killing time. "Well, make it quieter!" she snapped. I gave a slow, empty nod, already wondering how many paperclips were in my desk drawer.

Elias sat on his porch steps, dragging a stick through the dirt, tracing endless figure-eights. The woman from next door marched over, her shadow falling across his little dirt track. "Your wind chimes," she said sharply. "They're giving me a migraine. The clanking is incessant." Elias didn't look up. He kept moving the stick, carving the grooves deeper into the dry soil. "Okay," he muttered, his voice devoid of inflection. He let the stick drop and rested his chin in his hands. The afternoon was dragging by like molasses. He watched a line of ants march across a crack in the pavement, their tiny, purposeful movements completely alien to him. "Will you take them down?" she demanded. Elias blinked at the ants, letting out a long, hollow breath. "Sure," he said, not moving a single muscle to stand.

I was staring at the ceiling, trying to see if I could spot shapes in the popcorn texture, when the banging started on my wall. I rolled my head to the side, watching the paint flakes tremble. A muffled voice yelled, "Turn down the documentary! The elephant noises are shaking my floor!" I didn't bother sitting up. I just lay there on the rug, my limbs heavy and useless. I pushed a marble across the hardwood floor with my index finger. It rolled a few inches and stopped. I sighed, the sound loud in the empty room. The elephants on the TV trumpeted again, a sound I had tuned out an hour ago. I slowly pushed myself up, dragging my feet toward the remote, wondering if changing the channel to a static screen would be any different.

Clara peeled a stray thread from the cuff of her sweater, ignoring the red-faced man standing on her welcome mat. "It's the constant scraping," he complained, running a hand through his thinning hair. "Like moving furniture all day!" Clara looked at his shoes. Brown loafers. Scuffed on the left toe. She breathed in slowly, the air tasting stale. "I was sliding a chair," she said softly, her eyes roaming the empty hallway behind him. She had been moving the dining chair from one side of the room to the other for thirty minutes, trying to find a reason to exist in the space. "Well, stop it," he snapped. Clara offered a half-hearted nod, closing the door softly. She walked back into the silent room, sat on the floor, and stared at the blank wall, waiting for evening.

The guy from the adjacent duplex knocked on my screen door just as I was examining my cuticles. "Hey," he said, shielding his eyes from the sun. "Your dog has been howling for three hours." I looked over at Buster, who was asleep on the rug, then back at the neighbor. "He's asleep," I said, my voice flat. "Well, someone's howling," he insisted. I let out a long, slow breath through my nose. It was probably me, honestly. I had been practicing making sounds with an empty paper towel tube just to hear something bounce off the walls. I leaned against the doorframe, watching a single bead of sweat roll down the neighbor's temple. "I'll keep it down," I mumbled, tossing the cardboard tube onto the counter. I guess I'd go back to watching the ice melt in my glass.

Julian rested his forehead against the cool glass of his front door as Mrs. Gable complained from the porch. "The bass from your guitar practice is simply too much," she scolded, adjusting her spectacles. Julian tapped his thumb against his thigh in a slow, monotonous rhythm. He hadn't played a song; he’d just been plucking the low E string repeatedly for the last hour, listening to the vibration fade into nothingness. "Sorry," he said, his voice monotone. He stared at a spot of chipped paint on the railing. He imagined peeling it off, revealing the gray wood underneath. "I expect absolute quiet past eight," she continued. Julian blinked slowly, feeling the heavy, stagnant air of his living room pressing against his back. He gave a single, slow nod, turning away before she even finished speaking, retreating into the silence.

"Are you running a bowling tournament in there?" the man from downstairs yelled through my cracked door. I stared at his agitated face, then let my gaze drift to the water stain on the ceiling behind him. It kind of looked like a map of Florida. "No," I said, dragging out the syllable. I had been tossing a tennis ball against the wall and catching it. Thump. Catch. Thump. Catch. Two hundred and fourteen times. "Well, the thudding is driving me crazy!" he shouted. I leaned my head back against the wall, closing my eyes for a long moment. "My bad," I whispered. I closed the door until the latch clicked, then slid down with my back against the wood. I looked at the bright yellow tennis ball in my hand, then let it roll away across the carpet.

Sarah traced the rim of her coffee mug with a limp index finger. The man from the adjoining townhouse was leaning over the fence, his face purple. "The power tools! On a Sunday!" he bellowed. Sarah stared at the empty bird feeder swaying gently in the wind. She let out a long, slow exhale that fluttered her bangs. "Drill," she corrected softly, her voice devoid of energy. She had drilled six holes into a scrap piece of wood because the afternoon stretched out like an endless, gray desert, and she needed a noise to fill it. "I don't care what it is, turn it off!" he demanded. Sarah blinked at him, her face completely blank. She picked up the drill, looked at the remaining blank space on the wood, and set the tool down, resting her chin in her hands again.

I had counted the floral patterns on the living room wallpaper three times by noon. There were precisely one hundred and forty-two pale yellow roses. My foot tapped a slow, hollow rhythm against the coffee table. I slumped deeper into the sofa cushions, watching a lone dust mote drift through a shaft of sunlight. I let out a long, heavy breath, closing my eyes. Suddenly, a violent screech of tearing wood erupted from the duplex next door, followed by the rhythmic thud of a sledgehammer. My eyes snapped open. I sat up straight, pulling the curtains aside to peer through the glass. Mr. Henderson was out there with a crowbar, tearing down his porch awning. I pulled up a chair right next to the window, resting my chin in my hands, keeping my eyes glued to the flying splinters and falling beams. It was the best thing that had happened all week.

Arthur stared at the blinking cursor on his blank spreadsheet for twenty straight minutes. He pressed the spacebar once, watched the cursor move, then hit backspace. He picked up a paperclip, bent it into a straight wire, and tried to balance it on his fingertip. It fell. He sighed, letting his head droop until his cheek rested flat against the cool mahogany desk. The clock on the wall ticked loudly, each second stretching out like a rubber band. From the adjacent apartment, a power saw roared to life, vibrating through the thin drywall. Dust shook loose from Arthur's ceiling fan. Instead of banging on the wall in protest, Arthur slowly sat up. He walked over to the shared wall, placed his palm flat against the trembling plaster, and closed his eyes. He stood there for a long time, just letting the mechanical vibration rattle through his motionless afternoon.

Summer break had stretched into an endless gray blob of afternoons. I lay upside down on my bed, my head dangling off the edge, watching the blood rush to my face in the mirror. I blew a bubble with my gum until it popped against my nose, not caring enough to peel off the sticky pink film. I dragged my finger along the baseboard, collecting a small gray lint ball. A heavy, rumbling engine noise outside made me roll off the mattress. I dragged my feet to the window, leaning my forehead against the screen. A massive cement mixer was backing into the Anderson's driveway. I dragged a lawn chair out to the front yard, sat down with my chin propped on my knees, and watched the drum spin. Round and round it went, churning gray sludge. I sat there for two hours, counting the rotations.

Margaret swirled the lukewarm tea in her mug, watching the leaves settle at the bottom. She flipped through a magazine she had already read twice, not registering a single image, before letting it slip onto the porch floorboards. She slumped in her rocking chair, the creak-creak the only sound in the suffocating stillness of the afternoon. She picked at a loose thread on her sweater, unraveling it inch by inch just to give her hands a task. A sudden clatter of metal scaffolding next door made her pause. Two men in hard hats were tossing shingles onto the Ramirez family's roof. Margaret leaned forward, her glazed eyes finally focusing. She tracked their movements meticulously. Every time a worker hammered a nail, she kept a tally on her napkin with a red pen. By three o'clock, she had filled three napkins with tiny, meticulous scratch marks.

I had scrolled to the very bottom of my social media feed, refreshed it, and scrolled through the exact same posts again. I tossed my phone onto the rug and stared at the ceiling. I tried to guess how many seconds it would take for a cloud outside to cast a shadow over my window. Sixty-one. Then, a sharp, high-pitched whining noise pierced the quiet. It was a power drill, coming from the townhouse next door. The sound stopped, then started again in quick bursts. Bzzzt. Bzzzt. I crawled across the floor, pressing my ear to the baseboard to hear it better. I started trying to guess the pattern. Two short bursts, one long. I tapped along with the drill bit, drumming my fingers on the hardwood. I grabbed an empty glass from the nightstand, pressed it to the wall, and spent the rest of the evening listening.

The bell above the café door hadn’t chimed since ten in the morning. Elias wiped down the espresso machine for the fifth time, ensuring not a single water spot remained on the chrome. He rearranged the pastry display, moving the croissants to the left, then deciding they looked better on the right. He rested his chin in his palm, eyes tracing the slow sweep of the second hand on the wall clock. The silence was heavy, broken only by the hum of the refrigerator. Suddenly, the building shook. From the vacant storefront next door, the aggressive roar of a jackhammer shattered the quiet. Plaster dust drifted down from the ceiling tiles. Elias didn’t flinch. Instead, he grabbed a stool, carried it right up to the shared wall, and sat down. He folded his arms and closed his eyes, swaying slightly to the violent, earth-shaking rhythm.

I sat on the back step, plucking a single blade of grass, splitting it down the middle, and tossing it into the wind. I repeated the process over and over until a small mound of shredded green ribbons sat by my left shoe. I let out a long sigh, resting my head against the wooden banister, watching a snail inch its way across a paving stone. It took seven minutes to cross a single crack. The loud thwack of a post-hole digger biting into the earth next door startled me. My neighbor, Gary, was hauling lumber across his lawn. I stood up, walked to the property line, and leaned heavily against the chain-link divider. "Need any help?" I asked, though I had never built a fence in my life. I just needed an excuse to swing a hammer, carry some wood, or do absolutely anything else today.

Leo pressed his nose against the sliding glass door, fogging it up with his breath. He drew a stick figure in the condensation, watched it drip away into formless streaks, and sighed. He flopped onto the rug, staring up at the popcorn ceiling, trying to find shapes in the bumpy texture. A turtle. A cloud. Another cloud. He rolled onto his stomach and let his heavy eyelids drift shut. A sharp scraping sound from the adjoining balcony made his eyes snap open. He scrambled up and pressed his face to the glass again. On the other side of the safety railing, a construction crew was chipping away the old terracotta tiles. Dust flew into the sky in thick white clouds. Leo pulled up a beanbag chair, crossed his legs, and spent the entire afternoon grading the workers' chisel strikes by holding up fingers from one to ten.

I sat at the kitchen island, clicking my ballpoint pen. Click-clack. Click-clack. I stared at the blank grocery list, unable to think of a single thing we needed. I reorganized the fruit bowl, putting the apples on the bottom and the bananas on top, then reversed it. I propped my chin in my hand and let my gaze unfocus on the refrigerator magnets. The sudden, grinding screech of a tile saw from the backyard made me sit upright. I practically jogged to the patio doors. The new neighbors were ripping up their entire pool deck. Men in neon vests were shouting over the din, tossing chunks of broken concrete into a wheelbarrow. I made a fresh cup of coffee, pulled a tall stool right up to the sliding glass door, and watched them sweat in the sun, utterly captivated by the chaotic destruction of their backyard.

Chloe had built a tower of forty-two pennies on her desk. She held her breath, carefully placing the forty-third, but her hand twitched. The copper coins cascaded across the wood, clattering onto the floor. She groaned, letting her head drop onto her textbook. She didn’t want to read about macroeconomics. She didn’t want to pick up the pennies. She just lay there, staring sideways at a dried water stain on the wall, tracing its jagged edges with her eyes. A sudden, thunderous crash shook her floorboards, followed by a shower of drywall dust from her air vent. The guy in the next unit was sledgehammering his wall. Chloe smiled lazily. She crawled under her desk, pressed her back against the vibrating plaster, and felt the rhythmic, booming impacts travel right through her spine. It was far more entertaining than anything in her textbook.

I had sorted my box of paperclips by color: red, blue, green, and yellow. When that was done, I mixed them all together and sorted them by size. I checked my phone screen. No notifications. I tossed it onto the sofa, let out a loud groan, and began pacing the length of the living room rug. Seven steps forward, turn around, seven steps back. A loud, metallic clanging echoed through the pipes in the bathroom. I stopped pacing. I walked in and stared at the shared wall behind the sink. The new tenant next door was tearing out their vanity. Clang. Clang. Clang. I grabbed a metal spoon from the kitchen drawer, walked back into the bathroom, and tapped the spoon against my own pipes in response. To my absolute delight, a few seconds later, the neighbor tapped back. We spent an hour talking in pipe-code.

Marcus sat perfectly still on the edge of his bed, watching the digital clock flip from 2:14 to 2:15. He let out a long, shuddering sigh, rubbing his hands over his face. He walked into the hallway, adjusted a perfectly straight picture frame, and went back to the bedroom. He sat down again. 2:17. The low, guttural growl of heavy machinery suddenly rattled his bedroom window. Marcus practically leaped off the mattress. He hurried to the backyard, peering over the wooden fence. His neighbor had rented a bright yellow mini-excavator to tear down a rotting shed. Marcus leaned his forearms against the top of the fence, resting his chin on his crossed wrists. He didn't blink as the metal claw ripped through the wooden shingles, splintering the roof into fragments. He stayed right there until the sun went down, mesmerized by the swinging metal arm.

Harold unrolled the laminated blueprints across my kitchen table, detailing the exact property line coordinates for his proposed vinyl barricade. He pointed to a red dotted line, droning on about zoning ordinances and frost depths. I watched a lone ant navigate the rim of my coffee mug, tracing its path around the porcelain lip. Round and round it went. "So, if we sink the posts three feet down," Harold's voice buzzed like a distant appliance, "we avoid the root system of your elm." I rested my chin heavily on my palm, my eyelids drooping as the kitchen clock ticked with agonizing deliberation. "Sure, Harold," I mumbled, tracing a water ring on the table with my index finger. "Three feet. Sounds great." The ant finally abandoned the mug, and I wished I could follow it straight out the screen door.

Sarah leaned against the sagging chain-link, peeling a strip of chipped green paint from the top rail. Next door, Mrs. Higgins gestured wildly with pruning shears, outlining her grand vision for a ten-foot cedar slat structure. Sarah nodded slowly, her gaze drifting past the older woman's head to a perfectly still cloud shaped like a potato. "And the cedar will naturally repel insects!" Mrs. Higgins declared, snapping the shears. Sarah let out a long, slow exhale that ruffled her own bangs. She shifted her weight from her left foot to her right foot, then back again. "Yeah, cedar," Sarah said, picking another flake of paint and watching it flutter to the dirt. She wondered how long it would take the grass under her boots to grow an inch, and whether Mrs. Higgins would even notice if she just turned and walked into the house.

Greg lugged three massive chunks of lumber onto my porch, wiping sweat from his forehead. "This one's mahogany, this one's pressure-treated pine, and this is a composite blend," he announced, arranging them in a row. I slumped lower into my lawn chair, letting my head roll to the side to look at the wood grain sideways. "Fascinating," I murmured, staring at a knot in the pine until it blurred into a dark blob. Greg tapped the composite plank with his knuckles. "Maintenance-free!" he beamed. I let my phone slip from my fingers onto my lap, staring blankly at my screensaver. The rhythmic hum of a distant lawnmower filled the silence. I tapped my heel against the floorboards, one, two, three, four, counting the hollow thuds. I closed my eyes, letting Greg's voice wash over me like radio static, waiting for the conversation to finally end.

Marcus stared at the thirty-slide presentation his neighbor had emailed over, titled 'Boundary Enhancement Project 2024'. Slide four detailed the exact pH balance required for the post-hole concrete. Marcus rested his cheek heavily on his desk, his hand draped lazily over the mouse. He scrolled down once. Slide five was a pie chart of neighborhood fence heights. He clicked his pen. Click, clack. Click, clack. His eyes dragged themselves toward the digital clock in the corner of his monitor: 2:14 PM. He scrolled to slide six. 2:14 PM. It hadn't even been a minute. Outside his window, a single dead leaf fell from the oak tree, hitting the ground with a soft scratch. Marcus sighed deeply, his breath fogging the edge of his coffee mug. He highlighted a paragraph about galvanized nails, deleted it, undid the deletion, and went back to staring at the pie chart.

"Hold the dumb end of the tape, would you?" Dave asked, tossing me the metal tab. I caught it limply and stood by the rosebushes while he walked backward, the yellow tape hissing as it unspooled. He shouted numbers back at me: "Thirty-four feet! Write that down!" I didn't have a pen. I didn't have paper. I just stood there, letting the tape measure droop into the mud. I looked up at the sky. Completely blue. Not a single bird. Dave kept rambling about needing a permit for anything over six feet. I began counting the thorns on the nearest rosebush. One, two, three, four... I lost track and didn't care enough to start over. I let out a loud, shuddering yawn that cracked my jaw, stretching my free arm high above my head. "You got that?" Dave yelled. "Yep," I echoed, my voice completely flat.

The drone of Arthur’s voice vibrated through the warm afternoon air as he held up a glossy catalog of wrought iron gates. Penelope sat on her garden stool, her chin propped heavily on both hands. Arthur pointed out the difference between spear-top and flat-top finials, his finger tracing the intricate metalwork on page forty-two. Penelope blinked slowly, her focus shifting from the catalog to the slow, agonizing crawl of a caterpillar making its way up a blade of grass near her boot. She watched it inch forward, pause, and inch again. “Or we could go with the gothic arches,” Arthur suggested, turning the page. “Mhm,” Penelope replied, her tone completely devoid of inflection. She picked up a small pebble and tossed it aimlessly into the dirt, watching the tiny puff of dust it create. She rested her face back in her palms, waiting for page forty-four.

"Look at this lattice," my neighbor, Tom, insisted, dragging me down aisle fourteen for the third time. The harsh fluorescent lights hummed above us. He stroked the white PVC crisscrosses like they were fine silk. "Privacy, but with airflow." I leaned my back against a towering stack of fertilizer bags, letting my arms hang limp at my sides. I traced the grout lines in the linoleum floor with the toe of my sneaker, following the grid until it disappeared under a shelf. "Yeah, airflow," I repeated. I pulled my phone from my pocket, checked the blank lock screen, and shoved it back in. Tom moved on to hinges, comparing the tensile strength of three nearly identical pieces of black metal. A heavy sigh escaped my lips as I tipped my head back against the fertilizer, watching a moth bounce repeatedly against one of the long, buzzing light bulbs.

Chloe sat cross-legged on her porch, her chin resting heavily on her fist, while her neighbor swiped through digital renderings of a privacy fence on his tablet. "See how the shadow falls at 3 PM?" he asked, zooming in on the pixelated grass. Chloe let out a long breath, her eyes glazed over. She watched a drop of condensation slowly slide down the side of her iced tea glass, tracing its path until it pooled on the coaster. "Mhm," she offered, her voice flat. He switched to a 3D fly-through mode, narrating the virtual tour with breathless enthusiasm. Chloe started silently counting the wooden slats on her porch ceiling. One, two, three, four... She tapped her fingers in a slow, monotonous rhythm on her knee. When he asked if she preferred the 'chestnut' or 'walnut' stain, she simply shrugged, staring vacantly at the empty street beyond him.

Linda brought over a binder of neighborhood covenant guidelines to show me exactly why our new shared fence had to be scalloped picket. She sat at my kitchen island, flipping through heavily tabbed pages. I rested my forehead directly on the cool granite countertop. "Section four, paragraph B," she recited, her voice a steady, unvarying monotone. I turned my head sideways so my cheek was squished against the stone, staring at a crumb of toast left over from breakfast. I slowly blew on the crumb, watching it roll an inch to the left. "And the paint must be an approved shade of eggshell," Linda continued. I blew on the crumb again. It rolled right. I let my eyelids fall shut. The ticking of the wall clock seemed to grow louder, each second stretching out into an eternity, echoing the endless rustle of Linda's turning pages.

Sitting on the tailgate of his truck, Mark stared blankly at the pile of fieldstones his neighbor had dumped on the property line. Gary was currently explaining the ancient art of dry stone walling, arranging two rocks with exaggerated care. "It's like a puzzle," Gary said, stepping back to admire his work. Mark offered a weak, half-hearted thumbs-up. He leaned back on his elbows, letting his legs swing lazily over the bumper. A fly landed on his jeans, and he didn't even bother to swat it away, just watched it rub its front legs together. Gary launched into a history of Scottish sheep enclosures. Mark yawned, a wide, jaw-cracking stretch that brought water to his eyes. He started picking a loose thread on his shirt cuff, unraveling it millimeter by millimeter, letting Gary's voice fade into background noise, indistinguishable from the distant hum of traffic.

I was halfway to my car when Brenda popped out from behind her bushes, clutching a thick stack of paint swatches. "Which one says 'welcoming but secure'?" she asked, fanning out thirty shades of beige. I slumped against my car door, my keys dangling loosely from my limp fingers. "That one," I pointed randomly. She shook her head. "No, that's 'Sand dune'. I'm thinking 'Desert Whisper'." I stared directly into the sun for a brief second just to feel something. I rubbed my eyes, letting out a long, slow exhale that fluttered my lips. Brenda began comparing the light reflectivity values of two nearly identical taupes. I started counting the dead bugs plastered to my car's windshield. Fifteen. Sixteen. I shifted my weight, staring vacantly over her shoulder at a plastic bag caught in the branches of a distant oak tree, fluttering weakly in the wind.

The dinner had dragged on for two hours, entirely dominated by Julian’s proposal for a soundproof acoustic barrier between their yards. Elias rested his chin in his palm, his fork aimlessly pushing a single, cold garden pea around the perimeter of his plate. Julian unrolled a schematic right over the placemats. “Notice the soundwave deflection angle here,” Julian noted, tapping a diagram. Elias let his eyes glaze over, the harsh lines of the schematic blurring into a gray smudge. He stared intently at the slow drip of wax sliding down the side of the centerpiece candle. Drip. Pause. Drip. “Does the sound abatement appeal to you?” Julian asked eagerly. Elias offered a slow, deliberate blink. “It’s fine,” he murmured in a flat voice. He slumped deeper into his dining chair, resting his head back against the wood, praying the candle would burn down and end the evening.

I had already counted the floral patterns on my wallpaper three times when the scratching started at the screen door. Forty-two blue roses, thirty-eight pink ones. I dragged myself off the sofa, my slippers shuffling against the linoleum. Outside, the scruffy terrier from next door was digging a hole in Mrs. Gable’s petunias again. I leaned against the doorframe, resting my heavy chin in my palm, watching the dirt fly. It was the fourth time this week he’d squeezed under the chain-link fence. Normally, I’d march over and complain, but today, I just pulled up a lawn chair. I watched the dog systematically destroy the flowerbed, occasionally tossing a pebble in his general direction just to see if he'd notice. He didn't. I let out a long breath, listening to the hum of a distant lawnmower, and started counting the remaining intact petunias.

Elias stared at the unblinking cursor on his blank computer screen until his vision blurred. The grandfather clock in the hall ticked with agonizing slowness. Tick. Tock. A sudden, sharp bark shattered the heavy silence of the farmhouse. Elias blinked, peeling his face away from his palm, and peered out the window. The neighbor’s golden retriever was bounding through the tall grass of his backyard, chasing a completely imaginary rabbit. Elias sighed, a long, deflating sound, and pushed his chair back. The wheels squeaked loudly. He trudged downstairs, grabbed a half-stale biscuit from the jar, and pushed the back door open. "Again, Buddy?" Elias mumbled, tossing the treat onto the porch. He sat on the wooden steps, elbows resting on his knees, and watched the dog chew with mechanical precision, grateful for the slight disruption in the endless expanse of the afternoon.

The television had been muted for an hour. I was flicking a rubber band against my wrist—snap, snap, snap—when a commotion in the narrow courtyard caught my eye. The latch on Mr. Henderson’s gate had failed again, and his overweight pug, Barnaby, was currently wedged between my recycling bins. I let my head loll back against the couch cushions, staring up at the water stain on the ceiling that looked vaguely like a map of Florida. Snap, snap. I suppose I should go help the poor beast. I slowly peeled myself away from the worn upholstery and meandered out the back door. Barnaby snorted, his curly tail wagging weakly. I didn't rush. I simply stood there, hands deep in my pockets, watching him struggle against the blue plastic bins for a solid five minutes before reaching down to unstick him.

Sarah was tracing the woodgrain of her pristine dining table with her index finger for the twentieth minute straight. The silence in the model-perfect house was thick and suffocating. A flash of white darted past the sliding glass door. She paused her tracing. The fluffy Samoyed from number 42 was back, happily trampling her carefully manicured lawn. Sarah leaned her forehead against the cool glass of the patio door, her breath fogging up the pane. She drew a little smiley face in the condensation, watched it drip, and then wiped it away with a slow, sluggish swipe of her sleeve. The dog barked at a squirrel. Sarah didn't flinch. She just continued to stare blankly at the creature, calculating exactly how many seconds it would take for Mrs. Higgins to come running down the street in her fuzzy pink bathrobe waving a leash.

I sat on the porch swing, pushing off with one toe every ten seconds just to keep the rusty chains squeaking. Squeak. Pause. Squeak. The sun beat down heavily, turning the air thick. A rustle in the azalea bushes made me slowly turn my head. Old man Miller’s basset hound dragged its belly across my lawn, its ears sweeping the dead grass. I exhaled a slow stream of air, puffing my cheeks out, and watched the slow-motion invasion. The dog finally collapsed under the shade of my oak tree, panting. "Right there with you, pal," I muttered to nobody. I picked up a twig from the porch floorboards and started peeling the bark off in tiny, methodical strips, letting the pieces flutter down onto my boots while the hound snored lazily in the heat. It was going to be a long Sunday.

Marcus flipped the glossy pages of a luxury watch catalog, not really looking at the price tags or the faces. He tossed the thick magazine onto the glass coffee table with a soft thud. Outside, a familiar yip echoed through the manicured hedges. The Yorkie belonging to the heiress next door had slipped through the wrought-iron fence. Marcus rested his chin in his hands, his eyes glazed over as the tiny dog ran in frantic circles around his stone fountain. He mentally counted the rotations. Fourteen, fifteen, sixteen. The afternoon stretched out before him, a vast desert of hours. He grabbed a handful of almonds from a crystal bowl, chewing them in a slow, rhythmic cadence, completely unresponsive to the dog's shrill yapping. Eventually, he picked up a throw pillow, placed it over his face, and let out a muffled, drawn-out groan.

The snow was falling in straight, unbroken lines outside the window. I had arranged my collection of colored pencils in rainbow order, then by length, and was currently considering sorting them by brand. A dark shape broke the white expanse of my backyard. It was the neighbor’s husky, Diablo, who had dug under the fence for the third day in a row. He was joyously plowing his face into the deep snowdrifts. I slouched deeper into my beanbag chair, letting a heavy sigh escape my lips. I didn't even reach for my coat. I just sat there, twirling a yellow pencil between my fingers, watching the dog ruin the pristine blanket of snow. Part of me knew I should call his owner, but dialing the phone felt like too much effort. I just kept spinning the pencil, watching the snow continue to fall.

Chloe was lying flat on the rug, staring up at the ceiling fan turning on its lowest setting. Whoosh. Whoosh. A scratching sound at the back patio door made her roll her head to the side. The scrappy mutt from next door was pawing at the glass, a muddy tennis ball in its mouth. Chloe didn't get up. She slowly dragged herself across the carpet, inch by inch, until her nose was nearly touching the glass. The dog dropped the ball and wagged its tail enthusiastically. Chloe stared back, her expression perfectly flat. She raised one hand and lazily tapped the glass twice with her fingernail. The dog barked. Chloe let her hand drop heavily back onto the floor, closing her eyes and listening to the rhythmic thump of the dog's tail against the siding, waiting for the sun to finally set.

I had already refreshed my email inbox six times in the last ten minutes. Nothing new. I spun my desk chair in a slow circle, dragging my feet on the carpet to control the speed. As I faced the sliding glass door, I noticed the Jack Russell terrier from apartment 1B was back on my patio, furiously attacking my potted fern. I stopped the chair’s rotation with a heavy thud of my heel. I rested my cheek against the cool wood of my desk, watching the dirt scatter across the concrete. I didn't feel angry. I didn't feel anything, really. I just observed the destruction like I was watching a documentary on mute. I reached out and started clicking my retractable pen. Click-clack, click-clack. I matched the rhythm of my pen to the dog's frantic digging, wondering how deep it would go.

Arthur sat in the faded armchair by the window, the television playing an infomercial about garden hoses at an almost imperceptible volume. He had been staring at the same crossword puzzle for an hour without filling in a single letter. A shadow darted across the sandy yard. The neighbor’s dalmatian had jumped the low seawall again and was currently investigating a washed-up crab pot. Arthur let out a long, wheezing breath that ruffled his mustache. He slowly set the newspaper down on his lap, making no move to stand. He leaned his head against the high back of the chair, his eyes half-closed. He watched the dog sniff the rusted metal, his fingers idly drumming a slow, even beat on the armrest. He wondered dimly if the tide was coming in or going out, but couldn't muster the energy to check the clock.

I was tossing a tennis ball against the living room wall and catching it. Thump, smack. Thump, smack. The sun was baking the dirt outside, creating wavy heat lines above the ground. Through the window, I saw the lanky greyhound from the ranch next door trotting casually through my cactus garden. Thump, smack. He had squeezed through the gap in the wire fence again. I let the ball bounce away and roll under the sofa. I walked to the window, my bare feet dragging on the Saltillo tiles. The dog stood perfectly still, panting in the sparse shade of a mesquite tree. I stood perfectly still, leaning my forehead against the hot glass, mirroring him. We just stared at each other for a long, drawn-out eternity, neither of us moving a muscle, trapped in the heavy, stagnant heat of the endless afternoon.

Maya was peeling the label off a water bottle, carefully pulling it so it wouldn't tear. The rain drummed a steady, unchanging rhythm against the roof. Through the rain-streaked window, she saw a miserable-looking beagle shivering under her patio table. It had slipped under the broken gate once more. Maya tore a tiny sliver of paper, let it flutter to the floor, and stared at it. She shifted her gaze back to the damp dog. She knew she should grab an umbrella and walk him back to the Smiths. Instead, she slumped forward, resting her forehead on the kitchen counter. She let out a long, fluttering sigh that ruffled a stray hair on her face. She closed her eyes, listening to the rain, the occasional whine from the yard, and the ticking of the oven clock, waiting for the day to just end already.

I was tracing the erratic path of a single raindrop down the kitchen window, wondering if it would overtake the drop below it before reaching the sill. The television buzzed playing a talk show I hadn’t processed for two hours. My chin rested heavily on my palm, my coffee long cold. The rhythm of the wall clock seemed slower today, stretching the afternoon out like chewed bubblegum. I dragged a fingernail along the grout line of the counter, retracing the same groove. Then, a massive crack shattered the quiet, followed by a tremor that rattled my mug. I didn't even jump. I slowly turned my head toward the glass. The Hendersons' ancient oak tree was now horizontal, resting comfortably across my driveway, its branches tangled in my shattered mailbox. I stared at the foliage. "Well," I muttered to the empty kitchen, "I suppose I should go outside."

Elias sat on the porch step, tossing a pebble into the air and catching it. Toss. Catch. Toss. Catch. He had counted exactly seventy-four tosses. The summer heat hung thick over the empty road. A beetle crawled across his boot, and Elias simply watched it, lacking the energy to shake his foot. He mentally mapped the grid of wire on the screen door for the third time since lunch. A deafening splintering sound suddenly echoed from the property line, followed by a heavy thud. Dust bloomed where Mr. Miller’s dying elm had stood, its massive trunk now resting atop Elias’s crushed wooden fence. Elias caught the pebble one last time, let out a slow exhale, and rested his chin in his hands. He watched the dust settle. Maybe he’d walk over and look at the wreckage in an hour or two.

I flipped the television channel. A blender infomercial. I flipped it again. A sitcom rerun. I let the remote drop onto the carpet, sinking deeper into the couch cushions until my neck rested at an awkward angle. Outside, the snow was falling in straight, uniform lines. I began counting the flakes passing the uppermost left pane of the window. One, two, three. My eyelids felt heavy, weighed down by the sheer silence of the house. I picked at a loose thread on my sweater, unraveling it inch by inch, watching it coil into a messy pile in my lap. A sharp, violent snap shook the floorboards. The towering pine from the duplex next door plummeted through the frozen air, smashing directly into my backyard shed. I stared at the collapsed roof and the scattered planks of wood. I slowly blinked, rubbed my eyes, and picked the television remote back up from the carpet.

Maya spun slowly in her desk chair, pushing off the desk with one toe. Round and round she went, tracing the swirls in the popcorn ceiling until she felt dizzy. She stopped, grabbed a pencil, and began shading in the letter 'O' on every piece of scrap paper within reach. The house was completely silent, save for the rhythmic squeak of the chair's rusty wheel. She let her head loll back, staring at the wall clock. It was only 2:15. A thunderous crash outside vibrated through her sneakers, rattling the windows in their frames. Maya lazily rolled her chair toward the glass. The neighbor’s prized weeping willow had uprooted, its sweeping green canopy now completely burying her family's patio furniture. Maya rested her forehead against the cool pane, exhaled a long breath that fogged the glass, and lazily drew a smiley face in the condensation with her index finger.

My cursor blinked on the blank spreadsheet. Blink. Blink. Blink. I scrolled up, then scrolled down, achieving absolutely nothing. I picked up a paperclip and meticulously unbent it until it was a straight piece of wire. Then, I bent it back into a triangle. My phone sat face down on the desk. I rested my cheek on the cool mahogany, listening to the hum of the refrigerator two rooms over. The sudden, violent sound of tearing wood made me sit up, though not with any particular haste. I ambled over to the sliding glass door. The sprawling magnolia tree from the adjacent yard had surrendered to gravity, its thick branches now resting squarely atop my patio. I surveyed the crushed chairs and the splintered trunk blocking my view. I tapped the glass twice, shoved my hands deep into my sweatpants pockets, and wandered slowly back toward my blinking computer cursor.

Arthur sat on the floral sofa, staring at the pattern of the Persian rug. He counted the red medallions woven into the fabric. There were twelve. He counted them again to be sure. Still twelve. He let out a heavy sigh, shifting his weight. The grandfather clock in the hallway chimed three times, echoing through the deeply quiet house. He picked up yesterday’s newspaper, glanced at the same headline he’d read twice already, and set it right back down. An earth-shattering boom suddenly vibrated through the floorboards, knocking a porcelain figurine off the mantel. Arthur slowly stood and shuffled toward the picture window. The massive silver maple from next door had collapsed, its jagged trunk taking down the power lines and completely crushing his birdbath. Arthur stared at the mess of leaves on his lawn for a moment. He rubbed the back of his neck, turned around, and sat back down to count the rug's medallions again.

I rocked back and forth in the hammock, dragging one foot on the porch deck to keep the momentum going. Squeak. Swing. Squeak. Swing. I stared at the clouds, trying to find shapes in them, but they just looked like formless gray blobs. A single fly buzzed around my ear, and I didn't even bother to swat it away. The ice in my lemonade had melted hours ago, leaving a watery, tepid mess in the glass beside me. Without warning, a loud cacophony of cracking timber erupted from the fence line. The neighbor’s towering pine tree descended in a violent arc, smashing through the trellis and burying my tomato garden under a mountain of sharp needles. Dust plumed into the muggy air. I stopped my rocking with a flat foot on the boards. I looked at the devastation, looked down at my watery lemonade, and resumed my slow swinging. Squeak. Swing.

Leo lay on his back, tossing a tennis ball at the ceiling. It hit with a dull thud, dropped back into his waiting hand, and went right back up. Thud. Catch. Thud. Catch. He memorized every water stain on the plaster. He rolled onto his stomach, resting his chin on his crossed arms, blowing a stray speck of dust across the hardwood floor until it hit the baseboard. The silence of his bedroom was heavy, pressing down on him. A tremendous crash shattered the quiet, violently shaking the walls. Leo pushed himself up and trudged over to the window, leaning his elbows on the sill. The Johnsons' giant sweetgum tree had snapped at the base, its massive crown now draped completely over Leo’s driveway, trapping his mother's sedan beneath a cage of thick branches. Leo stared at the flattened car, rested his chin back on his hands, and wondered what was for dinner.

I sat on an overturned bucket in the garage, dragging a stick through a puddle of spilled motor oil. I drew a circle, crossed it out, and drew another one. The radio in the corner murmured a soft, unrecognizable tune. I tapped my boots against the concrete, matching the sluggish tempo. I pulled my phone from my pocket, unlocked the screen, swiped through my apps three times, and locked it again. The day stretched before me, vast and completely empty. A sudden groan of tearing wood echoed from the side yard, ending with a booming crash that sent crows scattering into the gray sky. I stood up, stretching my stiff back, and ambled outside. The neighbor's dead birch had toppled directly across my lawn, snapping the clothesline in half. I kicked a stray branch that had landed near my toe, let out a long sigh, and walked back to my bucket.

Claire scrubbed a spot on the kitchen counter that was already perfectly clean. She dragged the sponge in tight, overlapping circles, her eyes glazed over, staring right through the granite. She wiped her hands on her apron, leaned against the sink, and watched a single drop of water gather at the faucet's edge. It swelled, hung suspended for an eternity, and finally dropped. Plink. She waited for the next one. Plink. A violent shudder ripped through the house, followed by an explosive shattering of wood. Claire slowly turned her head. Through the window, she saw the sprawling oak from the property next door had fallen. Its thick trunk was resting on her back deck, crushing the barbecue grill and splintering the wooden railing into jagged toothpicks. Claire stared at the ruined deck for a long minute, then slowly turned back to the faucet. She waited for the next drop. Plink.

I sat in the driver’s seat of my parked car, the engine off, the keys dangling from the ignition. I flipped the sun visor down. I flipped it up. Down. Up. I stared at the dusty dashboard, tracing my initials in the grime with a lazy finger. There was nowhere to be, nothing to do. I slumped lower in the seat, watching a plastic bag drift lazily across the empty street. The clock blinked 4:00 PM. A loud, sharp crack ripped through the quiet neighborhood, causing the car to physically bounce on its shocks. The massive sycamore from the yard next door collapsed, landing with a terrifying crunch mere inches from my front bumper. A thick shower of green leaves plastered my windshield. I sat completely still, staring at the rough bark entirely blocking my view. I slowly reached up, grabbed the sun visor, and flipped it down one more time.

Julian had read the same paragraph four times. He held the thick paperback open on his lap, but the words had turned into a meaningless soup of ink. He closed the book, setting it on the coffee table. He propped his chin on his fist, staring vacantly at the geometric patterns of the wallpaper. He traced the repeating diamonds with his eyes, left to right, top to bottom. The house was utterly silent, stifling and still. A deafening crash suddenly ripped through the afternoon, violently shaking the framed photos on the wall. Julian didn't flinch. He slowly blinked, pushed himself up from the armchair with a heavy groan, and walked to the window. The neighbor's gigantic weeping cherry tree was sprawled across Julian's front walk, its blossoming branches mangling his iron gate. Julian exhaled a steady breath, scratched his chin, and wandered back to his armchair to open his book again.

Rain drops raced down the glass, and I watched the left one win, then the right. I rested my chin on my palm, letting out a long, slow breath that fogged the pane. Behind me, the house was perfectly still, filled only with the hum of the refrigerator. I pushed away from the window and slouched toward the oak desk, opening the bottom drawer just to hear the wood scrape. My fingers thumbed past old tax returns and blank notepads, landing on a yellowed envelope. The handwriting was my own, addressed to my daughter on her eighteenth birthday, a milestone that had passed five years ago. I traced the unlicked seal, shifting my weight from one foot to the other, waiting for a spark of something to break the heavy afternoon quiet.

Arthur sat on a plastic crate in the attic, watching dust motes drift through a single beam of sunlight. He tapped his knuckles against his knees—one, two, three, four—then sighed, letting his shoulders slump forward. The weekend stretched out before him, an endless expanse of ticking clocks and empty rooms. He dragged a cardboard box closer, lacking the energy to actually lift it, and peeled back the brittle tape. Inside, beneath a pile of frayed sweaters, lay a crisp white envelope. It was addressed to his son, dated the day the boy left for basic training. Arthur stared at his own jagged penmanship. He picked at a loose thread on his jeans, the unmailed words sitting heavy in his hand, though the silence in the attic remained exactly the same.

The cursor blinked on my monitor. Blink. Blink. Blink. I rolled my pen across the desk, caught it, and rolled it back. The spreadsheet had not changed in twenty minutes. I spun my chair in a slow half-circle, staring at the beige wall of my home office, trying to count the tiny bumps in the plaster. Deciding to organize my pen cup for the third time today, I pulled open the top drawer. Sandwiched between a dried-out marker and a stack of sticky notes was a folded piece of stationery. I smoothed it out, recognizing the letter I had written to my oldest boy when he first started walking. I read the first line, then let the paper drop onto the keyboard, leaning my head back to watch the ceiling fan spin in endless, repetitive circles.

Clara let her cheek rest against the cool mahogany of the dining table. She traced the wood grain with her index finger, following the same swirling pattern over and over. The television murmured in the other room, a meaningless drone of daytime commercials. Pushing herself up with a heavy exhale, she wandered into the hallway, opening the antique credenza for no particular reason. She shuffled a deck of playing cards, then tossed them aside, her gaze landing on a pale blue envelope tucked into the corner. It was the apology she had written to her daughter three winters ago, the one that never made it to the mailbox. Clara flipped the envelope over, running her thumb along the edge, then placed it back in the drawer, closing it with a soft click before wandering toward the kitchen.

I sat on the porch, peeling the label off a damp water bottle in tiny, erratic strips. The neighbor’s dog barked, a rhythmic, predictable sound that did nothing to break the heavy weight of the Sunday afternoon. I kicked a pebble off the steps, watching it roll into the grass. Needing something, anything, to occupy my hands, I pulled the battered cigar box from under my chair. It was supposed to hold fishing gear, but instead, my fingers brushed against a folded piece of notebook paper. I recognized the messy scrawl instantly—the letter I wrote to my kids the night I moved out. I unfolded it, the creases deep and worn. The dog kept barking. I folded it back up, matching the corners perfectly, and started peeling the rest of the label off my bottle.

Marcus sat in the garage, listening to the rhythmic dripping of the leaky faucet. Drip. Drip. Drip. He spun a socket wrench on the workbench, watching it rotate until it wobbled to a halt, then spun it again. The lawnmower was already fixed, the tools were already cleaned, and the afternoon stretched ahead like a vast, empty highway. He pulled open the bottom drawer of his toolbox, idly shifting a pile of rags. Beneath them lay a sealed letter, smeared with an old thumbprint of motor oil. It was addressed to his youngest son, written the night before the boy’s wedding. Marcus picked it up, staring at the unopened flap. He tapped the envelope against the workbench to the exact tempo of the dripping sink, waiting for the hours to pass.

The washing machine thumped against the laundry room wall in a slow, uneven beat. I sat on the linoleum floor with my knees pulled up, rolling a stray button between my thumb and forefinger. I checked my watch; only four minutes had passed since I last looked. Letting my head fall back against the dryer, I pulled open the small utility drawer beside me, sifting through loose batteries and expired coupons. Buried at the back was a thick envelope. It was the letter I wrote to my daughter when she left for college, full of advice I never quite had the courage to mail. I stared at the faded ink, then tossed the letter onto the pile of clean towels, going back to rolling the plastic button as the washing machine continued its endless thumping.

Evelyn rested her chin in her hands, blowing a stray lock of hair out of her eyes. It fluttered, then fell right back across her forehead. She let out a long, breathy sigh. The clock on the mantel ticked loudly in the silent living room. She reached out and began rearranging the decorative coasters on the coffee table, lining them up by their edges. Seeking a distraction, she opened the drawer of the end table, her fingers brushing against a stiff, cream-colored envelope. She recognized the thick cardstock immediately. It was the letter she had written to her newborn son, sealed but never given. She ran her fingernail over the embossed return address, listening to the tiny scratching sound it made, then stared blankly out the window at the motionless trees.

I must have clicked my tongue against the roof of my mouth fifty times. It was a stupid habit, but there was absolutely nothing else happening in the house. I dragged my feet across the carpet, the static charge building with every heavy step, and slumped into the armchair. Beside me, a stack of old books begged to be sorted. I grabbed the top one, flipping the pages just to hear the flutter, when a folded piece of paper slipped out and drifted to the floor. I reached down and picked it up. It was the letter I had written to my teenage son after our biggest fight, the one I had hidden away. I read my own desperate handwriting, then folded it back into squares, tossing it onto the table and listening to the clock tick.

Julian sat at the kitchen island, tracing the grout lines between the tiles with a toothpick. He had already read the back of the cereal box three times, memorizing the nutritional facts down to the exact milligram of sodium. The house was utterly quiet, save for the distant hum of the central heating. He slid off the stool, dragging his slippered feet toward the junk drawer. He pulled it open, aimlessly shifting a tangle of charging cables and dried-out pens. Beneath a pile of rubber bands was a sealed letter, written years ago to his teenage daughter, an apology he could not quite vocalize. Julian stared at the unfamiliar stamp on the corner. He sighed, letting the drawer slide shut with a dull thud, and returned to the island to find a new tile to trace.

The conference call droned on, a muffled voice talking about synergy and deliverables. I had been on mute for an hour. I drew a chain of interlocking circles on my notepad, shading every other one with heavy, dark strokes. When the page was full, I tossed the pen down and opened my desk’s bottom file drawer. I thumbed through hanging folders, not looking for anything, just letting the tabs flick against my thumb. Tucked in the back was a pale pink envelope. It was the letter I wrote to my little girl before her first day of kindergarten, full of worries I did not want to pass on. I traced the cursive letters of her name, then rested my chin on my fist, staring at the computer screen as the tiny volume bars bounced up and down.

Sarah lay on her back on the living room rug, counting the popcorn bumps on the ceiling. She got to one hundred and twelve before losing her place and letting out a heavy puff of air. She rolled onto her side, her eyes drifting toward the bookshelf. Without getting up, she reached out and pulled out a worn photo album, letting it fall open on the floor. A loose piece of paper slipped from between the pages. It was the letter she had written to her son when he first moved away, the one filled with all the things she had been too proud to say. She looked at the smudged ink, then looked back up at the ceiling, wondering if she should start counting the bumps from the other side of the room.

I rested my chin heavily on my palm, watching dust motes dance in the shaft of afternoon sunlight cutting through the empty bookstore. The clock above the register ticked in a slow, agonizing rhythm that felt like drops of water on my skull. I had already rearranged the display table three times and alphabetized the clearance bin. Desperate for any stimulation, I picked up my phone and drafted a text to my roommate: *Save me. Bring tacos and stage a fake emergency.* I hit send, my thumb dragging lazily across the screen, before looking up to see my boss, Mr. Henderson, walking out of the back room. His phone buzzed loudly in his shirt pocket. He pulled it out, adjusted his reading glasses, and frowned at the screen. I froze as he looked up, peering over the spectacles directly at me, taco request delivered entirely to the wrong supervisor.

Professor Higgins had been droning on about eighteenth-century agricultural trade for what felt like three lifetimes. Maya traced the same geometric pattern into the margins of her notebook until the paper wore thin, her eyelids drooping with the heavy weight of the unventilated lecture hall. She let out a long, quiet exhale, sinking lower into her molded plastic chair. To break the agonizing stillness, she slipped her phone under her desk and typed, *If he says 'crop rotation' one more time, I'm going to climb out the window.* She blindly selected a contact and pressed send, her eyes glazing over as Higgins clicked to the sixty-fourth slide of his presentation. A sharp ping echoed across the aisle. Maya’s head turned slowly to see her extremely strict grandmother, who had insisted on auditing the class today, staring down at the glowing screen of her iPhone with a highly unamused expression.

The waiting room featured a beige wall, beige chairs, and beige carpet. I counted the ceiling tiles—forty-eight full squares, twelve partials—while a daytime soap opera played on mute from a corner television. My foot tapped a hollow rhythm against the leg of the chair. I picked up a magazine from two years ago, flipped through a pictorial about decorative gourds, and tossed it back onto the stack. Needing an escape from the sterile vacuum, I composed a message to my girlfriend: *This place is stealing my will to live. I might chew my own arm off.* I hit send, let my head loll back against the wall, and waited for her laughing emoji. Across the room, the stern receptionist’s desktop chimed. She clicked her mouse, her posture stiffening. 'Mr. Davis?' she called out, her voice frosty. 'The doctor will see you now. And please leave your arms intact.'

Uncle Arthur was recounting the detailed maintenance history of his riding lawnmower for the third consecutive Thanksgiving. David stared at his half-eaten mashed potatoes, using his fork to build a small, lumpy fortress. He sighed, shifting his weight from his left hip to his right, desperately wishing the dining room clock would fast-forward to dessert. Underneath the tablecloth, he navigated his phone screen by memory. *Please call me and pretend the apartment is flooding,* he typed to his best friend, hitting send without looking. He rested his cheek in his palm, eyes unfocused on a gravy stain. Suddenly, his Aunt Martha’s purse vibrated on the chair beside him. She fished out her phone, adjusted her bifocals, and cleared her throat loudly, cutting off Arthur’s monologue about spark plugs. 'Well,' Martha announced, staring pointedly at David.
