'It seems David's apartment is experiencing a sudden, tragic plumbing failure.'

Four hours down, three to go. I slouched against my suitcase at Gate B14, watching a cleaning cart slowly polish the terrazzo floor. Back and forth. Back and forth. I’d already visited the newsstand twice, memorized the overpriced menu at the nearest kiosk, and watched planes taxi on the tarmac until they all blurred together into a gray smear. Desperately craving human interaction, I typed out a message to my sister: *I am wasting my youth in Terminal B. Send memes or rescue me.* I sent it, staring blankly at the 'Message Delivered' status. A second later, a businessman in a tailored suit sitting two seats away let out a startled cough. He looked at his phone, then slowly turned his head to look at me. 'I don't have any memes,' he said, adjusting his tie, 'but I do have a crossword puzzle if it helps.'

The digital clock in the corner of Liam's screen flipped to 3:42 PM. The marketing director had been sharing his screen for forty-five minutes, hovering his cursor over the same pie chart while discussing synergy. Liam rested his forehead against his desk, listening to the muffled drone through his headset. He rolled a solitary pen back and forth across his mousepad, watching it hit the keyboard and roll back. He pulled up a chat window, meaning to message his coworker, Sarah. *If Steve says 'leverage' again, I am going to throw my router out the window,* he typed, hitting enter with a heavy sigh. Instantly, a notification popped up in the main, company-wide presentation channel. The droning voice over the headset abruptly stopped. The pie chart vanished, replaced by the marketing director's rigid face taking up the entire screen. 'Well, Liam,' Steve said. 'Let's not break company hardware.'

The sea of red taillights stretched infinitely down the highway. I rested my forehead against the steering wheel, the engine idling in a low, continuous hum. The radio played a block of commercials for local car dealerships that I mouthed the words to without thinking. I picked at a loose thread on the steering wheel cover, then picked up my phone from the cup holder. *I will literally pay you fifty bucks to airlift me out of this metal prison,* I typed to my brother, hoping for a witty reply to break the standstill. I tossed the phone onto the passenger seat and stared out at the unmoving asphalt. My phone rang immediately. It wasn't my brother. It was the CEO of my startup, whom I was supposed to be meeting in twenty minutes. 'I don't have a helicopter,' his voice crackled through the Bluetooth, 'but I appreciate the offer.'

The security monitors glowed with static views of empty parking lots, empty hallways, and empty elevators. Marcus spun slowly in his squeaky swivel chair, doing a full 360-degree rotation before stopping to stare at a moth fluttering against the fluorescent ceiling light. He tapped his boots against the base of the desk, humming a tuneless melody to fill the heavy silence of the warehouse. He grabbed his phone and texted his wife: *I've reached the end of the internet. Nothing left to see. Bring coffee when you wake up.* He sent it off into the ether, letting his arms dangle limply at his sides. A notification chimed from the walkie-talkie clipped to his belt. It was the stern night-shift supervisor, stationed three buildings over. 'Marcus,' the radio crackled, the supervisor's voice echoing loudly in the quiet room. 'I'm not your wife, and I don't deliver coffee.'

Rain drummed a steady, hypnotic beat against the windshield while my mom shopped for groceries. I traced the condensation trickling down the glass, wiping it away only to watch it fog up again. The radio was playing soft jazz, making my eyelids feel like they were made of lead. I slouched low in the passenger seat, kicking the floor mat with my heel. Needing a lifeline to the outside world, I texted my friend Leo: *Please save me from this minivan. I am aging in reverse.* I hit send and watched a stray grocery cart slowly roll across the wet pavement. A sudden buzz from the driver’s seat made me jump. My mom had left her purse. I peered over the console, horrified to see her screen light up with my message. I sank even lower into the seat, preparing for a very long ride home.

Chloe stared at the large municipal clock on the courthouse wall. The second hand ticked with a loud, mechanical snap. She had finished her paperback novel an hour ago, and had spent the last thirty minutes counting the number of scuff marks on the linoleum floor. She let out a prolonged breath, resting her cheek against the cold cinderblock wall. Desperate for a distraction from the utter lack of events, she typed a quick text to her roommate: *I would gladly confess to the crime myself if it meant I could leave this room.* She pressed send without checking the recipient. Moments later, the heavy wooden door opened and the stern-faced bailiff stepped into the holding area. He pulled his buzzing phone from his uniform pocket, read the screen, and locked eyes with Chloe. 'Ma'am,' he said slowly, 'that's a highly unusual way to enter a plea.'

He was currently explaining the nuanced differences between six types of artisanal brewing hops. I gave a tight, practiced smile, nodding as he held up his glass to the candlelight. My fingers drummed an invisible rhythm against my thigh under the table. I stared at the melting wax cascading down the candle, calculating how long it would take to reach the tablecloth. I sneakily maneuvered my phone under my napkin, typing a distress signal to my best friend: *Fake an emergency. Call me. If I hear the word 'fermentation' again I will dissolve into dust.* I hit send and immediately took a long sip of water to hide my face. A phone vibrated on the table. My date paused his lecture, looking down at his screen. The color drained from his face as he read the notification, his eyes slowly rising to meet mine across the table.

The contemporary art exhibit had seen exactly zero visitors since Tuesday. Elias leaned his elbows on the glass display case, staring blankly at a sculpture made entirely of recycled coat hangers. He slowly blew a bubble with his gum until it popped loudly in the echoing gallery. He shifted his weight, feeling the heavy, suffocating stillness of the room press against his shoulders. He pulled out his phone and texted his fellow gallery attendant: *If I have to look at this wire trash for one more minute, I'm going to set off the fire alarm.* He sent the message, sliding the phone back into his pocket. At the end of the hall, the esteemed and highly temperamental artist who had sculpted the piece pulled her phone from her designer handbag. She gasped, her heels clicking furiously against the hardwood floor as she marched directly toward his display.

Walking to my old childhood home, I look at the front yard. The oak sapling I planted in the fourth grade is just a flat stump now, dusting the grass with pale sawdust. I kick a stray piece of bark, watching it skid onto the pavement. "Huh," I mutter, shoving my hands deep into my pockets. I pull out my phone, swiping past three screens of apps without opening a single one, noticing I only have two bars of service. The afternoon sun is warm, and the cicadas are buzzing in a slow, droning rhythm that makes my eyelids heavy. I guess I'm supposed to feel something profound about the missing branches, but all I can think about is the forty-minute train ride back to the city and whether the corner store will still be open when I get back.

Clara rested her chin on her palm, staring out the passenger window as the car idled at the curb. Her parents had insisted on this detour to see the old neighborhood. "Look, Clara! Your little maple," her father pointed. Or rather, he pointed at a jagged stump surrounded by dirt. Clara let out a long, slow exhale that fogged the glass. She traced a circle in the condensation with her index finger, watching a drop of water race downward. "Yeah. Neat," she said, her voice entirely flat. She checked her watch. It was 2:15 PM. Five more hours until dinner. She leaned her head against the headrest, closing her eyes and counting the rhythmic ticking of the turn signal. Tick. Tick. Tick.

The stump of my third-grade pine tree was sitting right where I left it twenty years ago, just much shorter. I chewed on a thumbnail, staring at the concentric rings in the wood. One, two, three. I lost count around fifteen and gave up, dropping my hand to my side. The new homeowners had paved over most of the grass, turning the yard into a gray slab. I scuffed my sneaker against the concrete. A plastic bag drifted by on a slight breeze, scraping loudly against the asphalt. I watched it until it caught on a chain-link fence. Pulling a piece of white lint from my dark sweater, I wondered if there was anything good on television this afternoon, or if it would just be reruns again.

Julian dragged his feet across the damp grass of his childhood park, stopping before the fresh stump of the willow he had grown from a cutting. He stood there for a long moment, swaying slightly from heel to toe. He let out a loud, drawn-out sigh, crossing his arms and looking up at the gray, featureless sky. A crow cawed somewhere in the distance. Julian pulled his phone from his pocket, stared at the lock screen for a moment, and shoved it back into his jacket. He nudged a woodchip with the toe of his boot. The park looked exactly the same as it had an hour ago. He checked his battery percentage again. Forty-two. He turned around and started the slow walk home.

They chopped down the elm I planted when I was ten. I stood in the driveway, looking at the empty space by the mailbox where it used to be. My mom was talking on the porch, her voice a low murmur blending with the distant hum of traffic. I picked up a twig from the pavement, snapped it in half, and dropped the pieces. I shifted my weight to my left leg, then to my right. There was a crack in the driveway shaped vaguely like a shoe. I stared at it, tracing the outline with my eyes over and over. "Are we leaving soon?" I called out, interrupting whatever she was saying. My stomach gave a slight rumble. I really just wanted a sandwich.

Maya sat on the edge of the freshly sawed stump, the remains of the cherry tree she’d planted with her grandfather. She picked at a loose thread on the hem of her jeans, unraveling it inch by inch until it snapped. She tossed the scrap of cotton into the wind. Resting her elbows on her knees, she cupped her cheeks in her hands and blew a stray piece of hair out of her eyes. It fluttered, then fell right back. She let out a groaning exhale. Her gaze drifted from the stump to a line of ants marching across the dirt. She watched them carry a breadcrumb for a solid ten minutes, entirely untroubled by the absence of the shade she used to sit under.

Standing in the courtyard of my old middle school, I found the memorial garden mostly paved over. The silver birch I had proudly lowered into the soil was gone, leaving only a patch of disturbed mulch. I crossed my arms and rocked back on my heels. A squirrel ran along the brick wall, stopped, twitched its tail, and disappeared. I let out a loud yawn, stretching my arms high above my head until my shoulders popped. "Well, that's that," I murmured to the empty courtyard. I started walking back to the parking lot, taking care to step only in the center of the concrete squares. Step. Step. Step. I really hoped the traffic on the interstate wouldn't be heavy today.

Elias stared at the massive gap in the forest canopy. The redwood sapling he had tagged and nurtured during summer camp was now just a flat, wide table of wood. He sat down right in the middle of it. The woods were quiet, save for the rustle of dry leaves. He pulled a small notebook from his pocket and began to doodle in the margins, drawing mostly cubes and interlocking triangles. After filling a whole page with geometric shapes, he closed the book and stared at the opposite tree line. His eyelids felt impossibly heavy. He laid back against the rough surface of the stump, staring up at the clouds drifting lazily across the blue expanse, wondering how long he had to wait for the bus.

The new owners of our old farm had cleared the entire front pasture, including the apple tree I grew from a seed. I stood by the wire fence, leaning my chin against the metal rail. I tapped my fingers in a repetitive rhythm against the cold steel. One-two-three-four. One-two-three-four. A cow mooed somewhere over the hill. I pulled a long blade of grass, stuck it between my teeth, and chewed on the bitter end. The sun beat down, making the asphalt behind me radiate waves of heat. I scrolled through my messages, saw nothing new, and shoved the phone back into my pocket. Dragging a stick along the fence, I started the long, uneventful trudge back down the dirt road.

The community center had expanded its parking lot right over the spot where Leo had planted a sycamore fifteen years ago. He stood in space number forty-two, staring down at the yellow painted lines that crossed right over the remaining stump. He let his shoulders slump, his hands hanging loosely by his sides. He kicked a small pebble, watching it skitter across the blacktop until it hit the tire of a parked sedan. He let out a long breath through his nose, his gaze wandering to the flickering neon sign of a nearby diner. The 'N' was burnt out. 'Dier', he read in his head. He shoved his hands into his jacket pockets and began counting his steps to the diner entrance.

I pushed the gate open, hearing its familiar squeak. The backyard was completely transformed, and my little dogwood was nothing but a stump flush with the earth. I stood over it, resting my weight on one hip. A fly buzzed past my ear, and I swatted at it lazily. I looked at the stump, then up at the neighbor’s roof, where a weather vane was spinning slowly in the wind. North. East. North again. I checked my reflection in the dark glass of the patio door, fixing a strand of hair that had blown out of place. Letting out a slow, noisy sigh, I stared at the blank wooden fence, wondering if I had remembered to start the dishwasher before I left the apartment this morning.

Marcus stood in the overgrown field, staring at the fresh cut where his oak tree used to stand. The scent of raw wood lingered in the air. He leaned against the handle of his walking stick, his eyes half-closed against the afternoon glare. He reached into his pocket, pulled out a handful of loose change, and began flipping a quarter. Heads. Tails. Heads. Heads. He caught the coin, slipped it back into his pocket, and stared blankly at the horizon. A distant tractor hummed a monotonous tune. Marcus shifted his weight, letting his jaw hang slightly slack. He stared at the rings of the stump, letting his vision blur out of focus until the wood looked like nothing more than a gray smudge.

I rested my chin heavily on the tiny, plastic desk, tracing a shallow groove in the wood with my thumbnail. The open house had started twenty minutes ago, but the hands on the wall clock seemed glued in place. The teacher stood at the front, her nasal voice an unbroken hum that blended perfectly with the buzzing fluorescent lights overhead. When she turned to write her name on the chalkboard—Mrs. Gable—I barely blinked. Thirty years ago, she had stood in that exact spot, wearing what might have been the exact same floral cardigan, writing the exact same name in the exact same cursive loops. "So, as you can see, our schedule is quite structured," she said, tapping the board. I let out a long, slow breath, shifting my weight on the undersized chair, watching a speck of dust drift lazily through a sunbeam.

Marcus propped his head up with one hand, idly swirling a spoon through his lukewarm oatmeal. His other hand held Leo’s kindergarten class assignment letter. He read the name "Mr. Henderson" at the top and let out a flat, heavy exhale. He remembered Mr. Henderson’s pacing from 1994, the way the man would take ten minutes to explain a single, simple instruction. Marcus rested his forehead against his knuckles, staring blankly at the wall calendar. He counted the little squares until the end of the school year. One hundred and eighty days. He took a slow, mechanical bite of his oatmeal, chewing with a rhythmic, unenthusiastic motion. "Looks like you have Mr. Henderson," he muttered to the kitchen wall, not really looking at his son. He picked up his phone, stared at the black lock screen for a moment, and put it back down.

The drop-off line crawled forward an inch at a time. I drummed my fingers against the steering wheel in a steady, monotonous rhythm: tap, tap, tap, pause. My daughter chatted excitedly in the backseat about her first day of second grade, but her words washed over me like the hum of an air conditioner. As we finally pulled up to the front, the car door opened. "Welcome back!" a voice croaked. I turned my head lazily. It was Mrs. Albright, looking identical to the day she taught me in 1998, down to the heavy glasses chain. "Have a good day," I murmured, my voice perfectly flat. I watched my daughter hop out, my jaw slack. I shifted the car back into drive, staring down the endlessly long stretch of suburban road ahead, wondering if I should just sit in the parking lot and stare at the dashboard.

Elena scrolled down the elementary school faculty page, her chin resting firmly in her palm. Her eyes glazed over the endless rows of smiling headshots, clicking the mouse wheel with a rhythmic, mechanical flick of her index finger. When she landed on 'Mr. Vance - 4th Grade', the scrolling stopped, though her expression didn't change. It was her old teacher. He still had the exact same graying mustache. Elena blinked slowly, letting out a long puff of air that fluttered her bangs. She slumped further back into her ergonomic office chair, the springs creaking in the quiet room. She minimized the browser window, stared at her blank desktop wallpaper for a full minute, and then opened the calculator app. She began idly typing random strings of numbers, dividing them by seven, watching the decimals stretch infinitely across the little digital screen.

I stared intently at the acoustic tiles on the ceiling, trying to find shapes in the random pores. There was one that looked a bit like a shoe. Across the tiny table, Mr. Harrison was explaining his grading rubric for my son's math class. It was the same rubric he had used when I was in his seat twenty-two years ago. "Participation is twenty percent," he stated, his voice maintaining a perfectly flat pitch. I tapped the side of my pen against my knee, counting the seconds between his blinks. Five. Seven. Six. "Are there any questions about the homework policy?" he asked. I stifled a yawn, pressing my lips tightly together, and slowly shook my head. "No," I said, my voice barely above a whisper. I looked back up at the ceiling tile. The shoe shape was actually more of an anvil.

David dragged his feet as he pushed the shopping cart down the school supply aisle, the wheels squeaking in an endless, unchanging loop. His daughter, Lily, tossed a pack of highlighters into the basket. "Ms. Higgins says we need the yellow ones," she chirped. David’s eyes slowly drifted toward her. "Ms. Higgins?" he repeated, his tone devoid of any inflection. "The one with the big bird earrings?" Lily nodded happily. David let his eyelids droop, resting his elbows on the handle of the shopping cart. He remembered Ms. Higgins. He remembered the infinite stacks of identical worksheets. He pushed the cart forward another two feet, stopping in front of the loose-leaf paper. He stared at the blank white rectangles, listening to the hum of the supermarket refrigerators. "Great," he murmured to no one in particular, slowly shifting his weight to his left leg.

I sat on the living room rug, resting my head back against the sofa cushions. Timmy shoved his spelling worksheet in my face. "Look, dad! Mrs. Glick put a star on it!" I slowly peeled my eyes away from the muted television. A silver star sticker sat neatly at the top of the page. It was the exact same brand of foil star Mrs. Glick had used on my spelling tests three decades ago. "Nice," I said, drawing the word out as I stared blankly at the paper. I handed it back to him and let my arm drop heavily back down to my side. The clock on the mantle ticked loud enough to echo in my ears. Tick. Tick. Tick. I picked up a stray piece of lint from the carpet, rolled it into a tiny ball between my thumb and forefinger, and flicked it away.

Sarah sat in the very back row of the auditorium, her posture completely collapsed against the stiff wooden seat. She was endlessly twisting the program into a tight paper tube, then unrolling it, over and over. The curtains parted, and Mr. Phillips stepped up to the microphone to introduce the kindergarten tree-themed play. It was her old drama teacher. He cleared his throat and began the exact same speech he used to give before every spring showcase. Sarah let out a long, heavy sigh that ruffled the collar of her shirt. She rested her temple against the cool cinderblock wall next to her seat. Her eyes drifted away from the stage, following a crack in the paint that traveled all the way up to the lighting rig. She started counting the unlit bulbs, her face completely slack in the dim auditorium light.

The envelope sat on the kitchen counter for hours before I finally dragged myself over to open it. I slid my finger under the flap, pulling out my son’s mid-term report. The signature at the bottom read 'Cynthia Barnes.' My old English teacher. I stared at the looping cursive 'C' for a moment. My shoulders slumped. I leaned my hip heavily against the counter, tracing the granite veins with a slow, aimless finger. I remembered her reading aloud in a voice that lacked any melody or rhythm. I tossed the paper onto the island, where it slid and hit the fruit bowl. Pulling out one of the barstools, I sat down, propped my chin in both hands, and watched a single fruit fly do lazy, endless loops around the brown spots on a bruised banana.

Greg was mindlessly pushing his grocery cart through the produce section, staring blankly at a pile of russet potatoes. "Greg? Greg Miller?" a voice called out. He slowly turned his head. It was his old middle school science teacher, Mr. Vance, holding a plastic bag of carrots. "I have your boy, Tommy, in my homeroom this year!" Mr. Vance said cheerfully. Greg blinked slowly, his face completely motionless. "Oh. Yeah," Greg said, his voice flat. He leaned his weight onto the cart handle, letting his eyes drift from Mr. Vance's face down to the bag of carrots. "He's a good kid," Mr. Vance continued. Greg let out a slow, steady exhale through his nose. "Mmhmm," he replied. He picked up a potato, stared at its dirt-speckled surface for a few seconds, and gently placed it back on the pile, waiting for the conversation to end.

I sat in the folding chair, my legs stretched out straight in front of me, arms crossed loosely over my chest. The middle school band was tuning their instruments, a chaotic blend of squeaks and honks. At the podium stood Mr. Davis, baton in hand, looking exactly as he did when I played clarinet in this very gym. He tapped the stand three times. I let my head loll back against the bleachers behind me, staring up at the gymnasium rafters. I tried to see how long I could hold my breath before the music actually started. The off-key rendition of a basic scale finally began. I exhaled a long stream of air, letting my eyes slide half-shut. I began tapping my foot, entirely out of sync with the music, just to give my leg muscles something to do.

Julia sat near the back of the classroom during parent orientation, mechanically clicking her pen open and closed. Click-clack. Click-clack. At the front of the room, Mrs. Higgins was explaining the bathroom pass system. Julia recognized the laminated wooden block from her own childhood. She stopped clicking the pen and started drawing endless, overlapping circles in the margins of the informational handout. She drew them until the blue ink completely saturated the paper, nearly tearing through. Mrs. Higgins kept talking, her voice a steady, unchanging drone. Julia rested her cheek flat against the cool laminate of the desk. She stared sideways at a piece of discarded chewing gum stuck under the desk next to hers, silently tracking the slow, agonizing crawl of the second hand on the wall clock until it finally reached the twelve.

Elias stared at the blinking cursor on his spreadsheet for what felt like hours, tracing the beige cubicle wall with a paperclip. When the automated HR email arrived announcing Mr. Henderson’s immediate retirement, Elias just rested his chin on his palm. His mentor of five years was gone, leaving no note, no parting wisdom. Elias picked up a red pen, clicking it open and shut, open and shut, watching a solitary dust mote drift across the harsh fluorescent lighting. The office was too quiet, the hum of the air conditioner droning on in a relentless, flat pitch. He slowly dragged his mouse to close the email, leaning back in his chair until the springs groaned. Tomorrow would be exactly the same as today, just without the Tuesday coffee run. He let his head roll sideways against the fabric partition, listening to the clock tick.

I rested my chin heavily on the stainless steel prep table, mindlessly peeling my fiftieth potato. The rhythmic scrape of the peeler was the only sound in the prep kitchen until Marco walked in and casually mentioned that Master Chef Julian had cleared out his locker last night and moved to Florida. My hands didn't even pause. Julian, the man who taught me everything, just vanished. I watched a long ribbon of potato skin spiral into the trash can, feeling a heavy slowness settle behind my eyes. I sighed, letting my shoulders slump forward, dragging the blade across another tuber in slow motion. Without Julian's sudden, fiery inspections, the kitchen was just a sterile room of metal and root vegetables. I flicked a potato eye across the counter, staring at the blank white wall, wishing the hands on the clock would move a little faster.

Grease coated Maya’s fingertips as she spun a wrench around a bolt, over and over, feeling the mechanical clicks vibrate up her arm. The shop radio crackled with static, playing the same pop song for the fourth time today. When the shop owner casually pinned a memo to the board stating Old Man Rick had hung up his overalls for good without a final word to anyone, Maya simply exhaled a long, noisy breath. Her mentor was gone. She wiped her hands on a rag, tossing it onto a pile of identical dirty rags. She sat on an overturned bucket, elbows resting on her knees, staring blankly at the oil stains on the concrete floor. The garage felt completely stripped of energy. Maya picked up a stray lug nut, rolling it back and forth between her palms, listening to the rhythmic tap of a leaky faucet.

I traced invisible circles on the parchment with my wand, watching the ink dry at a painfully slow pace. Professor Alaric’s chambers were completely empty when I arrived for my advanced runes lesson. A simple note on the door stated he had permanently retired to the coastal provinces. Not a single goodbye. I slumped down onto the stone floor of the corridor, stretching my legs out and resting the back of my head against the cold masonry. I began counting the cobblestones on the opposite wall, losing track around forty-two and starting over. The academy tower was dead silent, save for the whistling wind. Without Alaric’s erratic, unpredictable pop quizzes, the afternoon stretched ahead of me like an endless, grey wasteland. I let out a heavy sigh, letting my wand roll away across the floor, watching its slow, clattering journey until it hit the far baseboard.

The neon sign outside buzzed in a low, continuous drone that made Arthur’s eyelids droop. He was balancing a pencil on his index finger when he noticed the empty desk across the room. The drawers were pulled out, hollowed of their contents, with a note from the landlord confirming Detective Vance had terminated the lease and left the city. No parting handshake from the man who taught him the ropes. Arthur let the pencil drop onto his blotter with a hollow thud. He leaned all the way back, placing his hands behind his head and staring at the yellowed ceiling tiles. One, two, three water stains. He drummed his heels against the side of his desk, the rhythmic thumping doing nothing to wake up his heavy limbs. The city outside moved at a crawl, and Arthur just closed his eyes, waiting for the day to end.

I watched the centrifuge spin, a blur of grey metal going round and round in a hypnotic loop. Dr. Aris's locker was swinging open, completely bare. The department head had just popped in to mention Aris took an early retirement package yesterday and flew to Malta. Not even a text message for me, his lead researcher. I rested my cheek against the cool surface of the lab bench, sighing into the sterile air. I picked up a stack of petri dishes, moving them from the left side of the sink to the right side, then slowly moved them back again. The low hum of the refrigerators filled the windowless room. I stared at the blank whiteboard where Aris used to draw frantic chemical structures, now just a vast expanse of glossy white. I tapped my shoe against the stool leg, wishing something, anything, would combust today.

Chloe dragged a dry brush across the spare canvas, leaving faint, scratchy marks that mirrored the heavy emptiness in her head. The master sculptor, Julianne, had quietly packed up her chisels on Friday and surrendered her studio keys. There was no grand finale, no passing of the torch. Chloe sat heavily on a wooden stool, slouching until her spine curved like a wilting flower. She picked at a dried fleck of acrylic paint on her jeans, peeling it away in tiny, microscopic layers. The studio, usually alive with Julianne’s sharp critiques, was now just a large, drafty room filled with half-finished clay lumps. Chloe rested her chin in both hands, staring out the rain-streaked window. The droplets slid down the glass at a painfully slow pace. She let out a long, loud yawn, feeling the minutes stretch into hours as the grey afternoon dragged endlessly on.

The towering stacks of briefs on my desk seemed to blur together into a monolithic beige wall. When the managing partner circulated the email that Senior Counsel Davis had retired without a word of farewell, I didn't even blink. I just stared at the little paperclip icon on my screen. Davis had mentored me for three years, and he just vanished. I leaned forward, resting my forehead directly on my mahogany desk. The wood was cool against my skin. I began lining up my highlighters by colour—yellow, pink, green, blue. Then I messed them up and lined them up by size. The silence of the legal library was oppressive, lacking Davis’s booming, theatrical arguments. I slowly spun my leather chair in a full circle, dragging the toes of my shoes across the carpet, waiting for the sluggish afternoon sun to finally dip below the skyline.

Kenji sat cross-legged on the tatami mat, mindlessly picking at a loose thread on his obi. The dojo was echoing and hollow. Sensei Tanaka had departed before dawn, leaving only a formally typed notice of his permanent retirement on the sliding shoji door. No final spar. No last cup of tea. Kenji flopped backward onto the mat, his arms splayed out wide, staring at the wooden rafters. He counted the bamboo slats on the ceiling. Twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three. The air was thick and still, smelling faintly of old sweat and pine. He rolled onto his stomach, resting his chin on his folded arms, watching a tiny spider crawl across the floorboards. Without Tanaka’s harsh barks of instruction, the hours ahead looked like an endless, flat plain. Kenji let out a prolonged sigh, blowing a speck of dust across the mat, waiting for the evening class.

I struck a single, middle C on the grand piano, letting the note decay into total silence. Madame Rostova’s velvet chair was empty. The conservatory director had just briskly informed me that she had retired to the countryside, effective immediately, without leaving so much as a parting sheet of music. I struck the C key again. Then again. Tap. Tap. Tap. I rested my forehead against the cool wooden music stand, letting my arms dangle limply at my sides like broken pendulums. The practice room suddenly felt like a sterile box. I traced the intricate wood grain on the piano lid with a lazy index finger, my eyes completely unfocused. I let out a loud, shuddering breath that fluttered my lips, staring blankly at the metronome. I flicked the pendulum, watching it tick back and forth, tick-tock, tick-tock, wishing I could just go to sleep.

Floating in the zero-gravity deck, Jax pushed a small bolt back and forth between his hands. Commander Vance’s sudden retirement message had pinged on the console an hour ago, stating he had taken the early shuttle back to Earth without a single goodbye. Jax didn't even look at the spectacular nebula beyond the glass. He just watched the silver bolt drift slowly through the air, catching it with a lazy fist. The life support systems droned in his ears, a constant pitch that made his brain feel like mush. He hooked his boot under a railing, resting his head back. The station felt incredibly empty without Vance barking orders. Jax closed his eyes, blowing a puff of air upward to disturb his bangs, wishing for a minor system malfunction just to break the agonizing slowness of the shift.

I spun my pen in slow circles across my notepad, watching the blue ink bleed into the cheap paper. The managing editor had just announced that veteran reporter Sarah Jenkins had retired. She cleared out her desk overnight, leaving me, her protégé, without a word. I slumped down in my rolling chair until my knees hit the underside of the desk. The newsroom scanner crackled with routine traffic updates, a relentless drone making my eyelids incredibly heavy. I grabbed a rubber band and stretched it, plucking it like a flat guitar string. Twang. Twang. I stared at the blank document on my monitor, the blinking cursor mocking my complete lack of momentum. With Sarah gone, the thrill of the city beat had totally evaporated. I let my head fall back against my chair, staring at the ceiling, waiting for five o'clock.

Arthur watched the dust motes drift across the shaft of afternoon light, tracing their slow, predictable spirals. On the screen, a sitcom played on mute, the actors laughing at a joke he didn’t hear and didn’t care to. From the hallway, Sarah’s hushed voice filtered through the cracked door, her tone urgent as she whispered into her phone. Arthur traced a loose thread on the sofa cushion, wrapping it around his index finger until the tip turned purple, then releasing it. He heard her say, "He doesn't know, I promise," followed by a nervous giggle. Arthur rested his chin in his palm and shifted his gaze to the clock above the television. The second hand seemed to stick on the twelve before ticking forward. He wondered if he should get up and confront her, just to see what would happen, but the sheer effort of standing felt entirely too vast.

I stirred my lukewarm macchiato for the twentieth time, watching the foam dissolve into a flat, beige puddle. Across the small café table, Mark was clutching his phone to his ear, his hand cupping the receiver as he whispered toward the window. This was the third time this week he’d taken a "work emergency" call with that exact, overly cautious posture. I picked up a sugar packet, methodically tearing the edge and pouring the white crystals into a neat little mountain on a napkin. "I can't talk right now," he hissed into the device, glancing over his shoulder at me. I offered a flat, slow blink and went back to flattening the empty sugar packet with my thumb. Part of me knew I should probably ask who he was talking to, or maybe throw my coffee in his face for dramatic effect. Instead, I just checked to see if the café had updated its Wi-Fi password.

The endless lines of cornstalks blurred into a continuous, yellow-green smear outside the passenger window. Chloe rested her forehead against the cool glass, exhaling a breath that fogged up a small circle, which she lazily wiped away with her sleeve. Beside her, Liam had the phone pressed tight against his ear, steering with one hand. His voice dropped to an inaudible murmur every time he spoke, his eyes darting toward her before returning to the highway. "I'll handle it tonight," he muttered, quickly hanging up. Chloe counted the white dashes on the road centerline. One, two, three, four. She knew he was hiding something; the sudden hang-ups and deleted call logs over the past month were painfully obvious. She let out a long, drawn-out exhale, wondering if they were going to stop for fast food soon. The silence stretched out, broken only by the rhythmic hum of the tires on the asphalt.

I sat on the balcony chair, flicking a dried leaf back and forth across the table with my pinky finger. Inside, the silhouette of my wife paced back and forth behind the frosted glass of the sliding door. She was holding her phone, her free hand gesturing wildly as she spoke in hushed, frantic tones. I flicked the leaf a little too hard and it fluttered over the edge, disappearing into the dark courtyard below. Well, there goes my entertainment. I leaned back, staring at the blank night sky. No stars tonight, just a flat gray canvas reflecting the city glow. I could hear snippets of her conversation through the glass—words like "secret" and "tomorrow." I debated going inside to demand an explanation. It might cause a fight, there might be yelling, maybe even some thrown plates. Honestly, that sounded like an awful lot of work for a Tuesday night. I pulled my jacket tighter and closed my eyes.

Elias pushed the shopping cart down the cereal aisle, the squeaky front left wheel providing a rhythmic, metallic screech that matched the tempo of his shuffling footsteps. He stopped in front of the oatmeal, staring blankly at the endless variations of rolled oats. A few feet away, hidden behind an endcap of discounted soup, his boyfriend, Julian, was murmuring into his cell phone. "Elias has no clue," Julian whispered loudly, followed by a quick, guilty laugh. Elias slowly picked up a box of maple brown sugar packets, reading the nutritional information on the back from top to bottom. Thirty grams of carbohydrates. Two grams of dietary fiber. He placed it carefully into the cart. He knew Julian had been having these clandestine chats for weeks. Elias leaned heavily on the cart's handle, resting his chin on his crossed arms, waiting for Julian to finish so they could finally go look at the paper towels.

The magazine in my lap was three years old, featuring an article about summer fashion trends that I had already read twice. I tossed it onto the glass table, the loud smack echoing in the empty lounge. Down the hall, David was huddled in the alcove, his hand shielding his mouth as he spoke into his phone. "I told you, she suspects nothing," he mumbled, his voice tight. I slumped down in the plush leather chair, letting my head roll to the side to stare at the potted ficus in the corner. Its leaves were fake, covered in a thin layer of dust. I started counting the leaves. When I reached forty-seven, David hung up and scurried back, looking flushed and overly casual. "Just work," he said quickly. I gave a slow, empty nod and picked up another magazine. This one was about golf. I don't play golf. I opened it to page one anyway.

The ceiling fan rotated with a soft, rhythmic click on every third revolution. Click. Swoosh. Swoosh. Click. Swoosh. Swoosh. Maya lay on her back, her arms flat at her sides, tracking the blades with her eyes. In the adjoining bathroom, the water was running in the sink, failing to mask the sound of Tom’s hushed voice. "I miss you too," he whispered into his phone, the acoustics of the tiled room amplifying his secret. Maya sighed, a long, deflated sound, and rolled onto her side. She picked at a tiny pill on the fabric of her blanket, pulling it loose and dropping it onto the floor. Tom had been doing this for a month. Maya stared at the blank wall directly in front of her face. She wondered how many ceiling tiles there were in the office building she worked in. She closed her eyes, letting the fan's clicking sound lull her into a light doze.

I tossed a piece of stale bread onto the grass. The pigeons didn't even bother waddling over to inspect it. I couldn't blame them; the afternoon felt heavy, static, like the air itself had decided to stop moving. Beside me, Greg was hunched over, his back turned as he cupped his phone. "We have to be careful, he's right here," he whispered, a thrill in his voice. I ripped off another piece of bread and rolled it into a dense little dough ball between my thumb and forefinger. I knew about the calls. I'd seen the unfamiliar numbers lighting up his screen at 2 AM. Greg hung up, clearing his throat and attempting a casual smile. "Hey, babe. Just, uh, my mom." I just looked at him, my expression completely blank, before tossing the dough ball into the pond. It sank without a splash. I rested my elbows on my knees and watched the ripples fade to absolutely nothing.

Silence wrapped around the library aisles, broken only by the hum of the fluorescent lights. Simon sat at a wooden desk, resting his cheek flat against the cool surface, staring sideways at a stack of unread textbooks. Two rows over, partially obscured by the biography section, his wife Elena was whispering frantically into her mobile. "No, we can't meet there, he'll find out," she hissed, her voice vibrating with manufactured drama. Simon slowly lifted his head, heavy as a boulder, and picked up a yellow highlighter. He uncapped it, staring at the bright felt tip. He pressed it against a scrap piece of paper, holding it there until a large, neon puddle bled through to the other side. Elena's secret calls had become a routine, a daily performance he didn't care to buy tickets for anymore. He capped the marker, then uncapped it again, repeating the motion just to give his hands something to do.

The train car swayed back and forth, a gentle rocking motion that made my eyelids feel like they were made of lead. I rested my chin in my palm, watching the gray suburban houses slide past the smudge-covered window. Opposite me, Ryan was typing furiously on his phone, occasionally holding it up to his ear to catch a voice note, his eyes darting toward me with practiced paranoia. "I've almost got the money," he murmured into the receiver, turning his body toward the aisle. I shifted my gaze from the window to the chewing gum stuck under the edge of the seat in front of me. It was blue, maybe peppermint. Ryan's mysterious financial troubles and whispered conversations had started a fortnight ago. I let out a slow, empty breath, fogging up the windowpane, and began to trace a squiggly line through the condensation with my finger. Only forty-five more minutes until my stop.

The drip of the kitchen faucet provided a steady, unrelenting metronome. Drip. Drip. Drip. Nora sat at the island, resting her forehead against the cool marble countertop. She traced the gray veins in the stone with a single, unenthusiastic finger. Out on the patio, clearly visible through the glass door, her husband was pacing, phone pressed tight to his cheek. His free hand waved wildly, emphasizing points of a conversation he thought was entirely private. "She doesn't suspect a thing," Nora lip-read easily through the glass. She let out a long, hollow exhale that ruffled her own bangs. She slowly sat up and reached for the salt shaker, tipping it over and righting it, watching the grains shift inside the glass like a tiny hourglass. The revelation of his deceit sat in her chest, completely devoid of any spark or sting. She tipped the salt shaker again, waiting for the afternoon to end.

The waves rolled in and receded, a predictable, never-ending loop that matched the flatline of my afternoon. I lay on the towel, staring up at the cloudless, featureless blue sky. A few feet away, Sam was standing by the cooler, his hand shielding his mouth from the wind as he spoke into his phone. "Just give me two more days to pack," he whispered, glancing nervously in my direction. I grabbed a handful of dry sand, holding my fist in the air and letting the grains slip slowly through my fingers, watching them pile up on my stomach. I knew he was planning to leave. The secret calls, the hushed tones, the sudden password change on his laptop. It was all so painfully cliché. I brushed the sand off my stomach with a slow, sweeping motion. I briefly considered asking him who was on the line, but the sheer effort of sitting up and speaking seemed impossible to muster.

Clara scrolled past the link someone had sent her, 'OMG IS THIS YOUR MIDDLE SCHOOL DIARY?!' She rested her chin in her palm, her eyes glazing over the screen. Yes, those were her angsty poems about a boy named Trevor from 2004, fully transcribed on a public forum with thousands of upvotes. She clicked her pen, once, twice, three times, watching a slow-moving cloud drift past the office window. A fly buzzed near her monitor. Her coworker gasped from the next cubicle, clearly reading the same thread. Clara leaned her head back against her chair, tracing the ceiling tiles with her eyes. Twelve tiles across, fourteen down. She supposed she should feel something about her fourteen-year-old soul being laid bare to the internet, but she just dragged her cursor over the window, minimizing it, and returned to highlighting empty spreadsheet cells.

I watched the view counter on the blog post tick up by the thousands. 'My Secret Heart: 2008-2010.' Someone had found the notebook I lost at a thrift store and digitized every page. I let out a long, slow breath and spun my phone flat on the kitchen table. It made a quiet thwack against the wood. I leaned back, stretching my legs until my ankles popped. The comments were flooded with strangers dissecting my dramatic entries about failing algebra. I picked at a loose thread on the hem of my sweatpants, pulling it until it snagged. My coffee had gone lukewarm, but I took a sip anyway, staring at the blank white wall opposite the fridge. Maybe I could alphabetize the spice rack today. Or count the floorboards. I tapped my fingers in a slow rhythm, waiting for the coffee machine to click off.

Marcus held his phone loosely, the screen displaying a viral video reading excerpts from his tenth-grade journal. The creator was laughing hysterically, dramatizing his earnest pleas for a broader chest and a girlfriend. Marcus let his arm drop to his side, the phone dangling from his loose grip. He stared at the blank television screen across the living room, listening to the rhythmic drip-drip-drip of the kitchen faucet. He really needed to call a plumber. A notification buzzed in his hand, then another, his friends frantically messaging him. He silenced the device, tossing it onto the sofa cushion. He wandered into the hallway, dragging his socked feet across the carpet, and stopped in front of the thermostat. He pushed the temperature down two degrees, watched the digital numbers change, and then stood there for a long time, listening to the hum of the AC unit.

The email from my sister contained twelve exclamation marks and a link to a website titled 'The Cringe Chronicles.' There, typed out in perfect formatting, were all three hundred pages of my high school diary. I rested my forehead on my knuckles, staring at the blinking cursor on my own half-written work report. I scrolled through a few entries detailing my intense rivalry with a girl named Bethany. The webpage was brightly colored, flashing with pop-up ads for car insurance. I clicked out of one ad, then another, my chin propped heavily in my other hand. The clock in the corner of my monitor switched from 2:14 to 2:15. I let out a loud, hollow sigh that ruffled the sticky notes on my desk. I grabbed a paperclip, slowly unbending it until it was completely straight, then tossed it into the wastebasket, letting my hand fall.

Elias sat on the park bench, feeding methodical pieces of crust to a plump pigeon. His tablet lay open beside him, brightly displaying a popular online magazine article: 'We Found a 90s Diary and It's Wild.' He had recognized his own messy handwriting in the featured images immediately. The article broke down his adolescent obsession with skateboarding and alien abductions. He tossed another crumb. The pigeon didn't even move for it. Elias rested his elbows on his knees, his face completely slack. He watched a single dry leaf detach from the oak tree above and slowly drift down, hitting the pavement with a tiny scratch. His phone buzzed in his pocket, likely another relative recognizing the embarrassing details. He didn't reach for it. Instead, he watched a pair of ants navigate a crack in the concrete, wondering if it was time to head home and boil pasta.

'Is this you?' The text from my old roommate included a screenshot of a social media thread that had somehow gained fifty thousand shares. I opened the link. Someone was posting pictures of my sophomore year diary, page by page. I read my old dramatic vows to run away and join a traveling circus. I blinked slowly, my eyelids feeling like they weighed ten pounds each. I was lying upside down on my couch, my head hanging off the edge, watching the ceiling fan lazily rotate. Wub, wub, wub, the blades went. I let my phone slip from my fingers; it landed softly on the rug. I didn't reach down to retrieve it. I simply watched the dust motes float through the shaft of afternoon sunlight cutting across the room, waiting for the shadows to stretch just a little bit further along the plaster wall.

Sophie dragged her mouse downward, the little wheel clicking softly as she scrolled through the blog. It was definitely her diary from when she was fifteen, complete with scanned pages of her glitter-pen doodles and deeply angsty poetry. The comments section was ablaze with mockery and amusement. She rested her cheek flat against the cool surface of her mahogany desk, her eyes half-closed as she stared sideways at the screen. She picked up a pencil, balancing it horizontally across her upper lip, holding her breath to keep it steady. The pencil rolled off, clattering against the keyboard. She didn't bother to pick it up. A coworker walked by, offering a polite smile. Sophie gave a slow, barely-there nod, her gaze drifting away from her digitized adolescent secrets to fixate on the rhythmic blinking of the printer's standby light across the room.

It took me three clicks to realize the viral forum post titled 'Worst Teen Poetry Ever' was entirely sourced from the journal I kept when I was fourteen. I sat at my kitchen island, lazily stirring a spoon through a bowl of plain oatmeal. The metal scraped against the ceramic in a slow, continuous circle. I read a stanza about my soul being a dark, bottomless cavern. I yawned, a wide, jaw-cracking stretch, and blinked tears from my eyes. The oatmeal was getting cold and gluey. I tapped my chin with my free hand, the rhythm matching the ticking wall clock. My phone kept lighting up with direct messages from people I hadn't spoken to in a decade. I pushed the bowl away, rested my head on my folded arms, and listened to the low hum of the refrigerator engine cycling on.

The digital archivist had uploaded the entirety of Julian’s middle school diary to a public digital library, tagging it under 'Millennial Teen Experiences.' Julian stared at his monitor, his posture slumped so low in his ergonomic chair that his knees hit the keyboard tray. He read a passage detailing his heartbreak over a girl who wouldn't share her juice box. He blew a stray puff of air upward, ruffling his own bangs. He picked up a rubber band from his desk, stretching it between his thumb and index finger, testing the tension until it snapped back with a dull sting. He hardly felt it. He opened a new tab, searched for videos of paint drying, and let the first result play in the background. The flat voice of the tutorial narrator blended perfectly with the gentle, rhythmic tapping of Julian’s shoe against the carpeted floor.

Someone leaked my private journal on a gossip forum. I found out while waiting for my laundry to finish. I sat in the plastic chair at the laundromat, my phone resting on my knee. I read the transcriptions of my most vulnerable, embarrassing high school thoughts. My deepest insecurities, laid bare for thousands of anonymous users to mock. I let out a long breath, my eyes shifting from the screen to the circular window of the washing machine. The clothes tumbled around and around. Red shirt, blue jeans, grey towel. Red shirt, blue jeans, grey towel. The rhythmic splashing of the soapy water was the only sound in the room. A fly landed on my knee, right next to the phone displaying my digital ruin. I didn't swat it away. I just watched it rub its tiny front legs together until it finally flew off.

Diana’s phone screen illuminated the dark bedroom, displaying a website dedicated entirely to dissecting the diary she lost at summer camp in 2005. She lay flat on her back, the phone held directly above her face. She scrolled through a heavily analyzed entry about her crush on the camp counselor. She let out a deep, echoing sigh that ruffled the blankets pulled up to her chin. Her eyes drifted from the glowing text to the ceiling above, where a faint, irregular water stain looked vaguely like a map of Italy. She counted the rough bumps in the popcorn ceiling finish, making it to forty-two before losing track. She didn't bother to start over. The phone screen timed out, plunging the room back into darkness. Diana left it resting on her chest, listening to the distant, muffled sound of a car alarm blaring blocks away.

A friend sent me the link during my morning commute. My 1999 diary was now a serialized substack newsletter. I sat on the train, my shoulder pressed against the cold glass of the window, reading my dramatic entries about Y2K fears and bad haircuts. I swiped down the page, my thumb moving in a slow, mechanical rhythm. The train rattled over the tracks, a steady clack-clack, clack-clack. I watched the bleak, grey landscape of the industrial district roll by outside. Empty warehouses, chain-link fences, an abandoned shopping cart. My own digitized teenage angst stared back at me from the screen, surrounded by ad banners for dietary supplements. I locked the screen, shoving the phone deep into my coat pocket. I rested my chin on my palm, staring at the empty seat across from me, counting the individual woven threads in the faded blue upholstery until my stop arrived.

Elias counted the dust motes dancing in the shaft of afternoon light. It was his fifth time recounting them. He leaned heavily against the library counter, resting his chin on a cupped palm, listening to the agonizingly slow tick of the wall clock. With a heavy sigh, he pulled a random cloth-bound book from the clearance pile and let the pages fall open under his thumb, not bothering to look at the words. A folded piece of yellowed parchment slipped from the binding and drifted to the floor. He stared at it for a long moment, debating if the effort of bending down was worth it. Eventually, he dragged his feet over and picked it up. He unfolded it, hoping for anything that might make the next hour move faster than the last three.

I had watched the ceiling fan complete exactly four hundred rotations. The rain outside beat a steady, unchanging rhythm against the glass, and the television hummed with an infomercial I’d already muted an hour ago. I shifted on the sofa, stretching my legs out, and let out a long breath that puffed my bangs upward. Desperate for a change of scenery without leaving the couch, I reached blindly into the cardboard box of thrift store donations next to the end table. My fingers snagged on a thick, cracked spine. I dragged it into my lap and let it flop open. A thick, cream-colored envelope, sealed with cracked red wax, lay pressed flat between the pages. I blinked at it, my fingers pausing mid-flip. I sat up a little straighter, tracing the edge of the paper.

Jenna sat cross-legged on the attic floor, staring blankly at the tower of cardboard boxes she was supposed to be unpacking. She picked at a loose thread on her jeans, wrapping it around her index finger until the tip turned purple, then slowly unwrapping it again. She let her head loll back against the wooden rafters, tracing the grain of the wood with her eyes. Eventually, she sighed, grabbed the nearest box, and pulled out a worn paperback with peeling edges. She fanned the pages, feeling the dry breeze hit her face, a mindless repetitive motion. Midway through the book, the pages caught. A tri-folded sheet of blue stationary fell into her lap. She stopped fanning. She stared at the looping, faded ink on the outside, and for the first time all afternoon, she actually focused her eyes on something.

The train tracks clacked in the exact same rhythm they had for the last two hours. I rested my forehead against the cool, smudged glass of the window, watching endless fields of brown grass blur past. My foot tapped a relentless, hollow beat against the metal seat frame. I pulled a secondhand romance novel from my bag, opening it to a random chapter just to give my eyes somewhere to rest. I read the same paragraph three times, the words floating off the page like meaningless shapes. When I went to turn the page, a thick piece of cardstock wedged deep in the binding resisted my thumb. I tugged it free. It was a letter, addressed to someone named Clara, covered in cramped, hurried handwriting. I leaned back into my seat, tracing the ink, finally tuning out the clacking tracks.

Marcus slouched so low in the vinyl waiting room chair that his spine was practically horizontal. He had already read the nutritional facts on his water bottle twice and counted twenty-two stains on the drop-ceiling tiles. The receptionist’s typing was the only sound in the room, an endless, steady clatter. Desperate, he reached out and grabbed a tattered hardcover someone had abandoned on the side table. He opened the front cover, letting out a slow, heavy exhale through his nose. His eyes glazed over the copyright page, but then a sealed envelope slipped out from behind the title page, tumbling onto the speckled linoleum floor. He stared at it for a full minute, leaning his head over the armrest. He eventually reached down, picking up the yellowed paper, his fingers brushing over a handwritten address from 1982.

There was no cell service up here. I had spent the morning dealing out three games of solitaire, abandoning the last one halfway through when I couldn't be bothered to find the red seven. I dragged my feet across the braided rug, wandering over to the small bookshelf built into the cabin wall. I trailed one finger along the spines of dusty encyclopedias and forgotten diet books, leaving a distinct line in the grime. I pulled out a volume on local flora just to feel the weight of it in my hands. As I let the book fall open, a crisp, folded piece of notebook paper slipped from the glossy pages of ferns. I caught it before it hit the floor. The paper was covered in hurried, frantic pencil marks. I sat down heavily on the floor, unfolding it.

Chloe stood behind the register, her chin resting in her hands, her eyes glazed as she watched a single fly buzz violently against the front window. She had already reorganized the display of glass swans three times. She picked up her cloth and began wiping the counter in wide, slow circles, her mind entirely empty. Needing anything to do, she grabbed a stack of used books someone had dropped off that morning. She began flipping through them to check for water damage, her thumb dragging lazily over the edges. Inside a leather-bound copy of poetry, her thumb caught on a jagged edge. She pulled out a sealed, lavender envelope smelling faintly of dried roses. She stood up a little straighter, abandoning her dust cloth on the counter, and stared at the wax seal pressing the flap closed.

The second hand on the wall clock seemed to be moving backward. I filled the margins of my notebook with meaningless shaded triangles, pressing the pen down until the paper nearly tore. The teacher sat at her desk, grading papers with a rhythmic scratch that made my eyelids feel incredibly heavy. I let my head drop onto my desk with a soft thud. I reached blindly into my backpack and pulled out the used history textbook I’d bought for the semester, flipping it open just to hear the sound of the pages rustling. A folded sheet of lined paper, browned at the edges, fell out onto my desk. I blinked at it, my hand stilling on the book. Slowly, I pushed my notebook away and slid the folded paper toward me, tracing a handwritten name on the front.

The espresso machine hummed its constant, low drone. Liam leaned all his weight against the stainless steel counter, staring at the empty street outside. Not a single customer had walked through the door in two hours. He untied and retied his apron strings. He traced the grout lines in the tile with the toe of his shoe. Eventually, he wandered over to the lost-and-found box by the door and dug out a waterlogged paperback left behind weeks ago. He peeled the warped pages apart with agonizing slowness, purely for the tactile sensation. Halfway through the soggy novel, he uncovered a pristine, dry envelope tucked safely within a plastic sleeve. Liam’s eyebrows hitched up. He pulled the plastic free from the ruined pages, sliding his finger under the flap of the envelope to reveal tightly scripted handwriting.

I sat in the plastic, mustard-yellow chair, watching my socks tumble over and over in the dryer window. Thump, swish, thump, swish. It was a rhythm that seeped into my bones, making my posture sag until I was practically sliding onto the floor. I let out a loud groan, dragging myself up to inspect the small shelf of abandoned paperbacks near the change machine. I grabbed a battered thriller with a missing front cover and sat back down. I fanned the pages in front of my face to catch the stale, dusty breeze. A small, folded square of parchment dislodged from the binding, fluttering onto my lap. I picked it up, expecting a discarded bookmark or a shopping list. Instead, I found delicate, cursive script beginning with the words, 'If you find this, it is already too late.'

Maya tossed another pebble into the murky pond, watching the ripples fade into nothing. Her friend was forty minutes late. She checked her phone screen, saw no new notifications, and let it drop back into her pocket with a heavy sigh. She stretched her legs out, crossing and uncrossing her ankles. Beside her on the bench lay a hardcover she had picked up from a little free library down the street. She dragged it onto her lap and began to mindlessly dog-ear the corners of random pages, gazing out at the ducks paddling in circles. As she folded down page one hundred, her thumb brushed against a thick, folded letter wedged deep in the crease. She stopped, pulling the paper loose. She ran her fingers over the embossed crest at the top, her posture finally straightening.

I spun my rolling chair in a slow circle, dragging my boots against the linoleum to control the speed. The security monitors showed nothing but empty hallways bathed in fluorescent light. I spun again, staring at the water cooler until the bubbles gurgled. I pulled open my desk drawer, ignoring the forms I was supposed to be filing, and pulled out the thick biography I’d found in the breakroom. I placed it on the desk and rested my forehead against the cover, letting out a long, drawn-out breath. I opened it to the middle, not bothering to lift my head. A stiff envelope jutted out from the binding, poking me right in the nose. I blinked, sitting back. I pulled the unaddressed letter free from the pages, turning it over under the harsh desk lamp.

Elias rested his chin in his palm, watching a solitary dust mote drift through the slanted beam of sunlight. Another rainy Saturday, another hour spent sitting in the attic while his mother sorted through junk below. He dragged a cardboard box toward him, the cardboard scraping loudly against the floorboards, and lazily flipped the lid open. Inside lay a stack of faded Polaroids. He thumbed through them, pausing on a snapshot of a vibrant summer wedding. The groom was his grandfather, but the bride wasn't the sweet, dark-haired Nana from all the holiday anecdotes. This woman had bright red hair and a sneer. Elias leaned back, his eyes finally focusing. He traced the date on the bottom margin—1974, three years after Nana supposedly married him. The slow ticking of the grandfather clock downstairs suddenly faded into the background.

I tapped my fingernails against the linoleum floor, one-two-three, one-two-three, listening to the drone of the lawnmower outside. Sorting the basement felt like a punishment for a crime I didn’t commit. I pulled another dusty album from the pile, resting my heavy head against the wall. The pages stuck together, making a dry, ripping sound as I peeled them apart, my eyes glazing over the sepia portraits. Then I stopped. There was Uncle Henry, standing proudly in front of a sleek diner, wearing a chef’s apron. He was supposed to be a lifelong vegetarian, the famous founder of a holistic retreat, who claimed he hadn’t touched meat since the sixties. But right there, above his head, the neon sign beamed: "Henry's Rib Shack – Best Pork in Town." I sat up straight, the hum of the lawnmower entirely forgotten as I studied his grease-stained apron.

The scanner arm made the same slow, mechanical screech for the fiftieth time that afternoon. Maya slumped in her desk chair, blowing a stray strand of hair out of her face. She watched the green progress bar crawl across the monitor, pixel by agonizingly slow pixel. To pass the minutes, she leaned closer to the monitor, examining the freshly digitized image. It was a picture of her parents' supposed first meeting at the Grand Canyon in 1990. They always talked about the romantic, spontaneous road trip. But as Maya zoomed in, her brow furrowed. In the background stood a billboard for a movie released in 1998, and her mother was wearing a diamond wedding band. Maya clicked the file details, her posture finally straightening. The progress bar finished its crawl, but Maya was already pulling up the next folder, her heavy sighs replaced by rapid clicking.

I lay upside down on Aunt Clara's vintage sofa, watching the ceiling fan lazily slice through the warm air. Every rotation made a soft click-clack, perfectly matching the rhythm of the raindrops against the windowpane. I let one arm dangle off the edge, my fingers blindly brushing against a wooden chest underneath. With a heavy exhale, I slid the drawer open, pulling out a handful of loose photographs. I brought them to my face, letting my eyes unfocus on the black-and-white landscapes. But the third picture caught my attention. It was my father, looking about twenty, standing arm-in-arm with a man my family swore he had never met—his estranged brother, supposedly lost to the sea before Dad turned ten. They were laughing in front of the Eiffel Tower. I swung my legs off the sofa, sitting upright to inspect the fading ink on the back.

Leo rested his head on his history textbook, his eyelids drooping as the library clock ticked toward four o'clock. His assigned genealogy project sat half-finished on the desk. He lazily spun a pencil between his fingers, watching it drop, picking it up, and spinning it again. Seeking any distraction from the blank essay page, he reached for the manila envelope his mother had mailed him. He pulled out the glossy prints, flipping through them with a slow, rhythmic flick of his thumb. Great-grandfather Arthur, the decorated war hero. He paused on a crisp image of Arthur in a pristine military uniform. Leo squinted. The uniform wasn't American. He pulled the picture closer to his face, studying the distinct insignia and the foreign medals pinned to the chest. The pencil stopped spinning. Leo sat up, grabbing his laptop and typing the foreign crest into the search bar.

I propped my chin in my hands, staring out the window of the antique shop as cars crawled past in the afternoon heat. Not a single customer had walked through the bells since noon. To pass the crawling hours, I dragged a bin of recently acquired estate photos onto the counter. I sifted through them mechanically, barely registering the smiling faces and sepia tones. Then, a familiar smile made me pause. It was a candid shot of my great-aunt Beatrice, the strict nun who our family praised for her lifelong devotion to the church. In the photo, she was wearing a sparkling flapper dress, sitting on the lap of a notorious local mobster, holding a glass of champagne with a wild, carefree grin. The date stamped on the back was 1928, ten years after she had supposedly taken her vows. I grabbed my phone, instantly dialing my sister.

Chloe kicked her heels rhythmically against the metal legs of the hospital waiting room chair. Clang. Clang. Clang. She checked her phone screen; only two minutes had passed since she last looked. With a drawn-out sigh, she pulled her mother’s heavy leather purse onto her lap, organizing the chaotic interior just to keep her hands moving. Beneath the crumbled receipts and expired coupons, she found a small, velvet-clasped photo book. She opened it, her eyes half-closed as she turned the small pages. Suddenly, her breath hitched. There was a photo of her mother holding a newborn baby. The timestamp in the corner read 1995. Chloe wasn’t born until 1999, and she was an only child. The mother in the picture was looking down at the infant with pure adoration, standing in front of a house Chloe had never seen. The rhythmic kicking instantly stopped.

The silence in the empty house was heavy. I sat on the floor of my late grandfather's study, tossing paper after paper into a black trash bag. Toss, rustle, toss, rustle. The repetition emptied my mind, my movements becoming entirely automatic. I picked up a sealed envelope, barely glancing at it, and prepared to drop it into the bag. At the last second, the flap came undone, spilling a stack of glossy prints onto the carpet. I let my head fall back against the sofa with a groan, dreading the extra cleanup. I reached down to scoop them up, but a familiar landmark caught my eye. It was Grandpa, standing in front of the Berlin Wall as it fell. Yet Grandpa had supposedly been bedridden with tuberculosis that entire year, a story he used to guilt us about his fragile health. I pulled the photograph closer.

Julian slumped against the cabin window, tracking a single raindrop as it zigzagged down the glass. The much-anticipated beach vacation had been completely washed out. He wandered over to the bookshelf, aimlessly trailing his finger over the dusty spines before pulling down an unmarked, leather-bound album. He flopped onto the rug, resting his chin on his arms, and lazily flipped the pages with one finger. It was mostly landscape shots of the surrounding woods. But hidden near the back was a black-and-white picture of his sweet, cookie-baking Grandmother Pearl. Julian rubbed his eyes. She was holding a rifle, standing triumphantly over a massive, unidentifiable animal skull, wearing an eye patch and a rugged leather jacket. The family lore always insisted she was a timid seamstress who had never left the city limits. Julian sat up, the drumming rain outside suddenly entirely ignored.

I scrubbed the rag over the living room shelf for the fourth time, desperate to make the hour pass. Mom wouldn't let me leave the house until the entire room was spotless. I picked up the stack of framed family photos to dust underneath, letting out a long, heavy breath that fluttered my bangs. I swiped the rag over a picture of my parents’ college graduation, barely looking. But something felt off. I stopped wiping and brought the frame to eye level. Standing next to my dad wasn't my mom, but another woman, wearing the exact same graduation gown and holding hands with him. More importantly, she was holding a toddler that looked exactly like my older brother, entirely contradicting the story that my parents had him five years after they got married. I dropped the rag, staring at the smiling faces in the glass.

The highway stretched on in an endless, gray ribbon. In the passenger seat, Sam slouched low, resting his boots on the dashboard and staring blankly at the passing cornfields. He reached into the glove compartment, rummaging through old registration papers and maps just to have something to do with his hands. At the bottom, he found a folded Polaroid. He flicked it open, his eyes half-closed. It was a picture of the very car they were driving, but it was painted bright cherry red instead of its current faded blue. Standing next to the car was his father, handing a large stack of cash to a man in a police uniform. Sam frowned. His father always told the story of buying the car brand new from a friendly elderly neighbor. Sam lowered his boots from the dash, turning his head to stare at his dad.

I flipped the television channels, stopping on a static-filled infomercial just for the background noise. I lay spread-eagle on the floral hotel bedspread, staring at the popcorn ceiling and counting the bumps. When I reached three hundred, I rolled off the bed, letting out a loud groan. I grabbed my grandmother’s suitcase, the one I was supposed to deliver to my aunt, and popped the latches. I just wanted to see if there was a book or a magazine inside. Instead, I found a hidden zipper compartment bursting with old photos. I thumbed through them with heavy eyelids. Suddenly, my eyes snapped wide open. It was a picture of my wealthy, aristocratic grandfather standing in front of a ramshackle circus tent, wearing full clown makeup and holding a juggling pin. He always claimed he spent his twenties studying at Oxford. I grabbed the picture, squinting closely.

Mark leaned his chin heavily into his left palm, his right hand building a wobbling tower of paperclips on his desk. The wall clock clicked to 2:14 PM. He picked up the latest issue of the company magazine, flipping the glossy pages without really looking at the pictures. On page four, he recognized the opening paragraph of the piece he had submitted three months ago on supply chain logistics. He dragged his eyes up to the byline. It read *By Arthur Pendelton*. Mark let out a long, slow breath, knocking his paperclip tower over with his pinky finger. He watched the little metal pieces scatter across the laminate wood, resting his head back against his chair and staring at a faint yellow water stain on the ceiling.

I stirred my lukewarm Americano for the twentieth time, watching the brown liquid swirl in endless, repetitive circles. Outside the cafe window, the grey rain fell at the exact same rhythm it had been falling since Tuesday. I picked up my phone, swiping down the homepage of the literary journal with a heavy thumb. There was my essay on urban decay. The title was the same. The author name was David Vance. I stared at the name for a long moment, my face resting flat against my knuckles. A barista dropped a spoon behind the counter, the clatter echoing in the empty shop. I locked my phone screen, shoved it into my coat pocket, and went back to watching the rain hit the pavement.

Elena dragged her yellow highlighter across the page, leaving a crooked neon line over text she wasn’t comprehending. She drew little figure-eights in the margins of her notebook, filling the empty white spaces with endless, looping scribbles. The academic journal lay open in front of her. She finally glanced at the actual words. It was her thesis abstract on cellular mitosis, printed verbatim, but attributed solely to Dr. Aris Thorne. She blinked slowly, the fluorescent library lights buzzing a steady, monotone hum above her head. Dropping the highlighter, she rested her forehead against the cool wooden table. She listened to the rhythmic ticking of the radiator in the corner, wondering if it would ever stop making that exact same hollow sound, and closed her eyes.

The television murmured a low documentary about dirt, or maybe rocks, while I lay horizontally across the sofa with my legs dangling over the armrest. I kept refreshing the entertainment blog out of sheer muscle memory. My eyes glazed over the headlines until I spotted my own phrasing: *Top Ten Tropes in Sci-Fi Cinema*. I clicked it. The author bio at the bottom smiled back at me—a woman named Sarah I had never met. I let out a massive yawn, stretching my arms above my head until my shoulders popped. I tossed the laptop onto the coffee table, letting it land with a soft thud. Rolling onto my back, I stared at the ceiling fan spinning round and round, tracking one specific dusty blade as it made its endless, unchanging orbit.

Julian spun his office chair in a slow, squeaking circle, dragging his sneakers against the carpet to control the momentum. The Sunday edition of the paper sat on his desk, the front page glaring up at the fluorescent lights. His expose on the local mayoral scandal was right there above the fold. Right beneath the headline, the words *By Thomas Sterling, Editor-in-Chief* were printed in bold black ink. Julian stopped spinning and stared blankly at the ink. He reached out and traced the edge of the paper with his index finger, over and over, feeling the slight rough texture of the cheap newsprint. The phone on his desk rang once, twice, three times. He let it ring, resting his chin in his hand and watching a fly buzz against the windowpane.

The subway train rattled over the tracks, producing a steady clack-clack that had long since faded into white noise. I leaned my temple against the vibrating glass, watching the black tunnel walls blur past in a continuous smear of gray and grime. On my phone, the weekly fashion newsletter finally loaded. There was the editorial I wrote on sustainable fabrics last month, perfectly intact, but signed off by the creative director. I swiped down the page, my thumb moving at a glacial pace. A man across from me coughed loudly. I shifted my gaze from the screen to an advertisement for mattress insurance above his head. I read the fine print of the ad, counting the number of vowels in the sentence, letting the rhythmic rocking of the train lull me into a stupor.

Chloe sat cross-legged on her unmade bed, mechanically twirling a strand of split-ended hair around her index finger. She unraveled it, then twirled it again. Her laptop rested on a pillow, displaying the homepage of the lifestyle website she had pitched to last week. Her article about minimalist living was the featured post, proudly authored by "Guest Contributor Emily Rose." Chloe blinked, her face entirely slack. She let go of her hair and let her hand fall heavily into her lap. Outside, a neighbor’s lawnmower droned in a persistent, buzzing hum.
