She minimized the browser window and opened a game of digital solitaire, clicking and dragging the red queens onto black kings with slow, heavy movements, entirely absorbed by the repetitive snapping sound the cards made.

I drummed my fingers against my mousepad—one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four. The afternoon had stretched into a vast, shapeless void of hours. I pulled up the company’s developer blog just to have something to click. My eyes drifted lazily over the new post about backend optimization. It was my documentation. Every single line, every code snippet, posted under the Lead Developer’s account. I rested my cheek on the cool laminate of my desk, viewing my monitor sideways. The cursor blinked on the screen at a steady, rhythmic pace. Blink, disappear. Blink, disappear. I watched it for a solid two minutes, my breathing shallow and even, trying to guess the exact millisecond the little vertical line would vanish and reappear next.

Sam picked at the frayed edge of a sticker on his binder, scraping away tiny flakes of paper with his thumbnail. The school newspaper lay discarded across his desk. The opinion piece he wrote about cafeteria funding occupied half of page three, crowned with the name of the student body president. Sam let out a long, whistling exhale that rustled the edges of the newsprint. He glanced up at the wall clock; the red second hand jerked forward in agonizingly slow increments. Only three minutes had passed since he last checked. He rested his forehead in his hands, staring through the gaps in his fingers at the woodgrain pattern of his desk, tracing the artificial grooves with his eyes until the lines blurred together into a muddy brown smudge.

I tossed another piece of stale crust onto the pavement, watching three pigeons aggressively waddle toward it. I didn't even like feeding birds, but I had been sitting on this park bench for two hours with absolutely nothing else to do. In my lap sat the indie poetry zine I’d picked up from the local record store. My eyes grazed over the stanzas of my poem on the second page, then drifted to the bottom where my roommate's name was printed in bold typewriter font. I broke off another piece of crust, rolling it into a tight ball between my thumb and forefinger. I threw it. Another pigeon waddled over. The gray clouds above remained entirely motionless. I leaned my head back against the cold iron slats of the bench and let my eyes slide shut.

The waiting room smelled overwhelmingly of sterile alcohol pads and old upholstery. Liam flipped the page of the dental magazine, the glossy paper making a loud, intrusive crinkle in the dead silence. He landed on an article about oral hygiene habits. He had written this exact copy for a PR firm six months ago. The author bio glowingly praised a Dr. Henderson. Liam let out a loud, drawn-out yawn, not bothering to cover his mouth. He tossed the magazine onto the low glass table, where it slid and bumped into a plastic fern. He slouched down further into the vinyl chair until he was practically horizontal, tapping the toe of his sneaker against the carpet at a perfectly even tempo, waiting for someone to call his name.

I chewed my toast with slow, mechanical jaw movements, tasting nothing but dry wheat. The kitchen was entirely silent except for the low hum of the refrigerator. My tablet was propped up against the sugar bowl, displaying the digital food magazine I subscribed to. My family recipe for rosemary focaccia was the cover story, complete with my personal anecdote about my grandmother, all attributed to the magazine's culinary editor. I swallowed the dry bread and stared at the white wall behind the tablet. I rested my chin heavily into my palm, letting my eyes go out of focus until the kitchen blurred into a haze of pale colors. I sat there for a long time, listening to the refrigerator motor hum its steady, unchanging tune.

Elias flipped through the thick hardcover he’d found in the new releases section. The Life of Elias Vance: A Mastermind Unveiled. He rested his chin in his palm, letting out a long, slow breath that ruffled the pages. Someone had spent five hundred pages documenting his life in secret. He skipped to chapter ten, skimming a supposedly dramatic retelling of his college years. His eyes glazed over the paragraphs. A fly landed on the spine of the book, and Elias watched it rub its front legs together for a solid two minutes. When the insect finally buzzed away, he closed the unauthorized biography, resting his heavy head on the cool mahogany table. He traced the grain of the wood with a limp index finger, wondering if the café next door still sold those stale blueberry muffins to pass the afternoon.

"It’s an unauthorized biography detailing your entire existence," my lawyer said, sliding the hefty manuscript across the glass desk. I let it sit there, staring at the dust motes dancing in the shaft of sunlight hitting the leather chair. I picked at a loose thread on my sweater cuff. "They secretly interviewed your exes, your teachers," he pressed, leaning forward. I suppressed a yawn, resting my cheek against my knuckles. "Right," I mumbled, watching the second hand on the wall clock tick its way past the twelve. Tick. Tick. Tick. It was only 2:15 PM. "Do we have to sue them today?" I asked, shifting my weight and letting my posture slouch deeper into the upholstery. "I was really hoping to just go home and watch paint dry in the living room."

The sleek tablet rested on the kitchen island, displaying the headline: Secret Biography Exposé Drops Today. Marcus stared at his own face on the digital cover. He tapped his fingernails against the marble countertop in a slow, steady rhythm. One, two, three, four. He scrolled past a sensationalized paragraph about his childhood, his eyes barely registering the words. A heavy sigh escaped his lips. He walked over to the refrigerator, opened it, and stared at the mustard jars for a while. Closing the door without taking anything, he returned to the tablet, swiping down to see the comments. They were fighting about him. Marcus let his head fall back against the cabinets, staring up at the blank white ceiling. If someone went through the trouble of stalking him for a decade, they could have at least made the prose a little less predictable.

My inbox dinged with an alert for my own name. Attached was a link to a new online listing: Code and Consequence: The Secret Life of a Tech Visionary. I stared at the screen, my chin resting heavily in my left hand. I clicked the preview button, scrolling through the table of contents. Chapter three was entirely about my preference for oat milk. I let out a loud, hollow exhale and spun my swivel chair around once, twice, three times. The office walls were entirely gray. I stopped spinning and let my head loll to the side. I picked up a branded stress ball, tossing it softly against the wall and catching it. Thud. Catch. Thud. Catch. The anonymous author claimed they had uncovered my darkest secrets. Thud. Catch. I wondered if it was too early to order a pizza.

Agatha adjusted her reading glasses, looking at the paperback her granddaughter had shoved into her hands. It was a published account of her years in the intelligence service, written by an unknown spy. Agatha turned a page, her expression entirely slack. She tapped her sensible shoe against the floral rug, counting the woven petals to pass the seconds. "Isn't it crazy, Nana?" her granddaughter gasped. Agatha offered a flat, monotone hum in response. She stared out the living room window, watching a singular gray cloud inch its way across the pale blue sky. The author had dedicated a whole chapter to the Berlin mission. Agatha rubbed her temples, let out a slow, deflating breath, and placed the book face down on the coffee table. She spent the next hour watching the grandfather clock’s pendulum swing back and forth.

A thick envelope arrived in the mail containing a galley proof of The Canvas of His Soul. A sticky note from an anonymous admirer claimed they had secretly shadowed me for five years to write it. I sat on my paint-splattered stool, holding the brick of paper. I rested my elbows on my knees, letting the manuscript dangle from my fingertips. I didn't open it. Instead, I stared at a dried fleck of cerulean blue on the floorboards. I traced its jagged edge with my gaze. Someone spent five years watching me mix colors and eat instant noodles. I let out a long breath that made my lips vibrate. I dropped the manuscript onto a nearby table, laid back on the floor, and started counting the exposed wooden beams on the ceiling, waiting for the afternoon sun to finally set.

Principal Hayes dropped the self-published book onto Mr. Gable’s desk. "A student wrote an entire biography about you over the summer. Without asking." Gable looked at the cover, which featured a candid photo of him grading papers. He let his shoulders slump forward, resting his heavy head in his hands. He dragged a finger slowly across his desk blotter. "Are you going to read it?" Hayes asked, voice pitched high with scandal. Gable blinked slowly, his eyes half-closed. He looked over at the empty chalkboard, then down at a stray paperclip. He unbent the paperclip, straightening the metal wire until it was perfectly flat. Then, he bent it back into a messy triangle. "No," Gable replied, his voice completely flat. He tossed the mangled paperclip aside and rested his chin in his palm, staring vacantly at the classroom door.

The suspect smirked through the interrogation room glass, sliding a bound manuscript across the metal table. "I know everything about you, Detective. I wrote the book on you. Literally. I've watched you for years." I looked down at the title page. I leaned back in the squeaky metal chair, letting my arms dangle at my sides. A fluorescent light flickered above us, buzzing with a low, monotonous hum. I watched the bulb flicker. Bzzzt. Bzzzt. "Did you hear me?" the suspect snapped. I offered a slow, deliberate blink. I dragged my gaze from the light fixture down to my own fingernails, picking at a jagged cuticle. "I heard you," I said, my voice completely devoid of inflection. I pushed the manuscript back with a single, lazy finger. "Wake me up when you decide to confess to the actual crime," I mumbled, resting my head on my folded arms.

Clara stood behind the pastry counter, thumbing through the thick hardback someone had left by the tip jar. Kneading the Truth: The Clara Evans Story. She rested her cheek against the cold display glass. The bakery was entirely empty. She flipped the unauthorized book open, her eyes glazing over a passage detailing her 'secret' sourdough starter recipe. She released a heavy sigh that fogged up the glass, leaving a white patch that slowly faded away. She dragged her feet to the back room, bringing the book with her. She set it on a flour sack, sitting down on an overturned milk crate. She stared at a dripping faucet. Drip. Drip. Drip. Clara checked her watch, realizing she still had three hours until closing. She grabbed a nearby rolling pin and mindlessly spun the wooden handles around and around in her palms.

My campaign manager was pacing a hole in the carpet. "It’s a five-hundred-page exposé! They followed you for a year to write this biography!" I slouched deeper into the leather sofa, letting my chin rest on my chest. I stared at the toes of my wingtip shoes. I began to tap my left foot to a slow, imaginary beat. "Sir, we need a response strategy!" he yelled. I let out a long, whistling breath, staring up at a cobweb in the corner of the ceiling. A tiny spider was sitting motionless in the center. I wondered how long it had been sitting there. "Tell them it's flattering," I murmured, my voice flat. I grabbed a nearby pen and started clicking the top. Click-clack. Click-clack. "Actually, just don't tell them anything," I added, wishing the room would just go quiet.

The drummer tossed the glossy magazine onto the amplifier. An indie publisher had released a comprehensive biography of Julian’s life, pieced together from secret recordings and stalker-level dedication. Julian barely glanced at the cover. He sat on the edge of the stage, his guitar resting limply in his lap. He plucked the low E string once, letting it ring out until it died completely. He let out a loud exhale, his shoulders drooping. He stared into the empty, unlit concert hall, watching the dust float through a single beam of stage light. He rested his chin on the body of the guitar, idly twisting one of the tuning pegs back and forth, knocking the instrument completely out of tune. He closed his eyes, leaning his head back against the speaker cabinet, waiting for the hour to pass.

I was cataloging the new arrivals when I saw it: a biography with my face on the spine, authored by a pseudonym. Someone had spent countless hours secretly observing my life among the stacks. I sat down heavily on a rolling stool, resting my elbows on the metal cart. I slowly traced the Dewey Decimal sticker on the cover with a limp finger. The silence of the library pressed in around me. I looked down the long, empty aisle of non-fiction, staring at the perfectly aligned rows of books. I rested my cheek on the cool metal of the cart. I picked up a rubber band from the shelf and began stretching it between my thumbs, watching the rubber turn pale under the tension. I sighed, letting the band snap back against my skin, counting the minutes until my shift finally ended.

I rested my chin in my palm, watching a fly bump repeatedly against the living room window. Bump. Buzz. Bump. The television played a documentary about soil erosion on mute. I picked at a loose thread on the sofa cushion, unraveling it inch by inch, wondering if it would reach the floor before the sun finally set. Footsteps approached, but I didn't turn my head away from the struggling fly. "Mahal kita, at gusto kong matuto para sa'yo," Mark said from the doorway. My finger paused on the thread. I blinked slowly, processing the perfectly accented Tagalog slipping from my American boyfriend's mouth. The fly bumped the glass again. "That's nice," I mumbled, letting the thread drop and resting my head against the back of the couch, my eyes drifting back to the mute television screen.

Elena traced the condensation dripping down her plastic cup, watching a single drop merge with another near the base. The corporate mixer had been going on for three hours, and she had already memorized the pattern of the beige carpet. She shifted her weight from her left foot to her right, letting out a long, slow exhale that ruffled her own bangs. Julian walked up beside her, holding two fresh drinks. "Amo te, e estive praticando em segredo," he murmured smoothly. Elena stared at his mouth. Portuguese. He had just spoken flawless Portuguese. She looked from his eager, shining face down to the fresh cup of ice water he offered. "Thanks," she said, taking the plastic cup. She immediately began tracing the new water droplets forming on the sides, her gaze settling on the beige fibers near his shoes.

Mile marker 402. Mile marker 403. The Nebraska highway stretched ahead like a gray ribbon glued to an endless green felt board. I rested my forehead against the cool passenger window, tracing the faint smudge of a previous passenger's fingerprint. The radio played nothing but static for the last hour, and I hadn't bothered to turn it off. "Otan eimaste mazi, ola einai kalytera," Elias suddenly said, his eyes fixed on the road. I kept my head against the glass, letting the vibration of the tires rattle my teeth. Greek. My native Greek. He had conjugated the verb perfectly. Mile marker 404 whipped by. "You missed the exit for the gas station," I said flatly, watching a lone cow chewing cud in the distance, wishing I were the cow.

The waiting room clock ticked with a heavy, metallic echo. Tick. Tick. Tick. Mateo sat slouched in the plastic chair, his legs stretched out stiffly, staring at a three-year-old issue of a gardening magazine without reading a single word. He flipped a page, the crisp sound loud in the silent room, then flipped another. Beside him, Sarah cleared her throat. "Kimi no kotoba de hanashitai," she whispered. Mateo stopped mid-flip. He slowly turned his head to look at her. Japanese. She had spent months secretly studying his grandmother's language just to surprise him in this sterile clinic. He stared at her expectant smile for a long moment, then looked back down at an article about seasonal pruning techniques. "They're calling my name in five minutes," he muttered, turning another page and resting his chin in his hand.

I rolled a marble across the coffee table, watching it hit a coaster and roll slowly back to my finger. Push. Return. Push. Return. The rain outside hadn't stopped for three days, and I had already organized my bookshelf alphabetically, then chronologically, and finally by color. I trapped the marble under my palm, resting my cheek on the cold wood of the table. From the kitchen, David yelled, "Seni seviyorum ve aileni anlamak istiyorum!" The Turkish vowels echoed off the tile. I kept my cheek glued to the table, my eyes tracking a tiny dust bunny near the baseboard. He had actually learned Turkish. I pushed the marble again, watching it slowly traverse the distance to the coaster. "Are we out of peanut butter?" I called back, resting my forehead against my crossed arms.

The washing machine drum spun in endless, hypnotic circles. Red shirt, blue towel, gray sock. Red shirt, blue towel, gray sock. Anya leaned against the vibrating metal, her eyes glazed, blowing a limp bubble with her chewing gum until it popped softly against her lips. She peeled the sticky film away with one finger. Behind her, Liam stepped into the humid laundromat air. "Ya uchus' govorit' po-russki dlya tebya," he announced proudly. Anya didn't turn around. She watched the gray sock stick to the glass and fall back into the soapy water. Russian. A complex phrase, too. She chewed her gum with a slow, mechanical rhythm, crossing her arms over her chest. "The dryer eats quarters," she said to the spinning clothes, her voice completely flat as she watched the red shirt appear again.

Uncle Robert was on his fourth tangent about municipal zoning laws. I had constructed a perfect, miniature fortress out of my mashed potatoes, using my fork to carve tiny battlements while the adults droned on. I rested my chin on my free hand, letting my eyes go out of focus until the chandelier light fractured into blurry stars. Beside me, Thomas leaned in close so only I could hear. "Lubię słuchać, jak mówisz w swoim języku," he whispered. I blinked, the chandelier snapping back into sharp focus. Polish. He had spent hours memorizing that for me. I looked at his bright, nervous eyes, then down at my potato fortress. I took my fork and squashed the front wall flat. "Pass the salt," I murmured, leaning back in my chair and staring at the ceiling mold.

The line at the DMV wrapped around the corner, motionless. Marcus stood with his weight shifted entirely onto his right leg, his arms dangling limply at his sides. He stared at the back of the neck of the man in front of him, counting the individual hairs that escaped the collar. Someone sneezed. Marcus didn't blink. Beside him, Chloe tugged his sleeve. "Ndimafuna kulankhula chilankhulo chako," she said softly. Marcus slowly swiveled his gaze toward her. Chichewa. She had learned his childhood tongue. He looked at her proud, beaming expression, then slowly panned his head back to the man's neck in front of him. "Take a number, they said," Marcus mumbled, his voice carrying no inflection as he shifted his weight to his left leg and stared blankly at the peeling yellow paint on the wall.

I scrolled down my feed. Swipe. An ad for shoes. Swipe. A meme I saw three weeks ago. Swipe. Someone's breakfast. I sighed, letting the phone drop onto my chest and staring at the popcorn ceiling. I tried to find shapes in the stucco. That one looked like a cloud. That one looked like another cloud. From the doorway, Leo cleared his throat. "Ich habe Deutsch gelernt, um deine Großmutter zu überraschen," he said, his pronunciation rigid but completely accurate. I didn't lift my head from the pillow. My German. For my grandmother. I picked my phone back up, holding it above my face, and refreshed the feed. The same ad for shoes appeared. "She's deaf," I replied in a monotone voice, swiping past the shoes and letting my eyes glaze over the glowing screen.

The ceiling fan wobbled on its axis, making a rhythmic clicking sound every time it completed a rotation. Click. Whoosh. Click. Whoosh. Maya lay flat on her back on the rug, her arms spread wide, watching the blades blur into a dusty circle. She had been lying there for forty-five minutes. Sam walked into the living room, holding a textbook. "Wo xue le san ge yue de Zhongwen," he said, standing over her. Maya didn't move her eyes from the wobbly fan base. Mandarin. Three months of secret studying, just for her. She slowly brought her hands together and intertwined her fingers over her stomach. The fan clicked again. "Can you turn the speed down to one?" she asked, her voice hollow, not bothering to lift her head from the carpet.

The professor's voice droned on, a steady, unchanging frequency that blended perfectly with the hum of the overhead fluorescent lights. I used my pen to shade in the little circles in the letter 'O' on my syllabus, making sure each one was perfectly black. Once I finished the 'O's, I started on the 'P's. My boyfriend, auditing the class beside me, slid a folded note onto my desk. I unfolded it slowly, expecting a doodle. Instead, written in flawless Arabic script, it read: I am learning this so I can read your favorite poems. I stared at the elegant curves of the ink. I folded the paper exactly along its original creases, set it aside, and moved my pen to the first 'D' on the page, carefully filling the empty space with black ink.

Rain hammered against the bus window, blurring the city lights into streaks of neon. Jamal sat slumped in the corner seat, his hood pulled up, watching a stray wrapper slide back and forth across the sticky rubber floor as the vehicle lurched through traffic. Stop. Go. Slide. Stop. Go. Slide. Beside him, Kevin pulled out an app on his phone and confidently read aloud, "Siyabonga ukuba empilweni yami." Jamal slowly turned his head. Zulu. A perfect, melodious string of Zulu. He stared at Kevin's bright, eager eyes for a few seconds, listening to the hissing air brakes of the bus. Jamal turned his face back to the rain-streaked glass, his expression slack. "We're four stops away," Jamal muttered, watching the candy wrapper slide toward his muddy sneakers again.

The text message flashed across my wife’s unlocked screen: *Surprise party is a no-go. Tell everyone to stay home.* I stared at the illuminated letters for a moment, then shifted my gaze to the blank television. I rested my chin in my palm, feeling the heavy rhythm of the grandfather clock in the hallway. Tick. Tock. Tick. Tock. I picked at a loose thread on the sofa cushion, unraveling it millimeter by millimeter. The house was completely silent, save for the distant hum of the refrigerator. I let out a long, slow exhale that ruffled my bangs. With a heavy arm, I picked up the remote and began clicking through the channels. News, infomercial, static, news. Nothing caught my eye. I let the remote drop onto the carpet, leaned my head back against the cushions, and counted the water stains on the ceiling.

Marcus spun slowly in his ergonomic office chair, watching the grey cubicle walls blur into a continuous, muted stripe. On his monitor, an accidental CC on an email thread revealed that his team’s surprise afternoon birthday bash in the breakroom had been called off due to budget cuts. He stopped spinning and clicked his retractable pen. Click-clack. Click-clack. He rested his cheek against the cool wood of his desk, his eyes glazing over as he stared at a blinking cursor on a blank spreadsheet. Thirty minutes until five o'clock. He dragged his mouse in meaningless figure-eights across the mousepad, watching the little white arrow loop endlessly on the screen. The fluorescent lights overhead buzzed with a flat, electric drone. Marcus sighed, letting his eyelids droop half-shut, and waited for the digital clock in the corner of his screen to change from 4:30 to 4:31.

Sitting across from Sarah at the diner, I saw the group chat pop up on her phone resting between the salt and pepper shakers. *Venue flooded. Abort the surprise party for tonight.* Sarah hastily flipped her phone over, but I had already read it. I didn't say anything. Instead, I grabbed my straw and began stirring my iced tea, watching the ice cubes clink against the glass in slow circles. Around and around. I propped my elbow on the sticky table, resting my heavy head in my hand. Outside the window, a single plastic bag drifted across the empty parking lot, caught in a lazy breeze. I took a sip of the watered-down tea, tasting nothing but melted ice. "So," I said, my voice entirely flat, "what are we doing?" Sarah shrugged. I returned to stirring my drink, listening to the rhythmic clinking of the ice.

Through the thin floorboards, Leo heard his mother’s hushed voice on the landline, canceling the secret basement party they had been planning for his graduation. The pizza place had lost their order. Leo lay flat on his bed, his legs dangling off the edge, tossing a tennis ball straight up at the ceiling. Thud. Catch. Thud. Catch. He followed the ball's trajectory with half-open eyes. The afternoon sun cast long, unmoving shadows across his carpet. He let the ball drop, rolling away to gather dust under his dresser, but he didn't move to retrieve it. He simply lay there, staring at the popcorn texture of the ceiling, tracing the bumps with his eyes. Ten minutes passed. Then twenty. He crossed his arms over his chest, listening to the muffled drone of a lawnmower down the street, waiting for the sun to finally set.

I opened the hall closet to grab a jacket and saw a deflated bundle of "Happy Birthday" balloons shoved carelessly into a trash bag. Stuck to it was a Post-it note: *Surprise cancelled. Pipe burst at the hall.* I stared at the limp silver mylar for several seconds before closing the door. Walking into the living room, I collapsed onto the rug. I pulled my phone from my pocket and began swiping through my social media feed with a mechanical rhythm. Swipe. Swipe. Swipe. I wasn't reading any of the captions or looking at the photos. The colors simply washed over my screen in an endless stream. I let the phone fall onto my chest and stared at the dust motes drifting lazily through a shaft of sunlight. I let out a prolonged breath, tapping my fingers in a mindless, arrhythmic beat against the floorboards.

Elias stood by the mailbox, holding a crumpled flyer his neighbor had accidentally dropped in his lawn. It was an invitation to his own surprise retirement party, with a jagged red *CANCELLED* stamped across the front due to a scheduling conflict. He slowly folded the paper into a neat square, tucked it into his flannel pocket, and sat down on his wooden porch swing. He gave the ground a gentle push with his boot. Creak. Creak. Creak. He rested his chin on his hands, watching the cars pass on the highway in the distance. One silver. Two black. One red. He counted the seconds between each vehicle, his gaze fixed and unblinking. A fly buzzed lazily around his ear, but he didn't bother swatting it away. He simply sat there, swaying back and forth, matching the slow, heavy ticking of his wristwatch.

My phone buzzed with a message from Chloe. *Hey guys, we have to call off the surprise party for Alex tonight. I'm sick.* I am Alex. I locked the screen and let the phone slip from my fingers onto the mattress. I rolled onto my back and stared up at the blades of my ceiling fan. I clicked the remote to turn it on, watching the wooden paddles spin in a continuous, hypnotic blur. My room was entirely silent. I reached out to pluck a stray piece of lint from my blanket, rolling it between my thumb and forefinger until it formed a tight little ball. I flicked it away. It landed on the rug. I rested my hands on my stomach, matching my breathing to the rhythmic, mechanical whir of the fan, wondering how many rotations it would make before the day was over.

Maya found the catering invoice sitting on the kitchen counter, followed by a voicemail from the company stating the surprise anniversary dinner was officially called off due to the chef's emergency. Maya leaned heavily against the marble countertop, her eyes tracking a single drop of water slowly making its way down the side of the sink. She dragged her feet as she walked into the living room, flopping sideways onto the sofa. She picked up a magazine from the coffee table and flipped through the glossy pages. Flip. Flip. Flip. She didn't read a single word. She just watched the pages turn, listening to the crisp sound of the paper. When she reached the back cover, she tossed the magazine aside. She closed her eyes, letting out a loud sigh that echoed in the empty apartment, and began counting backwards from one thousand.

I walked into the garage and noticed a cardboard box labeled "Party Supplies" shoved into the recycling bin, complete with a printed email thread detailing how my surprise promotion celebration had been scrapped. I stood in the chilly garage, resting my weight against a stack of winter tires. I picked up a stray pebble from the concrete floor and tossed it lightly against the aluminum garage door. Ping. I found another pebble. Ping. I slouched against the rubber tires, my eyes wandering over the shelves of half-empty paint cans and old tools. The scent of gasoline and dust hung stagnant in the air. I crossed my arms, tapping the toes of my sneakers against the ground, listening to the low, continuous rumble of the water heater in the corner. I let my head fall back against the wall, staring blankly at a cobweb.

Victor saw the group chat left open on his husband’s laptop. The surprise weekend getaway with all their friends was officially cancelled because of the incoming snowstorm. Victor slowly lowered the laptop screen until it clicked shut. He walked over to the bay window, resting his forehead against the cold pane of glass. Outside, the world was completely still, blanketed in a flat expanse of grey clouds. He watched a single, leafless branch sway slightly in the wind. He began tracing the outline of the window frame with his index finger, over and over, memorizing the texture of the painted wood. He let out a long breath, watching the condensation briefly fog the glass before fading away. He crossed the room, sat on the edge of the ottoman, and stared at the dark fireplace, resting his heavy chin in the palms of his hands.

The restaurant hostess accidentally handed me the reservation book, pointing out where my "Surprise 30th - CANCELLED" was scrawled in red ink. My friends couldn't make the flight. I handed the book back with a slow nod and walked over to the waiting area. I sat down on a velvet bench, my posture sinking until my shoulders touched my ears. I pulled a loose receipt from my pocket and began folding it. Half. Half again. A tiny triangle. I unfolded it, flattening the creases with my thumb, and started the process all over again. The low murmur of diners and clinking silverware washed over me in a steady, monotonous wave. I stared at the pattern of the carpet—interlocking geometric diamonds—following the lines with my eyes until they blurred together. I rested my elbows on my knees, letting out a heavy, drawn-out sigh.

The banner reading "Surprise!" was stuffed unceremoniously into the back of her roommate’s car, along with a note that the park wouldn't allow their gathering. Clara closed the trunk with a soft click. She walked back into the apartment and laid facedown on the living room rug. Her arms were splayed out to the sides. She turned her head to the left, watching a line of ants march in a perfect, uniform row along the baseboard. She rested her cheek against the carpet fibers, tracking the insects’ painfully slow progress toward a crumb. She drummed her fingertips against the floor in a slow, aimless rhythm. The grandfather clock in the hallway chimed two o'clock. Clara closed her eyes, her face completely slack, listening to the endless ticking of the second hand as it marched in a circle, just like the ants.

Arthur clicked his ballpoint pen: click-clack, click-clack. The office clock ticked in a painfully slow rhythm. He spun his swivel chair a half rotation to the left, then dragged his loafers against the carpet to spin back. With a heavy sigh, he refreshed his personal email for the seventh time this hour. A notification from AncestryGenetics popped up. He rested his chin in his palm, lazily dragging the cursor to click the link. The screen loaded a pie chart, followed by a bold text box: Zero genetic matches to paternal or maternal lineage submitted. The words Non-Biological Child floated on the screen. Arthur blinked slowly at the glowing monitor. He let out a long, loud breath, picked up his lukewarm coffee, took a sip, and minimized the window. He leaned back, staring up at the fluorescent ceiling lights, waiting for five o'clock.

Rain drummed a relentless, steady rhythm against the bedroom window. I rolled onto my back, letting my arm dangle off the edge of the mattress, my phone hovering above my face. I dragged my thumb down the screen, swiping past the same three advertisements. The notification from the DNA registry finally chimed. I tapped it, stifling a yawn with the back of my hand. The page took forever to load. Finally, it showed my family tree. Under my parents' names, the line was broken, tagged with a prominent Adopted/No Biological Link tag. I stared at the bold red letters for a long moment, listening to the drip-drip-drip of the gutter outside. I locked the screen, tossed the phone onto the tangled blankets beside me, and watched a gray water stain on the ceiling spread imperceptibly.

Chloe tapped her acrylic nails against the steering wheel to the faint beat of a terrible radio commercial. She had been parked in the grocery store lot for twenty minutes, trying to delay going inside. She blew a bubble with her gum, letting it pop lazily before reeling it back into her mouth. Reaching into the passenger seat, she picked up the mail she’d retrieved yesterday. At the bottom of the pile was the DNA diagnostic report. She ripped the paper edge off in one slow, unbroken strip. The document stated starkly that she shared zero DNA with the swab she’d submitted from her mother. Status: Adoption Confirmed. Chloe chewed her gum, her eyes drifting from the paper to a plastic bag blowing across the empty asphalt in front of her car. She sighed, tossed the letter back onto the seat, and reached for the door handle.

The professor droned on about nineteenth-century agricultural reforms, his voice a flat, continuous hum that blurred into the background. I rested my heavy head on my textbook, tracing the wood grain of the desk with my pencil. Desperate for a distraction, I pulled my laptop closer and logged into the genealogy portal. I had sent the spit tube in weeks ago. The results populated the screen. Beside my name, the genetic markers flashed a stark mismatch with the rest of the uploaded family profiles, clearly labeling me as a non-biological adoptee. I rested my cheek against the cool desk surface, keeping my eyes half-open as I read the clinical breakdown of my true heritage. The professor switched to a slide about crop rotation. I let out a long, silent breath, minimizing the DNA results to pull up solitaire instead.

Marcus watched the washing machine drum spin in endless, sudsy circles. Left, then right. Left, then right. He let his head loll against the cold glass of the vending machine behind him, tapping his sneaker against the linoleum floor. To pass the dragging minutes, he pulled up his health and ancestry app. He scrolled past the Neanderthal traits and stopped at the family connections tab. The text clearly outlined that his genetic makeup had zero overlap with the parents who raised him, confirming an out-of-system adoption. Marcus rubbed his eyes, letting out a loud exhale that fogged the vending machine glass. He swiped away the notification, locked the screen, and went back to watching a pair of blue jeans tumble over and over in the wash, wondering if the dry cycle would take just as long.

I clicked the remote, jumping from an infomercial about mops, to a black-and-white movie, to a local news broadcast. Nothing held my attention for more than three seconds. I let my arm drop over the armrest, staring at the ceiling fan making its endless, lazy revolutions. My laptop chimed from the coffee table. I dragged myself forward, barely lifting my torso, and opened the message from the genetics clinic. The PDF detailed my genetic sequence, explicitly stating there was no biological connection to the family tree I had provided, officially confirming adoption. I rested my chin on my hands, my eyes drifting back to the television screen where a man was loudly demonstrating the absorbency of a sponge. I reached blindly for the remote, pressed the channel up button, and let myself sink back into the worn cushions of the sofa.

The commuter train rattled along the tracks, the same gray suburban houses flashing by the dirty window. Elena rested her temple against the glass, letting the vibration numb her jaw. She had read every article on her feed and played every puzzle game on her phone. She opened her email and clicked on the link from the genomic lab just for something to look at. The summary page displayed a bright orange banner reading: No maternal or paternal match found within submitted kin pool. Adoption status highly probable. Elena blinked at the glowing letters. A passenger across the aisle coughed loudly. She shifted her weight, crossed her legs the other way, and closed the browser tab. She pressed her face back against the window, watching the rain droplets merge and slide down the glass as the train rolled endlessly forward.

The security monitors displayed six different angles of an empty parking garage. I spun a paperclip around my finger, bending it until the metal snapped in half. It was only 2:00 AM. I groaned, leaning back in the squeaky leather chair, and pulled out my tablet. The DNA test results I ordered last month were finally ready. I navigated through the sluggish menus until I hit the family match section. The screen stated in plain, bold font that my genetic markers proved I was adopted, possessing zero ties to my supposed biological parents. I rested my elbows on the desk, resting my face in my hands, and let out a prolonged sigh. On monitor four, a stray cat walked slowly past a concrete pillar. I tossed the broken paperclip into the trash can and picked up another one from the cup.

Julian slumped in the vinyl waiting chair, flipping through a magazine from three years ago. The smell of ammonia and hairspray hung heavily in the air. He tossed the magazine onto the glass table and pulled his phone from his pocket, desperate to kill the remaining half hour of his mother's appointment. He opened the genealogy app. A new message sat in his inbox. He tapped it, resting his head back against the wall. The text plainly revealed that the DNA swab he submitted held no relation to the woman currently sitting under the drying hood ten feet away, officially classifying him as an adoptee. Julian stared blankly at the screen. He locked the phone, let his arms hang limply at his sides, and watched the second hand on the wall clock tick its way around the dial.

I stared at the seatbelt sign, waiting for the little chime that meant I could finally get up and stretch my legs. The airplane cabin smelled faintly of stale coffee and recycled air. I had already watched two terrible movies and finished my book. Desperate, I paid for the exorbitant inflight Wi-Fi just to have something to scroll. I logged into my emails and found the results from the ancestry site. The first line of the report indicated a complete lack of genetic continuity with my uploaded family data, confirming I had been adopted at birth. I propped my cheek on my fist, looking past the sleeping passenger next to me out the tiny window. Nothing but a blanket of white clouds stretched out endlessly. I sighed, shut my laptop, and closed my eyes, wishing the flight was over.

The digital counter clicked over to number forty-two with a harsh electronic beep. Maya looked down at her ticket: number eighty-seven. She groaned, sliding down in the hard plastic chair until she was nearly entirely horizontal. To avoid staring at the beige walls any longer, she opened the genetic testing portal on her phone. She navigated to the kinship section. A massive red alert stated she shared absolutely zero genetic material with the parents on her birth certificate, indicating she was legally adopted. Maya let out a long, low breath that fluttered her bangs. She rested her phone on her stomach, intertwining her fingers behind her head, and stared up at a flickering fluorescent tube on the ceiling. Another loud beep echoed through the room. Number forty-three. She closed her eyes and let her foot bounce rhythmically against the scuffed linoleum.

The silence in the library was so thick it felt heavy. I rested my chin on a stack of unread sociology textbooks, spinning a highlighter across the table and watching it roll to a stop. I did it again. And again. Eventually, I pulled up my email on the school computer, just for a change of scenery. The genetics lab results were sitting at the top of my inbox. I clicked the PDF icon. The second page held the bombshell: a clear, undeniable genetic mismatch proving I was adopted by the family I grew up with. I blinked slowly at the screen. The librarian shushed someone a few aisles over. I dragged my mouse up to the corner, closed the tab, and picked up the highlighter again, giving it a soft push so it rolled perfectly off the edge and onto the carpet.

I had refreshed the news feed five times in the last ten minutes. My cursor traced lazy figure-eights around the blank spreadsheet on my monitor while the office clock ticked loudly above the hum of the air conditioner. Propping my heavy chin onto my palm, I opened a new tab, typing in real estate websites just to look at places I couldn’t afford. I clicked randomly on my hometown, my eyes heavy and unfocused, scrolling past cookie-cutter suburban lawns. Then, a familiar blue front door stopped my endless scrolling. I blinked, leaning closer to the screen, suddenly awake. The listing read "Charming vintage colonial," but I recognized the crooked porch step where I’d scraped my knee at age seven. The endless afternoon stretched out behind me as I clicked through the photo gallery, staring at the yellow wallpaper of my old bedroom.

Marcus lay flat on his back on the living room rug, counting the faint water stains on the stippled ceiling. Rain lashed relentlessly against the windowpane, trapping him indoors for the third consecutive day. He let out a long, loud puff of air, picking up his phone from the floor and unlocking it with a sluggish swipe. He opened a property app, swiping aimlessly through listings in random states just to give his thumbs something to do. State after state blurred together in a haze of granite countertops and staged living rooms. He swiped right, then left, barely registering the pixels, until a specific oak tree anchored a familiar front yard. Marcus sat up, the phone suddenly gripped tightly in both hands. The beige siding of his childhood home in Ohio stared back at him, complete with the tire swing branch he’d claimed as a boy.

The receptionist’s keyboard clacked in a steady, unending rhythm. I slouched in the stiff plastic chair, flipping through a five-year-old magazine about home décor before tossing it back onto the glass table. I tapped my heel against the linoleum, checking my watch for the fourth time—only two minutes had passed. Desperate for a distraction from the beige walls, I pulled out my phone and typed in my old childhood address, a mindless habit I indulged in when time refused to move. Usually, it just showed a pixelated street view from a decade ago. Today, however, a bright red banner spanned the top of the search results: "New to Market." My posture straightened. I clicked the link, navigating through thirty high-resolution images of the house I grew up in, completely stripped of our old floral curtains and replaced with stark, modern gray furniture.

Elena’s eyelids drooped as the glowing numbers on the security monitor flipped to 3:14 AM. The warehouse cameras showed nothing but static empty corridors, just as they had for the last five hours. She rested her forehead against the cool edge of the desk, tracing the wood grain with her index finger. To keep her eyes open, she dragged her mouse to the browser, navigating to a housing portal and typing in the zip code of her youth out of pure muscle memory. She scrolled with half-lidded eyes, the bright screen illuminating her face in the dark booth. Suddenly, a thumbnail image made her breath catch. It was the Victorian house she’d grown up in. The listing photos showed the grand staircase where she used to hide during thunderstorms, now newly varnished, glowing brightly in the middle of her endless, quiet night.

The train swayed back and forth, the rhythmic clack-clack of the tracks lulling me into a heavy daze. I stared blankly at the back of the seat in front of me, letting out a long sigh as the gray landscape rolled past the smeared window. With an hour left until my stop, I pulled out my tablet, dragging my finger across the glass with zero enthusiasm. I opened a map application, zooming out and panning across the country, eventually dropping a street view pin onto my childhood street in Texas just to look at the neighborhood. Instead of the usual map view, a glowing real estate pin popped up directly over my old address. I tapped it, my posture straightening. The gallery revealed the same old brick fireplace where we hung our stockings, now staged with fake logs and a sleek glass screen.

David’s textbook had been open to the same page on macroeconomic theory for over an hour. He rested his cheek against the cool library desk, a pencil dangling loosely from his fingers, occasionally dropping it just to hear the faint clatter. He sighed, minimizing his essay document and pulling up a real estate website, an aimless habit he used to delay writing. He clicked on his hometown, scrolling past rows of properties with a glazed expression. His cursor drifted lazily downward until it hovered over a familiar wrap-around porch. David sat up slightly, dropping the pencil for good. The listing described a "cozy family retreat," but to David, it was the exact house where he had learned to ride a bike. He clicked through the gallery, examining the familiar backyard where the rusted swing set used to stand, perfectly preserved in digital clarity.

The washing machines hummed in a continuous, deafening drone. I sat on a cracked plastic folding chair, watching my clothes spin in endless, dizzying circles. I kicked a piece of lint across the scuffed linoleum, checked the timer—twenty minutes left—and groaned softly. I pulled out my phone, opening a browser tab and typing in random addresses of places I used to know, just to pass the agonizingly slow minutes. On a whim, I typed in the address of my childhood home in Seattle. The search engine immediately returned a listing with a bright "For Sale" badge. I leaned forward, elbows on my knees. The photos showed my old bedroom, the place where I had plastered glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling. They were gone now, replaced by fresh white paint, but the slanted roofline remained exactly as I remembered.

Sarah stirred her lukewarm coffee, watching the brown liquid swirl in endless, lazy circles. She checked the café door for the twentieth time, letting out a sharp puff of air. Her friend was thirty minutes late, and Sarah had already read the entire menu twice. She slumped back into the booth, propping her feet on the opposite bench, and unlocked her phone. She opened a property listing app, blindly tapping on her home state of Maine. She scrolled with a mechanical flick of her thumb, barely looking at the screen, until a familiar red door caught her eye. She stopped, her thumb hovering over the glass. It was her childhood home. The listing highlighted a "recently renovated kitchen," but Sarah only had eyes for the bay window where her mother used to read, now staged with an unfamiliar velvet armchair.

I tossed onto my left side, then my right, the digital clock glowing an unforgiving 2:47 AM. The ceiling fan spun in a hypnotic, endless rhythm that did absolutely nothing to pull me into sleep. I let out a loud groan, grabbing my laptop from the nightstand. I aimlessly clicked through Wikipedia articles, then local news, and finally, a real estate aggregator, searching for absolutely nothing. I typed in my childhood zip code, my eyes half-shut as I scrolled past overpriced split-levels. Suddenly, a familiar shingled roof jolted me fully awake. I clicked the image, sitting up against the headboard. It was the house I grew up in. The virtual tour took me through the front hall, past the spot where we used to mark our heights on the doorframe, now painted over in a sterile, pristine white.

Uncle Greg had been telling the same fishing story for forty-five minutes. Leo sat at the edge of the living room sofa, his chin resting heavily in his palm, eyes glazed over as he stared at a pattern in the oriental rug. He discreetly pulled his phone from his pocket beneath the coffee table. Desperate for any visual stimulation, he opened a real estate app, typing in the address of his childhood home across the country just to see what it looked like now. A vibrant "Just Listed" banner appeared on the screen. Leo blinked, his posture straightening as Uncle Greg’s voice faded into white noise. He swiped through the gallery, his heart doing a strange flutter as he recognized the oddly shaped kitchen island and the bay window where he used to wait for the school bus every morning.

The quarterly earnings presentation droned on, a cascade of bar charts and corporate buzzwords. I kept my webcam on but angled it slightly upward, letting my eyes drop to my second monitor. I rested my chin on my hand, my fingers drumming a slow, hollow rhythm on the desk as I clicked through a real estate portal. I typed in my hometown, scrolling past rows of beige houses with heavy, blank eyes. Then, a picture of a familiar stone chimney made my hand freeze. I clicked the listing, my eyes widening. It was my childhood home. The presenter's voice became a distant hum as I examined the photos of the backyard. The old oak tree was still there, casting a long shadow over the lawn where I used to spend my summers catching fireflies.

The line of brake lights stretched infinitely into the horizon. Mark put the car in park, leaning his head back against the headrest with a heavy, drawn-out sigh. He drummed his thumbs against the steering wheel, watching a fly buzz aggressively against the windshield. With nothing moving, he grabbed his phone from the cup holder and opened a browser, searching his old childhood address out of sheer lack of anything else to do. The results populated instantly, displaying a carousel of professional real estate photos. Mark leaned closer, completely forgetting the standstill traffic. The listing showcased the familiar wrap-around porch and the large attic window. He swiped through the images, marveling at how small his old bedroom looked now, completely cleared of his childhood posters and replaced with a perfectly made, generic guest bed.

I dragged the mouse across the screen, closing tab after tab of tax documents. A strange PDF caught my eye—an account in Mark’s name with forty thousand dollars. I stared at the numbers. The ceiling fan clicked rhythmically above me: tick, tick, tick. I leaned my chin onto my palm, my eyelids drooping under the weight of the afternoon. A secret account. I supposed I should be angry, or betrayed, or even curious. Instead, I just let out a long, slow exhale that fluttered the stray receipt on my desk. I minimized the window and opened up a game of digital solitaire, dragging a red seven onto a black eight. The clock on the wall said two-fifteen. It felt like it had been two-fifteen for three hours. I rested my head on the desk, staring blankly at the screen.

The rain sliding down the windowpane held more of Evelyn’s attention than the stack of mail in her lap. She sliced open an envelope with a blunt letter opener, not checking the addressee. It was a bank statement. A joint account? No, just David’s name. A balance of over two hundred thousand dollars. Evelyn blinked slowly, her face slack. She dropped the heavy cardstock onto the coffee table, watching it land next to a cold mug of tea. She picked at a loose thread on her sweatpants, pulling it until it snapped. Her husband was hiding a fortune. She rested her cheek against her knuckles, letting out a hollow, heavy breath. The ticking of the grandfather clock echoed in the silent living room. She watched a single raindrop merge with another on the glass, wishing she was asleep.

I found the passbook shoved behind the spare towels in the linen closet. I only looked because I was counting the towels for the third time today, just for something to do. The little blue booklet showed regular deposits—five hundred here, a thousand there, all siphoned away by Sarah over the last decade. My thumb traced the worn edge of the paper. I sat down on the edge of the bathtub, staring at the white grout lines on the floor. They needed scrubbing, but I couldn't muster the effort to get the sponge. I tossed the passbook back behind the folded washcloths and closed the closet door. The house was utterly silent, save for the hum of the refrigerator downstairs. I lay back against the cool porcelain of the empty tub, counting the bumps in the plaster ceiling until my eyes crossed.

Marcus tapped his pen against the desk in a steady, unvarying beat. Tap. Tap. Tap. His wife’s laptop had been left open, a browser window displaying a sprawling offshore investment portfolio solely in her name. Millions. He rested his chin on his free hand, his gaze drifting from the glowing numbers to the dust motes dancing in the shaft of sunlight across the room. He let the pen drop. It rolled off the edge and hit the carpet with a soft thud. He didn't bend down to pick it up. Instead, he swiveled his chair back and forth in slow, lazy arcs. A massive financial betrayal sat right in front of him, yet all he could focus on was the faint, persistent buzzing of a fluorescent bulb in the hallway. He closed the laptop lid, hoping the buzzing would stop. It didn't.

Unpacking my husband's suitcase, my hand brushed against a zippered compartment hidden in the lining. I unzipped it, pulling out a thick, leather-bound ledger. Pages and pages of offshore wire transfers, a secret financial life carefully documented over fifteen years. I flipped through the pages. The paper felt dry. I tossed the ledger onto the mattress. I sat on the edge of the bed, staring at the wall where the paint was starting to peel. I reached out and picked off a small flake, rolling it between my thumb and forefinger until it turned to dust. The television downstairs mumbled in a steady, incomprehensible drone. I lay back on the covers, throwing one arm over my eyes to block out the weak afternoon light, letting the heavy, suffocating quiet of the empty house press down on my chest.

Clara sorted the recycling with mechanical slowness. Cardboard, plastic, paper. She unfolded a crumpled bank receipt she’d pulled from Arthur’s jacket. Available Balance: $85,400. She flattened the paper against the kitchen counter, tracing the printed numbers with a limp index finger. The refrigerator kicked on with a low hum. Clara rested her forehead against the cool marble countertop. She closed her eyes, listening to the hum, letting it vibrate through her skull. Arthur had a secret life. She supposed she should confront him, yell, throw a plate. The thought alone made her want to go back to bed. She crumpled the receipt back into a ball, dropped it into the blue bin, and dragged her feet across the linoleum back to the living room sofa. She sank into the cushions, picked up the TV remote, and began clicking mindlessly through the channels.

I stared at the banking app on the iPad. My wife had forgotten to log out. Half a million dollars sat in a high-yield savings account I had never seen before. I swiped my finger left and right on the screen, watching the menu slide back and forth. Swipe left. Swipe right. Left. Right. The rhythmic motion was almost hypnotic. Outside the window, a squirrel ran up the trunk of the oak tree, stopped, and ran back down. I let out a long sigh, the air whistling faintly through my teeth. I locked the screen, plunging the device into blackness. I leaned my head back against the leather recliner, staring at the blades of the ceiling fan. I tried to calculate how many rotations the fan made in a minute, losing track around forty.

The lockbox in the floorboards was supposed to be empty. James pried it open with a flathead screwdriver, expecting old photographs. Instead, he found stacks of crisp, banded hundred-dollar bills and a passbook in his husband's name. James picked up a stack of bills. He flipped the edges like a deck of cards, listening to the rapid thwppp sound it made. He did it again. And again. The novelty faded quickly. He dropped the money back into the metal tin and let the lid fall shut with a flat clatter. He sat on the dusty floorboards, his shoulders slumped, staring blankly at a spider weaving a web in the corner of the room. It moved so slowly. James watched the arachnid for twenty minutes, his chin resting heavily in his palms, waiting for the sun to go down.

I found the hidden statement while searching for a spare phone charger. A Cayman Islands account, seven figures, all belonging to my wife. I sat cross-legged on the floor, the paper resting in my lap. A fly buzzed lazily around the lamp, hitting the lampshade with a faint thwack every few seconds. I watched it circle, my eyes tracking its erratic loops until they burned. I rubbed my face with both hands, letting out a heavy groan that echoed in the quiet room. The betrayal was sitting right there in black and white, but I just couldn't summon the energy to care. I folded the paper into a crooked paper airplane. I threw it toward the trash can. It missed, landing on the rug. I didn't get up to retrieve it. I just stared at it, waiting for dinner time.

The bank letter had slipped behind the radiator. Sylvia pulled it out, blowing the dust off the envelope. She read the contents without expression. Her husband was squirreling away thousands every month. She walked into the kitchen, the paper dangling loosely from her fingertips. She stuck the statement to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a banana. She pulled out a chair and sat at the dining table, resting her chin on the cool wood. She stared at the grain pattern, tracing a swirl with her thumbnail. The dishwasher gurgled and sloshed in the background. Sylvia let her eyelids drop halfway, her gaze fixing on a single crumb near the edge of the table. She flicked it onto the floor, then rested her head on her arms, letting the low hum of the appliances wash over her.

Going through the glove compartment for registration, I pulled out a leather checkbook. Not ours. Just his. The ledger showed hundreds of thousands of dollars. I flipped through the little blue pages, my thumb smudging the ink. The car engine idled, a low, constant vibration against my legs. I stared through the windshield at the empty parking lot. A solitary plastic bag drifted across the asphalt, pushed by a weak breeze. I watched it tumble over and over until it got stuck against a light pole. I sighed, letting my head loll back against the headrest. The digital clock on the dashboard blinked 3:14 PM. A whole afternoon still stretching out ahead. I tossed the checkbook back into the glove compartment, shut it with a soft click, and watched the blinking colon on the clock.

He discovered the offshore trust documents folded inside a hollowed-out book on her nightstand. Julian sat on the edge of the mattress, the thick parchment resting on his knees. He ran a hand over his face, his fingers pulling at his lower eyelids. He let out a loud, shuddering yawn that watered his eyes. Millions of dollars, secretly stashed away. He looked at the paperwork, then looked at the blank television screen across the room. He picked up the remote and turned it on, leaving it on a muted home shopping channel. He watched the host silently demonstrate a vacuum cleaner, his face totally slack. The documents slid off his knees onto the floor. Julian didn't look down. He just leaned back against the pillows, watching the silent vacuum suck up fake dirt over and over again.

The clinking of my spoon against the ice cubes was the only thing keeping me tethered to the present. Three partners had already spoken about Dad's thirty-year tenure at the firm, their speeches blending into an endless drone of tax season anecdotes. I stared at the geometric pattern of the hotel carpet, tracing the maroon loops with my eyes. When Mom nudged me, whispering that I was up next, I let out a long breath that rippled the surface of my ginger ale. I pulled the index cards from my pocket, the ink slightly smudged from how many times I had traced the edges with my thumb. "Right," I mumbled, pushing my chair back with a slow scrape. I trudged toward the microphone, wondering if anyone would notice if I just read the firm's mission statement instead of my prepared words.

Maya rested her chin heavily in her palm, her gaze fixed on a solitary ant navigating the rim of her paper plate. Around her, the backyard buzzed with retired teachers reminiscing about lesson plans and district policies. Her mother’s principal had been holding the microphone for fifteen minutes, his voice a steady hum that faded perfectly into the background noise of the cicadas. Maya checked her watch, then held it to her ear to ensure the second hand was actually moving. It was. Barely. She tore a tiny strip of cardboard from her plate, rolled it into a cylinder, and flicked it into the grass. "Maya, sweetie, get ready," her aunt hissed from the neighboring lawn chair. Maya blinked slowly, dragging her feet as she stood up. She took the microphone, staring out at the sea of beige cardigans.

There were exactly one hundred and forty-two square tiles on the ceiling of the banquet room. I knew this because I had counted them three times since General Hackett began his opening remarks. My speech was folded perfectly into a tiny triangle on the tablecloth, which I flicked back and forth between my index fingers like a sluggish paper football. Dad’s military buddies were roaring with laughter at a joke about a deployment in '98, and I forced the corners of my mouth to twitch upward. I checked my phone under the table. No new messages. I slid it back into my pocket and rested my forehead against my knuckles. Only two more officers to go before they passed the mic to me. I let out a slow exhale through my nose, closing my eyes and imagining the absolute silence of my living room.

Liam stood near the breakroom window, watching the slow crawl of evening traffic on the highway below. The taillights merged into a solid ribbon of red, inching forward with the same sluggish pace as this retirement party. Behind him, the regional manager droned on about his mother’s unparalleled dedication to quarterly margins. Liam took a sip of the lukewarm corporate coffee, swishing it around his teeth before swallowing. He picked a lint ball off his sweater sleeve, rolled it between his fingers, and dropped it into the trash can. Someone tapped a spoon against a glass, signaling the transition to the family portion of the evening. Liam released a heavy breath, dragging his gaze away from the highway. He shoved his hands deep into his pockets and shuffled toward the center of the room, fixing his eyes on a water stain near the ventilation grate.

I used the tine of my salad fork to carve abstract squiggles into the soft linen of the tablecloth. The senior partner had been speaking for what felt like an entire geological era, detailing Dad’s pivotal role in a 1992 corporate merger. I pressed my lips tightly together to trap a yawn, letting it escape as a silent, watering stretch of my eyes instead. The ice sculptures of the scales of justice were dripping steadily into their metal pans, the rhythmic plink, plink, plink capturing my absolute attention. When the applause finally erupted, I blinked, suddenly realizing it was my turn. I pushed up from the chair, my legs feeling heavy and stiff from an hour of sitting perfectly still. As I walked to the podium, I calculated exactly how quickly I could read my cue cards without it sounding like one continuous run-on sentence.

With meticulous precision, Chloe peeled the gold foil label from her soda bottle, ensuring it came off in one continuous strip. The VFW hall smelled of stale beer and floor wax, and the hum of the overhead fluorescent lights provided a constant drone beneath her father's coworkers' speeches. The postmaster was currently recounting a delivery route incident from a decade ago. Chloe rested her temple on the cool glass of her bottle, her eyes half-closed as she watched a dust mote drift slowly through a shaft of sunlight. Her mother elbowed her ribs. "You're up after Steve," she mouthed. Chloe gave a slight, loose-lipped nod. She gathered her crinkled speech notes, smoothing them flat on her thigh with the heel of her hand. Rising from the folding chair, she let out a long, quiet sigh, her gaze fixed securely on the microphone stand.

The gentle rocking of the harbor cruise ship made my eyelids droop. I leaned my elbows heavily against the brass railing, watching a solitary seagull float on an updraft. Inside the cabin, the head nurse of the oncology ward was delivering a heartfelt tribute to my mother’s compassion. I had heard these stories a dozen times at various hospital functions. I tapped out a slow, wandering rhythm on the railing with my thumbs. Someone inside called my name over the PA system. I didn't move for a solid three seconds, just tracking the seagull until it disappeared behind a mast. Pushing off the railing took more effort than I wanted to expend. I dragged my feet across the deck, grabbed the microphone, and cleared my throat, staring blankly at the sea of floral dresses and sensible shoes waiting for me to speak.

Julian slouched in the wicker chair, his long legs stretched out in front of him, crossing and uncrossing his ankles. He had been staring at the exact same fern for twenty minutes while his father’s colleagues discussed soil pH and cross-pollination techniques. Julian reached out, pinched a dead leaf off a nearby potted ficus, and shredded it into tiny green fragments, letting them drift onto his dress shoes. The head researcher’s voice was a low, steady murmur that blended seamlessly with the trickling of the indoor waterfall. Julian rested his chin on his chest, feeling his eyelids grow incredibly heavy. A sharp poke in the shoulder startled him. "It's time," his sister whispered. Julian rubbed his eyes, letting out a prolonged breath. He ambled toward the microphone, his hands shoved deep into his pockets, silently hoping his prepared speech was shorter than he remembered.

I zipped my jacket up to my chin, then unzipped it all the way down. Up. Down. The tiny metal rasp was the only thing keeping my brain active. The athletic director was recounting Dad’s 1985 championship season, a tale I could recite backwards in my sleep. I slumped against the hard plastic of the auditorium seat, tipping my head back to trace the water stains on the acoustic ceiling tiles. I started counting the rows of retracted bleachers on the far wall. One, two, three... I lost track around fourteen and didn't bother starting over. The applause jolted me. "And now, to say a few words, Coach's daughter!" I blinked, running a hand over my face. I stood up, my knees popping loudly in the quiet auditorium, and shuffled down the aisle toward the podium, grabbing my crumpled notes from my pocket.

Marcus had successfully constructed a three-story house out of pink and yellow sugar packets. He was halfway through adding a roof made of creamer cups when the structure collapsed. He didn't react, just stared blankly at the little mountain of sweeteners. At the front of the room, the Chief of Surgery was reading a poem dedicated to his mother’s steady hands. Marcus propped his chin on his fist, letting his gaze drift out the dark window where nothing was visible but his own reflection. He traced a slow circle on the glass with his finger. The microphone gave a sharp squeal of feedback. "Marcus, your turn to honor the guest of honor!" Marcus let his hand fall to his lap. He stood with a lethargic heave, grabbed the index cards he hadn't looked at in a week, and walked to the front of the room.

I sat cross-legged on the floor, dragging a rubber brush through the golden retriever’s fur over and over again. Uncle Dave had cornered the room with a sprawling, meandering story about Dad’s first day at the hardware store forty years ago. Every time Dave paused, I thought the speech was over, only for him to launch into another tangent. I watched the grandfather clock in the corner. The brass pendulum swung left, then right. Tick. Tock. I synchronized my breathing to the rhythm. The dog fell asleep, snoring softly. I stopped brushing and rested my forehead on my knees. Suddenly, my brother’s sneaker nudged my thigh. "You're up, kiddo." I let out a low groan that the dog grunted in response to. Pushing myself up from the rug, I trudged toward the center of the living room, smoothing the wrinkles from my jeans.

Elias sat in the front row, his gaze locked on the reference section directly behind the podium. He read the spine of a blue encyclopedia: Volume 4, D to F. Then he read it again. And again. The university Dean was delivering a deeply thorough, highly detailed history of his mother's contributions to the archiving system. Elias slouched until his shoulder blades touched the seat cushion, his arms crossed tightly over his chest. He tapped his thumbs in a slow, alternating rhythm against his biceps. The air in the room was warm, thick with the scent of old paper and dust, pressing heavily against his eyelids. He blinked slowly, fighting the physical weight of the room. When his name was called, he dragged himself upright, running a hand through his hair. He approached the podium, his expression completely blank, holding a single sheet of paper.

Arthur traced the embossed lettering on the heavy cream envelope with a limp index finger. "Notice of Condominium Conversion," the header declared in bold, uncompromising sans-serif. He dropped the paper onto his laminate kitchen counter, watching it settle next to a stack of grocery circulars. The refrigerator hummed its endless, steady tune. He picked at a stray thread on his gray sweatpants, pulling it slowly until it snapped. They wanted him to buy his unit or vacate by October. He rested his chin on his palm, staring out the window at the brick wall of the adjacent building. A pigeon landed on the ledge, pecked at a fleck of dried mud, and flew away. Arthur picked up his lukewarm cup of water, took a small sip, and wondered if he had enough peanut butter left to make a sandwich before the sun went down.

The landlord’s voice crackled through my phone speaker, buzzing like the trapped housefly bouncing against my living room window. "So, the developers are finalizing the condo paperwork next week," Mr. Henderson was saying, his pitch rising with manufactured excitement. I switched the television to channel four. An infomercial for a hose that expands with water pressure was just ending. "We're offering current tenants the first right of refusal," he continued. I laid my head back against the beige sofa cushions, counting the popcorn bumps on the ceiling. One, two, three, four. I switched to channel five. A man was demonstrating a vegetable chopper. "Did you hear me, Alex?" Henderson asked. I exhaled a long breath, letting the phone slide an inch down my cheek. "Yeah," I murmured. "First right. Sounds great." I watched the man on the screen dice a tomato.

The lobby buzzed with frantic tenant whispers as the property manager taped a large architectural rendering to the mailboxes. "Luxury Condominiums Coming Soon," the banner read. Clara leaned against the brass elevator doors, idly twisting a lock of hair around her finger, uncoiling it, and twisting it again. Mrs. Gable from 4B was waving her arms, her face flushed red as she demanded to know about eviction timelines. Clara looked down at her shoes. The right shoelace was slightly longer than the left one. She slowly dragged the toe of her sneaker across the speckled linoleum, erasing a scuff mark. The manager raised his hands, shouting over the din about mortgage assistance programs. Clara let out a slow, quiet breath through her nose, checking her watch. Ten more minutes until the mail carrier usually arrived. She went back to winding the hair around her finger.

A crisp white envelope slid under my front door, slicing through a dust bunny that had been gathering in the hallway draft. I didn't get up from the rug. Instead, I stayed on my back, watching the ceiling fan lazily push the warm, stale air around the room. After a long while, I rolled over and dragged myself toward the entryway, picking up the paper. It was an official notice. The building was being converted to luxury condos. Buy in, or move out. I tossed the paper onto the coffee table. It landed on a stack of unopened mail. I rested my chin on my knees, staring at the dust bunny the envelope had bisected. It was now two smaller, fluffier clumps. I traced the pattern of the rug with my fingernail, following a faded red vine until it disappeared under the couch.

Elias sat by the café window, stirring his black coffee in slow, uniform circles. Across the street, three men in expensive suits and hardhats were pointing at his apartment building, unrolling large blueprints over the hood of a sleek silver car. His neighbor, Sarah, rushed into the café, slamming her hands on his table. "Did you see? They're turning the whole block into condos! We're being pushed out!" Elias stopped stirring. The spoon rested against the side of the ceramic mug with a soft clink. He watched a bead of condensation slowly roll down the windowpane. "Yep," he said, his voice completely level. He took a sip of his coffee. It had gone cold. Sarah continued to gesture wildly, talking about tenant unions and legal action. Elias rested his head in his hands, watching the cars pass on the street outside, counting the silver ones.

"They're selling the building," my roommate announced, dropping the thick packet of condo conversion documents onto my lap. I didn't look up from my phone. My thumb moved in a steady, rhythmic swipe across the glass screen. A video of a cat jumping. Swipe. A picture of someone's lunch. Swipe. A joke I didn't understand. Swipe. "Did you hear me? We have sixty days to either secure a mortgage or find a new place," she insisted, her voice tight and frantic. I let my hand drop to my side, the screen of my phone still glowing against the couch fabric. I looked out the window at the gray, overcast sky. "Sixty days," I repeated softly, the words carrying no weight. I picked my phone back up. Swipe. Another cat video. "We should start packing, I guess," I murmured, watching the pixels move.

The real estate agent moved briskly through the living room, a laser measuring tape beeping sharply at every corner. "These original hardwoods will polish up beautifully for the condo conversion," the agent chirped, scribbling on a clipboard. Julian sat in the center of the room on a beanbag chair, tossing a tennis ball into the air and catching it. Thwack. Catch. Thwack. Catch. "We'll be out of your hair in just a moment," the agent promised, stepping over Julian's legs. Julian didn't blink. He watched the green fuzz of the ball spin against the white plaster ceiling. The agent rambled about granite countertops and open-concept layouts. Julian let the ball drop. It bounced twice, weakly, before rolling under the TV stand. He stared at the empty space where the ball had been, letting his arms hang loose over the sides of the chair.

My inbox chimed with a high priority message from the property management company. "URGENT: Condominium Conversion Notice," the subject line glared. I clicked it open. The text was a wall of legal jargon about buying options and termination of leases. I minimized the window. I opened a blank spreadsheet. I filled the first cell with the letter A. I moved to the next cell. B. C. D. I highlighted the entire row and changed the background color to a pale yellow. My phone buzzed on the desk—a text from my neighbor freaking out about the email. I let it buzz. I stared at the blinking cursor in cell E1. The office air conditioning hummed a low, steady note. I slowly tapped my spacebar, watching the cursor inch across the white screen, one tiny, empty step at a time.

The elevator jolted as it began its slow ascent to the eighth floor. Taped directly over the floor buttons was a brightly colored flyer: "Exciting Changes! Your Building is Going Condo!" Marcus leaned the back of his head against the mirrored wall. He watched the floor indicator numbers light up. Three. Four. He let out a long, heavy exhale that fogged the glass behind him. The elevator clanked and paused at floor five. No one got on. The doors closed again. Marcus reached into his pocket and pulled out a receipt from the grocery store. He folded it in half. Then in quarters. Then in eighths. He squeezed the tiny square of paper between his thumb and forefinger. The flyer had a QR code for "financing options." Marcus slid the folded receipt back into his pocket and stared out at the metal doors.

The heavy thud of sledgehammers echoed through the floorboards from the vacant unit below mine. They were knocking down walls to create the new open-concept condo layouts. The vibrations rattled the water in my glass, sending tiny ripples across the surface. I sat at my kitchen table, resting my chin on my folded arms. I watched the ripples form, fade, and form again with each strike. My eviction notice sat next to the glass, buried under a coupon flyer and a catalog for a clothing store I never shopped at. Another loud crash shook the floor. I slowly traced the rim of the water glass with my index finger. The sky outside was an uninterrupted sheet of gray. I blinked slowly, listening to the rhythmic, muffled pounding below, and wondered how long it would take for the ice in my water to melt.
