I found myself matching my breathing to the unrelenting swing of the metronome's arm. In, two, three, four. Out, two, three, four. I calculated how many days were left until her piano recital. Thirty-two. The scales started again from the very beginning.

Sarah sat on a wobbly stool in the basement, her chin propped on her hand, her eyes glazed over. Her son, Julian, was meticulously cleaning the vacuum tubes of a 1930s Zenith. "The filaments in this one are totally intact," Julian said, his voice echoing in the concrete room. Sarah blinked slowly. "Uh-huh," she managed to say. She looked down at her own hands, inspecting a small hangnail on her left thumb. She picked at it. The basement smelled of dust and old solder—a smell she once loved, now associated with agonizing hours of sitting completely still. She stared at a water stain on the concrete wall, noticing for the first time that it vaguely resembled a map of South America. Julian began reading aloud from a technical manual. Sarah rested her forehead on the cold metal of the workbench, closing her eyes entirely.

Elias stared at the email from Penguin Random House. "Thank you for your submission..." The cursor blinked rhythmically at the end of the boilerplate paragraph. He rested his chin on his palm, letting his eyes trace the path of a lone housefly buzzing against the windowpane. Tap. Tap. Tap. His index finger hit the desk in a slow, steady rhythm. The prestigious logo at the top of the screen had lost its luster months ago. He highlighted the text, hit delete without a change in his expression, and went back to organizing his paperclips by color. Silver, red, blue. Silver, red, blue. The rejection was the fifth this week, and quite frankly, the pattern of the spreadsheet he was supposed to be filling out for his day job held much more of his attention. He let out a long, flat exhale and checked his watch.

The crisp cream letterhead of HarperCollins lay flat on my kitchen counter. "While we appreciate the opportunity to review The Obsidian Spire..." I didn't bother reading the rest. I already knew the template by heart. I picked at a loose thread on my sweater, watching it unravel in a tiny spiral. I reached for my lukewarm coffee, taking a slow sip while staring at the beige wall above the sink. The paint was peeling slightly near the corner. I made a mental note to fix it someday. I tossed the heavy, expensive paper into the recycling bin with a soft thud, then scrolled through the channels on the small television on the counter. Infomercial, news, infomercial. Nothing caught my eye. The monumental rejection I had built up in my head for years had finally arrived, and I was just trying to decide if I should make toast.

"We wish you the best of luck placing your work elsewhere," the editor from Tor Books wrote. Jenna let her eyes glide off the screen. She leaned back in her ergonomic chair, spinning a half-empty water bottle by its cap. The plastic made a squeaking sound against the wood. Squeak. Squeak. Squeak. She slumped down, her chin resting on her chest, and stared at the dust motes dancing in the shaft of afternoon sunlight. Her dream publisher had finally responded after an eighteen-month wait. Jenna pushed herself up with a heavy sigh, walked to the window, and watched the traffic inch along the highway below. Red taillights, gray pavement. She walked back to her desk, collapsed into the chair, and started playing a game of Solitaire on her secondary monitor, dragging the black four onto the red five with a slow, mechanical drag of her mouse.

Another 'no' from Simon & Schuster sat in my inbox. I let out a long breath that puffed my bangs off my forehead and slumped onto the couch. My eyes drifted from the phone screen to the ceiling fan spinning slowly overhead. One, two, three blades. One, two, three. I drummed my fingers against my thigh in time with the ticking clock on the wall. It was the imprint I had dreamed of since childhood, but I just dragged my thumb across the screen, swiping the email into the trash folder, and stared at the empty inbox. I opened a mobile game, matching three shiny gems to clear a row, then matched three more, staring blankly as the digital bells chimed in the quiet, completely still room.

The letter from Macmillan was embossed with gold foil. Arthur traced the raised letters of the word "Unfortunately" with a limp finger. He yawned, his jaw stretching wide, and rested his head on the cool mahogany of his writing desk. He watched a snail inch across the glass of his terrarium on the other side of the room. The snail moved a millimeter, stopped, then moved another millimeter. Arthur blinked slowly. The rejection of his life's work by his absolute favorite press was sitting right in front of him, but his mind kept drifting to whether he had bought regular or pulp-free orange juice at the supermarket. He folded the thick paper into a haphazard airplane, threw it gently, and watched it nosedive immediately into the wastebasket. He let out a loud, empty sigh and rested his chin in his hands.

I stared at the words "Not a fit for our current list" from the Knopf editor I idolized. I sat perfectly still for ten minutes, listening to the hum of the refrigerator. It had a rhythmic buzz that dipped in pitch every few seconds. I propped my feet up on the desk and stared at my fingernails, noticing that the polish on my index finger was chipped. I peeled a flake of the blue paint off, letting it fall onto the keyboard. The rejection email was still open. I highlighted the word "Not," then un-highlighted it. Highlight, un-highlight. I leaned my head back until I was looking upside down at the bookshelf behind me, reading the titles in reverse. I closed my eyes, let out a slow exhale, and wondered how long it would take for the kettle to boil if I decided to get up.

Sitting in the crowded coffee shop, Marcus opened the attachment from the prestigious indie press he had spent years courting. "Dear Author..." it began. Marcus stopped reading. He set his phone face down on the sticky table and rested his cheek on his fist. He watched a barista wipe down the espresso machine, wiping the same spot in a circular motion over and over. A couple at the next table was arguing in hushed, repetitive whispers. Marcus stirred his Americano with a wooden stirrer, watching the black liquid swirl into a vortex, then slow down, then swirl again as he dragged the stick in circles. His masterpiece was rejected. He let out a prolonged, flat groan that was swallowed by the ambient noise, rested his head on his crossed arms, and stared blankly at the sugar packets sitting in their little ceramic bowl.

The notification chimed right as I was waiting for my laundry to finish. It was from the fantasy imprint at Orbit. I opened it, skimmed the highly standard "we regret to inform you" phrasing, and swiped it away. I sat on the plastic chair in the laundromat, watching the clothes tumble in the dryer. Orange shirt, blue jeans, gray towel. Over and over. Round and round. I rested my chin on my palm, my eyelids drooping under the harsh fluorescent lights. I had spent four years on that manuscript, dreaming of this specific publisher, but now the result felt like reading a terms of service agreement. I tapped my foot against the linoleum. Fifty-two tiles across, forty tiles down. I pulled a piece of lint off my sweatpants, rolled it into a tiny ball between my fingers, and flicked it at the floor.

Diana sat in the passenger seat of her parked car, staring at the physical letter from Scholastic resting on the dashboard. The standard rejection format offered no feedback, no encouragement, just a polite "no." She blinked slowly, the sound of passing cars providing a steady background noise. Whoosh. Whoosh. She rolled the window down an inch, then rolled it back up. She picked up the letter, fanned her face with it a few times, and let it drop onto the floor mat. She stared at the digital clock on the radio. 2:14 PM. She waited. 2:15 PM. Diana leaned her head against the cool glass of the side window, her eyes half-closed. The devastating news she had dreaded all month had arrived, and all she could muster was a wide, jaw-cracking yawn before she started picking at a frayed seam on the steering wheel.

My agent forwarded the rejection from Vintage Books at exactly noon. I read the polite dismissal, my face completely slack. I didn't cry. I didn't yell. I just sat there staring at the word "pass." I picked up a pen and started doodling on a sticky note. First a square. Then a smaller square inside it. Then an even smaller square. I filled the entire yellow pad with nested boxes until my hand cramped. I looked back at the screen. Still rejected. I spun around in my office chair, using my foot to push off the desk, doing three slow rotations before coming to a halt facing the blank wall. I peeled a piece of tape off the edge of my monitor, restuck it, and peeled it off again. I let out a long puff of air and rested my forehead on the cold desk.

The letterhead of Riverhead Books glowed softly on the tablet. Victor swiped past the "thank you but" and reached the bottom of the email in two seconds. He tossed the tablet onto the bed. It bounced once and settled perfectly flat. He flopped down on his back next to it, his limbs splayed out like a starfish. He stared straight up at the popcorn ceiling, his eyes scanning the bumpy white texture. He tried to find shapes in the stucco. That one looked vaguely like a cloud. That one looked like a blob. That one looked like another blob. He had queried them exclusively, waiting six months for this very moment. Victor let out a heavy sigh, rolling onto his side to watch the second hand of his wall clock tick away. Tick. Tick. Tick. He closed his eyes and waited for the afternoon to end.

The long-awaited email from the poetry editor at Farrar, Straus and Giroux consisted of exactly two sentences, both of them a polite rejection. I sat on my porch, holding the phone loosely in my hand. A lawnmower buzzed steadily three houses down. I watched a line of ants march across the wooden deck. One by one, they followed the exact same invisible trail toward a dropped piece of cracker. I leaned forward, resting my elbows on my knees, my chin in my hands. I watched them for twenty minutes. The dream of seeing my chapbook in their catalogue was officially dead. I shifted my weight, letting out a loud, empty breath. I picked up a twig and placed it directly in the ants' path, watching with heavy, half-lidded eyes as they simply walked around it and continued their slow, endless march.

Leo dragged his finger along the windowpane, tracing the slow path of a raindrop. The afternoon stretched ahead, an endless gray expanse of nothing. He sighed, letting his head loll against the back of the armchair. With a heavy thumb, he opened his gaming chat just to stare at the screen. A new picture loaded from 'PixelKnight'—a complaint about the weather ruining their walk. Leo blinked, his posture suddenly straightening. The photograph showed a brick-paved sidewalk, a vintage lamppost, and a green awning that read "Sal's Bakery." Leo pressed his face against the cold glass of his living room window and peered down. The exact same green awning sat directly across the street. He looked back at his phone, the slow ticking of the hallway clock completely forgotten.

I spun my favorite pen around my thumb, over and over, watching the ceiling fan complete its lazy, wobbly circles. Click, whoosh, click, whoosh. My open textbook lay untouched on the bed. I groaned, rolling onto my stomach to check my messages for the twentieth time this hour. My online co-op partner, 'ShadowMage', had just sent a video complaining about a loud noise interrupting their game. I clicked play. A distinct, rhythmic thudding filled my headphones, accompanied by the screech of a megaphone. I paused the video, pulling one earbud out. The exact same thudding and screeching drifted through my open bedroom window. I pushed myself up from the mattress, suddenly wide awake. ShadowMage was listening to the high school marching band practicing right down my street.

Maya slumped further down into the couch cushions until her chin rested on her chest. She flipped through sixty channels of daytime television, settling on a muted infomercial about garden hoses. She blew a stray lock of hair out of her eyes and blindly reached for her phone. Opening Discord, she saw a message from her digital art buddy, 'InkSpill'. "Just saw the weirdest guy unicycling past my window." Maya stopped her thumb mid-scroll. She looked up from the glowing screen and glanced out her apartment's bay window. Down below, weaving precariously through the afternoon traffic on Elm Street, was a man in a neon pink top hat riding a tall unicycle. Maya slowly sat up, her eyes darting between the street and the chat logs.

The spreadsheet on my monitor blurred into a sea of meaningless gray numbers. I rested my heavy head in my palm, tapping my foot against the cubicle wall in a slow, mindless rhythm. Is it really only two o'clock? I minimized the window and opened my chat with 'StarDust99'. We had been swapping memes for months. "Can't believe the coffee cart in the lobby ran out of hazelnut again," they wrote. I stopped tapping my foot. I sat up, staring at the message. The coffee cart? I looked past the edge of my cubicle toward the glass doors of the elevator bank. Our building had a coffee cart in the lobby. I quickly typed back, "Wait, does your lobby have a giant brass globe in the center?"

Julian stared at the blank document, listening to the rhythmic dripping of the kitchen faucet. Drip. Pause. Drip. He rested his forehead against the cool mahogany of his desk, letting out a long, hollow exhale. He picked up his phone, swiping aimlessly left and right on the home screen before finally opening his chess app. His longtime rival, 'KnightRider', had just logged on. Julian sent a quick greeting. "Hey," the reply came, "just waiting for the L train. It's delayed at Belmont station again." Julian lifted his head from the desk, his brow furrowing. Belmont station? He walked over to his balcony door, sliding it open to hear the faint rumble of the transit tracks. Belmont station was exactly three blocks away from his apartment.

I had already stacked my collection of loose paperclips into a pyramid three times. I knocked the metal structure over with a lazy flick of my index finger, watching the clips scatter across the wood. I let out a massive yawn, stretching my arms high above my head, desperate for the afternoon to end. I logged into the guild server, putting on my headset. "Hey," I mumbled into the mic. "Anyone alive?" 'GhostSniper' unmuted. "Yeah, I'm here. Trying to drown out this ridiculous thunderstorm." I frowned, looking toward my drawn curtains. A bright flash of lightning illuminated my bedroom, followed by a violent crack of thunder that rattled my floorboards. "Wait," I said, my voice suddenly sharp. "Are you getting hail right now, too?"

Chloe dragged her cursor across the desktop, highlighting and unhighlighting a cluster of folders. She rested her cheek on the cool surface of her desk, her eyes half-closed as she watched the digital clock flip to 3:14 PM. A notification pinged. Her forum friend, 'Wanderlust_99', had updated their status. "Finally checking out that new vintage bookstore on 5th Avenue." Chloe blinked slowly, the words taking a moment to register. She lifted her head, pushing her chair back. 5th Avenue? She grabbed her jacket from the back of the door. The vintage bookstore they had been messaging about for weeks wasn't just in her state. It was literally at the corner of her neighborhood. The heavy fog in her mind instantly vanished as she grabbed her keys.

The Sunday afternoon stretched out like a vast, empty desert. I lay completely upside down on the armchair, my legs draped over the top, idly watching a spider weave a web in the corner of the ceiling. I sighed so loudly it echoed in the silent room. I pulled my phone from my pocket, opening the language exchange app. 'Kitsune88' sent a voice note. "Sorry I didn't reply earlier," his voice crackled through the speaker. "The fire alarm at my dorm in Miller Hall just went off." I dropped the phone onto the carpet. I scrambled to sit upright, my heart suddenly racing. The shrill, piercing shriek of a fire alarm began blaring through my own ceiling. Miller Hall was my building.

Sam peeled the label off his water bottle in tiny, microscopic strips. He arranged the sticky scraps into a circle on the diner table, resting his chin heavily on his other hand. The waitress wiped the counter in a slow, hypnotic circle. Sam checked his messages for the seventh time. His coding mentor, 'ByteMe', had just sent a photo of their lunch. "Best cherry pie in the world," the caption read. Sam stared at the image. The pie was sitting on a distinctive checkered tablecloth, right next to a cracked yellow salt shaker shaped like a rooster. Sam slowly turned his head to the right. Two booths down, a woman was typing on her laptop, a cracked rooster salt shaker sitting next to her half-eaten cherry pie.

I counted the tiles on my bathroom floor. Seventy-two. I sighed, splashing cold water on my face just to feel something different. Returning to my bedroom, I collapsed face-first onto my mattress and blindly groped for my phone. I opened my chat with 'EchoBass', my long-time music production buddy. "Can't record vocals today," they complained. "There's a massive parade marching right down Oak Street." I rolled over, staring at my ceiling. Oak Street. A faint, rhythmic thumping vibrated against my windowpane. I stood up, walked to the glass, and pulled back the blinds. A brass band was marching past my front gate, tuba players gleaming in the sun. I typed a frantic reply: "What color are the tuba players' uniforms?"

Marcus slouched so low in his patio chair he was practically horizontal. He tossed a tennis ball against the brick wall, catching it with a flat thud. Throw. Catch. Throw. Catch. He checked his phone between tosses. His internet friend of five years, 'LunarMoth', posted a quick update: "Hiding from the heatwave at the Riverwalk Mall food court." Marcus stopped the tennis ball mid-air, clutching it tightly in his palm. He sat up straight, abandoning his slouch. The Riverwalk Mall was a ten-minute drive down the highway. He stared at the screen, the endless, dragging afternoon suddenly evaporating. Throwing the tennis ball into the grass, he rushed inside to grab his wallet and keys, dialing LunarMoth's number for the very first time.

Another hour of refreshing a social feed that hadn't changed. I groaned softly, letting my head thunk against the desk. I picked at a stray thread on my sweater, unraveling it inch by slow inch. Desperate for any distraction, I hopped into the voice channel. "Hey," I said to 'IronClad', the only other person online. "Hey," he replied, sounding just as deflated. "I'm just watching the construction guys tear up the pavement at the corner of 8th and Pine." I froze, the thread slipping from my fingers. I turned my chair toward my window, pulling the curtain aside. Sparks were flying from a jackhammer directly below my third-floor apartment—at the intersection of 8th and Pine. "Are you in the brick building or the stucco one?" I whispered.

I dragged my thumb up the cracked glass of my phone, watching the colors blur together. Another picture of someone’s latte. Swipe. Another lip-sync video. Swipe. I rested my cheek heavily against my palm, staring at the ceiling fan making its endless, slow circles. The phone buzzed lightly against my desk. Notification: @historyhenderson wants to follow you. I blinked slowly at the little blue icon. That was my AP European History teacher. I drummed my fingers rhythmically against my leg, tracing the wood grain of the desk with my eyes. The notification just sat there, waiting for a response, while I let out a long, heavy exhale and tossed the phone onto the bed. I watched a speck of dust drift lazily through a shaft of afternoon sunlight, wondering how many minutes were left until dinner.

Mia rested her chin on her knuckles, letting her eyes unfocus until the textbook pages became a gray haze. She tapped the eraser of her pencil against her notebook in a slow, steady rhythm—thump, thump, thump. Deciding to break the endless quiet, she picked up her phone and began a mechanical scroll through her notifications. A small heart icon caught her attention: Ms. Davis liked your post. She stared at her biology teacher's profile picture, a poorly lit selfie with a golden retriever. Mia let out a prolonged sigh, her shoulders slumping further into the cushions of the sofa. She didn’t smile, nor did she panic. She just watched the battery percentage drop from forty-one to forty, listening to the steady hum of the refrigerator in the kitchen. With a heavy blink, she set the phone face down on the glass table.

The gray highway lines whipped past the passenger window in an endless, repetitive rhythm. I leaned my head against the cool glass, tracing the condensation with a lazy index finger. To pass the crawling hours, I unlocked my phone and swiped down to refresh my feed for the fifth time in ten minutes. Nothing had changed. Among the usual spam was a notification: Mr_G_Chemistry follows you. I stared blankly at the screen, reading the handle twice. It was definitely him, judging by the beaker emoji. I let out a slow breath that fogged up the window again. "Huh," I murmured to the empty car interior, my voice completely flat. I locked the screen, letting the device slip loosely into my lap. I went back to watching the identical trees blur by, counting the mile markers as they emerged from the overcast gloom.

The ticking of the waiting room clock echoed loudly in Leo’s ears, each second stretching longer than the last. He slouched deep into the vinyl chair, his legs stretched out into the aisle. His thumb worked on autopilot, swiping through his Instagram feed without his eyes truly focusing on any of the images. He paused only when a notification dropped down from the top of the screen: Coach_Miller started following you. Leo stared at the gym teacher’s profile picture for a long moment. He rubbed his temples, letting out an audible exhale that ruffled his own bangs. He didn't block the account, nor did he follow back. He simply clicked the power button, plunging the screen into blackness. Tossing the phone onto the empty seat beside him, he returned to staring at the peeling wallpaper, waiting for the receptionist to call his name.

The thick summer heat hung in the air, making it too oppressive to move. I sat on the porch steps, resting my elbows on my knees, watching a line of ants march across the concrete. I picked up a stray twig and snapped it into increasingly smaller pieces. My phone vibrated in my pocket. I pulled it out, my arm feeling strangely heavy. An alert on the screen informed me that Mrs. Gable, my literature teacher, was now following my art account. I stared at the name, my face completely neutral. "Okay," I whispered to myself, the word carrying no inflection. I didn't even click on her profile. I dropped the phone back into my pocket and returned to the ants, watching them carry a breadcrumb toward the grass. The afternoon stretched out before me, an endless expanse of identical, humid hours.

Sarah rested her head entirely on her desk, using her folded arms as a makeshift pillow. The study hall was dead silent, save for the hum of the fluorescent lights. She clicked her mouse aimlessly, highlighting text on Wikipedia and then un-highlighting it. Opening a new tab, she logged into Twitter. A new follower notification popped up. It was Principal Vance. She blinked heavy eyelids at the little icon of the man in his usual gray suit. She clicked a pen with her free hand. Click, clack, click, clack. She didn't feel a rush of anxiety or a spark of amusement. It was just another piece of digital noise. Letting out a long breath that scattered some loose papers, she closed the laptop halfway. She rested her chin back on her arm and began counting the tiny perforations in the acoustic ceiling tiles.

Rain drummed a steady, unchanging beat against the roof. I lay upside down on the sofa, my legs resting against the wall, listening to the ticking grandfather clock. I held my phone above my face, idly scrolling through my followers list to prune inactive accounts. My thumb stopped. There, between my cousin and a bot account, was Mr. Harrison from geography. I stared at his smiling face in the tiny circle. I let my arm drop heavily to my chest, the phone resting against my ribs. The rain kept falling. The clock kept ticking. I blew a stray curl out of my eyes and watched it flutter back down. I supposed I should remove him as a follower, but the effort of lifting my hand back up felt monumental. I closed my eyes, letting the rhythmic drumming of the rain wash over the quiet room.

The bus stop was deserted. Jackson stood leaning against the glass shelter, his hands shoved deep into his coat pockets. He kicked a loose pebble onto the street, watching it skitter into the gutter. Pulling out his phone, he began mindlessly swiping through his social media feed. An alert popped up indicating that Madame Dubois, his French teacher, had viewed his story and started following him. Jackson’s expression remained entirely slack. He let out a slow, deflating breath, watching his breath turn to white mist in the crisp air. He pocketed the phone without a second glance. Shifting his weight from his left foot to his right, he looked down the long, empty road. There was no sign of the bus. He reached down, picked up another pebble, and tossed it toward the drain, listening for the faint splash in the puddle below.

The store was completely empty. I leaned heavily against the cash register, resting my chin on my palm, watching dust motes dance in the fluorescent light. To pass the crawling minutes, I pulled my phone from my apron. A little notification badge sat on my screen. I tapped it with a heavy thumb. Mrs. Albright, my chorus instructor, had sent a follow request. I stared at the screen, my face entirely blank. The store radio played the same pop song for the fourth time today. I slowly locked the phone and slid it back into my pocket. I grabbed a rag and began wiping down the already spotless counter, making slow, deliberate circles. I watched the wet trail evaporate into nothingness, then checked the wall clock. Only ten minutes had passed since the last time I looked. I sighed, leaning back against the register again.

Elena sat in the corner of her aunt’s living room, staring blankly at the floral wallpaper while the adults talked in endless circles about mortgages. She slumped down in the armchair, her legs dangling over the armrest. She unlocked her phone, her thumb swiping downward to refresh her feed over and over, though nothing new appeared. Finally, an alert popped up. Mr. Carter, English Lit, has requested to follow you. She stared at the notification with half-lidded eyes. A distant aunt asked her a question about school. "Fine," Elena replied in a flat monotone, not looking up. She didn't click accept or deny on the request. She simply let the screen go dark and dropped the phone onto the carpet. She picked at a loose thread on the armrest, pulling it slowly until it unraveled, listening to the endless drone of the adults' voices.

My textbook lay open in front of me, the words blurring into a meaningless gray block of text. I rested my forehead against the cool surface of the desk, letting out a long, loud groan. I reached blindly for my phone, just to look at something with a backlight. A notification glared at me: my physics teacher, Mr. Zhao, had requested to follow my private account. I kept my face pressed against the desk, looking sideways at the screen. I blinked once. Twice. My thumb hovered over the notification, but the effort to click it felt like moving through molasses. I pushed the phone away until it slid off the desk and onto the rug with a soft thud. Staring at the blank wall, I started counting the faint scuff marks near the baseboard, waiting for the evening to just be over already.

The rain trickled down the windshield in slow, mesmerizing rivulets. Mark sat in the passenger seat of the parked car, his head tilted back against the headrest. He had been staring at the same spot on the dashboard for twenty minutes. Seeking any kind of distraction, he opened his phone. A little red dot hovered over his notifications. He tapped it lazily. Coach_Higgins wants to follow you. Mark stared at the little icon. His face didn't change. He let out a long breath, inflating his cheeks before letting the air escape slowly through his lips. He tossed the phone into the cup holder. He turned his attention back to the windshield, picking one raindrop at the top of the glass and placing a mental bet on whether it would reach the wiper blade before the drop next to it. He watched it slide, agonizingly slow.

Dean Harrison dabbed his forehead with a handkerchief, stammering through an explanation about a clerical error regarding the prestigious Wellington Grant. Maya rested her chin on her palm, her eyes tracking a slow-moving housefly buzzing against the windowpane. The dean pushed a thick manila folder across the mahogany desk, detailing how the funds were actually intended for a 'Maya R. Lin' rather than 'Maya T. Lin'. Maya tapped her index finger against her cheek in a slow, rhythmic beat. "So, do I have to pack up my dorm today, or..." she trailed off, stifling a yawn behind her knuckles. The dean blinked, taken aback by the flat tone of her voice. She pulled out her phone, noting she had twenty minutes before the dining hall stopped serving those slightly stale tater tots. "Can I go now? I really don't want to miss lunch."

The financial aid email sat open on my laptop screen, glaring in bold red font. RE: Revocation of Apex Engineering Scholarship due to Recipient Misidentification. I scrolled down the four-page legal explanation with one finger, leaning back so far in my desk chair that the springs squealed. The administration had apparently mixed up my student ID with a grad student from overseas. I picked at a loose thread on my sweatpants, pulling it until the seam bunched up. "Huh," I muttered to the empty room. My gaze drifted from the screen to the bare cinderblock wall above my bed. I grabbed a rubber band from the desk, stretched it between my thumbs, and shot it at the ceiling. It bounced off with a soft thwack and landed near my dirty laundry pile. I let my head loll back. Guess I'd need to find a campus job eventually.

The financial aid counselor’s voice droned on like a broken fan. She kept pointing at the highlighted sections of the contract, emphasizing how the Founders Arts Fellowship had been awarded to Julian by mistake. Julian rested his elbows on his knees, staring intently at the carpet's geometric pattern. If he squinted, the intersecting blue lines looked a bit like a squashed frog. The counselor slid a pen toward him, her tone thick with manufactured sympathy as she asked for his signature to formalize the transfer of funds to the correct student. Julian slowly dragged his gaze up to her face, noting the way her left eyebrow twitched. He took the pen, twirled it twice between his fingers, and scrawled his name on the dotted line. "Will there be anything else?" he asked, letting out a long, slow breath as he checked the clock on the wall.

"It says here you're not the designated recipient," my advisor said over the phone, his voice crackling through my earbuds. I stretched my legs out across the stone bench and watched a squirrel dig furiously in the dirt. "The Chancellor's Fund was meant for the other David Miller in the biology department." I rested my head against the cold brick wall behind me, watching a cloud drift lazily past the library tower. "Okay," I said, popping a stale peanut into my mouth. "We're going to have to reverse the tuition credits," he continued, sounding breathless and panicked. "Right." I chewed the peanut slowly, finding it completely flavorless. The squirrel darted up an oak tree, disappearing into the canopy. I let out a heavy sigh, shifting my weight on the hard stone. "Listen, Mr. Vance, my battery is at two percent. Can we just email about this later?"

The senior partners arranged themselves around the glossy mahogany table, wearing matching expressions of grave concern. Clara sat slouched at the opposite end, resting her cheek against her fist. The managing partner explained that the full-ride diversity scholarship she received was a clerical error, intended instead for a candidate at their sister firm. Clara watched the second hand on the oversized wall clock tick forward. Tick. Tick. Tick. She reached out with her free hand and began peeling the paper wrapper off a complimentary peppermint, entirely focused on keeping the delicate paper in one continuous strip. The lawyers exchanged bewildered glances as they paused for her reaction. Clara popped the mint into her mouth, crunching it loudly in the silent room. She slowly blinked her half-lidded eyes. "So, do I just leave the check on the desk, or..." she asked, her voice entirely devoid of inflection.

The official university seal on the letterhead looked like a squashed bug. I stood in the dorm mailroom, tracing the embossed edge with my thumb while reading the text. Error in allocation... intended for... immediate restitution required. I leaned against the metal mailboxes. The fluorescent lights overhead flickered, emitting a steady, low-pitched hum that vibrated right through to my teeth. I folded the letter into a perfect half, then into quarters, then into eighths, pressing the creases flat with my thumbnail. A couple of freshmen hurried past, laughing loudly about a weekend party. I stared at the bare wall opposite the mailboxes, letting my eyes go out of focus until the beige paint turned into a blurry smudge. Dropping the heavily creased letter into the nearby recycling bin, I shoved my hands deep into my pockets and began the long, slow trudge back up to my room.

Professor Higgins burst into the practice room, waving a printed spreadsheet. "Elias, stop playing! The conservatory made a massive blunder. The Virtuoso Endowment wasn't yours!" Elias stopped mid-scale, his fingers resting lightly on the piano keys. He watched the professor gasp for air. Elias played a single C-major chord, letting the sound ring out until it faded into absolute silence. "It belongs to Elena Rostova," Higgins panted, leaning heavily against the grand piano. Elias slumped his shoulders, staring at the empty margins of the sheet music in front of him. He picked up a pencil, mindlessly shading in the loops of the treble clef until it was a solid black blob. "That's unfortunate," Elias said in a low monotone. He dropped the pencil, resting his chin on the music stand. "If you don't mind, Professor, I still have forty-five minutes left in my reserved practice slot."

The head chef pulled me aside just as I was julienning carrots. He held a tablet, his face flushed red as he explained the administration mixed up the recipient of the Parisian Culinary Grant. It was meant for my lab partner. I kept my face completely still, watching a single bead of sweat roll down his temple. I picked up my knife again, slicing the next carrot into identical, millimeter-thick matchsticks. "You'll have to step down from the elite track," he said, waiting for a reaction. I placed the knife down and wiped my hands on my apron, staring at my reflection in the stainless steel prep counter. I let out a slow, drawn-out puff of air that rustled my bangs. "Understood," I said, glancing over at the walk-in fridge. "Am I still required to prep the three crates of pearl onions for dinner service today?"

The stage manager held a clipboard to her chest, whispering the bad news to Chloe in the wings. The drama department's full-tuition waiver had been incorrectly filed. Chloe sat on an upturned milk crate, her legs stretched out in front of her. She picked at a loose thread on her rehearsal skirt, pulling it inch by inch as the stage manager profusely apologized for the department's incompetence. Chloe rested her chin in her hands, her eyes fixed on a dust bunny drifting across the dimly lit wooden floorboards. She let out a long, heavy sigh that fluttered her eyelashes. "This is terrible, I know," the stage manager murmured. Chloe shifted her weight on the hard plastic crate, tapping her heel against the floor in a slow, monotonous rhythm. "Yeah," Chloe said, stifling a yawn with the back of her hand. "What time is rehearsal over again?"

The email from the Dean of Medicine popped up while I was highlighting my anatomy textbook. Due to an algorithmic error, the National Vanguard Fellowship had been awarded to me instead of the rightful candidate. I read the words, then let my gaze drift away. I leaned back in the hard wooden library chair, staring up at the acoustic ceiling tiles. I counted them. One, two, three... twenty-four tiles across. I picked up my yellow highlighter, balancing it perfectly horizontally on my index finger. It wobbled, dipped to the left, and fell onto the desk with a soft clatter. I picked it up and tried again, completely ignoring the flashing notification icon on my screen as a follow-up email arrived. My phone buzzed in my pocket. I let it vibrate against my leg, keeping my eyes fixed on the balancing plastic tube.

The university's financial liaison stood in the drafting studio, clutching a briefcase. He had just delivered the news that Marcus's urban design scholarship was legally void, a victim of a typo in the donor's paperwork. Marcus didn't look up from his desk. He dragged his T-square across the large sheet of drafting paper, drawing a perfectly straight, entirely meaningless pencil line. "We are prepared to offer a payment plan for the tuition you now owe," the liaison offered, his voice tight. Marcus rested his chin on his forearm, his gaze drifting away from his blueprints to watch a pigeon waddling along the exterior window ledge. The bird bobbed its head, pecking at a speck of dirt. Marcus slowly rotated a mechanical pencil between his thumb and forefinger, over and over. "A payment plan," Marcus repeated flatly, letting out a heavy, slow exhale. "Sure. Leave the forms."

The financial aid officer's face filled my laptop screen. He was animated, his hands flying around as he explained how my athletic scholarship was supposed to go to the new point guard, not the backup kicker. I rested my cheek heavily against my palm, watching the pixelated video feed lag and stutter. Every time he froze, his mouth hung open in comical shapes. I started taking screenshots of his frozen expressions, dragging them into a neatly organized folder on my desktop. "Are you understanding the gravity of this?" his voice snapped over the laptop speakers. I blinked slowly, dragging my eyes from the folder back to his face. I slumped lower in my chair, picking at a chipped piece of polish on my thumbnail. "Yes. The point guard. Got it," I mumbled, leaning forward just enough to check the time in the bottom corner of my monitor.

Professor Higgins slammed the printed essay on the mahogany desk, jabbing a thick finger at the highlighted paragraphs. "This is entirely lifted from Wikipedia, Mr. Davis!" Leo didn't flinch. He watched a solitary dust mote drift through the slanted beam of afternoon sunlight cutting across the room. It danced in slow, lazy circles. "Well?" Higgins demanded, his face turning a mottled purple. Leo rested his chin in his palm, his eyes tracking the dust speck as it finally settled on the edge of a stack of graded papers. He let out a long, slow breath that barely ruffled the page. "I guess," Leo said, his voice flat. He glanced at the clock above the door. Three-fifteen. If Higgins dragged this out another ten minutes, he was going to miss the bus, which meant he'd have to wait another hour at the station. "Can I just fail the assignment now?"

The Dean’s voice droned on, a steady, rhythmic hum that blended perfectly with the buzzing fluorescent light overhead. She pushed my term paper toward me, tapping a red-inked URL written in the margins. "Do you understand the severity of academic theft?" she asked, adjusting her glasses. I traced the woodgrain pattern on her desk with my thumbnail, finding a groove that looked exactly like the state of Florida. "Yes, ma'am," I murmured, watching the second hand on the wall clock jerk forward. Tick. Tick. Tick. Thirty more seconds until it hit the twelve. She started listing the university's honor code policies. I shifted my weight, propping my heavy head against my fist, and switched my focus to the slight squeak her leather chair made every time she leaned forward. "Are you listening to me?" she asked. "Honor code, chapter four," I replied, blinking slowly.

The disciplinary panel sat in a semicircle, three stern faces staring down at Maya. Dr. Aris slid the comparative plagiarism report across the table. "Seventy percent match," he announced, crossing his arms. Maya didn't look at the paper. Instead, she uncapped her black ballpoint pen and began drawing interconnected triangles on the back of her syllabus. She shaded the corners of each shape with precise, methodical strokes. "We need an explanation, Maya. This is your final warning." Maya filled in the last triangle, creating a perfect geometric star, then drew a circle around the whole thing. The silence stretched. She let out a soft sigh, rolling the pen back and forth between her thumb and index finger. "It’s the same as the rough draft," she said, her tone perfectly level. She gazed past the panel, out the window, watching a squirrel bury an acorn in the dirt.

"You didn't write this," Mr. Henderson said, blocking the doorway as the rest of the class filed out. He waved my essay on the French Revolution in the air like a white flag. I leaned against the doorframe, letting my backpack slide down my shoulder until it rested on the floor. My stomach gave a loud, hollow rumble. The cafeteria was serving pizza today, the kind with the thick, greasy crust. "The vocabulary is collegiate level," he pressed, stepping closer. I stared at the faint coffee stain on his blue tie. It looked a bit like a sailboat. "It's a good essay," I said, shifting my gaze to the hallway where a janitor was slowly pushing a dustmop. Mr. Henderson was still talking about sentence structure and historical analysis. I tapped my shoe against the linoleum, counting the tiles between me and the exit. Fourteen tiles left.

Principal Thorne’s office was stiflingly warm. While her mother wept quietly and her father vibrated with anger, Chloe sat completely still, peeling a tiny corner of the rubber casing off her phone, then pressing it back down. Peel, press. Peel, press. "This essay was purchased online," Thorne stated gravely. "This violates our core values." Chloe watched her father stand up and begin pacing, his voice rising as he demanded to know how she could do this. She switched to picking at a loose thread on her jeans. It unraveled slowly, curling around her index finger. Her mother blew her nose loudly. Chloe rested her cheek on her shoulder, staring blankly at the ceiling fan lazily cutting through the thick air. "Chloe, do you have anything to say?" Thorne asked. "No," she replied, unwinding the thread from her finger.

My teaching assistant, Greg, cornered me in the quiet section of the library. He slammed his laptop on my table, waking me from a half-doze. "Your code for the final project," he hissed, keeping his voice to a loud whisper. "It's copied straight from a GitHub repository." I slowly rubbed my eyes, letting out a long, gaping yawn that made my jaw crack. "Did you hear me?" Greg demanded, his face inches from mine. I looked at the screen. Yep, that was the code. I leaned back in my chair, stretching my arms high above my head until my shoulders popped, then let them fall heavily into my lap. "I changed the variable names," I mumbled, staring at a fluorescent light bulb that was flickering rhythmically above the stacks. Flicker, buzz, flicker. "That doesn't make it yours!" he whispered furiously. I rested my chin on my hand.

Mrs. Gable towered over Toby's desk, her lips pressed into a thin, white line. "I ran your book report through the plagiarism checker," she announced to the silent classroom. Toby blinked slowly, his eyes heavy. He picked up his yellow pencil and began rolling it back and forth across the slanted groove at the top of his desk. It made a soft, wooden rattle. "It came back as ninety-nine percent copied," she continued, her voice echoing off the cinderblock walls. Toby watched the pencil roll. Back, forth. Back, forth. He wondered how many times he could roll it before the bell rang. He checked the clock. Two whole minutes. He let his head sink down until his cheek rested flat against the cool laminate of the desk, keeping his eyes fixed on the pencil. "Toby!" Mrs. Gable snapped. "Okay," Toby said quietly, closing his eyes.

Dr. Vance’s face took up my entire monitor, his webcam angled so low I could see straight up his nose. "This paragraph on photosynthesis," he was saying, his audio cutting out slightly every few seconds. "It is word-for-word from the textbook." I minimized his face, dragging his Zoom window to the bottom corner of the screen so I could scroll through my social media feed. "Are you understanding the implications here?" his tinny voice crackled through my cheap headphones. I clicked 'like' on a video of a cat falling off a couch. "Yeah, word-for-word," I replied, my voice a flat monotone. I opened a new tab and started looking up keyboard prices. Dr. Vance was still talking, his mouth moving in jagged, pixelated bursts. I rested my forehead in my palm, clicking my mouse rhythmically against the pad. The router lights blinked steadily on my desk.

Coach Miller intercepted Jason by the lockers, a crumpled sheet of paper clutched in his fist. "The history department says you stole this essay," Miller growled, blocking the way to the gymnasium. "If you fail history, you're off the team." Jason blew a bubble with his chewing gum, letting it grow until it popped with a wet snap. He peeled the pink residue off his lip, staring at the scuff marks on the linoleum floor. "Did you hear me, son?" Miller demanded. Jason leaned back against the cool metal of the lockers, his eyelids drooping. He pulled his phone from his pocket, checked the blank lock screen, and slid it back in. "Yeah, history," Jason muttered. He shifted his weight, tapping his sneaker against the baseboard in a slow, steady rhythm. Miller continued his lecture about integrity. Jason blew another bubble, watching it expand.

"I found this exact same poem on a blog from 2014," Sarah whispered aggressively, sliding my paper back across the library table. She looked appalled, her eyes wide behind her thick glasses. I rested my chin on my crossed arms, staring at the spinning loading icon on my laptop screen. "You literally just changed the title," she hissed, looking around as if the poetry police were about to raid the study room. I let out a heavy breath that fluttered the corner of the paper. "Cool," I said, my voice completely devoid of inflection. I picked up a paperclip from the table and started bending it out of shape, straightening the wire until it was just a jagged line of metal. Sarah was going on about artistic integrity. I tossed the straightened paperclip into my open backpack and reached for another one, stifling a massive yawn.

Professor Lin stood before Elias's easel, her arms crossed tight. "This character design," she said, pointing a laser pointer at the canvas, "is a direct trace of a concept from a popular video game. We run image-matching software now, Elias." Elias slouched on his drafting stool, resting his cheek against his fist. He was watching a fly buzz repeatedly against the studio windowpane. Thump, buzz, thump. "Plagiarism in the visual arts is career suicide," Lin warned, her voice echoing in the vast studio. Elias slowly blinked. He spun his stool in a lazy half-circle, facing the blank wall opposite the easel. "Okay," he said, his tone perfectly flat. He dragged the toe of his shoe across the paint-splattered floorboards, tracing the outline of an old crimson stain. Lin waited for a defense, a tear, an apology. Elias just let out a long, rattling sigh.

The guidance counselor slid into the desk next to mine. "The English department sent me your mid-term," Mr. Brooks said softly, adopting his best deeply-concerned tone. "They found the exact same text submitted by a student three years ago." I kept my eyes fixed on the ceiling tiles. I had already counted forty-two of them, and I was trying to figure out if the room was a perfect square. "Did you buy this from an upperclassman?" he asked, leaning in closer. I let my head roll to the side so I was looking at him. His tie was slightly crooked. "No," I murmured, turning my head back to the ceiling. Forty-three, forty-four. He started explaining the long-term consequences of academic dishonesty on college applications. I pulled my sleeve down over my hand and began polishing a smudge on my desk, moving my arm in slow, monotonous circles.

I opened the envelope from the Financial Aid Office with the exact same energy I reserved for watching laundry spin. The letter began with "We regret to inform you," which was how the last fourteen letters had started. I leaned my cheek against the heel of my hand, using my free hand to fold the thick parchment into a lopsided paper airplane. It flew halfway across the room before nose-diving into the trash can. I drummed my fingers against the laminate desk, staring at the rhythmic ticking of the wall clock. Tick. Tick. Tick. Three more rejection letters were probably in the mail, but tracking them down felt like too much effort. I let out a long, slow breath, resting my head flat on the wood. The grain of the desk was slightly crooked. I traced the little spirals with my thumbnail, wondering if the cafeteria was open yet.

Marcus didn't even blink when the bold red "STATUS: DENIED" popped up on the college portal. His mother had made him apply for the Merriweather Grant, insisting it would build character. He slumped into the plush leather sofa, letting the phone drop onto his chest. He stared up at the crystal chandelier hanging from the vaulted ceiling, counting the individual glass droplets. Thirty-two on the outer ring. Sixteen on the inner. He reached over to grab a handful of popcorn from the silver bowl, chewing slowly. The scholarship was only for a few thousand dollars anyway, barely a fraction of his trust fund. He picked up his phone again, swiping past the rejection email to open a mobile game. His thumb tapped rhythmically against the screen, harvesting digital corn while his mother's footsteps echoed down the grand hallway to ask him if he had checked the portal yet.

The counselor pushed the rejected foundation application across his cluttered desk. I didn't look at the paper. Instead, I kept my eyes fixed on the window behind him, watching a singular gray pigeon peck at a discarded fry on the pavement. "They went with another candidate," Mr. Harrison said, his voice dropping into a somber, practiced whisper. I rested my chin on my palm, blinking slowly as the pigeon finally swallowed the fry. "Okay," I muttered, my voice perfectly flat. Mr. Harrison leaned forward, interlacing his fingers. "We can look at other options." I dragged my gaze away from the window, tracing a faded coffee ring on his desk pad. My foot tapped a slow, endless rhythm against the linoleum. "Do I need to sign anything, or can I just go back to study hall?" I asked, letting out a heavy, dragging sigh. The pigeon had already flown away.

Sarah stood in the financial aid office line for forty-five minutes just to be handed a slip of paper that said her merit award was canceled. She stared at the blue ink stamp marking her file 'DENIED', her face completely expressionless. The fluorescent lights overhead buzzed with a relentless, mechanical hum. She shifted her weight from her left foot to her right, staring at the scuff marks on the tile. A student next to her was crying over a tuition bill. Sarah just rolled her shoulders, her eyes wandering up to a faded poster about campus safety. She read the bullet points backwards. Safe. Be. To. Remember. She folded the rejection slip into tiny, neat squares until it was the size of a postage stamp, then tucked it into her pocket. The line shuffled forward an inch. She checked her watch, hoping the campus bus wasn't running late.

My laptop chimed with a new notification right in the middle of Professor Lewis's two-hour lecture on macroeconomics. I clicked it open. The subject line read 'Update on Your Presidential Scholarship Application'. I skimmed the first sentence, saw the word 'unfortunately', and immediately dragged the message to the trash folder. Professor Lewis was drawing a massive supply and demand curve on the whiteboard, talking on and on about market equilibrium. I rested my head heavily against the cinderblock wall beside my desk. The bricks were cold against my temple. I opened a blank document and started typing out the lyrics to a jingle from a car commercial I saw last night. When I ran out of lyrics, I highlighted all the text, changed the font to Comic Sans, increased the size to 72, and changed it to neon green. The clock on the wall said we still had forty minutes left.

Chloe methodically slit open the envelope with a butter knife. The kitchen was quiet except for the hum of the refrigerator. She pulled out the letter from the arts foundation, her eyes scanning the dense, formal text. Denied. She tossed the paper onto the granite counter, not even bothering to read the second paragraph. She propped her elbows on the island, resting her chin in her hands, and watched a solitary ant crawl across the tile backsplash. It moved erratically, stopping at a fleck of dried tomato sauce before turning left. Chloe let out a long breath, blowing a stray strand of hair out of her eyes. It fell right back onto her forehead. She blew on it again. The letter sat untouched next to a bowl of fruit. She picked up a bruised Gala apple, turning it slowly in her palm, inspecting the mottled skin without taking a bite.

"Did you get the email?" Liam asked, leaning over my shoulder in the student lounge. I scrolled down my phone screen, my thumb swiping at a sluggish, rhythmic pace. "Yeah," I murmured, staring blankly at the rejection notice from the STEM diversity board. "Me too," he groaned, rubbing his face. "This ruins everything. What are you going to do?" I shrugged, locking my phone screen and tossing it onto the table. It slid a few inches and bumped into a napkin dispenser. I slouched lower into the beanbag chair, letting my arms dangle toward the carpet. "Nothing," I said, watching a piece of lint stuck to the toe of my sneaker. I tried to flick it off by rubbing my shoe against the table leg, but it stayed stubbornly attached. "I guess I'll just take out the loans," I muttered, my jaw stretching wide in a massive, noisy yawn.

The mailbox hinge squeaked as Julian pulled down the metal door. He shuffled through the stack: a grocery circular, a bill, and a crisp white envelope from the university trust. He ripped the flap open right there on the sidewalk. As his eyes glazed over the standard 'unable to offer you funding' paragraph, his expression remained entirely slack. He dropped the letter back into the envelope, his shoulders dropping in a slow slump. A neighbor's dog was barking in a slow, steady rhythm three houses down. Ruff. Pause. Ruff. Pause. Julian leaned his back against the brick mail post, staring up at the power lines stretching across the suburban sky. A pair of sneakers dangled from the highest wire, the laces knotted together. He stood there for a full five minutes, listening to the dog bark, before turning around to walk inside, leaving the mail sitting abandoned on the concrete porch step.

I sat in the dim glow of the library computer monitor, clicking the refresh button on the financial aid portal. Finally, the page loaded. Application Status: Unsuccessful. I rested my forehead in my palm and dragged the mouse in slow, deliberate circles, watching the little white arrow loop endlessly around the center of the screen. Loop, loop, loop. The guy at the desk next to me was furiously typing an essay, his fingers hammering the keys. I let out a heavy puff of air, making my lips vibrate in a soft horse-noise. I minimized the browser and opened the computer's built-in solitaire game. I moved a red seven onto a black eight. Then a black six onto the red seven. The rejection meant I'd be working at the bookstore again, but right now, my biggest concern was that I didn't have any moves left for my two of clubs.

Nina sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor, surrounded by neatly organized stacks of college documents. She opened the latest letter from the Rotary Club and scanned the polite refusal. Without a change in her blank expression, she placed the paper onto the 'Rejected' pile, which was now noticeably taller than the 'Accepted' pile. She slumped backward, lying flat on the carpet, and stared at the popcorn ceiling. She raised her arm, pointing her index finger at the plaster bumps and tracing invisible constellations between them. There was a bump that looked like a star, and another that looked like a lopsided shoe. She let her arm flop heavily back down to the floor. The rejection meant her budget was tighter, but she simply rolled onto her side, picking at a loose thread on her sock until it began to unravel completely.

"So what did the letter say?" my dad asked, his pixelated face freezing on the screen due to bad Wi-Fi. I held up the crisp rejection letter from the alumni association, blocking my webcam entirely. "Denied," I said, my voice flat and perfectly level. I dropped the paper onto my desk. "Oh, honey, I'm so sorry," my mom chimed in, leaning into the frame. I slumped back in my chair, resting my chin on my chest. "It's fine," I mumbled, peeling a worn sticker off my water bottle. The adhesive left a sticky residue. I rubbed my thumb over the gunk, rolling it into tiny gray balls. My dad started talking about alternative loan options, his voice buzzing through the tinny laptop speakers. I nodded slowly, timing my head bobs to the flashing green light on my router, tuning out the noise completely.

Elias sat at a corner table in the busy cafe, his iced coffee sweating a puddle of condensation onto the wood. He swiped down on his tablet, reading the rejection notification from the athletic scholarship committee. He didn't flinch. Instead, he locked the screen and stared at the water ring. He dipped his index finger into the moisture and slowly dragged it across the table, connecting the puddle to a rogue breadcrumb. The cafe was loud, filled with the clatter of porcelain and overlapping chatter. Elias rested his head on his hand, his eyelids drooping halfway. He watched the barista wipe down the espresso machine with agonizing slowness. Wipe left. Wipe right. Elias stirred his completely melted iced coffee with a plastic straw, the ice cubes having long since disappeared. He took a sip of the watered-down drink, chewing rhythmically on the flattened end of the plastic straw.

The email subject line read 'Important Updates Regarding Your Advising.' I clicked it, my chin resting heavily in the palm of my hand. Dr. Aris was transferring to Stanford. I watched a fruit fly circle my lukewarm coffee mug. It landed on the rim, walked a millimeter, stopped, then walked another millimeter. I dragged my mouse down the screen to skim the transition plan. Three paragraphs of administrative text. I clicked my pen. Click, clack. Click, clack. The lab clock ticked in perfect sync with my pen. Someone down the hall dropped a book, the muffled thud the most exciting thing to happen in the last hour. I supposed I needed to find a new supervisor for the cell biology project. I picked up a paperclip, slowly bending it until the metal snapped, then tossed the pieces into the wastebasket.

Maya stared at the text message from Professor Vance announcing his departure, then went back to peeling the label off her empty water bottle. She scraped a sliver of adhesive with her thumbnail, rolling it into a tiny grey ball. Vance was leaving for a corporate job in three weeks, effectively stranding her thesis on medieval economics. She exhaled a long, flat breath and rested her head on the cool surface of the café table. The barista wiped the counter in slow, sweeping arcs. Maya watched a drop of condensation slide down the windowpane, tracing its meandering path until it hit the sill. She picked up a stray sugar packet, flipping it end over end between her index finger and thumb. The prospect of explaining her dissertation topic to a new faculty member felt like a chore she might just put off until November.

'As you may have heard, I will be accepting a tenure position at Oxford,' Dr. Hemlock announced from the podium. I rested my forehead on my desk, tracing the deep scratches carved into the wood by previous students. Someone had carved 'J+K' inside a jagged heart. I colored it in with my highlighter. Hemlock kept talking about transition committees and academic continuity. I counted the ceiling tiles. Forty-eight across, twenty-two deep. A girl two rows ahead of me was playing Solitaire on her laptop, and I caught myself silently rooting for her to move the black eight onto the red nine. Hemlock cleared his throat, adjusting his glasses. I suppressed a yawn, stretching my legs out until my sneakers bumped the seat in front of me, wondering if the dining hall was serving those soggy tater tots again today.

David sat in the swivel chair, spinning slowly in half-circles while Dr. Lin explained her sudden resignation. 'The grant money fell through, so I am relocating to the private sector,' she said, organizing her files. David picked up a pipet tip, balancing it perfectly on the end of his index finger. It wobbled and fell to the linoleum. He didn't pick it up. Instead, he pulled a loose thread on his sweater, watching it unravel inch by inch. He had spent two years working under Lin on this polymer research. Now, he would have to start over. He leaned back, staring up at the flickering fluorescent light that had been humming in a steady, continuous pitch since September. 'Okay,' David murmured, his voice flat. He grabbed a blank sticky note and started drawing interconnected triangles, filling in every other space with heavy black ink.

The little green box illuminated around Professor Chen’s face as he explained his decision to take an indefinite sabbatical. I muted my microphone and turned my camera off. Leaning back on my bed, I tossed a tennis ball at the ceiling, catching it as it dropped. Thump. Catch. Thump. Catch. Chen’s voice droned on through the laptop speakers about finding alternative mentorship. I pulled my phone from my pocket and swiped through social media, barely registering the images as they scrolled past my thumb. A cat video. A cooking tutorial. An ad for shoes. Thump. Catch. I realized I hadn't heard a word Chen said for the last five minutes. I sat up, typed 'Understood, thanks' into the chat box, and went back to the tennis ball. I counted to one hundred, trying to see if I could hit the exact same smudge on the plaster.

Elias leaned against the brick wall outside the faculty lounge, listening to his advisor, Dr. Sterling, tell him about moving to a research institute in Geneva. Elias rhythmically tapped the heel of his boot against the baseboard. Tap... tap... tap. He watched a line of ants march along the grout between the floor tiles. One ant was carrying a crumb of a potato chip. Elias tracked its progress for a solid two minutes while Sterling outlined a list of potential replacement advisors. 'Are you getting all this, Elias?' Sterling asked. Elias blinked, shifting his weight to his other leg and shoving his hands deep into his pockets. 'Yeah. Geneva. Replacements.' He let out a long, heavy exhale that puffed his bangs off his forehead. He stared at the brass doorknob on the lounge door, wondering how long it would take to tarnish.

The campus newsletter lay open on my desk in the library, the headline declaring 'Dr. Harrison Departs for European Fellowship.' I rested my cheek flat against the cool pages of my open textbook. My thesis on Victorian literature was currently orphaned. I picked up a pencil and began shading in all the letter 'O's on the page of the newsletter. There were forty-two in the first column alone. The quiet hum of the library's HVAC system was a heavy blanket pressing down on me. I watched a dust mote drift lazily through a slant of afternoon sunlight. It floated up, then dipped, dancing with absolute aimlessness. I let out a slow breath, blowing the dust mote off its path. Finding a new supervisor meant rewriting my entire proposal. I closed my eyes and listened to the rhythmic ticking of the wall clock.

Sitting on the stone bench, Chloe read the departmental email about Professor Singh’s resignation. She locked her phone screen and tossed it onto her backpack. A squirrel ran up the trunk of a nearby oak tree. Chloe rested her chin in her hands, her eyelids heavy. She watched a dry brown leaf detach from a branch and float in slow, lazy circles down to the grass. She pulled a blade of grass from the ground and began tearing it into microscopic vertical strips. Singh had been the only faculty member who understood her algorithmic trading models. Now she would have to explain her math to someone else. She sighed, a long, hollow sound. She picked up a pebble and flicked it across the concrete path. It skittered and stopped. She found another pebble and tried to hit the first one, missing by several inches.

Dr. Evans bought me a pint to soften the blow before announcing he was leaving the geology department for a mining company. I dragged my finger through the condensation on my glass, drawing a smiley face, then crossing it out. The jukebox in the corner was playing a country song I had already heard three times today. Evans kept talking about salary bumps and industry opportunities. I stared at the foam sliding down the inside of my glass. It moved at a glacial pace. 'It's a great opportunity,' I mumbled, resting my head against the high back of the wooden booth. I took a cocktail napkin and started folding it into halves, then quarters, then eighths, pressing the creases down hard with my thumbnail until the thick paper threatened to tear. I wondered if the bartender was ever going to wipe down the sticky counter.

The letter from the dean’s office sat on Liam’s desk, outlining the procedure for students abandoned by Dr. Alarie’s sudden move to a rival university. Liam lay flat on his rug, staring straight up at the ceiling fan spinning on its lowest setting. Whir, click. Whir, click. He had memorized the rhythm of the faulty motor. He lazily raised his arm, holding his thumb up to eclipse the lightbulb with every rotation. His dissertation on modern political movements was due in six months. He rolled onto his side, dragging a finger along the pattern of the carpet, pressing the fibers flat. He reached under his bed and pulled out a shoe box, reading the label. Size 10. He closed his eyes, listening to the muffled bass of his neighbor's music thumping through the wall. He needed to write emails, but he just lay there.

My advisor, Professor Thorne, caught me in the campus greenhouse to tell me she was retiring early and moving to Florida. I nodded slowly, deadheading a wilted marigold with my thumb and forefinger. She went into a long story about her new beach house and the grandchildren. I pinched a piece of soil between my fingers, rolling it until it crumbled into dust. The air in the greenhouse was thick, heavy, and smelled like wet dirt. I dragged my boots along the gravel path, making slow, grating sounds with every step. 'You'll be fine with Dr. Hayes,' she said. I stared at a row of dormant ferns, counting the fronds on the nearest one. 'Sure,' I said, my voice barely above a whisper. I slumped against the wooden potting bench, tracing the grooves of the worn timber, waiting for the conversation to end.

Samir sat in the crowded student union, staring at the resignation letter Dr. Kapoor had forwarded to her advisees. He slouched down in the armchair until his neck rested on the top edge. He watched the second hand of the giant wall clock sweep its agonizingly slow path from the twelve to the six. People bustled past him, loud and hurried, but Samir just stared at a stain on the carpet that looked vaguely like South America. He pulled a stray thread on the armchair's upholstery, wrapping it tightly around his index finger until the tip turned purple, then releasing it. He did this five times. Kapoor’s departure meant he’d have to retake the entire methodology seminar. Samir let his head loll to the side, watching a plastic wrapper blowing lazily across the floor, caught in the draft of the swinging entrance doors.

Mr. Harrison slapped the essay onto Liam's desk with a dramatic sigh. A heavy red 'D-' bled through the top page. Liam stared at it for a fraction of a second before his gaze drifted back to the ceiling tiles. He started counting the tiny perforations in the acoustic panel above him. One hundred and four, one hundred and five... The teacher launched into a lecture about wasted potential and missed thesis statements, but the sound morphed into a low drone, like a refrigerator humming. Liam rested his cheek against his knuckles, tracing an endless loop-de-loop pattern on the edge of his desk with a yellow pencil. "Are you even listening, Liam?" Mr. Harrison snapped. Liam blinked slowly, suppressing a yawn that made his jaw pop. "Thesis statements," he mumbled, watching a single fly bump repeatedly against the classroom window. "Right. Can I go to the bathroom now?"

The screen refreshed, displaying a bold 42% next to 'Final Exam'. I leaned back in my spinning chair and pushed off the desk, doing three slow rotations before bringing myself to a halt with my heel. A 42. I picked up a rubber band from the keyboard tray and stretched it between my thumbs, plucking it like a bass guitar string. Twang. Twang. My phone buzzed with a frantic text from Sarah complaining about getting a B plus. I didn't reply. Instead, I minimized the browser window and clicked the icon for Solitaire. The cards cascaded down the screen in a green and red waterfall. I dragged the black eight onto the red nine. My mom would probably ground me, which meant no going out. I dragged a red seven onto the black eight, resting my chin heavily on my left palm, watching the cards stack.

Chloe sat between her parents in the principal's office, her legs swinging gently beneath the undersized chair. Across the mahogany desk, Mrs. Gable slid a transcript forward, tapping a manicured nail against the glaring 'F' in Chemistry. Chloe’s mother gasped, launching into a tearful interrogation about late assignments and tutoring schedules. Chloe picked at a loose thread on the hem of her skirt, winding it tightly around her index finger until the tip turned purple, then releasing it to watch the blood rush back. She repeated the process. Mrs. Gable asked Chloe directly how she planned to rectify the failing mark. Chloe let out a long, hollow exhale, her eyes fixed heavily on the beige carpet. "Do extra credit, I guess," she said flatly, pulling the thread again. The clock on the wall ticked with agonizing slowness, the minute hand taking an eternity to click past three-fifteen.

My professor handed back our midterm portfolios, heavily laden with red ink and sticky notes. I flipped to the back page and saw the 55/100 circled twice. I closed the folder and tossed it onto my unmade bed. The radiator hissed in the corner of my dorm room, blowing dry, stale air into my face. I lay on the floor, staring up at the popcorn ceiling, trying to find shapes in the stucco. A cloud. A distorted face. A turtle. The failing grade meant I'd have to retake Intro to Microeconomics next semester, but the thought just washed over me like lukewarm water. I rolled onto my stomach and pulled my laptop closer, scrolling endlessly through an auto-playing feed of cooking videos. A guy chopped an onion. Another guy chopped some celery. I watched the videos for an hour, my face propped up in my hands.

Marcus joined his study group at the library, tossing his marked physics exam into the center of the table. A giant '38%' was scrawled at the top. The rest of the group fell silent, their eyes wide with secondhand panic. "Dude, what are you going to do?" Kevin whispered, clutching his own paper. Marcus shrugged, slouching so far down in his chair that his knees hit the underside of the table. He took out his phone and started deleting old emails from his inbox one by one. Select, trash. Select, trash. "If you fail this, you lose your scholarship," Jenny pointed out, her voice pitching up. Marcus let out a slow breath that ruffled his bangs. He clicked on a promotional email for a shoe sale, stared at the image of a sneaker for a solid minute, and then deleted it. "Guess so," he muttered, opening another email.

Dad clutched the steering wheel, his knuckles white. He had just seen my report card, specifically the D in History, and the car was filled with his booming lecture about responsibility. I stared out the passenger window, watching the yellow lines on the highway blur into a continuous strip. Dash, dash, dash. I started tapping my foot against the floor mat in time with the passing telephone poles. Tap. Tap. Tap. Dad’s voice rose an octave as he threatened to take away my car keys. I rested my temple against the cool glass of the window, leaving a foggy breath mark. I traced a smiley face into the condensation with my pinky finger, watching it slowly fade away. "Are you even listening to me?" Dad yelled. "Yep," I said, letting out a heavy sigh and drawing another, slower smiley face on the cold glass.

Ethan stood by his locker, staring at the crumpled math test he had just shoved onto the top shelf. The score was a 45. He leaned his back against the cold metal lockers and slid down until he was sitting on the linoleum floor. People stepped around him, chattering loudly. Ethan pulled a loose thread from his shoelace, unwinding the aglet until the plastic tip snapped off completely. He tossed the little plastic piece across the hallway, watching it bounce twice before settling near a trash can. Someone stepped on it. Ethan rested his head back against his locker, his eyelids drooping halfway. He counted the tiles on the opposite wall, losing track at thirty and deciding it wasn't worth starting over. He remained seated long after the second bell echoed through the empty hall, watching a janitor slowly push a broom over the scuffed floors.

The red failing grade flashed on the digital rubric shared on the screen. My professor was breaking down exactly why my final project lacked depth, her tiny face talking animatedly in the little Zoom square. I minimized the window so her face disappeared, leaving only her muffled, continuous voice. I opened a new tab and typed 'types of moss' into the search bar. I scrolled through Wikipedia pictures of green fuzz, clicking on random links. Peat moss. Sphagnum. The professor paused, asking me if I understood where I went wrong. "Yes, completely," I said into the microphone, my voice completely flat. I muted myself again. I leaned my face heavily into my palm, squishing my cheek up to my eye. I clicked on an article about lichen. My leg bounced rhythmically under the desk as I scanned the text without actually reading a single word.

Maya sat at the café table, the D-minus literature paper resting under her half-empty iced latte. Her tutor, a frantic grad student named Greg, was waving his hands, explaining how her thesis totally missed the mark. Maya slouched in her chair, resting her chin on her folded arms. She watched the condensation glide down the plastic cup, forming a tiny puddle on her paper, blurring the red ink. A barista was wiping the counter behind Greg. Maya watched the rag move back and forth in perfect, even rhythm. "Maya, we need to rewrite this by Friday," Greg urged, tapping the soggy paper. Maya blinked slowly, letting out a long breath. "Sure," she muttered. She picked up a stray sugar packet and started folding it into microscopic accordions, staring blankly at the wall behind Greg's head while he continued talking.

"A twenty-two percent means you will have to attend summer school," the guidance counselor said, folding her hands on her desk. I let my head loll back against the headrest of the vinyl chair. The ceiling was composed of white squares dotted with random black specks. I started connecting the specks in my head to make constellations. A dog. A triangle. The counselor kept talking about my college prospects and plummeting GPA. Her voice blended completely into the hum of the air conditioner. I slowly spun my phone on the armrest, watching the shiny case catch the fluorescent light. Spin, stop. Spin, stop. "Do you have any questions for me?" she asked, her tone expecting tears or panic. I stopped the phone with my thumb. "No," I said, letting out a long, loud sigh. "Can I just go back to class now?"

The wind blew the marked biology test across the grass, the red 'F' flashing against the lawn. Julian didn't chase it. He sat on the stone bench, his legs stretched out in front of him, staring blankly at a squirrel burying a nut near an oak tree. His phone buzzed in his pocket—likely his lab partner asking about the grades. Julian ignored it. He leaned forward, resting his elbows on his knees, and picked up a dry twig. He began snapping it into the smallest pieces possible, dropping the tiny fragments into a pile between his shoes. Snap. Snap. The paper tumbled further away, catching on a rose bush. Julian watched it flutter in the breeze for a moment, resting his cheek in the palm of his hand. He let out a prolonged yawn, his eyes watering, and went back to breaking his little twigs.

I stared at the glowing monitor, the "F" for my digital art submission glaring back at me. I dragged the mouse cursor in slow, lazy circles around the grade, highlighting the text and un-highlighting it over and over. Highlight. Click. Highlight. Click. I rested my chin on the desk, the wood pressing into my jaw. The professor’s comment read, 'Lacks effort and composition.' I let out a heavy breath through my nose, blowing a stray piece of paper off my keyboard. I spun my chair away from the desk and stared at my closet door, counting the wooden slats. Forty-two slats. I rubbed my eyes, letting out a groan that stretched into a massive yawn. I rolled my chair back to the desk, closed the grade portal, and opened a blank document, staring at the flashing black cursor until my vision went completely blurry.
