Mr. Harrison rested his chin on his palm, his heavy eyelids drooping as he stared at the mountain of identical history essays. The fluorescent lights overhead hummed a monotonous, unbroken note. Tap, tap, tap went his red pen against the laminate desk. The classroom was empty, the ticking wall clock moving at a glacial pace. A small, brown-wrapped package sat next to his grading pile, delivered earlier with a note from a student he taught a decade ago. He let out a long, slow exhale that fluttered the corner of a student's paper. Without shifting his posture, he reached out with one sluggish finger and pushed the box an inch to the left, then let his arm drop back into his lap. He went back to watching the second hand make its excruciating climb toward three o'clock.

I sat in the back row of the faculty meeting, counting the acoustic tiles on the ceiling. Forty-two across, twenty-eight down. Principal Higgins droned on about the new district attendance policies, his voice a flat, continuous hum that blended with the whirring projector. I rested my forehead against my knuckles, tracing a scratch in the veneer of the table with my thumbnail. Earlier that morning, the front office had handed me a beautifully wrapped parcel from a girl I taught five years ago. It sat on my lap now, heavy and silent. I peeled a piece of tape off the corner, moving at a snail's pace, trying to stretch the action to fill the endless minutes. Once the tape was off, I rolled it into a tiny ball, squished it flat, and started counting the tiles again.

Ms. Vance propped her elbow on the armrest, letting her head loll slightly to the side as the students silently read chapter four. She pulled a loose thread on her sweater, wrapping it around her index finger until the tip turned purple, then slowly unwrapping it. A velvet box rested on her keyboard, hand-delivered by a former debate captain who had dropped by unannounced. She hadn't opened it yet. Instead, she stared blankly through the window at a single gray cloud that hovered motionless over the parking lot. She sighed, her breath fogging the glass of her coffee mug. She flicked the small silver latch on the velvet box, hearing a faint click, then pushed it shut again. Click, clack. Click, clack. The rhythmic sound gave her something, anything, to focus on while the afternoon stretched out like a lifeless desert.

Hallway duty on a Tuesday is an exercise in staring at painted cinderblocks. I leaned against the cold wall, my arms crossed shut, watching dust motes drift lazily through a shaft of sunlight. My phone buzzed in my pocket. "Whatever," I muttered, not bothering to pull it out. Beside my feet sat a massive gift basket of gourmet chocolates, mailed all the way from France by a graduate who had somehow remembered my birthday. I nudged the cellophane wrapping with the toe of my loafer, listening to the faint crinkle. The hallway remained completely empty. I picked up a stray paperclip from the linoleum, bent the metal into a straight line, and then tried to bend it back into a perfect triangle. When it snapped in half, I tossed the pieces back onto the floor and went back to watching the dust motes.

Professor Aris slumped back in his leather chair, the glow of the computer screen washing his face in pale blue light. He scrolled down a page of raw data, the wheel on his mouse squeaking with a repetitive, hollow chirp. On his blotter sat a delicate, hand-carved wooden metronome, a surprise shipment from a piano prodigy he had mentored years ago. Aris reached over and pushed the metal pendulum. Tick, tock, tick, tock. He watched the needle sway back and forth, matching the slow, heavy cadence of his blinking eyes. The rhythm did nothing to break the thick, stagnant air of the office. He pulled a yellow sticky note from a pad, folded it precisely in half, then in quarters, then into tiny eighths, until it was too small to fold anymore. He dropped the paper square onto the desk, exhaling heavily.

I linked another purple paperclip to the chain I was building, dragging it across the surface of my desk like a metallic snake. The seventh-grade study hall was perfectly silent, save for the scratching of pencils. I rested my chin flat on the cool wood, looking at the room from a sideways angle. An ornate envelope and a small wrapped book lay right in front of my nose, dropped off by an alumni who had suddenly felt nostalgic. I pushed the book with my nose, sliding it a few inches. Then I added a green paperclip to my chain. I checked the wall clock. Two minutes had passed. I let out a long, loud sigh, prompting a student to look up. "Just keep reading," I mumbled in a flat monotone. I picked up a yellow paperclip.

Mrs. Gable propped her chin on her stacked fists, her gaze fixed entirely on a water stain shaped like a mitten on the ceiling tile above the chalkboard. The intercom buzzed a static-filled announcement that she tuned out completely. Sitting directly in front of her was an expensive, leather-bound first edition of her favorite novel, sent by a student who was now a successful author. She traced the gold foil lettering of the title with a sluggish index finger, her expression entirely vacant. A fly buzzed against the windowpane, trapping itself in a corner. She watched the fly throw itself against the glass repeatedly. When the insect finally settled on the sill, Mrs. Gable let out a drawn-out breath, slumped forward until her forehead rested against the cold leather cover of the book, and closed her eyes to wait for the bell.

The continuous patter of rain against the glass sounded like a drum with only one beat. I sat at my desk, swiveling my chair a quarter turn to the left, then a quarter turn to the right. Squeak. Squeak. A glossy white gift bag with tissue paper spilling out sat on my filing cabinet, left there by a former theater kid who made it big. I leaned over, pulled out one sheet of the blue tissue paper, and slowly tore it into thin, even strips. I lined the strips up on my desk, making sure the edges were perfectly parallel. When I finished, I blew gently, watching the paper flutter to the carpet. Squeak went the chair to the left. Squeak went the chair to the right. "Is it three o'clock yet?" I whispered to the empty, gray room.

Coach Miller chewed on a blade of artificial turf, his elbows resting heavily on his knees. The gymnasium was silent during the off-period, the air smelling faintly of floor wax and old rubber. A pristine, engraved silver stopwatch lay in his palm, a token of gratitude mailed by a runner who had gone to the Olympics. Miller pressed the start button. The digital numbers began their rapid ascent. He watched the milliseconds fly by in a blur, his face completely slack. When it hit exactly sixty seconds, he clicked stop. He reset it to zero. He pressed start again. The hum of the vending machine down the hall echoed into the gym. He kicked the heel of his sneaker against the bleachers, tap-thud, tap-thud, watching the digital numbers cycle through another empty minute in the vast, quiet room.

Proctoring state exams requires standing perfectly still for three hours. I leaned my shoulder against the doorframe, mapping out the scuff marks on the linoleum floor. There was one that looked like a crescent moon, and another shaped like a boot. Inside my jacket pocket was a small velvet pouch containing a silver tie clip, an unexpected delivery from my very first graduating class. I slipped my hand into the pocket, rolling the cool metal between my thumb and forefinger, over and over. I counted the number of breaths the student closest to me took in a minute. Fourteen. I looked at the clock. It was 10:14 AM. I rolled the tie clip again, switched my weight to my other leg, and began counting the ceiling panels, wondering if I could calculate the total area of the room in my head.

Dr. Lin rested his cheek against his palm, his eyes glazed as the computer screen cycled through a series of generic screensavers. Flying toasters drifted across the monitor. A heavy, wax-sealed box of imported tea sat untouched by his keyboard, a surprise from a doctoral candidate he had advised years ago. He peeled a corner of the wax seal with his thumbnail, flicking the tiny red flake onto the carpet. He drew a long, slow breath through his nose and blew it out through his mouth, fluttering his lips. He spun a pen on his desk. It clattered to a stop. He spun it again, harder this time, watching it whirl until it rolled off the edge and hit the floor. He didn't bend down to pick it up. Instead, he just stared at the toasters floating across the screen.

The faculty lounge smelled faintly of burnt coffee and ancient microwave popcorn. I sat at the round plastic table, peeling the label off a water bottle in infinitesimal strips. Next to my elbow sat a custom-engraved golden apple, mailed by a former student who now ran a tech company. I picked it up, noting its heavy weight, and rolled it from my left hand to my right. Left, right. Left, right. The refrigerator motor kicked on with a loud shudder. I rested my chin on the table, putting myself at eye level with the golden apple, and flicked it with my middle finger. It spun in a slow, wobbly circle before coming to a halt. I let out a heavy sigh, resting my forehead on the cool plastic table, listening to the rhythmic, droning hum of the refrigerator.

Mr. Henderson slid the crisp white envelope across the table. Mark opened it, his eyes skimming the bold heading: Notice to Vacate. The landlord was talking, explaining the legalities, but Mark’s attention drifted to the font. It looked like Times New Roman, maybe size twelve. He rested his chin in his palm, letting a slow exhale escape his lips as he watched a dust mote drift slowly through a shaft of afternoon sunlight. Mr. Henderson’s voice droned on, a steady, unchanging hum in the quiet room. Mark picked up a pen from the table and began clicking it—click, click, click—staring blankly at the beige wallpaper. "Are you listening?" Mr. Henderson asked. Mark blinked slowly, dragging his gaze back to the landlord. "Thirty days," Mark said, his voice flat. He looked back at the dust mote.

I peeled the bright orange paper off my front door, taking care not to rip the tape. Eviction Notice. The landlord had used three exclamation points. I carried it into the kitchen, tossing it onto a stack of unopened junk mail, and turned on the faucet. I filled the electric kettle, hit the switch, and leaned against the counter. The water took exactly three minutes and forty seconds to boil; I knew because I timed it yesterday. I traced a water stain on the laminate counter with my index finger, going round and round the faded gray rim. The orange paper caught my eye again. I wondered if I should start packing boxes today, but the thought felt like too much effort. I watched the steam begin to rise from the kettle spout, waiting for the whistle.

The priority email landed in Sarah’s inbox just after lunch. She opened it, her eyes glossing over the legal jargon demanding she surrender the premises by the end of the month. She scrolled to the bottom, then scrolled back to the top, doing it again just to watch the scrollbar move. She minimized the window. The digital clock in the corner of her screen read 1:14 PM. She leaned back in her desk chair, lifted her feet off the floor, and pushed against the desk. The chair spun in a slow, lazy circle. One rotation. Two rotations. The ceiling tiles blurred together into a uniform field of speckled white. Her phone buzzed on the desk, but she didn't reach for it. She just let the chair spin until it eventually ground to a halt, leaving her facing the blank wall.

The knock was loud, authoritative. I dragged my feet across the carpet, opening the door to find the property manager holding a clipboard. He handed me a folded document and launched into a prepared speech about lease violations. I leaned my shoulder against the doorframe, letting my eyes glaze over as I watched a bead of sweat trickle down his temple. The document in my hand felt heavy, but I didn't bother unfolding it. "So, the locks change on the fifteenth," he finished, out of breath. "Okay," I said, my voice barely above a whisper. I shut the door, walked over to the sofa, and collapsed onto the cushions. I picked up the television remote, flipping through channels. Infomercial, news, cartoon, static. I left it on the static, staring at the black and white snow filling the screen.

Arthur found the envelope sitting on his welcome mat. Inside was a formal demand to leave the apartment within two weeks. He carried the paper to his recliner, sitting down heavily. He read the first paragraph, then his gaze drifted to the corner of the room where a spider was methodically weaving a web. Arthur watched the arachnid work for a long time, his chin resting on his chest. He let out a long, loud yawn, stretching his arms high above his head until his joints popped. The eviction notice slipped off his lap, fluttering to the rug. He didn't bend down to pick it up. Instead, he pulled out his phone and opened a solitaire app, his thumb swiping cards back and forth without really looking at the numbers. The quiet ticking of the wall clock filled the room.

A final warning to vacate had been slipped under my door overnight. I picked it up with two fingers, reading the bold black letters warning of legal action. I walked to the kitchen table and sat down. There was a bowl of stale cereal sitting from the day before. I picked up a spoon and started poking at the soggy flakes, mashing them against the side of the ceramic bowl. The notice sat next to my elbow. I began folding it. First in half, then into quarters, making sure the creases were perfectly sharp. I folded it until it was a tiny, thick square of paper that I couldn't compress any further. I flicked it with my middle finger, watching it slide across the table and drop onto the floor. I rested my cheek on the cool table surface, sighing deeply.

The landlord’s text was a wall of angry caps-lock letters, culminating in an eviction threat. Chloe swiped the notification away. She sat on her balcony, her feet propped up on the railing, staring out at the empty parking lot. A plastic bag tumbled across the asphalt, pushed by a weak breeze. She rested her elbows on her knees and rested her face in her hands, her eyelids drooping. The text message chimed again. She didn't look at the screen. She reached out, pinched a dead leaf off her potted pothos plant, and crushed it between her fingers, watching the dry flakes drift down to the concrete below. She picked up another leaf, rolling it between her thumb and forefinger, waiting for the sun to sink just a little lower so she could finally justify going to sleep.

The legal document was pinned to my door with a red thumbtack. I pulled the tack out, holding it up to the hallway light. The plastic head was chipped. I brought the notice inside, dropping it onto the coffee table. Thirty Days to Vacate. I lay down on the rug, staring up at the ceiling. There were exactly forty-two popcorn texture bumps inside the faint water stain above my head. I had counted them three times today. I closed my eyes, listening to the hum of the refrigerator kicking on. It was a low, steady vibration that rattled the loose floorboards in the kitchen. I rolled onto my side, grabbed a stray piece of lint off the carpet, and rolled it into a tiny ball between my fingers, letting the afternoon stretch out endlessly in front of me.

The sheriff stood in the doorway, handing over the pink slip. "You have until Friday," he said, adjusting his duty belt. David took the paper, nodding once. "Friday," David repeated, his voice utterly flat. The sheriff lingered for a moment, perhaps expecting tears or anger, but David just stood there, his shoulders slumped, blinking slowly. When the officer finally turned away, David closed the door. He walked to his desk, sitting down in front of a blank computer monitor. He took the pink eviction notice, reached into his drawer, and pulled out a pair of scissors. He began to cut the paper into thin, perfectly straight strips. Snip. Snip. Snip. The strips piled up on the desk like confetti. When he finished, he swept the pile into the trash can and stared at the empty black screen of his monitor.

My phone buzzed with an email from the property management portal. Subject: Notice of Lease Termination. I opened it, skimming the first sentence before my eyes drifted away. The font was Arial. I hate Arial. I tossed the phone onto my bed and walked over to the window. The street below was empty, save for a single parked car. I leaned my forehead against the cool glass. A raindrop hit the outside of the pane, slowly tracing a jagged path downward. I watched it until it merged with another drop, then picked a new one to follow. Down, down, down to the windowsill. My phone buzzed again, probably a follow-up warning. I let out a long, heavy breath, fogging up the glass, and drew a slow circle in the condensation with my fingernail, waiting for the fog to fade.

Elena found the certified letter in her mailbox. The contents were clear: she had broken the noise ordinance too many times, and she had to be out by the 30th. She walked up the stairs to her apartment, letting the paper dangle from her fingertips. Inside, she dropped it onto the kitchen counter. She opened the pantry, stared at the cans of soup for a full minute, and closed it. She opened the refrigerator, stared at the condiments, and closed it. She went back to the pantry. Nothing had changed. Elena dragged a chair out from the table, sitting down heavily. She picked up a ballpoint pen and began drawing interconnected triangles on the back of the eviction notice, filling the white space with dark blue ink until the legal warnings were completely obscured by geometric shapes.

The property owner stood on my porch, shouting through the screen door about unpaid rent and court dates. I sat on the living room floor, legs crossed, holding a Rubik's Cube. I twisted the top row to the right, then the right column down. His voice was a loud drone, blending with the sound of the neighbor's lawnmower. "Are you even listening to me?" he demanded, slapping a folded paper against the screen. I looked up, making eye contact but keeping my face completely blank. "Yes," I said, my tone perfectly level. I looked back down at the cube. Blue, red, yellow. I twisted the bottom row. I had solved this thing six times today. I heard him huff in frustration, heard the paper rustle as he shoved it into the doorframe, and listened to his heavy footsteps retreating down the driveway.

I’ve counted the acoustic tiles on the ceiling above gate B14 three times. There are exactly two hundred and forty-two. My sister’s wedding ceremony started an hour ago, but the "DELAYED" text glowing next to flight 881 hasn't blinked once. I slowly peel the remaining edge of the barcode sticker off my overpriced water bottle, rolling the sticky paper into a tiny grey ball between my thumb and index finger. I flick it. It bounces off my scuffed shoe and joins a rogue peanut shell on the speckled carpet. With a heavy exhale, I rest my chin on my palm, watching a luggage cart make its fifth slow loop around the tarmac outside the rain-streaked window. I trace the outline of a raindrop with my fingernail, waiting for the digital clock to flip from 4:12 to 4:13.

Marcus arranged his matching red candies into a row of five for the fiftieth time, the bright digital explosions reflecting in his glazed eyes. By now, the panel of directors across the country had already packed up their briefcases and given the VP position to someone else. He didn't even care anymore. He dragged his thumb across the cracked screen, swiping a yellow lemon shape to the left. Nothing happened. He let his head loll back against the rigid metal airport seat, staring at the fluorescent light fixture that emitted a constant, low-frequency hum. The hum seemed to stretch time itself into an endless, flavorless paste. He tapped his left foot, then his right foot, creating a slow, hollow rhythm that matched the ticking of the wall clock. Another sigh escaped him as he unlocked his phone to swipe more candy.

The opening chords of my favorite band's farewell tour are probably echoing through the stadium right now, but I am intimately memorizing the lint patterns on the carpet of Terminal C. I slide down slightly in the vinyl chair, letting my legs stretch straight out in front of me. To pass the time, I watch a man in a rumpled suit eating a soggy sandwich. I decide his name is Greg, and he prefers mayonnaise over mustard. When Greg finishes chewing, I shift my gaze to a flickering neon sign above the pretzel stand. Buzz. Click. Buzz. Click. I tap my boarding pass against my knee in time with the malfunctioning light. I’ve already read the safety manual in the seat pocket of the display chair twice, noting that in the event of an emergency, the animated figures remain perfectly, rigidly calm.

Evelyn had already walked the length of Concourse D four times. Her daughter was currently walking across a stage to receive her diploma, while Evelyn was inspecting a rack of overpriced travel pillows. She picked up a bright purple neck rest, squeezed its foam filling, and placed it back on the metal hook with a slow exhale. She wandered over to the magazine stand, flipping through a publication about exotic birds, a topic she cared absolutely nothing about. She read an entire paragraph on the mating habits of the blue-footed booby without processing a single word. Placing it back on the shelf, she watched the second hand of her watch sweep its slow circle. She leaned her hip against a pillar, picked at a loose thread on her sweater cuff, and watched a janitor push a broom back and forth, back and forth.

My professor warned me that no make-up exams would be given, so failing the semester is now a mathematical certainty thanks to the blizzard currently burying my plane. I take my black ballpoint pen and draw a tiny, imperfect circle on the back of my hand. Then I draw a slightly larger circle around that one. And another. The intercom chimes with a two-tone electronic jingle, followed by a muffled voice announcing a gate change for a flight I'm not on. I trace over the outer ring of ink on my skin, making the line thicker, pressing until it slightly hurts. Someone two rows over coughs. I count five seconds in my head, hoping they’ll cough again to break the silence. They don't. I sigh, dropping my chin into my folded arms on my carry-on bag, closing my eyes against the harsh overhead lights.

The memorial service for his uncle was supposed to commence at noon, but David was trapped in a seemingly infinite layover in Chicago. He sat cross-legged on the floor near an outlet, pulling every item out of his leather wallet. He stacked his credit cards in a neat pile on his knee. He smoothed out three crumpled receipts from last month, folding them into perfect squares before tossing them into a nearby trash can. Then he counted his spare change: forty-two cents. He lined the coins up—quarter, dime, nickel, two pennies—before sweeping them back into his pocket. He stared at the blank wall opposite him, a vast expanse of off-white paint. He blinked slowly, letting his vision blur until the edges of the wall softened into a grey smudge. He rested his chin on his knees, listening to the hum of the vending machine.

My husband is sitting alone at our favorite restaurant, while I sit under a buzzing fluorescent tube at Gate 7. I mentally list everything in my refrigerator back home. Half a carton of milk. Two bruised apples. A jar of pickles. I tap my fingers on the plastic armrest, pinky to index, over and over. I pull up the flight tracker app on my phone, watch the little blue airplane icon sit perfectly still on the map, and close the app. Ten seconds later, I open it again. The tiny plane remains motionless. I slump forward, resting my forehead against the cool, smooth handle of my rolling suitcase. A fly buzzes past my ear, and I follow its erratic flight path across the ceiling with heavy eyes until it disappears into the dark slats of a ventilation grate.

The real estate agent's voicemail had been polite, but Clara knew the sellers wouldn't hold the house. She let out a long breath that puffed her bangs up into the air. She slid down in the uncomfortable terminal chair until the small of her back hit the gap between the seat and the backrest. Crossing her arms, she let her head fall to the right, her cheek squished against the vinyl. She stared at the speckled linoleum floor. She found a black spot, connecting it to a grey spot with an imaginary line. Then to a brown speck. It looked like a constellation. She uncrossed her legs, crossed them the other way, and sighed again. A nearby toddler shrieked, but Clara didn't even flinch. She just watched the dust motes drift lazily through a single shaft of sunlight piercing the tall terminal windows.

This was supposed to be the night I finally met Sarah in person, but instead, I am getting intimately acquainted with the aesthetics of an airport lounge. I tie the laces of my left sneaker, pull them tight, and untie them again. I repeat the process on the right shoe. I rest my elbows on my knees and stare at the feet of the people passing by. Black loafers. Red heels. Scuffed boots. Neon running shoes. The parade of footwear blurs together. I twist the silver ring on my thumb around and around until the skin beneath it turns pink. Pulling out a pack of gum, I unwrap a piece, meticulously folding the foil wrapper into an origami triangle. I flatten it out, then fold it into a smaller square. The departures board clicks above me, but I don’t even bother looking up.

The million-dollar pitch was happening without him. Julian didn't care anymore. He scrolled through his phone's photo gallery, swiping past hundreds of pictures of his cat without really seeing any of them. Swipe left. Swipe left. Swipe left. He reached the end of his album, stared at the final image for ten seconds, and locked the screen. He placed the phone face-down on his thigh. He leaned forward, elbows resting heavily on his knees, and stared at the gap between his shoes. The low murmur of a hundred distant conversations blended into a single wall of white noise. He picked up a complimentary airline napkin from the side table and began tearing it into long, perfectly straight strips. When the napkin was completely shredded into a messy pile of white confetti, he brushed it all into his palm and threw it away.

My sister probably has her baby in her arms by now. I am currently standing in front of a brightly lit vending machine, studying the ingredients of a generic cheese cracker. I press my face so close to the glass that my breath fogs up the pane. Riboflavin. Thiamine mononitrate. I slowly drag my finger across the condensation, drawing a sloppy smiley face before wiping it away with my sleeve. I fish a crumpled dollar bill from my pocket, feed it into the slot, and watch the machine spit it back out. I feed it in again. It spits it out. I don't even want the crackers. I slide the bill back into my pocket, turn around, and lean my back flat against the cool glass. I stare at the ceiling vents, tracking the slow, rhythmic rotation of the internal fan blades.

Her name had likely just been called for the regional journalism award, but Maria was busy analyzing a crack in the drywall near Gate E4. The fissure resembled a map of Italy. She traced it with her eyes from top to bottom, then from bottom to top. She exhaled loudly, puffing her cheeks out as the breath escaped her lips. Sliding her phone across the sleek surface of the charging station, she watched it hit the metal edge, then slid it back. Back and forth. It made a rhythmic thud against the barrier. A woman nearby was frantically arguing with a ticket agent, her voice echoing shrilly through the concourse. Maria watched the argument with heavy, half-closed lids, completely detached from the drama. She propped her chin on her fist, letting her gaze drift past the angry woman to an empty baggage carousel.

I lie on my twin-sized bed, tracing the outline of the faded glow-in-the-dark stars my dad stuck to the ceiling fifteen years ago. There are exactly forty-two of them. Downstairs, the muffled sound of a game show blares from the living room TV. The contestant guesses the price of a blender. I mouth the exact same number before the announcer even speaks. My phone screen remains black on the nightstand, untouched for the last three hours. I pick at a loose thread on my childhood quilt, pulling it until it bunches up the fabric, then smoothing it out again. A car drives past the window outside, its headlights sweeping across the floral wallpaper. I count the seconds until the next car passes. One, two, three... twenty-seven. Nothing. I let out a long breath, shift my weight on the mattress, and begin counting the stars backward from forty-two.

David rested his chin heavily on his palm, staring at the pot of water on the stove. A single tiny bubble formed at the bottom, detached, and floated to the surface. Then another. The ticking of the grandfather clock in the hallway seemed to echo louder with every swing of its brass pendulum. "Did you know the Andersons painted their mailbox blue?" his mother asked, meticulously wiping down the immaculate granite countertops for the third time that afternoon. David offered a slow, noncommittal hum, dragging his finger through a stray dusting of flour. He traced a figure-eight, erased it, and drew a square. The refrigerator hummed to life, providing a brief symphony of mechanical noise before fading back into the oppressive quiet. David closed his eyes, listening to the agonizingly slow rhythm of the ticking clock, waiting for the water to finally boil.

The cul-de-sac is completely dead at 2:00 PM on a Tuesday. I sit on the porch swing, pushing off the wood floor with one toe every ten seconds just to keep the rusty chains squeaking. That squeak is the only proof I exist right now. Across the street, Mrs. Gable’s sprinkler rotates. Ch-ch-ch-ch-hissss. I memorize the rhythm. It takes fourteen sprays to complete a full semicircle. My dad comes out holding a pair of hedge clippers, asking if I want to help him trim the azaleas. I look at the bush. I look at the clippers. I look back at the rotating sprinkler. "Maybe later," I mumble, slouching deeper into the cushions. I pull out my phone, unlock it, swipe left, swipe right, and lock it again without opening a single app. The sprinkler finishes its cycle, and I wait for it to start again.

Maya sat on an overturned bucket in the center of the garage, watching her father arrange screwdrivers by size on a pegboard. He spent five minutes deciding whether the Phillips-head should go before or after the flathead. Maya exhaled a long breath that fluttered her bangs. She picked up a stray zip-tie from the concrete floor, bending it into a circle, then a triangle, before snapping it together and tightening it until it wouldn't move. She tossed the plastic loop toward a trash can, missing by three feet. Her dad hummed a song off-key, wiping a wrench with an oily rag. Maya leaned back against the workbench, sliding down until her shoulders slumped completely. She began tapping her sneakers against the floor—left, right, left, right—trying to match the tempo of her father’s tuneless humming just to give her hands and feet something to do.

I’ve been staring at the same open cardboard box for forty-five minutes. It’s filled with my old high school textbooks and a tangle of obsolete charging cables. My mom pops her head into the doorway, asking how the unpacking is going. "Almost done," I reply, not moving a single muscle. She nods approvingly and walks away. I pick up a calculator, pressing the '8' button until the screen fills up with eights, then I press clear and do it again with nines. Outside the window, a squirrel runs up the oak tree, pauses on a branch, and twitches its tail. I watch it until it disappears into the leaves. I let out a heavy sigh, dropping the calculator back into the box. I lie flat on the carpet, crossing my arms over my chest, and stare intently at the swirling texture of the stucco ceiling above me.

The muted television broadcast a golf tournament, the green fairways glowing in the dim living room. Marcus lay draped upside down over the armchair, his head dangling inches from the carpet. He watched a tiny white ball roll endlessly across the screen from this inverted perspective. His father was asleep on the recliner, a newspaper resting over his chest, snoring with the rhythmic consistency of a metronome. Marcus reached out, lazily plucking a piece of lint from the rug. He rolled it between his thumb and forefinger, examining it as if it held the secrets of the universe, before flicking it away. He stretched his arms above his head, groaning loudly, hoping the noise might wake his dad and prompt a conversation. The snoring simply grew louder. Marcus let his arms flop back down, his eyes glazing over as another golfer lined up a slow putt.

I am thirty-two, following my mother through the produce aisle like a lost duckling. She spends four full minutes inspecting heads of lettuce, turning each one over in her hands, checking for phantom bruises. I lean my forearms against the handlebar of the shopping cart, resting my chin on the cold metal. I spin the red plastic handle of the cart backwards, then forwards, listening to the plastic squeak against the metal rod. "Do you think we need Roma or Vine tomatoes?" she asks. "Vine," I say immediately, not looking up. She nods, then picks up the Romas anyway to examine them. I push the cart forward half an inch, then pull it back half an inch. The wheels click. Forward, click. Backward, click. I wonder how many floor tiles make up aisle four. I start counting them, beginning at the bananas.

Chloe rested her cheek against the cool wood of the kitchen table, using a damp toothpick to herd a breadcrumb in circles. Across from her, her parents read the morning paper in absolute silence. The only sound was the harsh crinkle of turning pages and the occasional sip of coffee. Chloe puffed her cheeks out, blowing a slow stream of air that made her bangs flutter. She picked up the salt shaker, tipping it slightly so the white grains piled up against the glass, then tipped it the other way to watch them avalanche back down. She did the same with the pepper. "Big news in the zoning board today," her father announced without lowering the paper. "Mhm," her mother murmured. Chloe dropped her toothpick, let out a heavy sigh, and dragged her fingernails along the grain of the wooden table, staring blankly at the toaster.

Dinner isn't at eight anymore; it’s at five-thirty sharp. It is currently five-fourteen. I stand by the bay window in the dining room, watching a stray dog sniff a fire hydrant. I trace the path of a raindrop sliding down the glass pane. It merges with another drop, speeding up, and I mentally declare it the winner of a completely imaginary race. My mom is in the kitchen stirring a pot of stew, the wooden spoon knocking rhythmically against the metal rim. Clack, clack, clack. I tap my fingers against the window sill in perfect unison with the sound. The dog lifts its leg, finishes its business, and trots away down the sidewalk. I check my watch. Five-sixteen. I slowly drag my hands down my face, pulling at my eyelids, before turning around to watch the dining room clock tick its way toward five-seventeen.

Elias sat cross-legged on the floor of the den, tasked with sorting through old mail his parents had hoarded in a shoebox. He held up a mattress store coupon that expired three years ago, staring at the bold red lettering until the words lost all meaning. He tossed it into the "recycle" pile. He picked up a glossy flyer for a local pizzeria, reading the description of their supreme pie backwards, letter by letter. E-m-e-r-u-p-s. He yawned, a wide, jaw-cracking stretch that made his eyes water. Elias leaned his back against the floral sofa, balancing a stack of envelopes on his head like a paper hat. He sat perfectly still, timing how long he could balance the mail before gravity took over, silently hoping the ensuing mess would take up another hour of his afternoon.

The hammock in the backyard used to be my favorite place. Now, it just feels like a very soft trap. I sway back and forth, dragging one foot through the freshly mowed grass. Every time I swing left, my heel catches a dandelion. Left, catch. Right, nothing. Left, catch. Right, nothing. My parents are at work, leaving me alone with the droning hum of the central AC unit. I hold my phone up to the sky, framing the camera so it looks like a passing airplane is flying into a cloud, but I don't bother taking the picture. I let my arm drop over the edge of the hammock, watching a line of ants march relentlessly toward a discarded popsicle stick. I start counting them. Twenty-three, twenty-four, twenty-five. I close my eyes, letting the steady sway lull me into a heavy, dreamless midday sleep.

Sam sat at the kitchen island, meticulously folding a paper napkin into a tiny, jagged accordion. His mother was upstairs searching for her missing reading glasses, an expedition that had already lasted twenty minutes. Sam flattened the napkin out, smoothing the creases with his thumb, and began folding it into a triangle instead. The refrigerator hummed, a low vibration that Sam could feel through the soles of his shoes. He repeatedly clicked a ballpoint pen—click-clack, click-clack—until his thumb ached. He set the pen down and rested his forehead directly on the cool quartz countertop. Through the ceiling, he heard the muffled thud of his mother’s footsteps pacing from the bedroom to the bathroom and back again. Sam squeezed his eyes shut, wishing he had brought his headphones, and silently began reciting the alphabet backwards in his head. Z, Y, X, W...

Elias rested his chin in his palm, watching a dust mote drift through a shaft of afternoon sunlight. For the fifth time in an hour, he rearranged the stack of business cards on his folding table, making sure the edges aligned perfectly. The craft fair had been dead since noon. He let out a long, slow exhale, tracing the wood grain of the table with his thumbnail. A shadow fell over his prints. "Excuse me," a voice said. Elias didn't look up immediately, taking his time to blink away the glaze in his eyes. When he finally shifted his gaze upward, a young woman was rolling up her sleeve. There, etched perfectly into her forearm, was the exact linework of the raven he’d drawn three years ago. Elias stopped tapping his thumbnail, his posture suddenly straightening as he stared at the living canvas.

I let the phone drop onto my chest, staring at the water stain on the ceiling that looked vaguely like a shoe. The ceiling fan clicked on every third rotation. Click. Swoosh. Swoosh. Click. I picked the phone back up, my thumb swiping upward in a robotic, endless rhythm. More food pictures. More terrible news. More blurry concert videos. My eyelids felt heavy, weighed down by the sheer repetitiveness of the afternoon. Swipe. Swipe. Stop. I blinked hard. The image on the screen was a forearm, red and irritated. It wasn't the skin that caught my attention, but the ink. The intricate mechanical heart with the cracked valve—my sketchbook drawing from last October. I sat up slowly, the phone now gripped tightly in both hands. The fan clicked again, but I didn't hear it this time. Someone out there was permanently wearing my late-night doodle.

The client had been talking for forty-five minutes about synergy and brand identity. Maya stirred her lukewarm latte, watching the swirl of milk merge with the coffee. She rested her cheek against her knuckles, letting the corporate buzzwords wash over her like white noise. She counted the bricks on the wall behind the client's head. Thirty-two. Thirty-three. "So, we want something impactful, like this," the client said, finally leaning across the table and pulling down the collar of his shirt. Maya suppressed a sigh, forcing her eyes to focus on his shoulder. Her breath hitched. Staring back at her was the geometric wolf she had painted for a local indie zine two years ago. The exact shading, the exact jagged angles. She dropped her stir stick. The endless drone of the meeting vanished, replaced by the pounding of her own heartbeat.

The bass from the speakers vibrated through the floorboards, rattling the ice in my plastic cup. I had been sitting on the same lumpy sofa for over an hour, swirling the melted water around and watching the room blur into a sea of unfamiliar faces. Someone tried to talk to me earlier, but I just nodded until they drifted away. I rested my head back against the wall, tracing the peeling wallpaper with my eyes, wishing I was in my sweatpants at home. A guy squeezed onto the sofa next to me, reaching across to grab a coaster. As his shirt rode up, a flash of black ink on his ribs caught the dim party lights. I sat forward, the ice in my cup spilling onto my hand. It was my weeping willow design. Every delicate, sweeping branch was precisely how I’d painted it.

Professor Vance tapped his dry-erase marker against the whiteboard in a steady, metronomic beat. Tap. Tap. Tap. The freshmen were supposedly working on their still-life sketches, but mostly they were whispering or checking their phones. He let his gaze wander out the window to the gray, overcast sky, imagining the paint drying on his palette at home. He checked his watch. Twenty minutes left. He began a slow lap around the room, dragging his feet slightly. He stopped behind a student in the back row who was wearing a tank top. Vance was about to offer a generic correction on her shading when he saw the back of her shoulder. The ink was fresh, the design unmistakable—his own chaotic, abstract cityscape from his first gallery show. Vance froze mid-step, his marker slipping from his fingers and clattering loudly onto the linoleum floor.

I leaned against the cash register, resting my chin on my folded arms. The store had been empty for two hours, leaving me with nothing to do but listen to the hum of the fluorescent lights. I organized the display of mints by color, then messed them up, then organized them again. A customer finally walked in, the bell above the door chiming loudly. I didn't stand up straight, just offered a flat, rehearsed greeting. He placed a bottled water on the counter. As I reached out to scan it, my scanner beeped, but my eyes locked onto his wrist. Wrapped around his forearm was the serpent biting its own tail, complete with the tiny, hidden initials I always snuck into my linework. I slowly looked up from his wrist to his face, the scanner beeping again as my thumb clamped down hard on the trigger.

The subway car rocked back and forth, lulling Chloe into a glassy-eyed daze. She stared at the advertisement for dental insurance across from her, reading the fine print over and over without absorbing a single word. She blew a strand of hair out of her face, checked the battery on her phone—fifty percent—and slouched deeper into the hard plastic seat. Three more stops until her apartment. A man wearing a sleeveless gym shirt stood near the doors holding the overhead rail. Chloe’s eyes drifted lazily over to him, tracing the lines of the car. Suddenly, she sat bolt upright. There, spanning the entire length of the man's bicep, was the intricate mandala she had posted on her art blog a month ago. She rubbed her eyes, leaning closer to verify the shading. It was undeniably, exactly her creation.

I flipped through a three-year-old magazine, not actually reading the articles, just listening to the crinkle of the glossy pages. The waiting room smelled faintly of antiseptic and stale coffee. I slumped down in the vinyl chair, letting my head loll to the side. The ticking of the wall clock echoed in the silent room. Tick. Tick. Tick. I tossed the magazine onto the low table and began picking at a loose thread on my jeans, trying to guess how many ceiling tiles were in the room. A nurse walked out with a clipboard, calling a name. The woman sitting across from me stood up, tossing her cardigan over her arm. I caught a glimpse of her calf. The breath caught in my throat. Tattooed just above her ankle was my watercolor fox, the one I had painted during my lowest slump last winter.

Julian lay flat on his beach towel, staring blankly at the underside of his umbrella. The rhythmic crashing of the waves, which had been relaxing an hour ago, now just sounded like a repetitive loop. He kicked lazily at the sand with his heel, sighing heavily. He hadn't brought a book, his phone was dead, and he was completely done with swimming. He rolled onto his stomach, resting his chin on his crossed arms, and watched people walk past. Legs, coolers, flip-flops. More legs. Then, a pair of calves stopped right in his line of sight. On the left calf, inked in stark black lines, was the exact weeping angel sculpture he had carved for his senior thesis. Julian blinked, thinking the heat was playing tricks on his eyes. He scrambled up onto his knees, sand clinging to his chest, staring at the walking masterpiece.

My feet slapped the treadmill belt in a slow, uninspired rhythm. I stared at the red digital numbers on the console, willing the timer to move faster. Only ten minutes had passed. I let out a long puff of air, draping a towel over the display so I wouldn't have to look at it anymore. I stared blankly at the wall in front of me, listening to the synchronized squeak of sneakers across the room. I considered just hitting the big red stop button and going home to lie on the floor. A guy hopped onto the machine next to me, adjusting his headphones. As he reached up to stretch, the back of his shirt lifted. Etched right between his shoulder blades was the sprawling oak tree I had designed for an album cover that never got released. My foot missed the belt entirely.

Clara tossed another stale piece of bread to the pigeons, resting her cheek in her palm. The park was quiet, the gray afternoon stretching out in a long, unbroken line of nothing to do. She watched a leaf float down into the pond, charting its incredibly slow progress across the water. She let out a long sigh, tossing the rest of the crusts into the grass all at once. She dusted her hands off on her jeans, preparing to trudge back to her apartment. A jogger stopped at the water fountain nearby, bending over to drink. Clara’s eyes wandered aimlessly toward him, but stopped abruptly at his exposed calf. The ink was dark and heavily shaded—a perfect replica of the charcoal gargoyle she had sketched during her semester in Paris. Clara gripped the edge of the wooden bench, leaning forward.

My aunt was explaining her new diet for the third time this evening. I pushed my mashed potatoes around with my fork, building a small, starchy mountain and then flattening it back out. I let out a slow, silent exhale through my nose, propping my heavy head up with my free hand. I stared at the floral pattern on the tablecloth, tracing the vines with my eyes. My cousin’s new boyfriend sat across from me, and he reached over to pass the salt shaker. As his arm extended, his sleeve hitched up, revealing a band of ink around his wrist. I stopped playing with my food. The design was unmistakable—a continuous line drawing of two faces interlocked, the very piece I had framed above my drafting table. I dropped my fork, the clatter echoing loudly against the good china, cutting Aunt Linda off mid-sentence.

Elias rested his chin in his palm, swirling a lukewarm latte with a wooden stirrer. Outside the café window, a massive billboard proudly displayed the digital illustration he’d posted on his obscure blog three years ago. The corporate logo of a tech giant was slapped directly over his signature. Elias watched a pigeon peck at a cigarette butt on the sidewalk. He counted the number of times the pigeon bobbed its head—twelve, thirteen. Someone from the firm had clearly ripped the JPEG right off his site. He let out a long, slow breath, watching the condensation drip down his glass. The café clock ticked, each second heavy and thick. He picked at a loose thread on his sweater sleeve, wondering if he should order another coffee just to give his hands something to do for the next hour until his bus finally arrived.

I’ve been staring at the stucco texture of the gallery ceiling for what feels like an eternity. Below me, wealthy patrons clink champagne flutes, murmuring about the raw talent of the featured artist. That artist is currently standing next to a canvas I painted in my garage last summer. He stole it from my ex-roommate. I leaned against the cool plaster wall, tapping my shoe against the baseboard. Tap, tap, tap. A woman in a velvet dress walked by, leaving a trail of heavy perfume. I checked my phone screen—only 8:14 PM. Still forty-six minutes until the open bar closed. I scrolled through old emails, deleted a few spam messages, and let out a heavy exhale. I suppose I should walk over there and confront the guy, but it feels like an awful lot of effort.

The washing machine drum spun in a hypnotic, rhythmic thump. Thump, thump, thump. Maya rested her forehead against the cool glass of the window, tracing the soapy water’s path with her eyes. Pinned to the community bulletin board beside the change machine was a neon green flyer for a local punk show. The centerpiece was a sketch she had drawn in her sketchbook last month—someone had photocopied it without asking, blowing up her delicate linework into a grainy mess. Maya blinked slowly, shifting her weight from one foot to the other. She pulled a piece of lint from her jeans and flicked it onto the linoleum floor. The dryer buzzed a loud, nasal tone from three rows down. Maya let her head fall back against the wall, staring at the flickering fluorescent light tube above her, waiting for the cycle to end.

My thumb swiped upward. Upward again. A brightly colored ad for a dropshipping t-shirt company slid into view. The design on the shirt was my charcoal study of a weeping willow, the one I’d uploaded to an old portfolio site. I rested my cheek on my fist, feeling the weight of my heavy eyelids. I opened a new tab, checked the weather for tomorrow—cloudy, 60 degrees—and closed it again. I clicked back to the t-shirt ad. The fabric looked cheap. I stared at the blinking cursor in the URL bar for a solid minute, listening to the hum of the refrigerator in the kitchen. I grabbed a pen off the desk and started clicking it. Click-clack, click-clack. I wondered what I should make for dinner. Pasta, maybe. Or just toast. The screen dimmed, and I didn't bother moving the mouse to wake it.

The receptionist had said “just five more minutes” twenty minutes ago. Julian slouched deeply into the beige leather waiting room chair, his legs stretched out like two wooden planks. Hanging directly across from him was a massive framed print of a misty mountain range. It was his photograph. He hadn’t sold it to them. He hadn’t even signed a release. Julian blew a stray hair out of his eyes and watched it flutter before settling back on his forehead. He picked up a dog-eared architectural magazine from the glass table, flipped to the middle without looking, and stared blankly at a picture of a minimalist kitchen. The clock on the wall clicked loudly with every second. Julian let the magazine drop back onto the table with a soft thud. He began counting the small circular perforations in the acoustic ceiling tiles, making it to forty-seven.

Professor Higgins droned on about cellular structures, his flat voice blending with the hum of the projector. I rested my chin on my crossed arms, staring at the screen. The diagram of the mitochondria glowing on the whiteboard was unmistakably mine—the precise shading and quirky labels I had uploaded to a study forum last semester, now stripped of my watermark. I let out a long breath, watching a dust mote drift lazily through the projector’s beam. I took my mechanical pencil and started shading a perfect square in the margins of my notebook. The graphite scratched against the paper in a slow, rhythmic hush. Higgins cleared his throat and switched to the next slide. I rested my cheek on the cold laminate of the desk, my eyes half-closed, wondering if the dining hall was serving those dry turkey wraps again today.

The boutique had slapped a neon pink filter over Leo’s gritty stencil art, using it as the backdrop for their spring mannequin display. Leo stood on the sidewalk outside, chewing slowly on a piece of flavorless gum. He popped a small bubble. It snapped softly. He shoved his hands deep into the pockets of his oversized jacket and watched a street sweeper trundle slowly down the avenue, its brushes rotating in endless, repetitive circles. The boutique owner hadn't paid him a dime, completely missing the anti-capitalist message of the piece. Leo stared at the mannequin’s plastic, lifeless hand. He shifted his weight, scuffing the toe of his sneaker against a crack in the pavement. A gray sedan drove by. Then a white one. Leo sighed, pulling his phone out just to check the lock screen, noting he still had three hours to kill.

I stirred my iced tea with the straw, watching the ice cubes bob up and down in the amber liquid. Right above my booth, hand-painted in loopy cursive, was the exact character design and typography I’d created for my thesis project. The café owner had clearly traced it, claiming the aesthetic for their rebrand without asking. I let my head loll back against the vinyl seat. The ceiling fan rotated at a sluggish pace, its blades coated in a thin layer of grey dust. I took a sip of the tea; it tasted mostly like melted water now. I pulled a napkin from the dispenser and began tearing it into tiny, perfectly even strips, lining them up along the edge of the table. A fly buzzed near the window. I watched it bump against the glass over and over, trapped in a pointless little loop.

Arthur pressed the spacebar. The character jumped. He pressed it again. Another jump. On the screen, the enemy boss loaded in—a grotesque, multi-eyed alien. It was the exact 3D model Arthur had posted on an open forum with a strict no-commercial-use tag. The indie developer had just lifted it wholesale. Arthur rested his face in his hands, peering through his fingers at the glowing monitor. He dragged the mouse in lazy circles, watching the cursor trace useless loops around the stolen alien. The game’s background music consisted of a repeating four-chord synth loop that seemed to drill slowly into his skull. He leaned back until his chair squeaked, staring at a water stain on the ceiling. He wondered how long it would take for the developer to notice if he just went to sleep right here at his desk.

The train clattered along the tracks, rocking me side to side in a steady, numbing rhythm. Out the smudged window, a billboard flashed by. It was advertising a new energy drink, but the background was undeniably my vector art—a sprawling cyberpunk cityscape I’d spent months detailing. They hadn't asked me for permission. I blinked, watching the telephone poles whip past. One, two, three, four. My phone battery was dead. I had nothing to look at but the frayed fabric of the seat in front of me. I traced the woven pattern with my thumbnail, feeling the rough texture. The passenger next to me coughed. I leaned my head against the vibrating glass of the window, letting the low rumble of the engine fill my ears. Only seven more stops. I let out a long, hollow exhale, wishing the train would move a little faster.

Chloe sank deeper into the plush beige sofa, her eyes fixed on the blank television screen reflecting the living room. Above the mantelpiece hung a canvas print of her watercolor sunset. Her host, Mark, had just proudly announced he bought it at a discount home goods store for fifteen dollars. He had no idea she painted the original. Chloe picked at a loose thread on the throw pillow, wrapping it around her index finger until the tip turned slightly purple, then unspooling it again. Mark's story about his weekend golf trip droned on, a steady stream of noise blending with the ticking grandfather clock in the hallway. Chloe stared at the way the fake gold frame caught the light. She let her jaw go slack, her eyelids drooping heavily as she mentally cataloged the contents of her own refrigerator back home.

I clicked the right arrow on the remote. Another row of terrible movies slid across the television screen. I clicked right again. A sci-fi thriller popped up, featuring a heavily filtered version of a digital painting I had commissioned for a private client. The studio had just stolen it for their thumbnail. I slumped down until my neck rested on the back of the couch. I stared at the ceiling fan, watching it spin on its lowest setting. I tossed the remote onto the coffee table; it landed with a dull plastic clatter. I peeled a label off my empty water bottle, taking extreme care to keep the paper in one continuous strip. The movie synopsis blinked on the screen, waiting for me to make a choice. I closed my eyes, listening to the hum of the air conditioner, entirely unmotivated to press play.

Julian scanned the final varsity roster taped to the locker room door. He had kept his entire autumn schedule open for the team, but his name wasn't there. He let out a slow exhale, his eyes drifting away from the paper to a flickering fluorescent bulb overhead. It hummed in a continuous, flat note. He tapped his knuckles against his thigh, one, two, three, four times. The coach was offering sympathetic pats to other rejected boys down the hall, but Julian just stared at a peeling chip of blue paint on the concrete wall. He traced the jagged edge with his thumbnail, flicking it onto the linoleum floor. Without afternoon practice, he had exactly four hours to kill before dinner. He kicked a stray piece of gravel, checking his watch. Only two minutes had passed.

The email from the university athletics department sat open on my laptop screen, detailing my failure to make the starting lineup I'd been guaranteed. I minimized the window and stared at the desktop wallpaper. A digital clock in the corner blinked 3:14 PM. I picked up a loose thread on the hem of my sweatpants and pulled it until the fabric puckered. Across the room, a fly banged repeatedly against the window glass, buzzing with a desperate energy I couldn't relate to. I leaned my head back against the sofa cushions, watching dust motes drift through a single shaft of sunlight. Without two-a-day drills, my schedule was an endless stretch of nothing. I picked up the TV remote, flipped through fifty channels of daytime programming, and turned it off again.

Maya sat on the cold bleachers, resting her chin in her palm as she watched the regional swim team begin their warm-up laps. The coach had delivered the news of her exclusion yesterday, despite her dominating the trials. Now, she simply watched the rhythmic splashing with heavy eyelids. Her leg bounced, a rapid, mechanical rhythm against the metal seating. She pulled a stray bobby pin from her hair and began scratching meaningless spirals into the frosted condensation of her water bottle. The smell of chlorine just smelled like chemical bleach today. She counted the ceiling tiles—forty-two across, twenty down. Eight hundred and forty tiles. A whistle blew sharply, echoing off the humid walls, but Maya didn't flinch. She checked her phone. Fifty-two percent. She locked the screen, unlocked it, and locked it again.

They posted the minor league draft results this morning. I had packed my bags weeks ago, but my agent didn’t call. I dragged a lawn chair onto the front porch and slumped into the plastic webbing. A neighborhood kid rode his tricycle up and down the sidewalk. Up. Down. Squeak, squeak. I found a stick on the floorboards and began dragging it back and forth across the toe of my sneaker, watching the dirt smudge into the white leather. I reached into my pocket, pulling out three coins, and started passing them from knuckle to knuckle. A dog barked three blocks away. I caught the coins, shoved them back into my pocket, and let my head loll to the side, listening to the agonizingly slow tick of my wristwatch.

Elena rested her forehead against the cool glass of the passenger window. Her mother had been driving in silence since they left the national qualifying center, where the judges had inexplicably passed Elena over for the Olympic squad. Outside, identical pine trees zipped past in a continuous, green blur. Elena sighed, fogging up the glass, and drew a smiley face in the condensation. She gave it a top hat, then wiped it away with the sleeve of her jacket. She popped the glove compartment open, stared at the neat stack of napkins, and clicked it shut. Open. Shut. Open. Shut. "Stop that, please," her mother murmured. Elena dropped her hands to her lap. She counted the dashed white lines on the highway, losing track around two hundred, and started over from one.

The rejection voicemail from the relay coach was still queued on my phone. I had already bought the matching team cleats, assuming my spot was locked. I deleted the message, tossing the device onto my unmade bed. I lay on the floor, staring up at the popcorn ceiling. I started trying to find shapes in the textured plaster. There was a blob that looked like a shoe. Another looked vaguely like a cloud. I rolled onto my stomach, resting my chin on my folded arms. Without track conditioning, the afternoon stretched out like a vast, empty desert. I grabbed a pencil from my desk and started rolling it back and forth across the hardwood floor. Push, roll, stop. Push, roll, stop. I let out a loud, drawn-out groan that echoed in the empty room.

Marcus leaned against the vending machine in the ice arena lobby, ignoring the printed cut-list clutched in his left hand. The varsity hockey team he’d anchored last year had moved on without him. He popped a piece of tasteless gum into his mouth and chewed with a slow, exaggerated motion. He stared blankly at the spinning coils behind the glass of the snack machine, watching a bag of pretzels teeter on the edge of its row. He shifted his weight from his left foot to his right, his hands buried deep in the pockets of his letterman jacket. A group of younger kids ran past, shouting, but Marcus barely blinked. He took out his phone, scrolled down his contact list to the very bottom, then scrolled all the way back up without tapping a single name.

I didn't make the travel club I was recruited to join. The realization settled over me not with a crash, but with a flat, hollow thud. I sat on the back patio steps, tossing a pebble up and catching it. Toss, catch. Toss, catch. The sun beat down on the parched yellow grass of our lawn. I pulled a blade of grass from the edge of the concrete and split it down the middle, perfectly bisecting the green ribbon. I tossed it aside and found another one to split. The distant hum of a lawnmower droned on, an endless, flat noise that matched the wide-open expanse of my afternoon. I rested my elbows on my knees and let my jaw hang slack. I picked up my phone, opened the weather app, and closed it.

The rejection letter from the academy, a place David was practically guaranteed to enter, lay crumpled in the wastebasket. David lay upside down on his bed, his head hanging off the edge, watching the blood rush to his face. From this angle, his desk chair looked like some weird, modern art sculpture. He batted at a loose string dangling from his blanket. Without the intensive summer tennis camp, he had absolutely nothing on his calendar for the next two months. He let out a long, heavy breath, blowing a lock of hair out of his eyes. It fell right back. He blew it away again. He dragged himself upright, grabbed a tennis ball from his nightstand, and threw it at the wall. Thwack. Catch. Thwack. Catch. He aimed for a smudge on the wallpaper, hitting it dead center ten times.

The final roster was pinned to the bulletin board. Despite my flawless tryout, my name was missing. I sat on the wooden bench in the locker room, listening to the dripping showerhead in the far stall. Drip. Drip. Drip. I laced up my sneakers, pulled the knot tight, then unlaced them just to tie them again. The smell of old sweat and liniment hung in the air, heavy and flat. Without two-a-days, I had the entire month of August completely free. I picked at a loose piece of athletic tape on my wrist, unrolling it inch by agonizing inch until it finally snapped off. I balled the sticky tape up and flicked it toward the trash can. It missed, bouncing softly against the tile. I just sat back, waiting for the clock to hit three.

Chloe sat at a small corner table in the cafe, her figure skating bag shoved carelessly beneath her chair. The pairs coach had told her they were going with another girl, even though Chloe had practically run the auditions. Chloe rested her cheek against the cold tabletop, tracing the grain of the fake wood with her index finger. She stirred her iced latte with a green plastic straw, watching the ice cubes swirl in a lazy circle. Clink, clink, clink. She took a sip; the ice had melted, watering down the coffee. She let out a long, theatrical sigh, resting her chin in both hands and staring at the barista wiping down the espresso machine. Wipe, rinse, repeat. She built a small pyramid out of sugar packets, then knocked it down with her pinky.

The crew team I was supposed to captain launched their eight-man shell without me, gliding away smoothly down the river. I sat on the grassy bank, leaning back on my elbows. I pulled a dandelion from the dirt and blew the white seeds into the wind, watching them float away into the gray, overcast sky. Without the morning regatta schedule, my days stretched out in an unbroken, featureless line. I picked up a flat skipping stone and side-armed it across the water. One, two, three skips before it sank. I reached for another stone without looking, my fingers brushing against the cool, damp earth. A barge moved sluggishly down the center of the river. I closed my eyes, wishing it was time for lunch already.

Coach Miller drew arrows on the clipboard, his face red with strategic passion. Liam watched a single bead of sweat track down the man’s temple. "So, we're putting you in right field," Miller said, slamming a fist into his palm. Liam traced the seam of his baseball pants with his thumbnail, slowly pulling a loose thread until it snagged. Right field. He imagined the vast, quiet expanse of grass where the ball rarely flew. He could probably count all the dandelions out there. "Got it, Coach," Liam said, his voice flat. He leaned his chin on his palm, blinking slowly as Miller continued detailing the defensive shift. The buzzing of the fluorescent locker room light seemed louder than the coach's voice. Liam wondered if he had left his phone charger in the car, his gaze drifting up to count the water stains on the ceiling tiles.

"I need you at left-back today," Coach announced, slapping my shoulder. I stared at the green turf, using my cleat to dig a perfectly symmetrical hole in the rubber pellets. Left-back. I’d be running up and down the sideline, making safe passes, watching everyone else shoot. "Sure," I mumbled, letting my arms hang limp at my sides. The whistle blew, and I jogged to my new spot, the defensive line stretching out beside me. The opposing team passed the ball around their own penalty box for what felt like an hour. I shifted my weight from my left foot to my right foot, then back again. I watched a pigeon waddle across the track surrounding the field. It pecked at a discarded sunflower seed. I let out a long, heavy exhale, watching my breath puff in the cold air, waiting for the ball to cross the midfield line.

Maya sat at the bench, absentmindedly spinning a basketball on her finger. It fell, and she nudged it back with her shoe. Coach knelt in front of her. "We're moving you off the point. I need you spotting up in the corner." Maya rested her elbows on her knees, letting her head loll to the side. "Okay," she exhaled, staring at the scuff marks on the hardwood. Spotting up meant standing still. Waiting. She watched the clock tick down the warm-ups. Fifty-eight seconds. Fifty-seven. She imagined standing in the corner, arms raised, just existing as a decoy while the offense ran elsewhere. She reached down and retied her perfectly tight shoelaces, taking an extra twenty seconds to make the loops exactly even, ignoring the hype music blaring through the gymnasium speakers.

"You're anchoring the line today, right tackle," the coordinator barked, grabbing my jersey. I blinked at him, my face completely neutral. I wouldn’t be running routes anymore. Just blocking. Step, push, hold. Step, push, hold. "Alright," I said, my voice barely carrying over the chatter. Out on the field, I took my three-point stance. The turf smelled like damp dirt. I stared at the defensive end across from me. He was hyped, jumping around, slapping his helmet. I just knelt there, staring at the white chalk of the yard line. The quarterback yelled the cadence. I calculated how many plays were left in this quarter. Probably fifteen. I let out a long breath through my nose. The ball snapped. I stepped forward, put my hands on the guy's chest, and pushed. He pushed back. We stood there, locked together, while the play went somewhere else.

Elena peeled a piece of loose tape from her knee pad, rolling it into a tiny, sticky ball. "I want you in the libero jersey," Coach Davis said, tossing the contrasting shirt onto her lap. "We need your passing." Elena looked at the bright yellow fabric. She flattened it out, tracing the number with a slow finger. "Got it," she said, her tone perfectly flat. She pulled the jersey over her head, her movements sluggish. During the scrimmage, she stood in the back row, her arms hanging loosely in front of her. The ball went back and forth over the net. A spike. A block. Elena watched a dust mote float through the shaft of sunlight illuminating the gym floor. She tracked its slow descent, entirely captivated by the floating speck, until the whistle blew. She shuffled two steps to the right, resetting her stance with a heavy sigh.

"Slide back to defense tonight," Coach instructed, tapping my helmet with his clipboard. "We're short on the blue line." I scraped my skate blade against the rubber matting, creating a pile of tiny black shavings. "Sure thing, Coach." Out on the ice, the cold air usually woke me up, but tonight I felt heavy. I glided backward across the blue line, watching the forwards chase the puck deep in the offensive zone. They battled along the boards. I stood by the point, leaning my weight onto my stick, resting my chin on my glove. I watched the Zamboni doors at the far end of the rink, wondering how many laps the driver takes to clear the ice. The puck popped out to center. I skated over, loosely chipped it back into the corner, and returned to my spot to lean on my stick once more.

The track coach pointed his pen at Marcus. "I'm moving you off the anchor. You're running the first leg today." Marcus rested his cheek against his fist, staring blankly at the rusted bleachers. The anchor leg had all the glory, the dramatic finish. The first leg was just a crowded start. "Fine," Marcus muttered, not breaking his gaze from a lone candy wrapper blowing across the stands. He walked to the starting blocks, his spikes dragging audibly against the synthetic track. He settled into the blocks, staring at the empty lane ahead of him. The starter raised the gun. Marcus analyzed the texture of the red track surface, noting how the tiny rubber granules looked like crushed gravel. The gun cracked. He pushed off, matching the pace of the runners beside him, feeling entirely robotic as he rounded the curve to hand off the baton.

"Switch to the bow seat today," the coxswain called out through the megaphone. I unclipped my feet and climbed over the riggers, taking my new spot at the very front of the shell. As the stroke, I set the pace. Now, I just followed the person in front of me. Catch, drive, finish, recover. I stared at the sweaty back of the rower in the two-seat. Catch, drive, finish, recover. The rhythm was established, locked in. I let my eyes glaze over, watching the rhythmic splash of the oar blades. A duck paddled by the boat, looking completely unbothered by our passing. I wondered what ducks thought about all day. Probably nothing. I matched the swing of the boat perfectly, my mind drifting completely away from the water, the race, and the burn in my legs, mentally rearranging the furniture in my bedroom.

"We need you at fullback," the captain said, tossing Sarah the number 15 jersey. Sarah caught it with one hand and let it dangle. As a fly-half, she orchestrated every play. Now, she would be the last line of defense, standing deep in her own half. She pulled the jersey on and walked out to the pitch, her cleats sinking into the muddy grass. The match started, and the forwards immediately collapsed into a chaotic scrum. Sarah stood forty meters back, hands on her hips. She watched a cloud shaped vaguely like a teapot drift slowly across the grey sky. The whistle blew for a penalty. Sarah shifted her weight, pulling a blade of grass from the ground and splitting it down the middle with her thumbnail. She dropped the pieces, watching them flutter to the mud, before looking up to see if the ball had moved.

"Get in the cage," Coach yelled, tossing me the red goalie cap. "We need someone to block." I tied the strings under my chin, my expression utterly flat. I swam over to the goal, treading water in the shallow end. The rest of the team started a highly contested scrimmage at the opposite end of the pool. The splashing echoed loudly off the natatorium walls. I leaned my elbows on the floating crossbar, resting my chin on my forearms. I watched the ripples radiate outward from the distant swimmers. One, two, three, four ripples. They gently lapped against my chest. I slowly dunked my head underwater to muffle the sounds of shouting, watching the drain grate at the bottom of the pool. It had twelve slots. I came back up, wiped the water from my eyes, and went back to leaning on the crossbar.

"Stay back on the baseline this set," Julian's partner panted, wiping sweat from his brow. "Let me handle the net." Julian twirled his racket in his hand, a slow, continuous loop. "Yep," he said, walking to the back of the court. He stood near the fence, resting the frame of his racket against his toe. His partner served, rushed the net, and volleyed the return for a winner. Julian hadn't moved a muscle. He watched a yellow butterfly flutter aimlessly over the net cord. The next point started. A deep lob came toward him. Julian took three measured steps, hit a routine groundstroke, and walked back to his spot. He began counting the hexagonal links in the chain-link fence behind him, losing track around forty and exhaling a long breath as he decided to start over from the top corner.

"Drop back to sweeper," Coach ordered at halftime. "Just clear the ball if it comes near you." I took a sip from my water bottle, staring blankly at the plastic nozzle. "Okay." I jogged onto the turf, taking my position just ahead of our goalie. The second half commenced, and all the action localized around the opponent's striking circle. I stood still, my stick resting across my shoulders, hands draped loosely over the ends. The minutes ticked by. I started tracing circles in the synthetic grass with the toe of my shoe. I wondered if the cafeteria was serving pizza today. Would it be the square kind or the triangular kind? A stray ball finally rolled slowly toward me. I didn't bend my knees. I just swung my stick like a pendulum, slapping it back to the midfield, and resumed tracing my circles.

The CEO stood at the front of the breakroom, his voice trembling as he announced the acquisition. I kept my eyes on the margins of my legal pad, meticulously shading in the tiny squares I’d drawn during the first five minutes of the meeting. "A new era," he proclaimed, gesturing wildly. I shifted my weight, feeling the hard plastic of the folding chair dig into my lower back. I checked my watch: 2:14 PM. Still three hours and forty-six minutes until I could leave. The woman next to me gasped, whispering something about layoffs. I picked up my blue pen and began drawing triangles inside the shaded squares. If the new owners used a different payroll system, maybe it would mean a new color scheme for the portal. I let out a long breath, watching the second hand on the wall clock tick forward.

Julian rested his chin in his palm, his scrolling finger moving on autopilot through the endless corporate email thread. The subject line, URGENT: MERGER AND ACQUISITION FINALIZED, had thirty-two replies. He dragged his cursor over a block of text detailing the restructuring plan, highlighting it in blue, then clicking away to remove the highlight, over and over. His cat jumped onto the desk, and Julian spent a solid minute inspecting a piece of lint caught in its whiskers. On his second monitor, the company-wide town hall played on mute. The regional manager was weeping visibly on camera. Julian leaned back in his ergonomic chair, staring at the spinning blades of his ceiling fan. He wondered if he should make a turkey sandwich now or wait until three o'clock. He slowly returned his hand to the mouse, spinning the scroll wheel to reach the bottom of the email.

"They’re buying us out," Sarah hissed over the cubicle wall, her eyes wide with panic. "TechNova is taking over everything." I stared at the blinking cursor on my screen. It flashed once, twice, three times. "Did you hear me?" she asked, waving a hand in my peripheral vision. "Yeah," I mumbled, resting my forehead against my knuckles. I dragged a window around my desktop screen, watching it ghost against the background wallpaper. The buyout probably meant another round of onboarding videos. Last year’s security compliance module took four hours to click through. I let my eyes unfocus until the lines of code blurred into gray streaks. "What are we going to do?" Sarah demanded. I peeled a loose sticker off the corner of my monitor. "I guess I’ll have to update my email signature," I said, tossing the sticky scrap into the wastebasket.

Marcus stacked the cardboard boxes in a perfect tower, flawlessly aligning the corners. Over the intercom, the warehouse manager’s voice crackled, announcing that the retail chain had been sold to a national conglomerate effective immediately. Marcus picked up his tape gun. He dragged the adhesive strip across the next flap, the harsh ripping sound echoing in the empty aisle. A few coworkers up front were shouting, their voices ringing with shock and uncertainty. Marcus sat on an overturned crate and stared at his scuffed steel-toed boots. He tapped his left foot. Then his right foot. He examined a jagged hangnail on his thumb, wondering if he had clippers in his locker. The intercom clicked off with a sharp pop.
