Marcus sighed, letting his shoulders slump as he reached for the next flat sheet of cardboard, folding the flaps in the exact same sequence he always did.

The PowerPoint slide transitioned with a swoosh sound, revealing the logo of our new parent company. Our director paused for dramatic effect, waiting for our reactions. I traced the condensation dripping down my plastic water cup. A drop reached the table, pooling against the fake wood grain. I tapped the puddle with my index finger, dragging the water into a long, thin line. "This acquisition changes everything," the director said softly. I looked past him, out the large conference room window. Two pigeons were fighting over a piece of bread on the ledge. I watched them peck and flutter until the victor flew away. I shifted my gaze to the wall clock. 11:42 AM. Lunch wasn't until noon. I leaned back, crossing my arms, and began counting the acoustic dimples in the ceiling tiles directly above my head. One, two, three, four.

Elena wiped the espresso machine with a damp rag, rubbing the same stubborn coffee stain in slow, wide circles. The bakery owner stood near the register, emotionally telling the morning crew that he was handing the keys over to a corporate franchise tomorrow. Two baristas were crying, hugging each other near the pastry case. Elena moved to the steam wand, unscrewing the tip with a metal scrape. She watched a bubble form and pop in the soapy sink water. The owner walked over, placing a heavy hand on her shoulder. "It’s going to be a big transition," he said gently. "Okay," Elena replied, her voice completely flat. She dried the metal wand, reattached it, and pushed the rag across the counter again. She stared out the front window at the gray sky, calculating exactly how many days were left until her apartment lease was up.

The red emergency light flashed, signaling a complete halt on the assembly line. The foreman climbed onto a forklift to announce that an overseas conglomerate had purchased the plant. The roar of the machines faded, replaced by murmurs from the floor. I stood at my station, leaning my hip against the cold metal railing. I took off my safety goggles, wiping a smudge of grease off the lens with my thumb. The foreman’s voice droned on about share prices and global synergy. I stared at a loose bolt rattling slightly on the conveyor belt. I imagined the bolt rolling off the edge, bouncing across the concrete, and escaping out the loading dock doors into the woods. A guy next to me swore loudly about losing his pension. I put my goggles back on and let out a long, slow breath, waiting for the line to start moving again.

Arthur sat at his mahogany desk, building a small pyramid out of paper clips. The memo about the hostile takeover sat printed on his blotter, stamped with urgent red letters. The entire floor outside his glass office was in chaos. Phones were ringing off the hook, and junior executives were power-walking down the hallways with stacks of files. Arthur connected a silver clip to a red one, balancing it carefully on the apex of his structure. He rested his chin in his hand, watching the flimsy metal sway under the air conditioning vent. The new CEO was supposedly arriving in an hour to clean house. Arthur picked up a yellow highlighter and slowly drew a thick, neon line around the border of a blank sticky note. He capped the marker with a soft click, placed it in his drawer, and reached for another silver paper clip.

I kept my expression perfectly neutral as the CEO cried on the Zoom call, explaining the terms of the buyout. I had minimized the video window so it only took up a tiny square in the corner of my screen. The rest of my monitor was dedicated to a game of Solitaire. I clicked and dragged the black eight onto the red nine. In the chat box, dozens of messages flooded in with exclamation marks and question marks. People were demanding answers about severance and stock options. I uncovered an ace of spades and double-clicked it to send it to the foundation pile. The CEO was still talking, his face red and blotchy. I rested my cheek heavily against my palm, staring blankly as I blindly dealt three more cards from the deck. None of them were a playable red six. I let out a heavy breath and clicked reshuffle.

Dr. Lin swirled the purple liquid in her beaker, watching it coat the curved glass. The intercom buzzed, and the chief of research announced the lab’s immediate acquisition by a rival pharmaceutical giant. Several technicians dropped their clipboards, breaking into hushed, frantic conversations about patent ownership. Lin set the beaker down and picked up her mechanical pencil. She clicked the eraser. Once, twice, three times. The graphite extended, then broke off when she pressed it against the countertop. She swept the tiny gray speck into her palm and blew it away. A colleague rushed over, grabbing her arm. "Did you hear? They’re liquidating our division!" Lin blinked slowly, looking at the colleague’s hand on her sleeve, then back to her beaker. "I need to run this sample through the centrifuge," she said, her tone completely level. "It takes forty-five minutes. Do you want to watch it spin?"

The editor-in-chief stood on a desk, yelling over the typing and ringing phones that a private equity firm just bought the paper. The newsroom erupted. Reporters yelled questions, interns cried, and someone knocked over a stack of archives. I sat in my chair, rolling back and forth by pushing off the edge of my desk with my toe. Squeak. Roll. Squeak. Roll. I watched the dust motes drift through a beam of sunlight pouring in from the skylight. The editor was talking about downsizing and a new digital-first mandate. I picked up a rubber band and stretched it between my thumb and index finger, plucking it like a guitar string. It made a flat sound. I pulled it tighter until it snapped against my skin, leaving a brief red mark. I rubbed my thumb, spun my chair in a slow circle, and stared at the ceiling.

The head chef burst through the swinging doors, waving a signed contract in the air. "I sold the place! A restaurant group from the city is taking over!" The dishwashers cheered, while the sous chefs argued about menu changes. Diego stood at his prep station, a massive sack of potatoes resting at his feet. He picked up a russet, dragged the peeler down its side in one long strip, and tossed it into the water basin. Splash. He reached for another potato. The kitchen buzzed with loud debates about the new management. Diego stared straight ahead at the stainless steel backsplash, watching his distorted reflection. He peeled another potato. Splash. He let his shoulders drop, his eyelids feeling heavy under the harsh fluorescent lights. He calculated that there were at least eighty potatoes left in the sack. He grabbed the next one, the peeler scraping in a steady, unchanging rhythm.

I watched the second hand of the wall clock tick past the twelve for the forty-seventh time since lunch. My screen displayed the same spreadsheet I’d been staring at for hours, the numbers blurring into a gray smudge. I picked up a paperclip, slowly bending it until it snapped. An email popped up from HR, accidentally cc'ing the whole floor on the new hire's compensation package. Twenty-two-year-old Kyle, fresh out of college, was pulling in fifteen grand more than me. I looked at the figure, then looked back at my broken paperclip. I pushed the pieces around my desk, forming a little silver T, then an L. The fluorescent lights overhead emitted a continuous, low drone. I rested my chin heavily on my palm, wondering if it was too early to go down to the cafeteria and watch the vending machine rotate.

Sarah scrolled down the payroll summary, her chin resting on her left hand while her right index finger flicked the mouse wheel with a slow, rhythmic cadence. The quarterly report lay forgotten under a coffee mug. She paused on the line for Jason, the intern they had hired full-time last month. His base salary was substantially higher than her own five-year tenure rate. She blinked at the screen, letting out a long, slow breath that ruffled the sticky notes stuck to her monitor. Outside her window, a squirrel ran across a telephone wire. She watched it for a full five minutes, tracing its path until it disappeared into the oak tree. Turning back to the spreadsheet, she highlighted Jason’s salary, changed the font color to bright pink, and went back to staring at the squirrel's empty branch.

The rhythmic thump-thump-thump of the store’s HVAC unit was the only soundtrack in the breakroom. I was slowly peeling the label off a water bottle, trying to keep it in one continuous strip. Beside me, the manager’s binder sat open. I glanced over, my eyes casually dragging across the new payroll sheet. The kid we hired last Tuesday, the one who couldn't figure out how to fold a sweater, was taking home three dollars more an hour than my supervisor rate. I finally detached the label, rolling it into a tight, sticky cylinder between my thumb and forefinger. I tossed it at the trash can. It missed, landing on the linoleum. I watched the clock on the microwave change from 2:14 to 2:15. Only four hours and forty-five minutes left until my shift ended. I started peeling the label off a second water bottle.

David leaned far back in his ergonomic chair, his eyes tracking the slow progress of a dust mote drifting through a beam of afternoon sunlight. On his monitor, the Slack channel dinged. Someone had mistakenly dropped the new junior developer’s offer letter into the general chat before hastily deleting it. David had caught the number. It was twenty percent higher than his own. He pressed his lips together, exhaling a long puff of air, and spun his chair in a slow, complete circle. When he faced the desk again, he opened a new browser tab and typed 'types of moss' into the search bar. He clicked on the first image, resting his forehead against his palm, and spent the next twenty minutes reading about the cellular structure of sphagnum, letting the low hum of the servers wash over him.

The VP was on slide forty-two of the quarterly alignment presentation. I balanced a pencil perfectly on my index finger, watching it dip and sway. The guy next to me, a fresh graduate named Leo who still wore a suit to our casual office, slid his open laptop toward me to show me a meme. Instead, my eyes caught his open digital paystub on the adjacent tab. The net deposit was considerably larger than the one I’d received that morning after four years of service. The pencil tumbled off my finger and tapped against the mahogany table. I didn't bother picking it up. I just stared at the beige wall behind the projector screen, tracing the faint outline of a scuff mark that looked a bit like a dog. The VP’s voice continued as a steady, flat drone, blending seamlessly with the hum of the cooling fan.

Marcus leaned against the stainless steel prep counter, absently tapping a pair of tongs against his thigh. The lunch rush was completely dead. He watched a single drop of water gather at the tip of the faucet, swell, and eventually fall into the drain. The new sous-chef, a culinary grad who still burned the roux, left his phone unlocked on the cutting board. A text from his bank flashed on the screen, showing a direct deposit amount that dwarfed Marcus's paycheck. Marcus blinked slowly at the glowing screen. He picked up a rag and wiped down the spotless counter for the fourth time in an hour. He tossed the rag into a bin, grabbed a potato, and began peeling it with slow, deliberate strokes, counting each strip of skin as it fell into the sink. One. Two. Three. Four.

I spent the last twenty minutes clicking my pen: click-clack, click-clack. The cursor blinked steadily at the end of a half-written email on my screen. Through the thin glass wall, I heard the director laughing with Chloe, the junior designer who started last week. A misrouted memo sat on my desk, clearly detailing Chloe’s starting salary, which eclipsed mine by a comfortable margin. I stared at the bolded numbers, then looked up at the ceiling tiles. I started counting the tiny holes in the acoustic foam above my head. I lost track around two hundred and had to start over. Click-clack, went my pen. The cursor kept blinking, keeping perfect time with the slow, heavy thud of my heartbeat. I wondered how many clicks a standard ballpoint spring could endure before the metal finally gave out completely.

The fluorescent lights buzzed, a sound Elena usually tuned out, but today it was the only thing occupying her mind. She sat at her reception desk, staring blankly at the wall calendar. The month had already ended, but she hadn’t bothered flipping the page. An envelope meant for the new triage coordinator had ended up in her inbox. She had opened it without looking. The salary printed inside was ten thousand dollars higher than what she made after a decade in the department. Elena let the paper drift onto the desk. She rested her cheek on her folded arms, tracing the grain of the fake wood laminate with her pinky nail. A phone rang three desks away. She didn't move to answer it, just watched the dust particles dancing lazily in the cold, artificial light of the waiting room.

Staring at the endless blocks of text in the contract, my vision started to swim. I highlighted a paragraph, un-highlighted it, then highlighted it again. A misfiled HR document had landed in my inbox an hour ago, revealing that the fresh-faced associate sitting two doors down was pulling in a heftier retainer than I was. I leaned back, letting my head hit the headrest with a soft thud. I stared at the geometric pattern of the carpet. I traced the interlocking squares with my eyes, trying to find a break in the design. Finding none, I rolled my chair back, opened my bottom drawer, and began organizing my collection of highlighters by color gradient, from a bright neon yellow to a faded, pale pink. When I finished, I messed them all up and started the entire process all over again.

Arthur sat in the breakroom, listening to the drip of the coffee maker. He was building a small tower out of sugar packets. He had just seen the open employment file on the printer. The newly hired copywriter, a kid who wore sneakers and graphic tees, was salaried well above Arthur’s senior manager bracket. Arthur placed a pink sweetener packet on top of his tower. It swayed, but held. He sighed, a long exhale that deflated his shoulders, and slumped further into the plastic chair. He watched a fly land on the rim of a discarded mug, rub its front legs together, and fly away. He tapped the bottom of his sugar tower with a single finger, watching the packets cascade onto the table, before slowly beginning to stack them up once more.

The AutoCAD grid on my monitor looked like an endless, grey net. I scrolled out until the lines blurred into a solid, flat grey field. The new drafter, a guy who still asked me how to use the plotters, had accidentally left his paystub on the communal printer. I’d seen it. His take-home was laughably higher than mine. I rested my forehead on the edge of my desk, feeling the cool wood against my skin. I closed my eyes and listened to the rhythmic, muted clicking of keyboards around the open-plan office. I opened one eye and watched a spider weaving a web in the corner of the window frame. It moved with slow, methodical precision. I stayed completely still, watching it loop the silk over and over, wishing the afternoon would just evaporate.

Greg dragged his steel-toed boot across the concrete floor, leaving a faint grey streak. He was holding a clipboard with the monthly budget. An accounting error had left the warehouse supervisor's salaries fully visible, showing the twenty-year-old rookie making significantly more than Greg did after eight years. Greg let the clipboard hang loosely from his fingers. He leaned his back against a towering stack of cardboard boxes and stared up at the high, corrugated metal ceiling. A single, deflated mylar balloon from someone’s birthday months ago was trapped in the rafters, swaying slightly in the draft of the industrial fans. He watched the silver foil catch the dim light. He stood there for a long time, listening to the distant beep of a reversing forklift, waiting for five o'clock to finally arrive.

Martin rested his chin on his palm, watching the cursor blink on line 402. Next to him, the eager new hire, Kevin, excitedly scribbled every word Martin said into a pristine notebook. "So, you just drag this formula down to the bottom," Martin instructed, his voice entirely flat. He watched a single speck of dust drift slowly across the fluorescent light overhead, tracking its descent until it landed on his lukewarm coffee. "And then?" Kevin asked, eyes wide. Martin let out a long, heavy exhale that ruffled the rim of his paper cup. "And then you wait for the macro to run." He tapped his index finger against the mousepad—one, two, three, four—staring at the spinning blue loading wheel as seconds dripped by like molasses.

"The syrup pumps go here," I mumbled, gesturing vaguely toward the sticky counter. The teenager beside me nodded frantically, adjusting her oversized apron. I leaned my weight onto my left hip, picking at a loose thread on my sleeve. "Two pumps for a tall, three for a grande." My gaze drifted to the street outside, tracing the path of a pigeon pecking at a cigarette butt. The espresso machine hissed, a sound I had heard exactly ten thousand times, blending into a background hum that vibrated behind my eyes. "Do I wipe the steam wand now?" she asked. I blinked slowly, pulling my attention back from the pigeon. "Yeah. Always wipe the wand." I rested my forehead against the cool metal of the pastry case, counting the seconds until my shift ended.

Sarah’s eyes glazed over as she pointed a pen at monitor four. "That’s the south gate. You just press this green button if a delivery truck pulls up," she stated, her voice completely lacking any inflection. Beside her, Julian leaned in closely, analyzing the grainy footage of an empty parking lot. Sarah slumped back into her squeaky leather chair, twirling the pen between her fingers. Drop. Catch. Drop. Catch. The rhythmic clicking echoed in the tiny security booth. She stared at a water stain on the ceiling, trying to decide if it looked more like a map of Florida or a squashed shoe. "What if it's a passenger car?" Julian asked. Sarah let out a slow, deflating breath and didn't bother sitting up. "Press the same green button."

I watched the conveyor belt hum, a steady, endless stream of gray plastic caps moving from left to right. "You check for cracks on the rim," I said, not looking at the guy standing next to me. I picked up a cap, turned it over, and tossed it into the bin. Pick, turn, toss. Pick, turn, toss. He mirrored my movements with intense, nervous concentration. My eyelids felt incredibly heavy, sinking downward like lead weights. I began counting the dark scuff marks on the concrete floor, trying to calculate exactly how many steps it would take to reach the exit door. "Am I doing this fast enough?" he asked. I rested my chin on my folded arms over the guardrail, watching the gray blur. "Sure. Whatever works."

The hum of the servers vibrated through the floorboards, a continuous noise that matched the completely blank expression on Greg’s face. He pointed a laser pointer at the rack of tangled wires. "Port 22 is for the main cluster," he said, the words slipping out automatically from muscle memory. The new technician, Lisa, squinted at the tangle, taking frantic notes on her tablet. Greg let his arm drop, the laser dot moving to the floor to draw lazy figure-eights around the toes of his scuffed boots. He wondered what he was going to make for dinner. Maybe pasta. Boiling water took time, but at least watching it bubble was a form of movement. "Should I document the IP addresses?" Lisa asked enthusiastically. Greg stared at the wall of blinking green lights, his jaw slack. "If you want."

"You push the lever forward to engage the blades," I instructed, my voice devoid of any pitch. I leaned against the trunk of a massive oak tree, sliding down until I was sitting flat in the damp grass. The new kid hopped onto the riding mower like it was a spaceship waiting for launch. I plucked a blade of grass and began to tear it into microscopic slivers. The engine roared to life, drowning out the buzzing of the cicadas. I stared up at the clouds, trying to find shapes but only seeing white blobs dragging across an agonizingly blue sky. He drove in a wobbly circle, looking back at me for approval. I gave him a slow, limp thumbs-up, resting my chin on my knees and waiting for the sun to finally set.

Elena rested her cheek against her fist, her eyes half-closed as she watched the new girl, Maya, organize the receptionist sticky notes by color. "The phone will ring. You say 'Good Morning, Miller and Sons'," Elena recited mechanically. She tapped a pencil against her notepad in a slow, hypnotic rhythm. Tap. Pause. Tap. Pause. The lobby was completely empty, the ticking of the wall clock echoing loudly in the sterile space. Elena watched a small spider weave a web in the upper corner of the window frame, mesmerized by the slow, repetitive motion of its tiny legs. "How do I transfer a call to HR?" Maya asked. Elena blinked slowly, letting out a long sigh that fluttered her bangs. "Button three," she murmured, returning her gaze to the spider.

"Tab, enter, copy, paste," I muttered, my chin propped up by my left hand. "Tab, enter, copy, paste." The recent graduate beside me was furiously typing away, his brow furrowed in deep concentration. I scrolled down the endless spreadsheet, a sea of identical numbers blurring into a gray smudge across the wide monitor. I started playing a game with myself, trying to see exactly how long I could hold my breath before the sheer silence in the cubicle drove me crazy. Thirty seconds. Forty. "Does this column need currency formatting?" he whispered. I let out my breath in a long, quiet hiss, my eyes tracking the slow crawl of the digital clock on the bottom right of the screen. "No. Just tab, enter, copy, paste."

Mr. Henderson leaned heavily on the circulation desk, his face a mask of complete neutrality. "You scan the barcode on the back, not the front," he stated, his voice a flat, continuous drawl. The young volunteer fumbled with a massive stack of returned children's books. Henderson stared at the wooden grain of the desk, counting the dark rings in the laminate. Seventeen rings. Eighteen. Nineteen. He felt his jaw crack as he stretched his mouth wide, his eyes watering from the pure effort of keeping them open. The scanner beeped—a sharp, piercing noise that failed to break the heavy fog wrapping around his mind. "Like this?" the boy asked. Henderson gave a single, slow nod, his gaze drifting to a patch of dust gathering on the metal cart.

"The fries take exactly three minutes," I said, staring blankly at the bubbling vat of oil. The trainee nodded aggressively, his uniform crisp and smelling strongly of fabric softener. I stood with my weight shifted entirely onto one leg, my arms dangling uselessly at my sides. A large housefly buzzed past my ear, and I followed its erratic flight path across the fluorescent lights with half-lidded eyes, tracking every loop and dive. "Do we shake the basket halfway through?" he asked eagerly. I didn't answer right away. I was too busy calculating how many more times I would have to hear the fryer timer go off before I could take my apron off. "Yeah," I finally mumbled, my voice trailing away. "Shake the basket."

Chloe’s cheek was smooshed against her palm, warping her mouth into a permanent pout. "Use the clone stamp tool to remove the blemishes," she directed, pointing a lazy finger at the screen. The new designer eagerly clicked away, zooming in on the model's digital face. Chloe slumped lower in her ergonomic chair until her knees practically hit the underside of the desk. She spun a plastic stylus between her thumb and forefinger, watching the ceiling fan complete rotation after rotation. Round and round. She wondered if the fan was moving slightly slower than it was yesterday. "Is the skin tone matching up?" the rookie asked. Chloe barely glanced at the monitor, her heavy eyelids drooping. "Looks fine," she murmured, returning her attention to the fan's endless, spinning journey.

"Add two drops of the reagent," I instructed, my voice completely flat. The new grad student pipetted the clear liquid with trembling, reverent hands. I leaned back against the black laboratory countertops, crossing my arms and staring at a tiny hairline crack in the white tile wall. It looked a bit like a squiggly river. I traced the path of the river with my eyes, from the ceiling down to the rubber baseboard, then back up again. The centrifuge hummed in the background, a continuous vibration that made my brain feel like it was stuffed full of cotton. "Should I log the exact time?" she asked, her eyes shining with academic zeal. I let out a slow, deflating exhale. "Sure. Log the time." I closed my eyes, letting the humming noise wash over me.

Mark stared at the blinking cursor on the new spreadsheet. His transfer to Logistics was meant to be a fresh start, but the beige walls of this cubicle looked exactly like the beige walls of Accounts. He picked up a paperclip, bent it straight, and then twisted it into a tiny, jagged spiral. The clock on the wall loudly ticked to 10:14 AM. It had been 10:11 AM the last time he checked, which felt like three hours ago. Someone two desks down was loudly chewing an apple. Mark rested his chin in the palm of his hand, letting his eyelids droop as he counted the acoustic tiles on the ceiling. Forty-two tiles. He picked up another paperclip from the plastic cup. Only seven and a half hours until he could go home.

They moved me from the sales floor to inventory control yesterday. I spend my shifts now surrounded by brown cardboard boxes, scanning barcodes with a laser gun that beeps a flat, atonal note every three seconds. Beep. Box of winter scarves. Beep. Box of leather gloves. I slide my foot across the concrete floor, drawing a lazy circle in a patch of dust. The radio in the corner plays the same top forty station we had up front, and I’ve already heard this pop song three times since my shift started. I lean my forehead against the cool metal of the shelving rack, closing my eyes while the scanner dangles from my limp fingers. Maybe if I organize the packing peanuts by size it will make the afternoon pass faster. Beep.

Sarah’s reassignment to the legacy systems maintenance team involved a desk in the basement and a dual-monitor setup that displayed endless streams of automated green text. She tapped her polished fingernails against the laminate desk—index, middle, ring, pinky, repeat. A fly buzzed near the fluorescent light fixture above her head, and her eyes tracked its erratic flight path with intense dedication. It was the most action she’d seen all morning. "Hey, Sarah, did you run the diagnostic?" Greg asked from over the partition. "Running it now," she replied, her voice completely flat. She hit the spacebar once. A progress bar appeared on the screen, crawling from one percent to two percent at an agonizingly slow pace. Sarah let out a long breath, inflating her cheeks, and spun her swivel chair in a slow, full circle.

Medical Records is a windowless room that smells strongly of old paper and industrial floor cleaner. Since they pulled me off the reception desk, my primary duty is alphabetizing patient files that date back to the early nineties. I open a manila folder, glance at a name, and slot it into a cabinet. "Aarons, Aaron." "Abbott, Abigail." My jaw cracks as I stretch my mouth wide, drawing in a massive breath of recycled air. I pull my phone out of my pocket, swipe through five pages of apps without opening a single one, and put it back. The silence in the room is heavy, broken only by the rhythmic swish of paper against paper. I rest my cheek against the cold metal of the filing cabinet drawer, staring cross-eyed at the little plastic label holder.

The conveyor belt hummed its steady, unending mechanical drone. Julian had been bumped from quality assurance down to the packaging line, where his sole responsibility was to place a tiny silver sticker on the top right corner of every passing box. Box, sticker. Box, sticker. He shifted his weight from his left foot to his right, staring blankly at a smudge of grease on the belt. His mind drifted to the grocery list he needed to write, then to whether he left his porch light on, and finally to the exact number of steps it took to walk from his car to his front door. Box, sticker. Julian didn't even look at the items anymore. His hand moved on pure muscle memory while his eyes glazed over, fixed on a spot on the opposite wall.

Moving to the Department of Motor Vehicles' archives meant trading angry citizens for absolute, suffocating silence. I sit at a metal desk under a flickering fluorescent tube that hums in B-flat. In front of me is a stack of vehicle registration forms that need to be stamped in triplicate. I press the red rubber stamp onto the ink pad. Thwack. I press it onto the paper. Thud. Thud. Thud. I lean back in my chair, balancing on the back two legs, and trace the outline of a coffee stain on my desk with a dried-out highlighter. I wonder how long it would take for someone to notice if I just stopped stamping and started making paper airplanes out of these forms. Probably days. I let the front legs of my chair hit the floor and sigh deeply.

Professor Higgins’s lateral move from active teaching to the historical archives committee sounded prestigious on paper. In reality, he was stationed in a dust-mote-filled room in the library basement, cataloging nineteenth-century alumni records. He flipped a brittle page, staring unblinkingly at the faded cursive script until the letters blurred into meaningless black squiggles. He picked up his fountain pen, clicked the cap on and off, on and off, the rhythmic plastic snapping echoing off the stone walls. Beside him, an electric fan oscillated back and forth, blowing his sparse grey hair just a fraction of an inch every ten seconds. He followed the fan’s movement with his eyes—left, right, left, right—completely ignoring the ledger in front of him. A heavy sigh escaped his lips as he slumped forward, resting his forehead on his arms.

They switched me from the bustling front desk to the overnight switchboard. It’s 3:00 AM, and the phone hasn’t rung in four hours. I’m sitting in a small room behind the main office, staring at a bank of unlit buttons. I peel a post-it note off a pad, fold it in half, fold it again, and press it flat with my thumbnail until it’s a tiny, dense yellow square. I flick it across the desk. It lands next to five other identical yellow squares. I prop my chin on my hands, feeling the heaviness in my eyelids, and stare at the digital clock. 3:02 AM. I softly tap my foot against the leg of the chair, trying to remember the lyrics to a song I haven't heard since middle school just to give my brain something to do.

The transition from litigation to compliance meant Elena no longer went to court. Now, her days consisted of reviewing hundreds of pages of corporate policy manuals to ensure formatting consistency. She scrolled down the PDF on her monitor, her index finger mechanically spinning the mouse wheel. Line after line of twelve-point Times New Roman text washed over her vision like gray static. She stopped scrolling and picked up a pencil, balancing it horizontally across her upper lip. She held her breath to see how long she could keep it there before it fell. It dropped to the desk with a clatter. Elena slouched deeper into her ergonomic chair, letting her arms hang limp at her sides, and stared at a water stain on the ceiling that looked vaguely like a map of South America.

After the restructuring, I was shifted from the investigative reporting team to writing blurbs for the lifestyle section’s catalog. "Refresh your living room with these vibrant throw pillows." I type the sentence, delete it, and type it again. My chin rests heavily in my palm. I stare out the window at the parking lot, watching a plastic grocery bag drift across the asphalt in the wind. It catches on a bush, flutters for a moment, and goes still. I find myself intensely invested in whether the wind will pick it up again. "Hey, you got that copy?" my new editor asks as she walks by. "Almost," I say, my voice carrying no inflection whatsoever. I drag my cursor over the sentence I just wrote, highlight it in blue, click off, and highlight it again.

Reassignment to the soil testing division meant David’s afternoon consisted of shaking plastic vials of dirt. He held a rack of test tubes, gently agitating them left to right for exactly two minutes. He stared blankly at the brown particles swirling in the water. One minute left. He blew a stray lock of hair out of his eyes and shifted his weight. The lab was dead silent except for the low hum of the centrifuge in the corner. He started counting backward from one thousand in his head. Nine hundred ninety-nine. Nine hundred ninety-eight. He watched a single drop of condensation slide slowly down the side of a glass beaker on the next bench over. When his timer finally beeped, he let out a long, slow breath, set the rack down, and reached for the exact same rack of vials next to it.

The head chef decided I needed to learn the fundamentals again, moving me from the hot line to the prep station in the back corner. My current task is peeling fifty pounds of potatoes. I hold a potato, scrape the peeler down its side, rotate, and scrape again. The skin falls into a giant plastic bucket. I grab another potato. Scrape. Rotate. Scrape. I gaze blankly at the stainless steel wall in front of me, observing the distorted reflection of my own face. I wonder if I could peel an entire potato in one single, unbroken ribbon of skin. I try it. The skin breaks halfway through. I drop the potato in the water bin and let my arms hang heavily by my sides for a moment, staring at the massive mountain of unpeeled potatoes still waiting in the sack.

I dragged my stocking feet across the living room floor, tracing the wood grain with my big toe. I’d arranged the furniture three times already, and the clock on the mantel still only read two-fifteen. With a heavy exhale, I flopped onto the rug and stared at the popcorn ceiling, counting the little bumps. When I reached four hundred, I rolled over and picked at a peeling edge of floral wallpaper. A whole strip tore away, revealing not plaster, but a solid wooden door with a tarnished brass knob. I let out a long, slow breath, resting my cheek against the cold floorboards. I suppose pulling the handle is marginally better than counting ceiling bumps again, I thought, extending a heavy arm toward the brass fixture. The hinges groaned as the heavy wood swung inward, smelling of dust and stale air.

Rain lashed against the tall windows of the Victorian manor, turning the sprawling gardens into a gray blur. Leo sat on the bottom step of the grand staircase, his chin propped heavily in his hands. He watched a single bead of water trace a sluggish path down the glass, silently urging it to move faster. When it finally hit the sill, he let out a loud groan and kicked the wooden panel beneath the stairs. The wood didn't thud; it clicked and swung inward. Leo stared at the dark, yawning gap. He slowly stood up, brushing lint from his jeans. He checked his watch—three more hours until dinner. Shrugging his drooping shoulders, he stepped into the cramped, pitch-black space, pulling his phone out to use the flashlight. At least the dust in here was different from the dust in the living room.

The cursor on my laptop screen blinked in a steady, mocking rhythm. I clicked my ballpoint pen thirty times, then switched to tapping it against my coffee mug. The spreadsheet was exactly where I had left it an hour ago. I spun my desk chair in a slow circle, dragging my sneakers on the carpet to control the speed. On the third rotation, I noticed a slight draft ruffling the edge of the curtains near the built-in bookshelf. I slumped out of the chair, padding over to investigate. Pressing my hand against the back panel of the shelf, the wood suddenly gave way with a soft mechanical clack. The entire unit pivoted outward, exposing a narrow, windowless stone chamber. I leaned against the doorframe, chewing on the end of my pen, wondering if I could set up my desk in there just to change the view.

Maya lay upside down on her bed, her head dangling over the edge while she watched the ceiling fan make endless, sluggish rotations. She had already reorganized her sock drawer by color, fabric, and length. She let out a prolonged sigh that fluttered her bangs. Sitting up, she grabbed a measuring tape from her desk and began walking heel-to-toe across the bedroom, measuring the walls for absolutely no reason. Twenty feet on the left. Fifteen feet on the right. She frowned, tapping the metal casing against her chin. The hallway was thirty feet long. The math didn’t add up. She shuffled to the back of her closet, pushed aside a row of empty hangers, and pressed firmly against the drywall. It popped open like a hidden latch, revealing a dusty servant's quarters. Maya stared at the space, her expression flat, and slowly walked inside.

I sat cross-legged in the center of the empty dining room, watching the fresh coat of gray paint dry. Literally. I watched a slightly wet patch near the trim slowly turn matte, timing it with the stopwatch on my phone. Two minutes and fourteen seconds. I blew a stray hair out of my face and picked up a putty knife, scraping aimlessly at a patch of old floral wallpaper behind the door. A large chunk flaked off, and the blade slipped into a deep groove. I leaned closer, dragging the knife down. It wasn't a crack in the plaster; it was the outline of a door. I dug my fingers into the seam and pulled. The wall swung open on rusted hinges, revealing a dark, cobweb-filled parlor. I let my arms drop, staring into the gloom, hoping there wasn't any more painting to do.

Arthur refolded the morning newspaper for the fifth time, aligning the corners with agonizing precision. He already knew the crossword answers by heart, and the weather report promised nothing but more clouds. He rested his chin on his cane, staring blankly at the floral rug in his newly purchased cottage. He reached into his pocket, retrieved a tarnished penny, and let it drop. It rolled across the floorboards, slipping beneath a heavy oak wainscoting panel. Arthur sighed, a long, rattling breath, and used his cane to pry at the wood. To his surprise, the entire panel slid sideways on a hidden track. Beyond it lay a subterranean wine cellar, thick with dust and draped in spider silk. Arthur didn't gasp or smile. He simply adjusted his glasses, leaned his weight on his cane, and shuffled forward into the dark, glad for a break from the crossword.

Thump. Catch. Thump. Catch. I threw the yellow tennis ball against the living room wall, catching it with a rhythmic smack. There was no cell service out here, the router was still in a moving box, and the nearest neighbor was two miles down a dirt road. Thump. Catch. I threw the ball a little harder. It hit a wooden panel near the fireplace with a hollow, echoing clunk. The panel shuddered and swung slightly ajar. I stopped tossing the ball, letting it roll under the sofa. Approaching the gap, I pushed the wood fully open. The air inside smelled of dried lavender and old paper. A narrow stone staircase spiraled downward into pitch blackness. I leaned against the doorframe, idly spinning the tennis ball in my left hand, debating whether climbing down into the dark was worth the effort of finding a flashlight.

Chloe lay motionless on the futon, staring at a water stain on the ceiling that vaguely resembled a lopsided teapot. The house was entirely unpacked, her roommates wouldn't arrive until tomorrow, and the television wasn't hooked up yet. She scrolled through her phone contacts, found no one she wanted to call, and tossed the device onto the floor. It slid under the radiator with a plastic clatter. Groaning loudly, Chloe rolled off the futon and flattened herself on the hardwood, reaching blindly into the gap. Her fingers brushed against a cold iron ring set into the floorboards. With a heavy sigh, she gave it a half-hearted tug. A trapdoor groaned open, exhaling a puff of musty air from a hidden basement room. Chloe rested her chin on the floorboards, peering down into the darkness without moving, her eyes slowly blinking in the dusty silence.

I plucked the low E string of my bass, letting the heavy note vibrate until it faded completely into the silent room. I waited a full minute, then plucked it again. The blank sheet music on my stand mocked my utter lack of ideas. I spun around on my stool, dragging my boots across the carpet, and rested my head against the wood-paneled wall. I began tapping a slow rhythm against the wood with my knuckles. Tap, tap, thud. I paused. The third strike sounded entirely hollow. I pressed both hands against the paneling and leaned my weight into it. The wall clicked and gave way, pivoting to reveal a small, soundproofed recording booth covered in velvet drapes. I stared at the vintage microphones gathering dust inside, scratched the back of my neck, and slowly dragged my bass by the neck toward the hidden doorway.

Sarah dragged the vacuum cleaner across the carpet with one hand, her other arm hanging limply at her side. She had already watered the fake plants and reorganized her spice rack alphabetically. The vacuum droned with a steady, endless hum as she pushed the nozzle against the back wall of her walk-in closet. The plastic head bumped against the baseboard, causing a section of the wall to unlatch and pop inward. Sarah turned off the vacuum. The sudden silence was heavy. She nudged the plasterboard with the toe of her slipper, pushing it open to reveal a hidden alcove filled with antique mirrors. She stared at her own slumped reflection repeated a dozen times in the dusty glass. Letting out a slow, drawn-out exhale, she dropped the vacuum hose, resting her head against the doorframe, watching the dust motes dance in the filtered light.

The blank page in the typewriter glared at me. I rested my chin on the keyboard, letting the keys press painfully into my jaw. The grandfather clock ticked in the corner, each second stretching out like taffy. I had walked around the perimeter of the cabin four times already. I slumped back into my leather chair, grabbed a paperclip from the desk, and began bending it back and forth until it snapped in half. Tossing the pieces over my shoulder, I heard one of them drop behind the bookshelf with a metallic ping. I dragged myself out of the chair to retrieve it, blindly reaching behind the oak trim. My fingers caught a hidden lever. The bookshelf swung smoothly outward, revealing a cramped, windowless study lined with leather-bound journals. I stared blankly at the secret room, let out a long breath, and leaned against the wall.

Toby sat cross-legged in the middle of his new room, surrounded by sealed cardboard boxes. He held a blue glass marble between his thumb and forefinger, letting it drop to the floor. It rolled a few inches and stopped. He picked it up, dropped it again, and watched it roll back. The afternoon stretched ahead, vast and empty. He laid his head on the floor, his cheek pressing against the cold laminate, and flicked the marble hard toward the closet. It disappeared under the baseboard with a sharp clink. Toby dragged himself across the floor on his stomach to fetch it. Pushing on the wood to reach under, the entire back of the closet shifted, gliding smoothly away to expose a secret, low-ceilinged playroom. Toby didn't gasp. He just blinked slowly at the dark space, crawled inside, and sat back down, waiting for the marble to stop rolling.

I sat across from Mark in the empty diner, stirring my lukewarm coffee into a slow, endless whirlpool. For the past hour, he had been monologuing about his stressful life as a senior hedge fund manager. I rested my heavy chin in my palm, watching a single fly bump repeatedly against the glass window. The diner bell chimed. A woman walked past our booth and casually thanked Mark for unclogging her pipes that morning, mentioning his plumber’s van parked outside. Mark’s face flushed scarlet, his grand financial tale dying in his throat. I didn't sit up or change my expression. I simply let out a long, slow exhale, watching the brown liquid settle in my mug, and wondered if the minute hand on the wall clock had actually moved since the last time I checked.

Sarah traced the rim of her water glass with a slow, dragging finger, listening to the rhythmic hum of the refrigerator. David paced the kitchen, waving his hands as he detailed the intense demands of directing independent films. Sarah’s eyelids drooped. She began counting the faded floral patterns on the wallpaper. Someone knocked, and a neighbor popped their head in, tossing a bright yellow vest onto the counter and thanking David for taking the crossing guard shift. David froze, mid-gesture. Sarah just kept her cheek pressed against the cool granite countertop. She blinked slowly, her gaze drifting past the fluorescent vest to a speck of dust floating lazily through a shaft of sunlight, wishing the afternoon would just end already.

I kept myself on mute, staring blankly at the grid of faces on my monitor. Lisa was dominating the video call, dropping buzzwords about her high-stakes marketing agency. I drummed my fingers against my desk—one, two, three, four—and checked the time. 14:02. Still forty minutes left. Lisa clicked the wrong button and shared her entire screen. Instead of a brilliant campaign portfolio, a bright pink dashboard appeared, showing her upcoming schedule as a local dog walker. The chat fell completely silent. I sank lower into my ergonomic chair until my head rested against the backrest. Staring up at the white ceiling tiles, I focused on a tiny water stain in the corner, letting my eyes glaze over as the silence stretched out.

Greg kicked a solitary pebble across the empty expanse of the parking lot, watching it skitter and stop. Beside him, Mike was animatedly recounting his supposed adventures as a private investigator. Greg let his arms hang limply by his sides, his gaze fixed on the cracked asphalt. A beat-up sedan suddenly pulled up, and the driver rolled down the window, tossing a stack of menus at Mike and yelling at him for missing his food delivery shift. Mike stammered, his face turning pale. Greg merely yawned, stretching his arms high above his head with a loud groan. He let his shoulders slump back down, looking toward the distant highway traffic, and asked in a flat, uninflected voice if they were ever going to get those burgers.

I swiped through my phone with a heavy, mechanical motion, barely registering the images on the screen. Jenna sat beside me on the couch, rambling about the exclusivity of the culinary institute she attended. I swiped past an ad for soap, then an ad for shoes. A notification popped up at the top of my screen: Jenna had been tagged in a photo. I tapped it. There was Jenna, wearing a bright orange uniform, handing a basket of fries through a drive-thru window. She stopped talking and looked over my shoulder, her eyes widening. I didn’t laugh or confront her. I just let the phone drop flat onto my chest, tipping my head back against the cushions to stare at the spinning blades of the ceiling fan.

Maya rested the side of her face against the bus window, watching the grey, uniform buildings blur past in an endless, rhythmic stream. Leo sat next to her, enthusiastically detailing the architectural blueprints he had supposedly drafted for a new downtown high-rise. The bus lurched to a halt at a red light. A man outside waved frantically, shouting through the glass to thank Leo for fixing his lawnmower yesterday at the repair shop. Leo shrank down in his seat, suddenly speechless. Maya didn't even turn her head to look at him. She simply exhaled, her breath leaving a patch of fog on the cold glass, and began tracing small, meaningless circles in the condensation with her index finger as the bus idled.

I systematically arranged my peas into a perfect geometric circle around the edges of my dinner plate. Across the table, Pete was mid-sentence, painting a vivid picture of his life as an international airline pilot. I rested my chin heavily in my palm, my eyes half-closed. The restaurant's kitchen door swung open, and the manager marched out, slamming a crumpled apron onto our table and demanding to know why Pete had abandoned his dishwashing station. Pete choked on his water, coughing violently into his napkin. I slowly pushed a single green pea to the exact center of my plate with the very tip of my fork, letting out a soft sigh as the ambient chatter of the restaurant washed over us.

Julian tapped his yellow pencil against his notebook: tap, tap, tap. A steady, endless rhythm. His roommate, Alex, stood by the window, boasting about his aggressive stock market trades and the massive returns he was expecting. Julian’s gaze drifted to a piece of mail left open on the coffee table—a brightly colored pay stub from the local petting zoo, made out to Alex. The pencil tapping didn't pause or change its tempo. Julian’s heavy eyelids drooped further as he shifted his focus back to the wall clock. He watched the second hand make its agonizingly slow sweep, silently counting the ticks, waiting for the shadows in the room to stretch just a fraction of an inch longer.

We had been sitting on this same park bench for nearly an hour. Even the ducks in the pond were asleep. I was hunched over, dragging a dirty twig through the dirt to form jagged, meaningless lines. Sam was standing, dramatically describing the boardroom negotiations he handled for a tech firm. His phone suddenly rang at maximum volume, the screen flashing 'Molly's Cleaning Service - Boss' in bright letters. He scrambled frantically to silence the device, shoving it deep into his pocket. I tossed the broken twig onto the grass. Leaning all the way back against the hard wooden slats of the bench, I tilted my head to stare blankly at the grey, featureless expanse of clouds overhead.

Chloe flipped the glossy magazine page to the right, then immediately back to the left. The soft crinkle of paper was the only thing keeping her awake. Ryan leaned against the fireplace mantel, gesturing wildly as he described his thriving corporate consulting firm. A folded piece of paper slipped from his inner jacket pocket and fluttered to the floor: a laminated nametag for the front desk of a local laser tag arena. Ryan stared at it in horror. Chloe let her eyes glaze over completely, staring right through the colorful plastic tag. She rested her temple against the cool leather of her armchair, letting out a long, hollow breath that ruffled her bangs.

I picked at the edge of my beer bottle label, trying to peel it off in one continuous, perfect strip. Derek was leaning over the sticky bar top, loudly going on about the intense neurosurgery residency he claimed to have just started. A girl with a backpack walked up, tapped him on the shoulder, and asked if he was scheduled at the Best Buy Geek Squad desk tomorrow because her laptop was acting up again. Derek’s mouth hung open. I managed to detach a long ribbon of paper from the glass. I let out a heavy sigh, resting my forehead directly against the cool, damp wood of the bar counter, letting the ambient noise of the pub drown out his stammering.

Elias counted the square ceiling tiles in the small waiting room. Forty-eight. Forty-nine. Fifty. Nina sat beside him on the hard plastic chair, weaving a highly detailed narrative about her glamorous life as a globe-trotting fashion photographer. The glass partition slid open, and the receptionist leaned out, calling loudly, 'Nina, your background check for the nighttime mall security guard position cleared.' Nina stopped mid-sentence, her hands freezing in the air. Elias didn't shift his slouched posture or raise his eyebrows. He simply blinked at a slow, deliberate pace, rested his head against the painted cinderblock wall, and began counting the ceiling tiles all over again, starting backward from fifty.

Julian dragged his palm down his face, letting out a prolonged exhale that ruffled his bangs. His mother knelt beside a towering plastic bin, reverently lifting a stack of third-grade multiplication worksheets. “Look at your little sevens,” she cooed. Julian shifted his weight from his left leg to his right, then leaned his shoulder against the dusty attic wall. His gaze drifted away from the faded pencil marks, settling instead on a solitary spider weaving a web near the rafter. He watched the arachnid's slow, repetitive movements, finding the geometry of the silk far more engaging than the math papers. He pulled his phone from his pocket, pressed the side button to illuminate the screen, noted that only three minutes had passed since he last checked, and slid it back, letting his head thunk softly against the drywall.

I propped my chin firmly in the cup of my hand, feeling my eyelids droop as mom pulled yet another laminated folder from the cedar chest. "1994," she announced, smoothing out a crumpled spelling test. "You got a gold star on 'dinosaur'." I offered a mechanical nod, my eyes completely glazed over as I stared at the geometric pattern of the living room rug. I started counting the blue triangles woven into the fabric. One, two, three... maybe if I reached a hundred, the box would magically empty itself. Mom continued to narrate the teacher’s handwritten comments at the top of the page. I tapped my index finger against my cheek in a slow, rhythmic beat, letting a heavy sigh escape my lips while wondering if the paint on the hallway wall had finally finished drying.

Elena sat cross-legged on the floorboards, staring blankly as her mother opened the fourth heavily taped cardboard box. Inside lay an endless sea of middle school essays, chronologically organized by semester. Her mother held up a ten-page report on the American Revolution, her eyes shining with nostalgia. Elena blinked, her face devoid of expression, and began to pick at a stray thread on the hem of her jeans. She pulled it slowly, watching the fabric unravel millimeter by millimeter. "You worked so hard on the bibliography," her mother murmured. "Mhmm," Elena replied, letting her chin drop to her chest. She stretched her legs out, crossing and uncrossing her ankles, before tilting her head back to study the slow, lazy rotation of the ceiling fan. The blades spun in a hypnotic circle, offering a quiet escape from the mountain of loose-leaf paper.

A massive binder landed on the kitchen table with a heavy thud, kicking up a tiny cloud of dust. "I kept them all," Mom whispered, flipping it open to reveal hundreds of my high school geometry assignments, each carefully slipped into a plastic protector. I let out a long breath through my nose, resting my forehead against the cool wooden table. "That's great, Mom," I mumbled into the grain of the oak. I reached out a hand, blindly turning a plastic page. A theorem. Another page. A proof. I pulled away and started peeling a tiny, translucent sticker off an empty water bottle sitting near my elbow. I scraped at the adhesive with my thumbnail, focusing entirely on getting the sticky residue off the plastic while Mom's voice droned on about my dedication to angles and hypotenuses.

Marcus slumped deep into the floral sofa cushions, his posture practically horizontal as his mother emerged from the hallway dragging a trunk. She popped the rusty latches to reveal a mountain of his elementary school vocabulary quizzes. Marcus let out a loud groan, dragging his feet across the carpet. "Look, your first spelling bee practice sheet!" she beamed, holding up a yellowed piece of paper. Marcus stared at it with half-closed eyes, offering a slow, synchronized blink. He reached for a nearby pen and a scrap of paper, aimlessly sketching jagged lines and interlocking circles until the ink began to run dry. When his mother handed him a stack of quizzes to look through, he simply rested them on his stomach, letting his head loll to the side to watch the second hand tick around the face of the mantel clock.

I sat at the edge of my childhood bed, my shoulders hunched forward, staring at a box labeled "Kindergarten-2nd Grade." Mom was on her knees, carefully extracting finger-painted turkeys and wobbly handwriting exercises as if they were ancient artifacts. "Look at this 'A'," she murmured, tracing the crayon lines. I offered a flat "Wow," letting a yawn stretch my jaw so wide my ears popped. I leaned back on my hands, kicking my heels rhythmically against the wooden bed frame. Thump. Thump. Thump. I caught sight of a dust mote floating lazily through a shaft of afternoon sunlight and tracked its entire descent to the floor. Mom handed me a story I’d written about a magical frog. I held it limp in my hand, staring through the paper rather than at it, wishing the hands of my watch would spin faster.

The attic was stifling, but Chloe barely registered the heat as she sat paralyzed before three plastic tubs. Her mother knelt beside her, pulling out endless stacks of lined paper filled with clumsy cursive. "I couldn't bear to throw away a single stroke," her mother explained, presenting a second-grade book report on caterpillars. Chloe’s eyes drifted toward a cracked windowpane. She propped her elbows on her knees and rested her heavy head in her hands, her cheeks squished between her palms. She let out a long, fluttering breath that made her bangs dance. "Uh-huh," Chloe murmured softly, her voice flat. She began absentmindedly arranging a pile of loose staples she found on the floor into a perfect square, completely ignoring the towering stack of historical timelines her mother was diligently laying out across the dusty floorboards.

We were supposed to be cleaning out the garage, but mom had firmly hit the brakes upon discovering my middle-school science fair materials. She sat on an overturned bucket, reading aloud my hypothesis on bean plant growth from 2004. I stood shifting my weight from my left foot to my right, staring at the concrete floor. I dragged the toe of my sneaker across a faded oil stain, trying to erase it with friction. "You used such descriptive words here," Mom said, holding up a daily observation log. "Yep," I replied, rolling my neck until it popped. I picked up a tennis ball from a nearby shelf and started bouncing it against the cinderblock wall. Catch. Toss. Bounce. Catch. I timed the rhythm of the rubber hitting the wall to match the endless drone of her reciting my old temperature recordings.

David slouched in the dining chair, his chin resting flush against the tabletop as his mother proudly displayed a thick scrapbook of his high school Spanish worksheets. "Remember Señor Martinez?" she asked, smoothing a page filled with verb conjugations. David blinked slowly, his eyes half-shut. He exhaled a long, steady stream of air out of the corner of his mouth, watching it ruffle the edge of the paper. Without lifting his head from the wood, he extended one arm and began spinning a salt shaker in slow circles. Round and round it went, the glass catching the kitchen light. "You got a B-plus on this quiz," she noted. David didn't respond. He just watched the salt shaker spin, waiting for it to wobble and stop before initiating another slow, lazy rotation with the flick of his index finger.

"I just knew you'd want to see these," Mom said, hauling a massive canvas tote into the living room. I sank deeper into the armchair, my spine sliding down until I was practically sitting on my neck. She reached in and pulled out a stack of my fourth-grade fractions homework. I stared at the endless rows of numerators and denominators, feeling my brain completely shut off. I started picking at a loose thread on the armrest, winding the rough fabric tightly around my index finger until the tip turned purple, then slowly unwinding it to watch the blood rush back. Mom handed me a worksheet covered in red checkmarks. I held it in my lap without looking down, my gaze fixed firmly on the television screen across the room, which was currently powered off, reflecting my own blank expression.

The basement smelled of damp earth and old cardboard. Sam sat on a folding chair, drumming his fingers in a mindless rhythm against his thigh. His mother pulled another crumbling notebook from the bottom of a banker's box. "Oh, your poetry phase!" she gasped, opening a binder stuffed with wide-ruled paper. Sam’s eyelids drooped. He leaned his head all the way back, staring straight up at the exposed pipes running across the basement ceiling. He began counting the small beads of condensation clinging to the cold copper. "Listen to this one about the autumn leaves," she prompted. "Sure, Mom," Sam muttered, his voice devoid of any inflection. He shifted his jaw, letting out a cavernous yawn that he didn't bother covering, before returning his vacant gaze to the water droplets, waiting patiently for a single one to finally fall.

Mom cleared her throat, adjusting her reading glasses as she pulled out the very first draft of my seventh-grade term paper. She had three whole boxes of this stuff. I sat on the floor, crossing my arms over my chest and letting my shoulders slump forward. I stared at the carpet, tracing an invisible maze into the fibers with my thumb. She read the introductory paragraph with intense dramatic flair. I nodded on autopilot. "Mhm. Cool." I looked at my phone screen, noting the time, then placed it face down. Ten seconds later, I picked it up to check the time again. Nothing had changed. I rested my forehead on my knees, closing my eyes while she moved on to the second paragraph, silently praying the phone would ring, the doorbell would chime, or the house would lose power.

I sat on my sagging porch, resting my heavy chin in my hands. The ceiling fan clicked with agonizing slowness. One Mississippi. Two. I watched a fly buzz against the screen door. Seven cars had passed in the last hour. I picked at a splinter on the armrest, letting out a long breath as I waited for the sun to sink just a fraction lower. Across the street, old Mr. Henderson struggled with his rusty mailbox. I dragged my feet across the asphalt to help him, hoping the walk would eat up at least three minutes. A glossy brochure slipped from his mail stack and fluttered to the cracked sidewalk. I bent down to retrieve it. It wasn't junk mail. It was a private banking portfolio and a deed to a Mediterranean villa, all bearing Henderson’s name in gold foil. My eyes widened, the slow ticking of the afternoon suddenly vanishing.

Elias tapped his pen against his desk. Tap, tap, tap. He stared at the blank apartment wall, tracing a faint water stain with his eyes. He had already reorganized his sock drawer twice and checked the refrigerator five times. The silence in his room stretched out like an endless, empty highway. He let out a loud groan and pressed his ear against the thin drywall separating him from Mrs. Gable’s unit, hoping to catch a snippet of her daytime soap operas just to hear a human voice. Instead, he heard the sharp rustle of paper, followed by a voice speaking in hushed, commanding tones. "Yes, transfer the four million from the Cayman account. No, leave the Swiss assets untouched." Elias froze, his pen slipping from his fingers. Mrs. Gable, the frail woman who regularly clipped twenty-cent coupons for canned soup, was casually negotiating a multimillion-dollar international corporate buyout.

The shears made a hollow snip as I butchered the top of my front hedge. I leaned back, blowing a stray hair out of my face, and watched a completely stationary cloud in the pale blue sky. It looked like a sheep. Or maybe a cotton ball. I sighed, letting my arms hang limp at my sides. Every day here felt exactly like the one before it. I dragged the clippers over to the property line I shared with Greg, the guy who drove a rusted 1990 hatchback. A drone suddenly whined overhead, hovering above Greg's overgrown backyard. I followed its path, peering over the wooden fence. My jaw dropped. Beneath the canopy of untamed oak trees sat a pristine, custom-built helipad, and Greg was currently stepping out of a sleek, black chopper in a tailored Brioni suit. The shears slipped from my grip, burying themselves in the dirt.

Maya kicked a pebble down the dirt road, watching it bounce into a ditch. She kicked another one. Then a third. The summer sun beat down on the quiet rural street, and the only sound was the distant hum of a tractor. She collapsed onto a wooden fence post, resting her forehead against her knees, counting the ants marching in a straight line across her sneaker. One, two, three. It felt like time had completely stopped. She glanced over at crazy Old Man Miller’s ramshackle cabin, the one with the collapsed roof and boarded-up windows. A massive transport truck quietly pulled up behind the treeline. Maya squinted, her chin resting heavily in her palm. The back of the truck lowered, and out rolled a pristine, vintage Ferrari 250 GTO. Miller stepped out of his shack, tossed a solid gold bar to the driver as a tip, and patted the car's hood.

I swirled the dregs of my lukewarm coffee, watching the brown liquid coat the sides of the mug. The clock on the cafe wall ticked loudly, each second feeling like a full minute. I rested my head on the cool table glass, tracing endless circles in the condensation left by my cup. Out the window, the empty street offered nothing but the occasional pigeon pecking at a cigarette butt. My neighbor, Sarah, sat two tables away, seemingly doing the exact same thing. She lived in the tiny studio below mine and worked part-time at the bakery. I let out a slow, dramatic exhale, practically melting into my chair. Then, a man in a sharp suit approached Sarah’s table. He placed a velvet briefcase in front of her. It popped open, revealing stacks of bearer bonds and diamond necklaces. "Your dividends for the quarter, Your Highness," the man whispered.

Arthur watered his plastic fern, entirely forgetting it didn't need water. He stood by the window of his high-rise, his chin propped heavily on his hand, staring at the concrete of the adjacent building. He counted the bricks. Four hundred and twelve on the top section. He let out a long, whistling breath that fogged the glass, drawing a smiley face in the condensation and immediately wiping it away. Below him, his neighbor from 4B, the scruffy college kid who survived on instant ramen, was walking an old golden retriever. Arthur watched them meander aimlessly. A sleek, armored limousine pulled up to the curb. The tinted window rolled down, and a uniformed chauffeur handed the kid a silver briefcase. The briefcase popped open, catching the afternoon sun and blinding Arthur with the gleam of solid gold bricks. The kid grabbed one, tossed it to the dog, and kept walking.

I sat by the community pool, dangling my feet in the lukewarm water. Kick, splash. Kick, splash. I stared up at the cloudless sky, wondering if I could guess the exact moment the sun would dip behind the clubhouse. I picked at the frayed edge of my towel, tossing tiny threads into the water and watching them float. Nothing moved. Nothing changed. The silence was heavy. I glanced over at Mrs. Higgins, the sweet elderly lady next door who always smelled of mothballs and cheap peppermint. She was digging through her canvas tote bag. I rested my head back on the concrete, closing my eyes, desperate for the day to just end. "Pardon me, dear," her voice broke the stillness. I opened one eye. She was holding a diamond the size of a golf ball. "Do you think this looks too gaudy for my grocery run?"

Clara slumped in her desk chair, her face illuminated by the blue light of a blank spreadsheet. She scrolled down to row 10,000, then scrolled all the way back up. She clicked her mouse five times in rapid succession, just to hear the sound. She let her head fall back against the headrest, staring at the popcorn ceiling and counting the little bumps. Across the alleyway, her neighbor, a struggling artist named Leo who painted on discarded cardboard, left his blinds open. Clara watched him slowly, resting her cheek against the cold surface of her desk. Leo pulled back a large canvas resting against the wall. Behind it wasn't a collection of paint tubes, but a massive wall safe. He spun the dial, pulled the heavy door open, and began casually tossing bundles of hundred-dollar bills into a gym bag, using them to cushion a priceless Renaissance tiara.

The washing machine tumbled round and round. Red shirt, blue jeans, white towel. Red, blue, white. I sat on the hard plastic chair of the basement laundromat, my chin resting heavily on my fists. I watched a drop of water slowly slide down the glass of the machine door. I sighed, tapping my heel rhythmically against the linoleum. Tap-tap-pause. Tap-tap-pause. I felt like I was sinking into the floorboards. Pete from down the hall walked in carrying a laundry basket full of threadbare sweaters. He nodded at me, pulling a crumpled box of detergent from his pocket. He dropped the box. Instead of white powder, heavy, glittering gemstones cascaded across the dirty floor—rubies, emeralds, and sapphires the size of walnuts. They bounced and rolled beneath the washing machines. Pete groaned, muttered something about his Swiss vault being too full, and started sweeping the priceless gems into a dustpan.

Marcus sat on his apartment balcony, throwing bits of stale bread at the pavement below. He watched a solitary pigeon peck at the crumbs, willing the bird to do something interesting. It didn’t. He leaned back, letting out a heavy groan, and began peeling the label off his soda bottle in microscopic strips. The afternoon dragged out, thick and motionless. He pressed his palms against his eyes until he saw colorful shapes. On the adjacent balcony, his neighbor—a quiet man who drove a delivery van—was watering a dying cactus. Marcus watched him through half-closed eyelids. The man accidentally knocked the terracotta pot off the railing. It shattered on the street below. Instead of dirt, hundreds of flawless diamonds spilled across the asphalt, sparkling violently in the afternoon sun. The delivery driver simply shrugged, pulled a solid gold phone from his pocket, and made a call.

I sat cross-legged on my driveway, pulling blades of grass from the concrete cracks and shredding them into tiny green piles. The neighborhood garage sale had been going on for four hours without a single customer. I rested my head on my knees, staring blankly at the rusted bicycle I was selling for ten bucks. The silence made my ears ring. Next door, Mr. Vance sat in a lawn chair, offering a collection of dusty bowling balls. I watched a fly land on his knee, wishing I could trade places with it just to fly away. Suddenly, a black SUV rolled up. A man in a tailored suit stepped out, handed Mr. Vance a leather briefcase, and whispered, "The cartel accepted your bid for the private island, sir. The remaining fifty million is secure in the offshore accounts."

The snow fell in completely straight, uniform lines. Jenna pressed her forehead against the icy windowpane, fogging the glass with her heavy sighs. She drew a tic-tac-toe board in the condensation, played a game against herself, and lost. She slid down the wall until she hit the floor, staring up at the ceiling fan that hadn't moved in months. The silence of the cabin was making her count the wooden floorboards. She hauled herself back up to the window, gazing blankly at the dilapidated shack next door where old Mr. Abernathy lived. A heavy snowplow suddenly cleared the driveway, revealing not gravel, but a massive steel vault door embedded in the earth. The door hissed open, and Abernathy emerged in a floor-length mink coat, followed by three men carrying towering stacks of gold bullion. He casually directed them to load the literal treasure into a waiting armored helicopter.

Elias sat on the edge of the bed, watching Sarah excitedly wave a thick stack of printed pages. "It's all about you," she breathed, eyes wide. "Our first year together, fictionalized." Elias let out a long breath, his gaze drifting from her flushed face to the water stain on the ceiling. It looked vaguely like a turtle. He picked at a loose thread on his sweatpants, watching it unravel slowly. "Cool," he mumbled, letting his chin drop heavily into his palm. He wondered if the deli down the street was still doing the two-for-one sandwich deal. Sarah was reading a passage aloud now, her voice trembling with emotion. Elias shifted his weight, checked the blank screen of his phone, and let out another heavy breath. "Are there going to be sequels?" he asked, not really waiting for the answer.

"So, the protagonist is literally me?" I asked, resting my head against the cool glass of the living room window. Outside, a single gray car drove past. Then another. Mark nodded frantically, tapping the manuscript on his desk. "Every quirk, every habit! The way you drink coffee, the way you sleep!" I slowly dragged my eyes away from the street and looked at the pile of paper. It was very thick. I imagined having to read all of it. A deep, hollow yawn forced its way up my throat, which I barely managed to cover with the back of my hand. "That's a lot of pages," I said, leaning my full weight against the wall and sliding down an inch or two. "Do I have to read the whole thing today? The paint is drying in the hallway and I was sort of watching it."

The cursor blinked at the top of the document: The Muse of My Life. Clara stared at her husband’s laptop screen, leaning her cheek against her fist. David was pacing the kitchen, explaining the narrative arc he had spent three years secretly developing around her personality. Clara traced a water ring on the mahogany table with her index finger, around and around in endless circles. She listened to his footsteps—squeak, thud, squeak, thud. He was talking about a climactic scene based on their trip to Maine. Clara let her eyelids droop. She tried to calculate how many tiles made up the kitchen backsplash. Forty across, maybe twenty down? She interrupted David mid-sentence. "Did you take the trash out?" she asked, her voice entirely flat. David stopped pacing. Clara just kept tracing the water ring, her eyes glazed and fixed on the wood grain.

I sat cross-legged on the rug, flipping through the bound manuscript Elena had just dropped into my lap. She stood over me, practically vibrating with nervous energy. "It's a romance," she whispered. "About us. About you." I turned a page. Then another. There were so many words. So much dialogue. I rested my chin on my knee and let out a long, slow exhale. The ticking of the grandfather clock in the hallway seemed incredibly loud. Tick. Tock. Tick. Tock. I flipped a chunk of fifty pages at once, barely registering the chapter breaks. "Is there a dragon in it?" I asked, staring at the dust motes dancing in the shaft of sunlight between us. "No," she said, her smile faltering. I closed the book with a soft thud and let it slide onto the rug. "Oh. Okay." I stared at the dust motes again.

When Marcus found the hidden files on Julian's desktop, neatly labeled "The Marcus Chronicles: A Novel", his first reaction was a heavy, drawn-out sigh. He clicked open the first document. He rested his head in his hands, his eyes struggling to stay focused on the blocky text. Julian had written seventy thousand words about his enigmatic charm and mysterious aura. Marcus scrolled down. Down. Down. The scroll bar barely moved. He tapped his foot against the desk leg—one, two, three, four. He minimized the window and opened a tab for solitaire, mechanically dragging a black four onto a red five. He could hear Julian coming up the stairs. The big reveal was imminent. Marcus slumped lower in the ergonomic chair, his eyes half-closed, bracing himself for the monumental effort of having to feign surprise for the next hour.

"I've been writing a book about you," my wife announced over dinner. I kept my eyes on my plate, slowly pushing a single pea across the porcelain with the tines of my fork. It rolled into the mashed potatoes and stuck there. "A book," I repeated, my voice an even monotone. "Yes! A psychological thriller based on your life!" I watched a drop of condensation slide down my water glass, merging with another drop halfway down. It felt like it took hours. I picked up the glass and took a slow, deliberate sip just to give my hands something to do. "Will I need to go on a book tour?" I murmured, feeling the weight of my own eyelids pulling downward. She launched into a detailed plot summary. I went back to the pea, nudging it out of the potatoes and toward the carrots.

Sophie sat in the passenger seat, watching the highway lines dash past the window in an endless, rhythmic blur. Dash, space, dash, space. Beside her, Liam was practically shouting over the radio, confessing his great secret. He had penned a sweeping historical romance, using her as the exact model for the heroine. Sophie rested her temple against the cool glass of the window. "A duchess," she repeated, her tone entirely devoid of inflection. "Yeah! And you lead a rebellion!" Liam cheered. Sophie closed her eyes. The hum of the tires on the asphalt was a steady, droning vibration. She imagined the remaining four hours of the drive, stretching out before them like a vast, featureless desert. She slowly reached over and turned the radio volume up a few notches, drowning out the sound of his plot explanation with an old mattress commercial.

The manuscript was tied with a red ribbon. Sam handed it to me with trembling hands, tears welling in his eyes. "You are my absolute inspiration," he choked out. I pulled the ribbon loose. It fell to the floor. I didn't pick it up. I leafed through the first few pages, resting my chin heavily in my palm. My eyes scanned the paragraphs, but the words just looked like gray smudges. "Chapter One," I read aloud, my voice flat. "The Boy With the Amber Eyes." I looked up at the ceiling fan spinning slowly, its rhythmic clicking the only sound in the room. Click, swoosh, click, swoosh. "We're out of milk, by the way," I said, shifting my gaze back to the thick stack of paper. "Just remembered. Did you want to go to the store, or should I?"

The revelation happened over coffee. Jenna slid a beautifully bound proof copy across the cafe table. The title read: Through Her Eyes: A Memoir of Us. Mia stared at the cover. She rested her elbow on the table, letting her cheek squish into her palm. She tapped her spoon against the edge of her mug. Clink. Clink. Clink. "It took two years," Jenna whispered, reaching for Mia's free hand. Mia let her hand be taken, though it remained limp in Jenna's grip.
