She looked past Jenna to the barista, who was wiping the counter with slow, methodical strokes. Left, right, left, right. "Two years," Mia echoed, blinking very slowly. She let out a long breath that ruffled her bangs. "Are we going to order food soon? I've been looking at the menu for twenty minutes."

"So you're the hero," Chris said, pointing to the screen. "And you save the galaxy." I sat back in the computer chair, letting my head loll against the headrest. I stared at the acoustic foam on the ceiling. "The galaxy," I repeated, stretching my legs out until my heels rested on the carpet. "Yeah! Look at the stats I gave your character!" Chris scrolled through endless pages of lore and attributes. My eyes drifted to the corner of the monitor. The clock read 4:12 PM. It felt like it had been 4:12 PM for a century. I let out a loud, hollow yawn, stretching my arms over my head until my joints popped. "That's great," I mumbled, pulling out my phone and opening a mindless bubble-popping game. "Tell me when we get to the part where I blow up."

Arthur stood in the doorway of the study, holding the printed email from a literary agent. His wife had apparently sold a manuscript. A fictionalized, highly dramatized account of their marriage. He watched his wife beaming at him from her desk. Arthur leaned his shoulder heavily against the doorframe. He crossed his arms, staring vacantly at a spot just above her left shoulder. He began counting the books on the shelf behind her. One, two, three, four... he lost track and didn't care enough to start over. He let his head tip back against the wood with a soft thump. "A six-figure advance," she said, her voice piercing the quiet. Arthur sighed, a long, deflating sound. "Does this mean we can afford to hire someone to clean the gutters?" he asked, rubbing his drooping eyes with the back of his hand.

The dedication page literally said, 'To the one who sits across from me'. I flipped it over. Three hundred pages of prose about me. Tom was watching my face, waiting for a reaction. I sank deeper into the couch cushions, feeling the leather stick to the back of my legs. I grabbed a throw pillow and hugged it to my chest, resting my chin on its edge. "Wow," I said, drawing out the vowel into a flat, emotionless line. I looked out the window. A squirrel was burying a nut. Then it dug the nut back up. Then it ran away. I watched the empty patch of grass for a while, wondering if the squirrel would come back. Tom cleared his throat loudly. I blinked, dragging my attention back to the heavy book in my lap. "Is it double-spaced?" I asked.

I dragged my thumb down the phone screen for the hundredth time, watching videos play on mute while the train bumped along the tracks. A glossy video popped up: "Chef Antoine’s Sensational Lavender Honey Cake." I stopped scrolling. The measurements—three-quarters of a cup of almond flour, exactly two tablespoons of crushed dried lavender—were identical to the post I’d put on my tiny blog five years ago. He was even using my trick of adding a pinch of white pepper. I let out a long breath, watching the chef grin as he sliced the cake for the camera. My eyes drifted to the smudge on the train window, then to the gray sky outside. I swiped up, letting the video vanish, and rested my chin heavily against the cold glass.

The café was entirely empty, the espresso machine emitting a low, continuous hum. Elias rested his chin in his palm, tapping a rhythm on the counter with a single knuckle. A customer finally pushed the glass door open, bells jingling, holding up a phone. "Do you guys make the viral 'Gold Coast Muffins'? The ones from that influencer?" Elias leaned forward slowly, squinting at the screen. The picture showed his own creation—orange zest and cardamom muffins—renamed and branded by someone else with millions of followers. "We don't," Elias said, his voice completely flat. The customer sighed and walked out. Elias watched the door swing shut, picked up a damp rag, and resumed wiping the exact same spot on the counter he had been cleaning for the last twenty minutes.

The morning talk show droned on in the background, a symphony of forced laughter and clattering pots. I sat on the sofa, picking a loose thread on the throw pillow. On the television screen, a celebrity chef was presenting his "groundbreaking" Sunday Chili. I glanced up just long enough to see him dump a quarter cup of cocoa powder and half a bottle of dark stout into the pot—my exact, highly specific additions from a forum post in 2012. "A culinary masterpiece!" the host cheered. I dropped the throw pillow, let my head loll back against the cushions, and stared at the slowly rotating blades of the ceiling fan. "Yep," I muttered to the empty room. "Masterpiece." I closed my eyes and listened to the steady tick of the wall clock.

At the neighborhood potluck, everyone crowded around Mrs. Gable’s casserole dish. "It’s from that new bestselling cookbook!" she announced loudly. "The Tuscan Sunset Bake!" Maya sat at a folding table at the back of the yard, resting her cheek on her fist. She knew the recipe. It was her grandmother’s eggplant dish, the one Maya had submitted to a community magazine years ago, down to the odd addition of smoked paprika. She stirred a plastic fork through her potato salad, making small, deliberate circles. Someone offered her a plate of the famous bake. "No thanks," Maya said, her gaze drifting past them to a squirrel burying a nut near the fence. She let out a long, heavy exhale and went back to dragging her fork through the mayonnaise.

The waiting room smelled of old magazines and industrial cleaner. I flipped through a glossy culinary journal from two years ago, the pages crinkling softly in the silent room. Right there on page forty-two was my distinct pear and Gruyère tart, complete with the thyme-infused crust I spent weeks perfecting. Only here, it was credited to a Michelin-starred bistro in Paris under the name "Tarte Rêverie." I stared at the photo. The caramelized edges looked exactly like mine. I flipped the magazine shut and tossed it onto the glass coffee table with a soft thud. I slouched down in the plastic chair, stretching my legs out in front of me, and began counting the tiny perforated holes in the acoustic ceiling tiles to pass the time until my name was called.

Sitting in front of his dual monitors, Leo clicked through the list of winners for the national street food competition. First place went to a food truck in Austin for their "Revolutionary Yuzu Brisket Tacos." Leo pulled up the recipe. The marinade, the slaw, the specific ratio of soy to citrus—it was copied verbatim from his defunct college recipe diary. A congratulatory banner flashed across the winning website with digital confetti. Leo’s face remained entirely motionless. He blinked slowly, his shoulders slumped against the ergonomic mesh of his desk chair. He minimized the browser window, revealing a half-finished game of digital Solitaire. With a heavy sigh that barely parted his lips, he dragged a red seven over a black eight, the faint click of his mouse echoing in the quiet room.

"You absolutely have to try the Miracle Soup at The Gilded Spoon," Sarah said, leaning over my cubicle wall. "It’s changing the culinary world." I kept my eyes on the blinking cursor of my spreadsheet. She held up a picture of the broth. I recognized the floating specks of charred ginger and toasted fennel seeds immediately. It was the winter immunity broth I’d shared on a public recipe exchange last December. "Wow," I said in a monotone voice, not looking away from my monitor. "That’s crazy." Sarah kept talking about the complex flavor profile. I rested my chin on my hand, my eyes glazing over the endless columns of data. I pressed the down arrow key, watching the highlighted cell drop one row at a time. Down. Down. Down.

The library was overwhelmingly quiet, save for the hum of the air conditioning. Clara turned the thick, glossy pages of a famous baker’s new memoir. She paused on chapter four, where the author revealed the "secret" to his globally acclaimed sourdough. Clara read the exact hydration percentages and the unusual resting temperatures she had developed in her own kitchen, which she had naively posted in a baking group. The baker claimed it came to him in a dream. Clara’s expression didn't shift. She let the heavy book close on its own. She rested her forehead against the cool wooden surface of the reading table. For several minutes, she just watched a speck of dust float lazily through a shaft of sunlight, her arms hanging limp at her sides.

My roommate burst through the front door, waving a grease-spotted paper bag. "I stood in line for two hours to get the viral Brooklyn Brioche!" he gasped, out of breath. He handed me a glazed pastry. I took a bite. The distinct flavor of browned butter, cardamom, and a hint of white miso flooded my mouth. It was my college finals week recipe, the one I had shared on an open-source baking wiki. "Isn't it mind-blowing?" he asked. I chewed slowly, my face blank. "It’s fine," I mumbled, swallowing. I handed the rest of the pastry back to him. I walked over to the sofa, collapsed face-first into the cushions, and let my arms dangle off the edge toward the floor, staring at a stray crumb on the rug.

Julian stared at his tablet screen. The YouTube video titled "The World's Greatest Secret Sauce" had amassed fifteen million views. The host enthusiastically whisked together the exact blend of gochujang, maple syrup, and smoked salt that Julian had created for a failed local pop-up restaurant. The host claimed it was a generations-old family secret. Julian’s eyes drooped half-shut. He reached out with a heavy arm and tapped the screen to pause the video right on the host's beaming face. He let his head rest on his palm, squishing his cheek, and watched the battery icon in the corner of the screen slowly drop from fourteen percent to thirteen percent. He let out a long, low breath that barely disturbed the quiet of his dim apartment.

At the fancy dinner party, our host proudly served a steaming platter of "Giovanni’s Famous Truffle Risotto." Everyone oohed and aahed. I recognized the unusual garnish of crispy fried capers and lemon zest instantly—it was the signature dish I’d submitted to a cooking contest last year. Giovanni had clearly lifted it. "Incredible, isn't it?" the man next to me whispered. I nodded slowly, my eyes half-closed. I picked up my silver fork and began dragging it through the creamy rice, pushing the capers into a neat little line on the edge of my porcelain plate. The lively chatter of the dining room washed over me in a dull roar. I propped my heavy head on my left hand and continued making tiny, meaningless patterns in my food.

Walking down the aisles of the high-end grocery store, Nina pushed her shopping cart at a glacial pace. She stopped in front of the artisanal dessert display. Prominently featured was a box of "Earth’s Bounty Vegan Fudge Bites." Nina looked at the ingredient list. The inclusion of pureed black beans and avocado oil matched the recipe she had posted on her old nutrition blog perfectly. A giant corporate logo was stamped on the front. Nina’s face remained slack. She leaned her forearms against the cold metal handle of the shopping cart, gazing upward at the flickering fluorescent tube light on the ceiling. The store radio played a faint, generic pop song. She exhaled slowly, her shoulders slumping, and eventually pushed the cart forward, the wheels squeaking rhythmically.

The second hand on the kitchen clock possessed a loud, rhythmic click that echoed through the empty house. Click. Click. Click. I rested my chin on my palm, tracing the wood grain of the table with a loose fingernail. Seventy-two lines of grain. I sighed, letting my head drop onto my folded arms. Beside my elbow sat Chloe’s abandoned tablet. With a slow, heavy drag of my finger, I swiped the screen awake, just needing a change of scenery from the beige walls. I tapped a folder labeled 'Math Apps' with a heavy thud of my thumb. Inside, nestled between calculator icons, was a blue bird logo, logged into an account named 'Chloe_Chaos_99'. I stared at the feed of late-night selfies and inside jokes with strangers, blinking slowly as the clock continued its endless clicking in the background.

Arthur clicked his ballpoint pen. In. Out. In. Out. He spun around in his office chair, watching the ceiling tiles pass by in a slow, white blur. He had organized his inbox by date, then by sender, and finally by subject line, but there were still three hours left in the afternoon. He picked up his son's old hand-me-down phone, which he used for testing mobile software, and started swiping back and forth between the two home screens. Left, right, left, right. His thumb caught on an unnamed folder, revealing a vibrant pink and purple camera icon. Arthur tapped it, leaning back until his chair creaked. A video immediately started playing—his son, Leo, lip-syncing to a loud rap song under a neon light, captioned 'My parents are so clueless.' Arthur just stared at the looping video, his pen clicking rhythmically against the desk.

Raindrops raced each other down the windshield of the minivan. I picked a plump droplet near the rearview mirror and bet my imaginary fortune on it reaching the wiper blade first. It merged with another and stopped halfway. I let out a long breath that fogged the glass, drawing a smiley face in the condensation, then wiping it away. An hour left of soccer practice. Maya’s laptop sat on the passenger seat, open and sleeping. I reached over and tapped the spacebar, hoping to play solitaire or read a recipe. The screen flared to life, bypassing the lock screen entirely to reveal a private message board. The username was 'MayaTheRebel', and the current thread was a detailed breakdown of how she sneaks out the basement window. I rested my head against the cool glass of the window, watching another raindrop stall out.

Elena matched the gray socks, then the black socks, then the white socks. She stacked them in perfectly aligned towers on the ironing board. She stared at the wall, listening to the hum of the dryer, wishing the machine would break just so she would have a puzzle to solve. She reached into the pocket of her teenager’s denim jacket, pulling out a sleek black smartphone that definitely wasn't the cracked model she paid the bill for. Elena pressed the power button with a slow, heavy thumb. Notifications flooded the screen from a hidden photo-sharing app. Messages from boys she didn't know, photos of parties she thought her daughter was sleeping through. Elena set the mystery device on top of the gray sock tower, folded her arms, and went back to listening to the rhythmic, unchanging tumble of the dryer drum.

There are exactly four hundred and twelve floral patterns on the living room wallpaper. I counted them twice. With my son away at his weekend retreat and the dog asleep on the rug, the silence in the house felt thick and heavy. I dragged my feet across the carpet, sinking into the computer chair. I nudged the mouse. I didn't want to read the news, and I had already checked the weather for the next ten days. I absentmindedly clicked through the browser history, looking for a distraction. A string of unfamiliar URLs caught my eye, leading to a sprawling profile page under a fake name. It was full of my son's artwork, edgy poems, and complaints about his suffocating home life. I rested my cheek in my hand, scrolling the mouse wheel down, down, down, watching the complaints blur together on the bright screen.

Marcus lay on the living room rug, tossing a tennis ball straight up into the air and catching it. Thwack. Catch. Thwack. Catch. The television had been off for hours. He had already read the back of the cereal box during breakfast and sorted the junk mail. Beside him on the carpet rested his daughter's school tablet. He rolled onto his side, propping his head on one hand, and poked the screen to see what time it was. A notification banner lingered on the lock screen: "New comment on your secret reel." Marcus swiped it down. A hidden profile opened, showcasing his quiet, straight-A daughter performing elaborate dance routines in the school bathroom. He watched three of them in total silence. Then, he locked the screen, picked up the tennis ball, and threw it back up toward the ceiling. Thwack. Catch.

The magazine on the table was from 2018. I had already read the article about autumn knitwear twice. The receptionist was typing at a speed of exactly one keystroke per second. I let my head loll back against the vinyl chair, staring at the fluorescent light fixture until my eyes watered. My own phone was dead, so I pulled my son's spare phone from my purse—the one I was supposed to drop off for repairs. I powered it on, hoping it had a snake game. Instead, the browser opened directly to a profile page for 'NightHawk_Jake'. I scrolled sluggishly. There were hundreds of posts tracking local street races, complete with photos of my son hanging out in industrial parking lots at 2 AM. I let the phone rest on my lap, returning my gaze to the slow, blinking cursor on the receptionist's computer monitor.

The keynote speaker had been talking about synergy for forty-five minutes. Sarah rested her chin in both hands, her eyes glazed over as she watched a fly buzz in lazy circles near the projector screen. She dragged her laptop bag up onto her lap, pulling out the silver MacBook she had borrowed from her daughter for the trip. She flipped it open, ignoring the spreadsheet she was supposed to be reviewing. Instead, she clicked aimlessly through the applications folder. A strange icon shaped like a ghost caught her attention. She clicked it. It was a secret messaging account, flooded with disappearing photos of her daughter scaling the town's water tower with older kids. Sarah stared at the images, her expression blank, while the speaker's monotone voice echoed through the hall, rambling about Q3 deliverables and vertical integration. She slowly closed the lid, tracing the metallic apple logo.

The crossing gate bells clanged in a steady, monotonous rhythm. The freight train passing in front of my bumper seemed to have no end. Boxcar after rusty boxcar clattered over the tracks. I drummed my fingers on the steering wheel, counting them. Forty-one, forty-two. I picked up my teenager’s phone from the center console, abandoned during the morning rush. I unlocked it just to check the battery percentage, swiping a screen over. Nestled in a folder called 'School Notes' was a bright yellow app icon I didn't recognize. I tapped it. A map populated, showing my son’s secret profile 'KingOfSneak' tagged at a downtown club two nights ago, surrounded by thousands of likes from strangers. Boxcar fifty-seven passed. Boxcar fifty-eight. I let the phone slip from my fingers back into the cup holder, staring blankly at the endless blur of rusted metal passing by.

The lobby was completely silent, save for the faint hum of the vending machine in the hallway. David sat at the front desk, resting his cheek against the cool laminate surface. He had already straightened the stack of brochures four times. He slowly dragged his daughter's tablet toward him, intending to mindlessly swipe through a puzzle game. As the screen brightened, it revealed a social platform he had never seen before. A profile named 'Echo_Whispers' was logged in, filled with dark, gothic poetry and complaints about how suffocating her parents were. David rested his heavy eyelids, scrolling through the posts with a lethargic flick of his index finger. The vending machine hummed. The neon vacancy sign buzzed outside. He rested his chin back on the desk, watching the brightly colored icons on the tablet screen slowly dim and fade to black.

I sat on the porch swing, pushing off the floorboards with one toe. Creak. Creak. Creak. The neighborhood was dead. Not a single car drove past, not a single neighbor was out walking a dog. I had the family laptop balanced on my knees, staring at the blank Google search bar, trying to think of a single thing I actually wanted to look up. Nothing came to mind. I opened the browser settings to clear the cache, just for the sake of clicking something. A saved password for a site called "VibeCheck" popped up under my son's initials. I clicked the autofill. The screen populated with a secret life—skatepark videos, loud music, and a girl he was apparently dating. I stopped swinging. I just stared at the screen, letting the heavy summer humidity press down on me, the quiet street remaining absolutely motionless.

Clara sat at the reference desk, resting her chin on a stack of returned paperbacks. The library was empty, the quiet so profound it felt like a physical weight. She traced the edge of a barcode with her thumbnail, staring at the dust motes drifting lazily through a shaft of sunlight. She booted up her teenager’s old laptop, which she brought to catalog books, and aimlessly poked around the hard drive. A hidden bookmark folder labeled "Homework" revealed a link to a massive streaming channel. Clara clicked it. A video played of her son streaming a violent video game, swearing loudly to an audience of ten thousand live viewers. Clara watched his face in the corner of the screen, her own expression completely slack. She let out a long, slow breath, watching another speck of dust drift aimlessly through the quiet air of the library.

I watched the clock tick from 2:14 to 2:15. An entire minute, gone forever. I let my head fall back against the sofa, tracing the popcorn ceiling pattern until my eyes glazed over. Desperate for any movement, I dragged myself out to the backyard with a rusty trowel, poking at the dry earth just to hear the sound of the metal scraping dirt. Scrape, pause. Scrape, pause. On the tenth scrape, the metal made a sharp clink. I brushed away the dust with a heavy hand, revealing a dented biscuit tin. Inside sat a faded Polaroid of me at twelve, a handful of marbles, and a letter in my own messy childhood scrawl. I stared at the contents, completely blank. I had absolutely no memory of putting these things in the ground, but at least the afternoon was finally moving forward.

Marcus tossed a crumpled receipt into the wastebasket, missed, and didn't bother getting up to retrieve it. He exhaled a long, noisy breath that fluttered his bangs, slumping over the dusty workbench in his garage. To his left, a rusted screwdriver lay perfectly parallel to a wrench. He nudged the wrench so it rested at a slight angle, then nudged it back. Looking for any excuse not to sit completely still, he began dragging the heavy workbench away from the wall. A hollow scrape echoed from the floorboards. Marcus crouched, prying up a loose plank with the tip of the screwdriver. Beneath it lay a sealed PVC pipe wrapped in duct tape. He peeled the tape away to find a stack of baseball cards and a handwritten note from 1998 bearing his own signature, a secret stash he couldn't recall hiding.

I must have reorganized the bookshelf three times before noon. Alphabetical, then by color, then by genre. When the clock struck one, I collapsed onto the floor, pulling at the frayed threads of the rug. I rolled onto my back, watching a solitary dust mote float lazily through a shaft of sunlight. I reached under my bed, blindly sweeping my hand across the floorboards in search of a stray sock or a lost coin—anything to occupy the next five minutes. My fingers brushed against a cold, hard lockbox shoved deep against the baseboard. I dragged it out into the light. The combination dial was covered in cobwebs. Miraculously, my fingers instinctively spun the numbers to my old locker code, popping the lid open. Inside were concert tickets and a diary from my sophomore year, a buried treasure I had entirely forgotten.

Elena sat on the porch steps, resting her chin heavily in her palms. She watched a pair of ants carry a breadcrumb across the concrete, her eyes half-closed. When the ants disappeared into a crack, she let out a loud, hollow sigh and picked up a stick, dragging it aimlessly through the mulch of her mother’s flowerbed. She traced circles, then squares, then a wobbly figure-eight. The stick suddenly caught on something solid, snapping in half. Elena barely reacted, just lazily pawing at the dirt with her bare hands until a small, rusted coffee can emerged. She popped the plastic lid. Inside was a collection of folded notebook paper, a dried rose, and a braided friendship bracelet. She recognized her own messy handwriting on the notes, but the memory of burying this little vault was completely missing from her mind.

Rain lashed against the windowpane in a steady thud. I sat on the basement stairs, counting the wooden slats. Fourteen stairs. I walked up to the top, then walked back down. Fourteen again. I grabbed an old hammer from the tool belt hanging on the banister and lightly tapped the drywall, listening to the hollow echo. Tap. Tap. Thud. I paused. I tapped the spot again. Solid. With nothing better to do with my afternoon, I chipped away at the crumbling plaster until a fist-sized hole appeared. I reached into the dark cavity and pulled out a tarnished cigar box. Inside lay a collection of my milk teeth, a plastic dinosaur, and a note reading DO NOT OPEN UNTIL 2020 in my own jagged handwriting. I stared at the rusted hinges, trying to summon a single memory of hiding it.

Julian lay flat on the living room floor, staring at the ceiling fan making its endless rotations. Click, swoosh. Click, swoosh. He rolled onto his side, his cheek pressed against the hardwood, and picked at a piece of lint. He blew it away, watching it settle a few inches further. Seeking the slightest change of scenery, he crawled under the staircase to inspect a loose floorboard he had noticed weeks ago. He wedged his fingers under the wood, lifting it with a groan. Beneath the dust and cobwebs sat a neon green plastic lunchbox. Julian unclasped the latch, revealing a pristine collection of mid-90s pogs, a defunct pager, and a list of New Year's resolutions written by a teenage version of himself. He rubbed his temples, genuinely baffled, unable to remember the day he had sealed it away in the dark.

I had been throwing a tennis ball against my bedroom wall for an hour. Thwack. Catch. Thwack. Catch. The rhythm became white noise. I aimed a little to the left, and the ball struck the edge of my loose wooden headboard, knocking a small, decorative panel to the floor. I let my arm drop, staring at the exposed gap in the wood. It was an excuse to move. I reached into the hollow space and my hand closed around a cool metal cylinder. I pulled out an old aluminum water bottle tightly sealed with wax. Chipping the wax away over the trash can, I shook out a dozen folded letters addressed to my future self, alongside a dried four-leaf clover. I recognized my own cursive, but the act of sealing this strange capsule was a total blank.

The pendulum clock in the hallway chimed four times, a slow, drawn-out sound that matched the heavy slump of Clara’s shoulders. She sat at the kitchen table, swirling her lukewarm tea until a small vortex formed, then waiting for it to stop so she could swirl it again. Unable to endure another silent minute, she wandered into the backyard and grabbed a rusty trowel, jabbing it into the soil around the old oak tree. She dug without purpose, just tossing scoops of dirt aside to pass the hour. The trowel scraped against heavy plastic. Clara unearthed a sealed Tupperware container, heavy with dirt. Popping the lid, she found an old MP3 player, a beaded necklace, and a crumpled map of the neighborhood labeled in her own childish print. She turned the map over, entirely unable to recall leaving it there.

Swiveling my desk chair left to right, I let my shoes scuff against the carpet. I clicked my pen twenty times, then unclicked it twenty times. The silence in the attic room was thick. I dragged myself out of the chair and began peeling away the wallpaper near the window, just to hear the satisfying paper tear. Underneath a particularly stubborn strip, a loose brick jutted out from the exposed masonry. I wriggled the brick free and peered into the dark recess. I pulled out a velvet pouch tied with a golden string. Inside were three smooth river stones, an expired arcade token, and a Polaroid of me smiling gaps between my teeth. I traced my own signature on the back of the photo, totally mystified by the secret stash I had apparently hidden away.

Leo lay on the grass, watching clouds drift at a slow pace. That one looked like a sheep. That one looked like a blurry sheep. He chewed on a blade of grass, sighing heavily into the summer air. He rolled over, letting his fingers dig into the soft earth near the edge of the patio. His nails caught on a piece of hard plastic buried beneath the turf. Grateful for a distraction, he grabbed a nearby rock and scraped the dirt away until he freed a small, sealed lockbox. The code was set to 0-0-0. He popped it open to find his old middle-school glasses, a mixtape, and a letter detailing his tenth-grade crushes. Leo laughed softly, turning the cassette tape over in his hands, completely unable to remember the afternoon he had decided to bury his adolescence.

I rested my forehead on the cold steering wheel of the rusty car sitting in the barn. The rain outside meant my outdoor plans were ruined. I tapped my thumbs against the dashboard, playing an imaginary drum solo that quickly lost its charm. I popped the glove compartment, slammed it shut, then popped it again. The third time I slammed it, the back panel of the compartment cracked and fell inward. I reached into the dusty void of the dashboard and pulled out a tightly rolled leather pouch. Unfurling it, I found an old pocket watch, three foreign coins, and a handwritten list titled Things to do before turning twenty. It was undoubtedly my handwriting, but I stared at the aged paper, completely disconnected from the teenager who had stashed it deep inside the broken car so many years ago.

Maya tapped her fingernails against the glass of the window, a slow, methodical click, click, click. She watched a solitary drop of water trace a sluggish path down the pane. With a heavy exhale, she turned her back on the gray afternoon and began pacing the length of the attic. Ten steps forward, turn, ten steps back. She dragged her boot across the dusty floorboards, catching the toe on a raised knot in the wood. She knelt down, wiggling the loose plank until it gave way. Hidden in the joists was a dented metal tinbox. Maya dusted it off and opened the lid. Inside lay a collection of dried leaves, an old diary, and a silver locket. She recognized the locket as her own, yet the memory of hiding the tin beneath the floorboards eluded her entirely.

I watched the ceiling fan complete its three-hundredth rotation, the rhythmic click-clack of the blades the only sound in the empty laundromat. I traced the cracked laminate of the folding table with my thumb, letting out a long, slow breath that fluttered a stray receipt. Kicking my heel against the metal chair leg, I stared at the rotating drum of dryer number four. A scuffed leather square resting beneath the adjacent bench caught my eye. I nudged it out with the toe of my sneaker, leaning down with a heavy sigh to flip it open. Thick stacks of hundred-dollar bills stared back at me, strapped in crisp paper bands. I blinked at the green paper, looking back at the slowly spinning laundry, drumming my fingers against the wad of cash as I waited for the spin cycle to finally end.

Martin rested his heavy head in his hands, watching the digital clock on his monitor change from 4:13 to 4:14. He dragged his cursor across the desktop, highlighting and unhighlighting a folder labeled 'Q3 Reports' for the past ten minutes. A loud sigh escaped his lips as he kicked his trashcan, knocking over a thick, overstuffed brown wallet someone had dropped near his cubicle earlier. He leaned down, moving with the sluggishness of molasses, and flipped open the leather fold. Dozens of crisp fifty-dollar bills spilled onto the gray carpet. Martin stared down at the fortune, his expression remaining perfectly blank. He let out another slow puff of air, nudged the bills back into the leather folds with his shoe, and leaned back in his swivel chair to watch the clock click to 4:15.

Counting the cracks in the pavement was losing its appeal by the third block. I scuffed my boots against the concrete, watching a lone gray cloud inch its way across a perfectly flat blue sky. My headphones played a podcast I hadn't been listening to for at least twenty minutes. As I kicked a pebble, watching it skitter into the gutter, I noticed a bulky designer wallet resting on the curb. I picked it up, flipping it open to find it bursting with more hundred-dollar bills than I had ever seen in my life. I stared at the Benjamin Franklins, then looked down the empty suburban street where nothing had happened since 1998. "Huh," I muttered to the empty sidewalk. I shoved the overflowing wallet into my coat pocket and went back to timing the interval between my footsteps.

Chloe leaned heavily against the register counter, blowing a loose strand of hair out of her eyes. The mall was a ghost town, the only movement the slow drip of a fountain three storefronts down. She picked at a chipped piece of polish on her thumbnail, peeling it off in one tiny strip. Under a display rack of discounted sunglasses, a black leather bifold sat abandoned. She dragged her feet across the tile, retrieved the wallet, and pried it apart. A massive wad of banded cash practically leaped out, at least ten thousand dollars in fresh currency. She blinked slowly at the money, then looked up at the empty concourse. With a loud, drawn-out exhale, she set the small fortune next to the receipt printer, rested her chin back in her palm, and returned to peeling the polish off her index finger.

I sat on the green slatted bench, watching a pigeon peck at a cigarette butt with a blank expression. The park was entirely still, the afternoon air thick and unmoving. I checked my phone—no new messages. I locked the screen, unlocked it, swiped left, and locked it again. My foot tapped a rhythmic, hollow beat against the asphalt, striking something soft. It was a bulging, zippered clutch. Peeling back the zipper, the neon green of banded cash greeted me, a seemingly bottomless stack of fifty-dollar bills. I sifted through the crisp paper, my face resting heavily in my other hand. The pigeon abandoned the cigarette and waddled a few feet away to inspect a leaf. I tossed the open wallet onto the empty space beside me, leaned my head back against the wood, and watched a cloud slowly dissolve.

Elias swirled the cold, black coffee in his mug, watching the dark liquid climb the ceramic walls before settling. The diner’s fluorescent lights hummed a low, constant drone that made his eyelids droop. He rested his cheek against the cool Formica tabletop, tracing a coffee stain with the tine of a fork. Beneath the table, his shoe brushed against a heavy object. Slowly sitting up, he reached down to retrieve a thick alligator-skin wallet. Flipping it open revealed a staggering amount of cash, thick stacks of hundreds wedged into every slot. Elias looked at the money, then at the single waitress wiping down the far counter for the fifth time. He let the wallet fall onto the table with a dull thud, slumped back into the vinyl booth, and went back to swirling his cold coffee.

The ticking of the wall clock echoed through the empty waiting room, each second feeling longer than the last. I flipped through an automotive magazine from three years ago, not reading a single word, just listening to the crinkle of the glossy pages. I slid down in the plastic chair until my knees hit the coffee table, letting my arms hang limp at my sides. My fingers brushed against a faux-leather wallet wedged between the cushions. I pulled it free, opening it to find a brick of twenty-dollar bills so thick the leather seams were splitting. I flipped through the wad, feeling the raised texture of the paper. A nurse walked by the glass partition without looking in. I shoved the wallet onto the coffee table, picked the magazine back up, and flipped to an ad about spark plugs.

Jenna stood by the auditorium doors, her flashlight dangling limply from two fingers. The credits for the romantic comedy had been rolling for five minutes, and the sweeping orchestral music was putting her to sleep. She shifted her weight from her left foot to her right, then back again, staring blankly at the sticky carpet. Beneath an empty back-row seat, a red leather wallet lay discarded. She shuffled over, picking it up with a slow sigh. Inside was a driver's license and enough cash to buy a used car. She stared at the thick stack of bills, her face devoid of any surprise. The screen finally went completely black, the house lights buzzing on. Jenna tucked the small fortune into her uniform pocket, grabbed her broom, and began sweeping popcorn kernels with agonizingly slow, half-hearted strokes.

I stared at the dark tunnel rushing past the subway window, my reflection staring back with half-closed eyes. The rhythmic clack of the tracks was the only sound, lulling me into a hazy trance. I rested my head against the vibrating glass, letting out a long puff of air. On the empty plastic seat across from me sat a simple brown wallet. I leaned forward, retrieved it, and popped the snap closure. A ridiculous amount of hundred-dollar bills sat inside, neatly organized and completely out of place on the empty train car. I ran my thumb over the edge of the money, looking up at the illuminated route map above the door. Still four stops away. I dropped the wallet onto my lap, crossed my arms over my chest, and went back to staring at my blurry reflection in the dark glass.

The lobby was perfectly silent except for the faint hum of the vending machine down the hall. Arthur rested his chin on his folded arms, watching a single fly buzz in lazy circles around the chandelier. He blew a stray hair off his forehead, wishing the phone would ring just to break the silence. A guest had left a sleek black wallet resting near the complimentary mints. Arthur pulled it toward him, opening it to reveal tight, banded stacks of hundred-dollar bills. There had to be fifty thousand dollars in there. He stared at the money for a moment, his expression completely flat. He slowly reached out, took a single peppermint from the bowl, unwrapped it, and popped it into his mouth. He slid the wallet into the lost and found drawer, resting his chin back on his arms.

I dragged my pen across the notebook, drawing endless, looping spirals until the ink began to run dry. The library was suffocatingly quiet, the smell of old paper making my eyelids feel heavy. I let out a long breath, slumped forward, and rested my forehead against the cool wooden desk. Something pressed uncomfortably against my knee. I reached under the desk and pulled out a bulging, worn leather wallet. Prying it open, I found it completely stuffed with crisp fifty-dollar bills, more money than my college tuition. I stared at the green paper, listening to the muffled sound of a librarian re-shelving a book three aisles over. I closed the wallet, set it next to my notebook, grabbed a fresh pen from my bag, and began drawing spirals on a brand-new page.

Marcus watched the black-and-white monitors, his eyes glazing over as he stared at the empty parking garage feed. He tapped his pen against his knee, the rhythmic sound echoing in the tiny booth. He let out a loud yawn, stretching his arms above his head until his shoulders popped. On the floor beside his rolling chair, a silver money clip held together a thick, folded stack of large bills and a few credit cards. He leaned over, scooped it up, and thumbed through the cash. It was thousands of dollars, completely untraceable. Marcus stared at the monitor showing camera four, where a stray cat was slowly walking across the concrete. He tossed the money clip onto the desk next to his half-eaten sandwich, propped his boots up next to the monitors, and let his eyes drift shut.

I had already arranged my spice rack alphabetically and color-coded my t-shirts by the time the mail carrier finally walked up the driveway. I watched him from the living room window, tracing the path of a lone raindrop down the glass with my index finger. The hollow metallic clack of the mailbox lid shutting was the loudest sound I’d heard all afternoon. Shuffling outside in my slippers, I found a single envelope. Inside was a birthday card, bright yellow, with no signature, no return address, just a pre-printed greeting. My birthday was six months ago. I stared at the blank space where a name should be, then looked at the empty street, the gray sky, and the dormant hydrangeas. I brought the card inside, placed it on the kitchen counter, and went back to watching the second hand sweep across the wall clock.

Elias sat on the porch swing, pushing off with one foot every ten seconds just to hear the rusted hinges squeal. Squeak, pause, squeak, pause. The neighborhood was dead silent, save for the occasional drone of a distant lawnmower. He walked to the mailbox just for something to do, opening it to find a heavy cardstock envelope. It was a birthday card, featuring a cartoon dog wearing a party hat. Elias flipped it open. Blank. No name, no message. He flipped it to the back. Made in China. $3.99. He let out a long, slow breath, puffing his cheeks out as he exhaled. He put the card back in the envelope, walked over to the recycling bin, dropped it in, and returned to the swing. Squeak, pause, squeak, pause. Maybe he would see how many times he could bounce a tennis ball against the garage door later.

The television had been playing an infomercial about copper pans for the last forty minutes, and I hadn't changed the channel. I already knew they were scratch-resistant and could melt a penny. The mail arrived at three o'clock, offering a brief five-minute excursion to the end of the driveway. I pulled out a stack of grocery circulars and a blue envelope. The envelope held a birthday card that read 'To a Special Someone'. I opened it, expecting a gift card or at least a signature, but there was nothing. Just empty white paper. I brought it inside, dropped it onto the coffee table next to a half-empty mug of room-temperature tea, and sank back into the indent on the sofa. The infomercial host was now making an omelet without oil. I propped my chin in my hand, staring unblinking at the screen.

Maya lay on the carpet, tracing the geometric patterns in the rug with a dry pen. She rolled onto her back, staring at a water stain on the ceiling that looked vaguely like a turtle. When the mail slot clattered in the front door, she didn't get up immediately. Five minutes later, she dragged herself down the hallway to retrieve a lone square envelope from the welcome mat. Inside was a birthday card sprinkled with loose glitter. There was no signature. She shook the card over the trash can, watching the tiny metallic flecks cascade down into yesterday's coffee grounds. She didn't wonder who sent it. She didn't wonder why they forgot to sign it. She just sat on the linoleum floor of the kitchen, picking the remaining pieces of glitter off her thumb, one by one, until the clock chimed four.

I scrolled to the bottom of my social media feed until I started seeing posts from three days ago, then I locked my phone and tossed it onto the bed. I paced from the bedroom to the kitchen, opened the refrigerator, looked at the jar of pickles and the carton of milk, and closed it again. I walked out to the mailbox. There was an unsigned birthday card inside, decorated with silver foil balloons. I held it in my hand, reading the generic wishes printed inside. I didn't know whose handwriting was missing, and my birthday wasn't until November. I walked back inside, placed the card on the dining table, and sat in the chair. I started tapping my index fingers against the wood, trying to match the rhythm of the dripping faucet in the sink. Tap. Drip. Tap. Drip.

Arthur had reorganized his bookshelf by color, then by author, and finally by the height of the spine. Now, he sat in his armchair, staring out the window at a squirrel burying a nut in the lawn. The mail truck pulled away, leaving a solitary white envelope in its wake. Arthur padded outside in his socks, indifferent to the damp concrete, and fetched it. It was a birthday card with a picture of a sailboat. Inside, the space for a signature was completely blank. Arthur examined the card, then looked back at the yard. The squirrel was gone. He took the card inside, grabbed a black marker, and carefully wrote 'From Nobody' on the bottom line. He propped it up on the mantelpiece, stepped back, and let out a heavy sigh, crossing his arms and waiting for the afternoon sun to shift across the floorboards.

The ceiling fan rotated at exactly one revolution per second on its lowest setting. I had been counting the spins for twenty minutes. When the mail arrived, I slowly pushed myself up from the mattress, my joints popping in the quiet apartment. In the metal box downstairs, I found a pink envelope. Inside was a birthday card smelling faintly of cheap perfume, with a picture of a laughing clown. No name, no message. I stared at the creepy painted smile for a few seconds. I thought about trying to solve the mystery of who sent it, but the effort felt like walking through molasses. I left the card on the kitchen counter next to a pile of unpaid bills. Returning to the living room, I laid flat on my back on the rug and focused my eyes back on the ceiling fan. One. Two. Three. Four.

Chloe’s chin rested on her palm, squishing her cheek as she stared blankly at her computer screen. The screensaver bounced from corner to corner. Every time it almost hit perfectly in the angle, she held her breath, only to exhale loudly when it missed. She checked the mail just to break the silence. A bright green envelope waited inside. She ripped it open to find a birthday card with a generic floral print. She scoured the inside for a name, a note, even a stray mark, but found nothing. Just a crisp, blank white void. She tossed the card onto her desk. It landed next to a cup filled with twelve identical ballpoint pens. She picked one up, clicked the top ten times in rapid succession, and went back to watching the DVD logo drift lazily across her dark monitor, waiting for five o'clock.

I had spent the last hour meticulously peeling a label off a water bottle, trying to keep it in one piece. When I failed, I balled up the sticky plastic and missed the trash can. I went out to the porch to fetch the mail, dragging my feet along the gravel. There was a thick envelope with no return address. I opened it to find an unsigned birthday card featuring a watercolor landscape. My birthday was today, but seeing the empty signature line sparked no curiosity. I just stared at the painted trees. They looked fuzzy. I brought the card inside, sat on the edge of the sofa, and picked up a deck of playing cards. I began dealing them out for my fifth game of solitaire of the afternoon, slipping the unsigned birthday card under the pile of discards.

Marcus leaned his head against the cool glass of the living room window, watching cars occasionally roll past on the damp street. There was a fly buzzing near the lamp, but he couldn't muster the energy to swat it. When the mail arrived, he ambled out to the front gate. Amidst the junk mail was a square envelope containing a birthday card. The front declared 'Have a blast!' in bold, neon letters. Inside, the white space was completely untouched by ink. Marcus flipped the card over, read the copyright year, and let out a long, drawn-out puff of air. He walked back inside, dropping the card onto a stack of old magazines. He slumped back onto the couch, propped his feet up on the coffee table, and continued tracking the erratic flight path of the lone housefly circling the lampshade.

I chewed on the plastic cap of my pen until it cracked. My notebook was full of meaningless doodles—cubes, spirals, and block letters of my own name. I stood up, stretched my arms overhead, and decided to check the mail again, even though I had checked it an hour ago. This time, there was a lavender envelope sitting at the bottom of the rusty metal box. I tore it open. It was a birthday card with a picture of a cat hanging from a branch, reading 'Hang in there!' The inside was completely blank. No signature, no heartfelt note. I held it for a moment, listening to the hum of the refrigerator leaking out through the open screen door. I slipped the card into my back pocket, went back to my desk, picked up the cracked pen, and started shading in a row of tiny triangles.

Sylvia was attempting to balance a silver spoon on the tip of her nose when she heard the mailbox snap shut. She let the spoon clatter onto the kitchen table and trudged to the front door. The lone item inside was an envelope containing a birthday card covered in holographic stars. She opened it up, her eyes scanning the blank, unsigned interior. No clues, no handwriting, nothing to decipher. She sighed, her shoulders slumping as she closed the card. She returned to the kitchen, leaving the card leaning against the salt shaker. She sat back down in her wooden chair, resting her chin on the table surface. She stared at the spoon for a long minute. Finally, she picked it up, tilted her head back, and tried to find the precise center of gravity on her nose all over again.

Chloe leaned her chin against her palm, tracing the grain of the coffee shop table with a torn sugar packet while Sarah wept into a napkin. "I’m serious this time, I got the job in Seattle," Sarah sobbed, her mascara running. Chloe watched a pigeon peck at a cigarette butt outside the window. "Seattle," Chloe repeated, her voice perfectly flat. She checked her phone screen; no new notifications. Sarah had declared she was moving to Austin in May, Denver in August, and Brooklyn last week. Chloe shifted her weight, feeling the hard wooden chair digging into her lower back, and wondered if it was too early to order a second iced latte. "You’re not even listening!" Sarah cried. "I am," Chloe sighed, resting her chin on her other hand and watching the second hand sweep across the large wall clock above the barista station.

"So, the movers come on Tuesday for the cross-country haul," Mark announced, pacing the length of my living room with wild, sweeping hand gestures. I picked at a loose thread on my sweatpants, slowly pulling it until the seam began to pucker. He was talking about New York, the big city, the adventure of a lifetime. I let out a long, slow exhale and stared blankly at the TV screen, which was currently playing a documentary about the history of cardboard with the volume muted. "Are you going to help me pack?" he asked. I looked up, blinking slowly. "Sure," I murmured, leaning my head back against the sofa cushions. The ceiling fan rotated at a sluggish pace, click-clack, click-clack. I wondered if I had enough frozen peas left for dinner, or if I’d have to make the five-minute drive to the grocery store.

The clinking of silver against porcelain did nothing to drown out Julian’s impassioned monologue about relocating to Los Angeles. Arthur slumped lower into the velvet armchair, his thumb rhythmically swiping up on his phone screen. Another picture of a latte, another sunset, another meme he didn't laugh at. "It’s three thousand miles away, Artie. I leave tomorrow," Julian insisted, leaning across the marble table. Arthur stifled a yawn with the back of his hand, his eyes glazed over as he stared at the ornate wallpaper pattern directly behind Julian's head. "Tomorrow. Wow," Arthur offered in a monotone drawl, letting his phone drop onto his lap with a soft thud. He drummed his fingers against the armrest, counting the seconds until the waiter would return. "Do you think they have that potato soup today?" Arthur asked, entirely missing the incredulous look spreading across his soon-to-be-absent best friend's face.

The bell was fifteen minutes away when Mia slid the folded note across my desk. I unfolded it slowly, smoothing the creases. My dad got transferred to Miami. We're leaving forever on Friday. I stared at the blue ink, then let my eyes drift toward the whiteboard, where Mr. Harrison was droning on about soil erosion. I picked up my pencil and began shading the letter 'O' on my worksheet until the graphite turned shiny and black. Miami. Friday. I rested my cheek on the cool laminate of the desk, watching a speck of dust dance in a sunbeam. I tapped my foot against the metal chair leg in a steady, repetitive rhythm. I flipped the note over, drew a tiny stick figure, and slid it back, checking the clock above the door. Fourteen minutes to go.

"I just can’t believe I won’t see you every day," Lisa’s voice crackled through the phone’s speaker. Jenna placed the device on the kitchen counter, grabbing a damp sponge. She wiped down the granite surface, her eyes following the circular motions of the soapy suds. "Mmhmm," Jenna replied, her voice entirely flat. "Boston is just so far from San Diego," Lisa continued, her tone trembling. Jenna peeled a dried speck of tomato sauce off the stovetop with her fingernail, letting out a long, heavy exhale through her nose. She wandered over to the refrigerator, opened it, stared at the mustard and half-empty milk carton for twenty seconds, and let the door swing shut. "Are you even there?" Lisa asked. Jenna picked up the phone, collapsing onto a nearby dining chair. "Yeah. Boston. Crazy," she muttered, staring blankly at the blank television across the room.

Boxes were piled high against every wall of Leo’s bedroom, stenciled with the words 'Oregon or Bust'. I sat in his spinning desk chair, pushing off the floor with my sneakers to rotate myself in slow, lazy circles. "I'm really going to miss this town," Leo said, taping up a carton of books. I caught a tennis ball from his desk and tossed it against the ceiling, catching it as it fell. Thwack. Catch. "Yeah," I mumbled, tossing it again. Thwack. Catch. The ceiling had exactly forty-two popcorn bumps in the square section right above my head. I had counted them three times since I arrived. Leo went on a tangent about the mountains in Portland and the coffee scene. I let my head loll back over the edge of the chair, watching the room upside down, wondering if my mom was making meatloaf tonight.

Derek didn't look up from his monitor when Kyle dropped the bomb about the move to Chicago. His thumbs continuously flicked over the thumbsticks of his controller. "So, my mom said we're packing up the truck on the twenty-first," Kyle said, hovering awkwardly in the doorway. "Cool," Derek grunted, his eyes half-closed as his character jogged across a barren, digital wasteland. There were no enemies around, nothing to loot, just endless gray polygons. Derek let his character run into a wall, watching the walking animation loop against the unyielding stone. He sighed loudly, letting the controller drop into his lap. "Chicago," Kyle repeated, hoping for a reaction. Derek stared at the looping animation, resting his chin on his chest. "That's the windy one, right?" he asked, his voice devoid of any inflection. He picked the controller back up and began making his character jump in place.

"I signed the lease in Maine," Trevor announced, racking his dumbbells. I sat on the edge of the bench press, chewing my gum in a slow, rhythmic cadence. I stared at the gray rubber flooring, counting the little blue flecks mixed into the pattern. "Maine," I echoed, my voice flat. I leaned forward, resting my elbows on my knees, and let out a long breath that ruffled my bangs. "We leave next weekend. It's a huge step for my career," he said, his face flushed with excitement. I blew a bubble, letting it pop softly against my lips before pulling it back into my mouth. The gym music bumped a monotonous bassline. I picked up my towel, wiped an imaginary spot of sweat from my forehead, and looked at the wall clock. "Right," I murmured. "You want to do legs now, or are we done?"

Samantha sat cross-legged on the park grass, aggressively tearing blades of green into tiny pieces while Harper detailed her upcoming move to Alaska. "It's completely off the grid," Harper gushed, throwing her arms wide. Samantha let out a heavy sigh, tipping her head back to stare at a completely cloudless, empty stretch of blue sky. She dropped the shredded grass and began poking at a nearby ant hill with a discarded popsicle stick. "Uh-huh," Samantha droned. She watched an ant scramble over a pebble, wondering how long it would take the insect to realize it was going in circles. "I'm going to have to buy a whole new winter wardrobe," Harper continued. Samantha rested her cheek against her knee, her eyelids drooping to half-mast. "Yeah. Coats," she replied in a monotone whisper, her gaze remaining rigidly fixed on the dirt in front of her.

The windshield wipers squeaked back and forth in a hypnotic, slow rhythm. Squeak-thwump. Squeak-thwump. "So, the transfer came through. I'm moving to Texas," Ben said from the driver's seat. I rested the side of my face against the cold glass of the passenger window, watching the endless, gray highway lines blur together. "Texas," I repeated, barely moving my lips. I reached out and adjusted the air conditioning vent, pointing it directly at my face, then immediately pointed it away again. "I'll be gone by the end of the month," he added, his voice tinged with melancholy. I let out a prolonged exhale through my nose, fogging up the glass, and traced a lazy circle in the condensation with my index finger. "Cool," I murmured, watching the circle fade away. The wipers dragged across the glass again. Squeak-thwump. "Are we stopping for food soon?" I asked.

In the sterile glow of the breakroom fluorescents, Greg stirred his lukewarm coffee for the fourth consecutive minute. "HQ is relocating me to the London branch," Marcus said, leaning against the vending machine. Greg’s eyes remained locked on the swirling brown liquid in his paper cup. The tiny wooden stirrer scraped against the cardboard bottom with a dull, repetitive scuff. "London," Greg stated, his face entirely slack. Marcus nodded eagerly. "Across the pond! I have to pack up my whole apartment by Sunday." Greg finally stopped stirring, resting his chin heavily in his palm. He looked past Marcus, his gaze settling on a peeling safety poster on the far wall. The silence stretched out, accompanied only by the low hum of the refrigerator. "Do you know if Linda brought donuts today?" Greg asked, his voice devoid of energy, tossing the wooden stirrer into the trash can.

I sat on the porch swing, pushing off the floorboards with my heel. Creak, sway, creak, sway. "I got accepted into NYU," Elena announced, sitting on the railing. "I'm moving to Manhattan in August." I peeled a strip of chipped white paint from the armrest, rolling it into a tight little ball between my thumb and forefinger. "Manhattan," I mumbled, tossing the paint ball into the overgrown bushes. "I can't believe we won't be neighbors anymore," she said, her voice catching slightly. I slouched deeper into the wooden slats of the swing, letting out a loud, hollow sigh that seemed to stretch on forever. I watched a lone car drive past our house at exactly the speed limit. The street was totally empty again. "Yeah," I said, my voice flat. I pushed off the floorboards with my heel again. Creak, sway, creak, sway.

Arthur traced the faded seam of his corduroy pants, looping his finger back and forth across the thread. Dr. Evans burst into the consultation room, his face flushed, clutching a manila folder to his chest. "Arthur, there's been a catastrophic error," the doctor panted. "The lab mixed up your biopsy results with a man named Arnold." Arthur watched a dust mote drift through a shaft of sunlight cutting across the desk. "So... no surgery?" he asked, his voice flat. "No! You're completely healthy! It was a false alarm!" Dr. Evans beamed, expecting a celebration. Arthur slowly exhaled, resting his chin in his palm. "Right. Do I need to validate my parking ticket at the front desk, or does the machine do it?" he asked, already mentally reviewing the contents of his refrigerator to see if he had enough bread to make a sandwich.

The phone wedged between my ear and shoulder was getting warm. I clicked the remote, cycling past a cooking show, a home shopping network, and a documentary about sea sponges. On the other end of the line, the hospital administrator was using a lot of dramatic pauses. "Ma'am, it appears your blood panels were swapped with an elderly patient. You don't have severe anemia after all." I chipped a flake of dry polish off my thumbnail. "Mhm," I murmured. "This is highly unusual, we are so terribly sorry for the emotional toll," she continued. I watched the sea sponge filter water. It looked like a very slow, repetitive existence. "Okay. So do I stop taking the iron pills?" I asked, suppressing a yawn. "Yes, absolutely." I hung up and stared at the blank television screen, wondering if the grocery store was still open.

Marcus sat at his kitchen island, his laptop camera capturing the top half of his face while he carefully shaded in a series of interlocking triangles on a sticky note. The pixelated face of Dr. Chen filled the screen, her expression grave. "Marcus, I need you to listen carefully. The pharmacy dispensed someone else's heart medication to you under your profile. Your actual chart shows perfect cholesterol." Marcus switched from a black pen to a blue one, filling in the next geometric shape. "Uh-huh," he said, not looking up. "You could have experienced a severe drop in blood pressure," she emphasized, her voice climbing an octave. "I see," Marcus replied flatly, his eyes tracing the grid of his notepad. He capped his pen, leaned back, and spun his chair in a slow, drifting half-circle. "Does this mean I owe a different copay?"

I spent twenty minutes counting the anatomical inaccuracies on the digestive system poster before the nurse practitioner finally hurried in. She practically slammed the door, her eyes wide behind her wire-rimmed glasses. "Your X-rays," she gasped, out of breath. "They belong to a sixty-year-old woman with advanced osteoporosis. The technician labeled the digital files backward." I rested my head against the cool plaster wall, letting my eyelids droop halfway. The hum of the fluorescent light above pitched into a steady, unbroken drone. "So my ankle isn't crumbling," I stated, staring at the floor tiles. "Exactly! It's just a mild sprain!" she said, offering a bright, nervous smile. I slowly pushed myself up from the crinkly paper covering the examination table. "Great. Can I just leave the walking boot in the hallway, or do you guys have a specific bin for it?"

The official hospital letterhead demanded attention, but Elena was far more focused on waiting for the coffee machine to finish its slow, sputtering drip. She ripped the envelope open, scanning the dense paragraphs. Notice of Data and Diagnostic Mix-Up. The text explained that her MRI had been swapped with another patient, meaning she did not have a developing mass in her frontal lobe. Elena folded the letter neatly in half, then into quarters, and set it next to the sugar bowl. She tapped her fuzzy slipper against the linoleum, keeping time with the final drips of the brew. The cat rubbed against her ankles, and she stared blankly out the window at the overcast sky. Her phone buzzed with an urgent follow-up email from the neurology department. She swiped the notification away without opening it, poured her coffee, and went back to bed.

The line at the pharmacy counter hadn't moved in ten minutes. I shifted my weight from my left foot to my right, staring at a display of travel-sized toothpaste. The pharmacist motioned me forward, looking frantic. "We caught an error just in time," he whispered, leaning over the counter. "Your physician's office sent over a prescription for heavy immunosuppressants. But we checked the national database, and those belong to a transplant patient with the same name." I blinked slowly at him. "So, no pills for me?" I asked, my voice a flat monotone. "No, it was a massive administrative error," he wiped his brow. I looked past him to the clock on the wall. "Does that mean my nasal spray is ready, or do I need to keep waiting?" I asked, pulling out my phone to scroll mindlessly through photos of my own cat.

The dental surgeon rushed into the small operating room just as the assistant was adjusting the bib around Julian’s neck. "Stop everything," the surgeon ordered, holding up an iPad. "We pulled the wrong panoramic scans. Julian, you don't need all four wisdom teeth extracted. Those records belong to the patient in room three." Julian let out a long breath, staring up at the blinding overhead light. He reached up and slowly peeled the paper bib off his chest, dropping it beside the chair. The dental drill continued to emit a high-pitched whine from its resting dock. "Okay," Julian murmured, rubbing his temples. He swung his legs over the side of the chair and stared at the blank beige wall for a long moment. "Am I supposed to take this complimentary toothbrush, or is that only for the people who actually get surgery?"

I stirred my iced latte until the ice cubes melted completely into small, rounded slivers. My phone lit up with an urgent message from the patient portal, marked with a red exclamation point. I clicked the link. The clinic administrator confessed that my genetic screening results had been switched with my cousin's, who had the same last name. I didn't actually have the rare hereditary marker they'd called me about yesterday. I set the phone face down on the table. Outside the cafe window, a pigeon pecked rhythmically at a discarded piece of chewing gum. I watched it for five solid minutes, resting my chin heavily in my palm. The waitress walked by, asking if I wanted the check. "Yeah," I mumbled, tracing a water ring on the glass table. "And maybe another napkin. This one got wet."

Clara lay flat on the hospital bed, staring at the textured acoustic tiles on the ceiling. She had counted forty-two full tiles and twelve partial ones around the edges when the chief resident scurried in, followed by two nurses. "Ms. Higgins, we have incredible news. There was a mix-up with the pathology lab. The tissue sample was benign. You don't need the chemotherapy protocol." Clara turned her head at a glacial pace toward the doctors. She offered a slow, singular nod. "Oh. Good," she said softly, her face completely still. The resident waited for a smile, tears, or a hug. Instead, Clara picked at a loose thread on the thin cotton blanket covering her knees. "Since I'm not staying," she droned, "do I still get to eat the pudding cup that came with the lunch tray, or do you have to take it back?"

The doctor’s office had a ticking clock that echoed off the sterile white walls. Tick, tick, tick. I slumped in the plastic chair, watching the second hand drag itself around the dial. Dr. Aris finally entered, looking profoundly apologetic. "I cannot express how sorry we are. Your ultrasound was logged under the wrong identification number. You aren't expecting twins. You just have a small, harmless cyst." I stared at the potted fern in the corner, noticing its leaves were turning brown at the tips. It desperately needed watering. "Alright," I sighed, pulling a piece of lint off my sweater. "We have launched a full investigation into how this happened," she assured me. I rested the side of my head against the cold wall. "Sure. Just... email me the bill, I guess," I said, wondering if I had enough gas to make it home without stopping.

Victor sat in the darkened examination room, resting his chin on the metal contraption while staring blankly at the blurry letters on the distant wall. The optometrist burst back into the room, flipping frantically through a thick file. "Mr. Vance, I apologize. The retinal scans I showed you earlier? They belong to a diabetic patient with severe macular degeneration. Your eyes are perfectly fine." Victor slowly pulled his head back from the machine, his eyelids drooping. He let out a long, loud breath that fluttered his lips. "So I don't need the injections," he stated, his voice completely devoid of inflection. "Exactly!" the doctor cheered. Victor picked up his phone, thumbing aimlessly through his lock screen notifications. "Right. Well, I’ve been sitting here in the dark for twenty minutes," he said, staring at his unlaced shoe. "Can we just wrap this up?"

I sat on the overstuffed couch, tracing the floral pattern woven into the fabric. My psychiatrist, Dr. Miller, cleared his throat for the third time. "It seems the reception desk swapped your intake forms with another client. The severe personality disorder diagnosis I’ve been referencing... that isn't yours." I didn't sit up. I kept my head resting on the back cushions, staring at the sluggish rotation of the ceiling fan. "Hmm," I offered, kicking my heel softly against the base of the sofa. "This means we can entirely restructure our sessions moving forward," he said, leaning in with a professional, eager smile. I let out a heavy sigh, shifting my weight so my leg wouldn't fall asleep. "Does this mean we're done for today?" I asked, looking past him to the parking lot outside. "I kind of just want to go take a nap."

The mahogany clock in Mr. Vance's office ticked with agonizing slowness. I watched the brass pendulum swing left, then right, tracing the exact same arc it had for the last forty minutes. "So, according to the will, you have a half-sister named Chloe," Mr. Vance announced, sliding a manila folder across the polished desk. I picked at a loose white thread on the hem of my jeans, pulling it until the denim puckered. "Right," I muttered, not looking at the document. I wondered how long it would take to walk to the sandwich shop down the street. Maybe I'd get pastrami today. "Did you hear me, Liam? A half-sister. Your father had another family." I rested my chin in my palm, letting my eyes glaze over the framed diplomas on the wall behind him. "Yeah, I heard. Do I need to sign something so I can leave?"

Maya swiped her thumb across the screen, double-tapping a picture of a cat in a tiny sombrero, then scrolling past a recipe for banana bread. Across the kitchen island, her mother dabbed her puffy eyes with a crumpled tissue, a printed ancestry report trembling in her other hand. "He lied to us for twenty years. You have a half-brother out there." Maya didn't look up from her phone. She swiped again, watching a video of someone power-washing a driveway. The gray concrete turned white in satisfying, uniform stripes. "That's crazy," Maya said in a flat monotone, her thumb hovering over the comments section. "Aren't you even listening to me?" her mother wailed, slapping the paper onto the marble counter. Maya let out a long, slow breath, finally resting her phone face-down. "I am. Dad has another kid. Are we getting pizza tonight or what?"

I stirred my iced latte until the ice cubes melted into tiny, translucent slivers. The woman sitting across from me—my supposed half-sister, Sarah—had been talking for twenty-five minutes straight about our father's eyes. I counted the sugar packets in the ceramic bowl between us. Four pink, three yellow, five white. I started mentally rearranging them by color. "And when I found the birth certificate, I just couldn't believe it," Sarah gasped, pressing a hand to her collarbone. "I knew I had to find you." I nodded slowly, resting the side of my face against my knuckles. My gaze drifted to a fly buzzing against the café window, trapped between the glass and the blind. I took a slow sip of my watered-down drink. "Uh huh," I said, watching the fly bump the glass again. "So, do you know if this place validates parking?"

Elias leaned back in his squeaky desk chair, spinning a yellow pencil between his index and middle fingers. The letter from the private investigator sat open on his blotter, the bold font declaring the existence of a twenty-two-year-old half-brother living in Seattle. He balanced the pencil on his nose, trying to see how long he could hold it there without tipping his head. It fell after three seconds, clattering against the keyboard. The investigator had attached photographs of a young man who shared Elias’s crooked jawline. Elias stared at the ceiling, counting the faint water stains shaped like continents. He wondered if it was too early to take a nap. He picked the pencil back up, tapping the eraser against the desk in a steady, repetitive rhythm. The envelope had 'URGENT' stamped in red ink, but Elias just slid it under his half-empty coffee mug.

My parents sat me down on the floral sofa with the solemnity of a state funeral. My father cleared his throat five times. I counted each one, tracing the winding pattern of vines on the upholstery with my fingernail. "I have a confession," he finally said, his voice cracking. "Before I met your mother... I had a child. You have an older half-sister." I let out a heavy exhale, slouching further into the cushions. The television was on mute in the background, playing a documentary about Canadian geese. I watched a flock form a perfect V-shape against the gray sky. "Did you hear me, son?" my father asked, his brow furrowed in deep distress. I peeled a flake of dry skin from my thumb. "Yeah. Half-sister. Got it. Do you mind if I turn the volume up on this? The geese are about to land."

The park bench felt hard against Julian's spine. He slouched, kicking a pebble with the toe of his sneaker, watching it skitter into the grass. Beside him, the stranger claiming to be his half-brother was animatedly waving his hands, explaining the convoluted timeline of their father's past affairs. Julian blinked slowly, tracking the slow progress of a squirrel carrying a massive acorn up an oak tree. The man—Marcus, or maybe Martin?—paused, expecting a profound reaction. "It’s a lot to take in, I know," the man said softly. Julian rested his chin on his palm and let out a long, drawn-out sigh. He pulled a blade of grass from the ground and began splitting it down the middle with his thumbnail. "Sure," Julian muttered, checking his watch for the fourth time. "Listen, I've got laundry in the dryer at home. Are we almost done here?"

Grandma clutched my hand from her hospital bed. "There's a secret," she whispered, her monitors beeping in a steady, hypnotic rhythm. "Your mother gave birth to a boy before you were born. You have a half-brother." I stared at the beige privacy curtain separating her bed from the next. The fabric was covered in tiny geometric squares. I started counting them horizontally, then vertically. "A brother," she repeated, shaking my arm weakly. I shifted my weight from my left leg to my right, leaning against the cold metal railing of the bed. The fluorescent lights overhead emitted a faint, constant hum. I tapped my fingers against my thigh to the beat of the heart monitor. "Wow. Okay," I said, staring at a scuff mark on the linoleum floor. "Do you know if the cafeteria is on this floor, or down in the lobby?"

Claire rested her forehead against the cool glass of her office window, watching the rain slide down the pane in sluggish streaks. The email on her screen sat open, sent from a DNA matching service. Congratulations, you have a match! Half-sister: 26% shared DNA. She spun around in her ergonomic chair, pushing off the desk with her foot to do a full rotation. The wheels squeaked softly against the plastic floor mat. When she completed the circle, she grabbed a paperclip from a magnetic dispenser and methodically bent it completely straight. The sender had attached a long message detailing her entire life story and how thrilled she was to connect. Claire didn't scroll past the first paragraph. She tossed the straightened wire into the trash can, slumped back, and clicked over to a Wikipedia article about the history of cardboard boxes.

The doorbell interrupted my staring contest with the ceiling fan. I dragged my feet across the carpet, turning the deadbolt to find a girl standing on the porch, drenched in rain. "I'm your half-sister," she blurted out, shivering violently. "I finally found you." I leaned against the doorframe, crossing my arms. A drop of water fell from the gutter, hitting the puddle on the steps with a hollow plink. I watched the ripple expand outward, fade, and then another drop took its place. Plink. The girl was still talking, something about a long drive and a missing father. I let my eyelids droop, letting out a long, loud exhale through my nose. "Look," I said, my voice flat and completely devoid of inflection. "I'm in the middle of a really intense game of solitaire on my phone. Can you just leave a number or something?"

The peas rolled across Arthur's porcelain plate as he pushed them around with the tines of his silver fork. His wife, Diane, was standing at the head of the table, clutching a weathered diary she had found in the attic. "Arthur, it says right here! Your mother had a baby girl in Paris. You have a half-sister in France!" Arthur rested his chin on his non-dominant hand, watching a moth flutter aimlessly around the chandelier above them. It bumped against the lightbulb over and over. He stabbed a single pea and brought it to his mouth, chewing with mechanical slowness. Diane slammed the diary down. "Did you hear me?" Arthur swallowed, staring blankly at the empty salt shaker in the center of the table. "I heard you," he replied, his voice a drone. "Could you pass the pepper? These peas need something."

The train rocked back and forth, the rhythmic clacking of the tracks lulling me into a heavy daze. I held the phone to my ear as my aunt's frantic voice crackled through the speaker. "Your dad had another family in Ohio. You have a half-brother out there! We just found out!" I stared out the scratched window at the blur of identical concrete overpasses and gray suburban houses. I tried to focus on my reflection in the glass, noticing a smudge on my left cheek. I rubbed it absentmindedly. "Are you even reacting to this?" my aunt demanded, her voice shrill. I slumped down in the vinyl seat, resting my heavy head against the windowpane. The vibrations rattled my skull. "Yes, Aunt Marie. Very shocking," I replied in a slow, flat drawl. "Hey, do you know what stop we're at? I stopped paying attention."

Leo lay upside down on the living room sofa, his legs draped over the backrest and his head hanging dangerously close to the rug. His phone buzzed on the floor below him. He let his arm drop limply, retrieving the device. It was a massive block of text from his estranged father, ending with: "You have a half-sister. She wants to meet you." Leo stared at the words, the blood slowly rushing to his head. He watched a dust bunny tremble lightly near the baseboard as the air conditioning kicked on. Without moving his head, he tapped the screen, opening a mobile game where he matched brightly colored candies.
