The notifications kept sliding down from the top of the screen—his father begging for a response. Leo just swiped them away, his glassy eyes fixed solely on crushing a digital row of four green jellybeans.

Marcus kicked a loose pebble across the cracked driveway, watching it bounce into a pile of rusted garden tools. He checked his phone for the fourth time in ten minutes; no new messages. His mother was still haggling over a cracked ceramic rooster three tables away. He let out a long, slow exhale, letting his chin rest heavily in his palm as he leaned against a folding table filled with chipped Tupperware. His gaze drifted slowly over a cardboard box labeled "50 cents each." There, wedged between a plastic fire truck and a tangled jump rope, sat a faded brown plush bear with a missing left button eye and a familiar green velvet bowtie. Marcus blinked, straightening his posture slightly. He reached into the dusty box, his fingers brushing the matted fur of the exact bear he had lost at a rest stop sixteen years ago.

The afternoon heat pressed down on me as I swiped aimlessly through my social media feed for the fifth time, barely registering the photos. "Just five more minutes," Sarah promised from the next lawn over, sifting through a rack of moth-eaten cardigans. I dragged my feet along the sun-baked pavement, letting out a loud sigh that earned me zero attention. I picked at a loose thread on my jeans, staring blankly at a folding table displaying old VHS tapes. I shifted my weight, tapping my toe against a cardboard box. Glancing down, I stopped mid-tap. Sticking out from beneath a pile of faded baby blankets was a worn, yellow stuffed bear with a crookedly sewn red smile. I dropped my phone into my pocket, suddenly recognizing the patch on Barnaby's worn stomach.

Elias leaned heavily against the side of his station wagon, letting out a massive yawn that made his jaw pop. He watched a squirrel dart up a nearby oak tree, tracing its path until it disappeared into the canopy. The neighborhood yard sale stretched endlessly down the cul-de-sac, a sea of discarded lamps and stained novels. He crossed his arms, tapping his fingers against his bicep in a slow rhythm. To pass the time, he wandered toward the nearest driveway, aimlessly dragging a finger along the edge of a plastic folding table. He stared into a plastic bin of stuffed animals, his mind completely blank, until a flash of denim overalls caught his eye. He reached in, pulling out a matted grey bear with a chewed-off ear. Elias rubbed his thumb over the initials 'E.M.' scrawled in faded sharpie on the paw, his yawning entirely forgotten.

I had already counted thirty-two ceramic figurines on the wobbly picnic table when my husband announced he needed to inspect the tools in the garage. I let my head drop back, staring up at the cloudless sky and exhaling a long, loud breath. I shuffled to the next table, picking up a snow globe and shaking it without enthusiasm, watching the flakes drift down before setting it back exactly where it was. The minutes stretched like chewing gum. I knelt by a damp cardboard box on the lawn, digging through mismatched mittens just to give my hands something to do. Beneath a wool scarf, my fingers brushed against something soft. I pulled it free, staring at the purple plush bear with the missing nose. The faint scent of my childhood laundry detergent lingered on its fur, instantly pulling me out of my mid-afternoon slump.

Chloe dragged her sneakers across the asphalt, deliberately scuffing the rubber soles. She rolled her eyes as her dad examined a set of golf clubs for the third time. She leaned her forearms against a stack of milk crates, resting her forehead on her wrists. The buzzing of a nearby fly was the only thing happening in the entire driveway. She swatted it away with a limp hand, wandering over to a pile of unwanted toys. She nudged a plastic dump truck with her toe, watching it roll an inch and stop. Kicking aside a tangled mess of action figures, she noticed a flash of corduroy. She squatted down, pulling out a small, lopsided bear wearing a knitted red sweater. Her breath hitched. The sweater had the exact same snagged thread on the left sleeve that she had caused with a pair of safety scissors in second grade.

My eyelids felt like they were lined with lead. I propped my chin in my hand, sitting on the bumper of my car while my sister negotiated the price of a mid-century side table. I watched a drop of condensation slowly slide down the side of my iced coffee, tracing its path until it pooled at the bottom. The suburban street was painfully quiet, save for the occasional chirp of a bird. Needing to stretch my legs, I ambled over to the neighbor’s driveway, scanning a table of discarded knick-knacks with half-open eyes. I picked up a tarnished spoon, put it down, and moved to a basket of plush toys. My hand idly sifted through the soft pile until I grabbed a familiar, chunky paw. I pulled it up, staring wide-eyed at Captain Fluff, the missing eye patch and sewn-on pirate hat exactly as I left him.

Liam checked his watch. Only two minutes had passed since the last time he looked. He let out a slow groan, shifting his weight onto his left leg and crossing his arms tightly over his chest. The summer humidity was oppressive, making the endless rows of old paperbacks and rusted kitchenware look even less appealing. He began counting the cracks in the concrete driveway to keep his mind occupied. Reaching crack number fourteen, he found himself standing in front of a wire basket overflowing with children's items. He idly poked at a plastic dinosaur, sending it toppling over. Underneath it, a tuft of blue faux fur peeked out. Liam dug it out, revealing a stuffed bear with a stitched-on star on its chest. He froze, recognizing the ink stain on the star where he had accidentally dropped his favorite fountain pen ten years ago.

"Uh huh. Yeah, that’s great," I mumbled, not really listening to the elderly woman explaining the history of her soup tureen. I stared past her shoulder, watching a plastic bag tumbleweed its way across the street. I shifted from foot to foot, silently pleading for my mom to finish browsing the linen pile. I walked away mid-conversation, letting my shoulders slump as I wandered toward a folding table at the back of the garage. I picked at a chipped piece of wood on the table's edge, my gaze sweeping over a pile of stuffed animals without actually seeing them. Then, my eyes locked onto a familiar green ribbon. I grabbed the scruffy brown bear from the pile. It still had the jagged scar across its belly where my grandmother had stitched it back together after our golden retriever had gotten hold of it.

Priya rested the back of her head against the brick exterior of the stranger’s house, letting her eyes lose focus. The voices of the yard sale shoppers blurred into a flat, rhythmic hum. She slid down the wall until she was squatting on the pavement, drawing aimless circles in the dust with a stray twig. "Five minutes," her roommate called out, holding up a hideous floral lamp. Priya just gave a slow thumbs-up without looking. She tossed the twig aside and rummaged lazily through a cardboard box by her knees, pulling out a handful of wooden blocks and tossing them back. Her hand brushed against a soft texture at the bottom. She yanked it free. It was a pink bear with a velvet snout, wearing the exact tiny silver locket she had put around its neck in fourth grade.

I let out a massive yawn, covering my mouth with the back of my hand as I trailed behind my wife. She was completely engrossed in a box of vintage vinyl records. I slouched against a nearby lamppost, staring at the asphalt and watching an ant carry a crumb across a crack. I sighed, kicking a small pebble into the grass. Looking for any distraction, I shuffled over to a folding table displaying old toys. I picked up a Rubik’s cube, twisted it once, and set it down heavily. Next to it sat a clear plastic bin full of stuffed animals. I reached in blindly, grabbing a handful of fuzz and pulling it up. I blinked hard. Dangling from my hand was a white polar bear with a distinctive blue knitted scarf. The faint smell of mothballs and my grandmother’s attic instantly flooded my senses.

Julian rolled his eyes at the sky, letting his arms dangle loosely at his sides as his partner haggled over a set of rusted lawn darts. He exhaled noisily through his nose, meandering toward a shaded corner of the driveway. He picked up a snow globe, shook it gently, and set it down without waiting to see the flakes fall. He leaned against a stack of plastic storage bins, picking at a loose thread on his cuff. His gaze wandered to a laundry basket labeled "Free." He lazily poked through the tangled mess of jump ropes and deflated soccer balls with his index finger. At the bottom, a familiar patch of plaid fabric caught his eye. Julian dug past a pile of mismatched socks and pulled out a stuffed bear. It was missing its right ear, exactly like the one he had lost at summer camp.

I rested my chin heavily on my hands, leaning against the hood of my truck while my dad debated the merits of a used lawnmower. The humid morning air felt thick, and the endless tables of mismatched dishware and outdated electronics blurred together. I let out a long breath, checking my phone screen just to look at the time. To keep from falling asleep standing up, I pushed off the truck and wandered over to a pile of old blankets on a tarp. I nudged a floral quilt with the toe of my boot. Underneath it lay a matted, cinnamon-colored bear. I bent down, picking it up. One glass eye was scratched, and a crude zigzag stitch held its left arm in place—my own amateur sewing job from when I was ten.

Chloe rested her chin heavily in her palm, using her free hand to spin the mouse wheel down, then up, then down again. The admissions prep website blurred into a wall of gray text. She counted the number of times the word 'leadership' appeared on the page—fourteen. She let out a long, slow breath that fluttered her bangs, clicking a link to 'Sample Essays' just to give her index finger something to do. Her eyes dragged across the first paragraph. Wait. She sat up, the fog lifting slightly. The anecdote about the broken toaster and the stray cat was unmistakable. It was her own essay from three years ago, sitting right there under "Exemplary Personal Statements." Chloe blinked, reading the words she had painstakingly typed in high school, realizing she hadn't felt a spark of interest all afternoon until this exact second.

I must have read the "Prepare for Your Future!" brochure at the guidance office six times, memorizing the stock photos of smiling students sitting under generic oak trees. The clock on the wall made a loud, rhythmic tick-tock that seemed to slow down with every passing minute. To escape the droning sound of the receptionist typing, I pulled out my phone and tapped randomly on the university's online portal, navigating to their 'Tips for Applicants' page. I swiped up without really looking, my eyes glazing over the text until a specific sentence caught my attention. 'When the stage lights failed, I found my true voice.' I stopped tapping. I knew that sentence. I wrote that sentence last November. Suddenly, the sterile waiting room faded away as I stared at my own deeply personal story, plastered across the screen as an anonymous 'Outstanding Submission'.

Marcus stirred his iced latte until the ice cubes completely melted into a watery, tan puddle. He rested his forehead against the cool glass window of the café, watching a plastic bag drift lazily across the empty street. He had been staring at the "College Prep 101" textbook for two hours without absorbing a single concept. Flipping toward the back appendix out of sheer desperation for a distraction, he let his gaze drag lazily over the sample writing section. His heavy eyelids suddenly snapped open. The essay on page 342 began with his exact opening line about collecting vintage fountain pens. Marcus dropped his stirring straw. He scanned the paragraph, his heart rate picking up as he recognized his own metaphors and quirky formatting. The textbook he had been mindlessly ignoring for the past three weeks had secretly published his very own admissions essay.

Click. Click. Click. I pressed the top of my ballpoint pen until my thumb ached, staring blankly at the blank document on my laptop. It was a rainy Tuesday afternoon, and my roommate was asleep, snoring softly in the corner. I had already organized my sock drawer by color and alphabetical order of brand. Needing any excuse to delay my history paper, I started browsing the English department's 'First-Year Composition Guide' PDF. I scrolled down, resting my head on the cool surface of my desk. On page twelve, under 'Crafting a Narrative', a familiar paragraph greeted me. It was my essay. The one about baking bread with my grandmother. I rubbed my eyes, reading the exact phrases I had agonized over a year ago. The heavy, stagnant feeling in my chest vanished, replaced by a sudden jolt of disbelief as I read my own words.

The computer lab was entirely silent except for the hum of the air conditioner. Elena rested her cheek on the cool laminate desk, watching the bouncing DVD logo hit the corners of the monitor. She had been sitting there for an hour, doing absolutely nothing. Finally, she jiggled the mouse to wake the screen. A browser tab from the previous user was still open, displaying a test prep company's blog post titled "What Makes a Great Application?" Elena leaned back, letting out a heavy sigh that ruffled the collar of her shirt. She began reading the first highlighted excerpt, but stopped halfway through the second line. She leaned closer to the monitor. The story about fixing the old rusted bicycle was hers. The exact same adjectives, the same punctuation. The lethargy that had pinned her to the chair evaporated as she stared at her own memories.

The train rattled along the tracks, blurring the gray industrial buildings into a continuous, unbroken streak. I counted the power lines dipping and rising outside my window. Fifty-one, fifty-two, fifty-three. The journey from campus took forty-five minutes, and my phone battery was at four percent. I pulled a crumpled alumni newsletter from the seat pocket in front of me, flipping through it just to have something in my hands. The pages were filled with donor lists and upcoming gala announcements. I let my eyes unfocus on the text until a bold header caught my attention: "Inspiring the Next Generation: A Sample Statement." I scanned the text. 'The smell of rain on hot asphalt always reminds me of my first debate tournament.' I froze. I wrote that. It was my admissions essay from three years ago, printed right there between an advertisement and a crossword puzzle.

Leo shaded in the little squares of his graph paper, transforming them into an intricate, meaningless checkerboard pattern. The teacher at the front of the room was reading from a handbook in a flat, monotone voice, but Leo wasn't listening. He rested his temple against his knuckles, staring at the generic "Guide to Admissions" packet placed on his desk. He flipped to a random page in the middle, tracing the printed letters with the tip of his pencil. Halfway down the page, his pencil stopped moving. He blinked, sitting up slightly. The paragraph described a summer spent painting murals in downtown Chicago. It mentioned a specific spilled can of yellow paint on a pair of ruined Converse sneakers. Leo looked down at his own paint-splattered shoes. The school district had literally published his personal statement as the prime example of narrative voice without telling him.

There were exactly forty-two acoustic tiles on the ceiling of Mr. Henderson's office. I knew this because I had counted them three times while he took a phone call that seemed to stretch into eternity. I picked at a loose thread on the armrest of the waiting chair, wrapping it around my finger until it turned purple. To give myself something to do, I reached for a thick spiral-bound 'Success Manual' sitting on the glass table. I opened it to the middle, letting my eyes glaze over a section labeled 'The Hook'. I read the first sentence, and my stomach dropped. 'I have never been able to whistle, but I can mimic the call of a red-tailed hawk.' I dropped the manual on the table. That was my opening line. My secret party trick, my essay. I stared at the page, wide awake now.

Sam threw a tennis ball at the ceiling. Thump. He caught it. Thump. He caught it again. The weekend stretched out before him like a vast, empty desert of unstructured time. He rolled over on his bed, his arm hanging off the edge, and aimlessly swiped through a forum for high school seniors. Post after post blurred together into a wall of generic advice and panicked questions. He clicked on a stickied thread titled "Hall of Fame Admissions Essays," letting out a long breath as the page loaded. He began to skim, his chin resting on the mattress, until he saw a piece about learning to play the cello backwards. Sam stopped breathing for a second. He scrolled up, checking the URL. It was unmistakable. There, immortalized in pixelated text on a highly trafficked message board, was the exact personal statement he had submitted last year.

I bent the paperclip until it snapped into two pieces, then tossed the metal fragments onto the desk. I had been sitting in the basement of the campus library for three hours, supposedly researching a sociology paper. Instead, my head was resting heavily on my forearm, and I was clicking randomly through the university's archive portal. I navigated to the 'Admissions History' tab, my eyelids drooping as I scrolled through digitized handbooks from the past decade. A document titled "Exceptional Narratives 2021" caught my cursor. I opened it, intending to mock the overly earnest tone of past applicants. But as I read the first paragraph about a disastrous camping trip in the Blue Ridge Mountains, my posture straightened. The description of the raccoon stealing the marshmallows was verbatim. My essay. I sat up completely, staring at the screen, the silence of the library suddenly feeling deafening.

Maya lay upside down on the living room sofa, her legs resting against the wall. The television was on mute, playing an infomercial about garden hoses. She scrolled through her tablet with her thumb, letting out a loud groan that echoed in the empty house. She opened the university's official magazine app, swiping aimlessly through glossy photos of campus buildings and smiling alumni. She paused on an article titled "The Art of the Personal Essay." Maya let her eyes drift over the text, not really processing the words until the name of her hometown jumped out at her. She flipped her body around, sitting upright on the cushions. The article featured a full-length essay about building a greenhouse out of recycled plastic bottles. It was her exact project, her exact words, published for the entire alumni network to see, sitting right there on her screen.

The second hand on the wall clock seemed to be moving backward. I rested my cheek against the cold surface of my desk, listening to the rhythmic tapping of Mrs. Gable's chalk against the blackboard. We were doing a workshop on college applications, and I had already submitted mine a month ago. I slouched lower in my seat, aimlessly flipping through the district-provided workbook she had handed out. My eyes dragged across the pages, looking at the stock images of graduation caps. I stopped on page twenty. The header read "Sample 4: The Overcomer." I started reading the text, tracing the words with my finger. 'The engine sputtered, leaving me stranded with nothing but a wrench and my grandfather's advice.' I froze, my jaw dropping. That was my grandfather. That was my essay. I looked up at Mrs. Gable, suddenly entirely present in the room.

I had been staring at the fifty-third dust mote floating in the shaft of afternoon sunlight for what felt like an hour. The attic was quiet, save for the hum of the central air that ticked on and off every fifteen minutes. I shifted my weight on the hard floorboards, letting out a long, flat breath that rustled the cobwebs above. My thumb traced the edge of a cardboard box I’d opened an hour ago but hadn’t actually looked inside. Seeking anything to break the heavy stillness, I lazily dragged a weathered leather journal from the top of the pile. The pages smelled of mildew and old paper. I flipped them open with a flick of my wrist, fully expecting blank lines. Instead, a loose sheet drifted onto my lap. In my dad’s unmistakable scrawl, the heading read: Things to Do Before I Go.

Marcus leaned his chin against his palm, his elbow propped on the handle of a push broom. He pushed a single stray screw back and forth across the concrete garage floor, listening to the tiny metallic scrape. Back. Forth. Back. Forth. The radio played a static-filled commercial for a local car dealership that he had already heard three times today. He let go of the broom, letting it clatter to the ground, and dragged his feet toward his late mother’s old metal toolbox. He flipped the latch, not looking for any tool in particular, just needing to hear the mechanical click. Inside, resting atop the socket wrenches, lay a piece of faded pink stationery. He picked it up, expecting a hardware store receipt, but his eyes focused on her neat cursive: My Ultimate Bucket List. He read the first line: See the Northern Lights.

The rain had been drumming a steady, unchanging rhythm against the windowpane all afternoon. I sat cross-legged on the rug, peeling a loose thread from the hem of my jeans until it snapped. I checked my phone. 3:14 PM. No new notifications. I tossed the phone onto the cushion and rolled onto my back, staring up at the popcorn ceiling, trying to find shapes in the bumpy texture. Eventually, I pulled open the bottom drawer of the coffee table with my bare foot. It was filled with mom’s old junk. I reached down blindly and pulled out a stack of cocktail napkins, flipping through them with a heavy sigh. One napkin was stiff, covered in blue ink. I brought it closer to my face. Life Goals, it said in her handwriting. 1. Ride a hot air balloon. 2. Learn Italian.

Chloe clicked her pen. Click-clack. Click-clack. She spun slowly in her father’s oversized desk chair, letting her head loll back against the leather headrest. The ceiling fan rotated at a sluggish pace, the blades cutting through the silent room with a rhythmic squeak. She stopped spinning and let out a prolonged exhale, watching her breath disturb a stack of old mail. Reaching over, she began opening her father's desk drawers, randomly lifting paperclips and dropping them back into their plastic compartments. In the bottom drawer, tucked beneath a stack of blank tax forms, was a spiral notebook. She dragged it out to doodle in the margins, flipping to the middle. The page wasn't blank. It was titled My Grand Adventures, followed by a numbered list. Number one was crossed out: Hold a koala. Number two remained untouched: Visit the Grand Canyon.

I sat on the porch swing, pushing off the floorboards with one toe just enough to keep it moving. Creak, sway. Creak, sway. The heat was thick, pressing down on the neighborhood and keeping everyone indoors. I watched an ant carry a breadcrumb across the railing, following its agonizingly slow progress for ten minutes. Needing some sort of distraction, I pulled my dad’s old guitar case toward me. I didn't know how to play, but I popped the latches anyway, just to pluck a single string and listen to the hollow twang fade into the humid air. Inside the velvet-lined pocket where he used to keep his picks, I felt a folded piece of thick parchment. I pulled it out, smoothing the creases. It was a list, dated ten years before he died. Dreams to Chase, the header read in his heavy block letters.

Elias dragged the cursor across his computer screen, highlighting a block of text, clicking away, and then highlighting it again. He leaned back, letting his arms dangle off the sides of the office chair. The ticking clock on the wall sounded louder than usual, each second stretching out indefinitely. He kicked his foot out, nudging a cardboard box his mother had left behind. He leaned over, pulling out a battered copy of Moby Dick, a book he had no intention of reading. He held the book by its spine and shook it, watching a single, yellowed envelope flutter to the carpet. He picked it out of the dust, opening the unsealed flap. It was a handwritten list titled Before My Time is Up. The first entry, Skydive over the Alps, seemed entirely unlike the quiet woman he remembered.

Laying upside down on the sofa with my legs draped over the backrest, I watched a muted infomercial about a blender. The man on the screen enthusiastically chopped tomatoes while I blew a stray hair out of my face. I counted the tassels on the throw pillow. Fourteen. I reached an arm down to the floor, my fingers grazing the edge of a plastic tote bag that belonged to my dad. Without getting up, I blindly rooted around inside, feeling cold plastic and rough fabric. My hand closed around a small leather-bound pocketbook. I pulled it up, flipping it open right-side up while my head remained inverted. The ink was faded, but the words My Ultimate To-Do List were perfectly legible. I read the first bullet point: Write a novel. I rolled off the couch, finally sitting upright.

Sitting in the parked car, Sarah drummed her index fingers on the steering wheel, matching the tempo of the hazard lights. Click. Click. Click. She rested her forehead against the cool glass of the driver's side window, watching a plastic bag tumble across the empty asphalt. The tow truck was at least another forty minutes away. With a heavy sigh, she popped open the glovebox of her late mother’s sedan. She pulled out the car manual, flipping the glossy pages without registering a single diagram. Tucked near the back was a folded diner placemat. She smoothed it out over the steering wheel. Beneath a grease stain, her mother had written Things I Must Do. The list included Swim in the ocean at midnight and Forgive Sarah for the fight. Sarah stared at the ink, the silence in the car suddenly feeling very heavy.

I had rearranged the salt and pepper shakers into a perfect square, then a diamond, and finally a straight line. The kitchen clock read 4:00 PM. I dragged my fingernail along the groove in the oak dining table, gathering tiny specks of dust. I opened the junk drawer, staring at the tangled charging cords, dried-out markers, and loose batteries. I picked up dad’s old leather wallet from the corner of the drawer. I unzipped the coin pouch, expecting to find a few tarnished pennies to stack. Instead, I pulled out a tightly folded receipt. I carefully pried the fragile paper apart. On the blank back, he had written Life List. The items were small, written in hurried cursive: Take a cooking class. Learn to play chess. See the redwoods. I traced the faded ink, the ticking of the clock fading away.

David sat on the edge of the bed, slowly bouncing a tennis ball against the floor. Thud, catch. Thud, catch. He watched the laundry spinning in the hallway machine through the open door, mesmerized by the tumbling colors. He let the ball roll away under the dresser, making no move to retrieve it. Instead, he pulled his late mother’s wooden jewelry box onto his lap. He opened the tiny drawers one by one, picking up tangled necklaces and dropping them back into piles just to hear the clinking sound. Beneath a velvet insert in the bottom drawer, he spotted a folded piece of lined notebook paper. He unfolded it, rubbing the creases flat. At the top, she had written Bucket List. The very first item was Tell David about his real father. David stopped breathing, the rhythmic thudding of the washing machine entirely forgotten.

I clicked the television remote twenty times, cycling through the channels without letting a single image stay on screen for more than a second. News, cartoons, static, cooking show. I tossed the remote onto the rug and stared at the blank wall next to the TV. I picked at a loose thread on my sweater, unraveling it inch by inch. I needed to move, but I didn't want to go anywhere. I dragged myself over to a stack of my dad’s old vinyl records, pulling one out just to read the liner notes. Inside the sleeve of an old jazz album, a piece of graph paper slipped out and drifted to the floor. I picked it up, staring at his precise architectural lettering. My Life's Final Project was written at the top. The list below detailed places he wanted to travel, completely ignoring his illness.

Maya dragged her heels across the carpet, leaving two distinct tracks in the plush fibers. She walked to the window, stared at the empty street for five minutes, and then walked back to the center of the room. She picked up a deck of cards from the side table, shuffling them clumsily, letting half of them spill onto the floor. She didn't bother picking them up. She slumped into her mother’s old reading chair, pulling a dusty poetry anthology from the side pocket. She fanned the pages, feeling the brief breeze on her face. A small, stiff piece of cardstock wedged between the pages caught her thumb. She pulled it out. It was a beautiful watercolor bookmark, and on the back, her mother had written: Things to experience before I leave. The first item was Take a train across Europe.

I traced a smudge on the glass counter for the fourth time, my chin resting heavily in my palm. The pawn shop smelled of old dust and brass polish, a scent that did nothing to make the ticking clock on the wall move any faster. My sister was taking an eternity haggling over a used acoustic guitar, leaving me to stare blankly at the rows of forgotten jewelry. I let out a long, slow breath, watching a speck of dust drift lazily toward the floor. I shifted my weight to my other leg, blindly scanning the velvet trays just to give my eyes a task. That’s when the sapphire caught the fluorescent light. The twisted silver band and the unique star-cut stone—it was unmistakable. Nana’s ring, the one lost during the estate sale, sitting right next to a cheap digital watch.

Elias swiped to the next screen on his phone, closed the app, and opened it again without looking at anything. He slumped against the brick exterior of 'Golden Exchange', staring at the grey pavement as a single ant carried a crumb in circles. His friend had been inside for twenty minutes trying to sell a video game console. Groaning loudly to an empty street, Elias kicked a loose pebble into the gutter and finally pushed through the heavy glass door, desperate for a change of scenery. He leaned heavily against the jewelry counter, drumming his fingers in a slow, erratic rhythm on the glass. He let his gaze drift lazily downward, barely registering the tarnished trinkets, until a familiar gold filigree band made him stand up straight. His grandmother's missing diamond, sitting under a hand-written price tag.

Rain streaked down the pawn shop window, and I tracked a single drop as it crawled down the glass. Plop. Then another. Plop. I pulled my sleeves over my hands, wandering the narrow aisles without looking at anything in particular. Tools I didn't need, DVDs I'd never watch, electronics that probably didn't work. I let out a heavy sigh that fogged the glass of the display case. I wiped the condensation away with a lazy swipe of my sleeve, letting my eyes go out of focus on the velvet jewelry trays below. I started counting the rings. One, two, three, four... wait. My eyes snapped into focus. The ruby surrounded by tiny, chipped emeralds in the shape of a flower. I pressed my face against the cold glass. It was my grandmother’s engagement ring, missing since 1998.

Maya sat on a folding chair in the corner of the shop, swinging her legs so her heels hit the metal legs with a rhythmic clink, clink, clink. She peeled a fleck of silver nail polish off her thumb, then inspected her hand as if expecting it to do a trick. The shop owner was explaining the history of an antique clock to another customer, his voice a low, unchanging hum that made Maya’s eyelids heavy. To keep herself awake, she stood up and dragged her feet toward the nearest brightly lit case. She rested her forehead against the cool glass, tracing aimless circles on its surface. Beneath her finger, something caught her attention. A pearl setting flanked by twin amethysts—her grandmother's engagement ring, stolen years ago from the family safe, staring back at her.

I had scrolled through my entire social media feed twice. Finding nothing new, I pocketed my phone and slumped against the counter of Pawn Stars & More, letting my head loll back to stare at the water stains on the acoustic ceiling tiles. I started counting them. Thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three... I let out a long breath, puffing my cheeks. Trying to kill another ten minutes until my bus arrived, I dragged myself upright and peered into the jewelry case, letting my vision blur. Shimmering blobs of silver and gold merged together. Blinking away the glaze in my eyes, I noticed a very specific, oddly asymmetrical cluster of diamonds. I leaned in, my heart giving a sudden jolt. The bent prong. The engraving on the inner band. It was Grammy’s ring, sitting beside a plastic tiara.

Marcus tapped a steady, irritating beat against his thigh. He had been trapped in the downtown pawn broker's shop for what felt like three hours, waiting for the rain to stop. He aimlessly flipped through a bin of scratched CDs, recognizing none of the artists and not caring to learn. He dragged his feet across the linoleum, the squeak of his wet sneakers the only sound breaking the drone of a sports game playing on a muted television. He paused by the jewelry counter, resting his chin on his folded arms upon the glass, watching the second hand of a wall clock tick at a torturous pace. Glancing down simply to give his eyes a destination, his vision locked onto a platinum band with an emerald-cut diamond. The very ring his grandmother claimed she flushed down the toilet in 1985.

Chewing on a plastic coffee stirrer, I wandered the aisles of the pawn shop, reading the price tags on old power tools just to give my brain something to process. Fifty dollars for a drill. Twenty for a sander. Fascinating. I tossed the chewed plastic into a nearby bin and leaned against a display case, resting my weight on one hip. I let my eyes trace the cracks in the linoleum floor before looking down at the rows of rings inside the cabinet. Most were generic, gaudy things. I idly scanned them, my mind wandering to what I was going to make for dinner. But as my eyes passed a cluster of vintage rings, I froze. The twisted rose gold, the opal center stone flanked by tiny pearls. It was Nana's engagement ring, stolen during the break-in five years ago.

The drone of the pawn shop’s old air conditioner hummed a single, unchanging note. Clara rested her chin in her hands, sitting on a dilapidated leather sofa meant for testing used amplifiers. She watched a dust mote slowly descend from the ceiling, tracking its agonizingly slow journey to the carpet. Deciding that anything was better than sitting still, she stood up with a heavy sigh, stretching her arms above her head. She ambled over to the glass cases at the front, leaning her elbows on the counter and letting her eyes glaze over the rows of discarded jewelry. She picked at a loose thread on her sweater, staring vacantly at a tray of silver bands. Suddenly, an oddly shaped turquoise stone set in tarnished silver snapped her back to reality. It was her late grandmother’s custom engagement ring.

I blew a strand of hair out of my face, watching it flutter and settle back onto my forehead. The pawn broker was in the back room appraising my roommate's camera, leaving me alone with the quiet hum of a neon window sign. I tapped my fingernails on the glass counter—pinky, ring, middle, pointer, over and over. I read the 'All Sales Final' policy four times, dissecting the typography. Desperate for a distraction, I began inspecting the jewelry case beneath my hands, judging the ugly pieces. A tacky gold chain here, a fake-looking Rolex there. Then, nestled between two thick class rings, I saw a delicate silver band woven like vines around a modest sapphire. I stopped tapping my fingers. My breath hitched in my throat. It was Abuela's engagement ring, lost before I was even born.

Leo let out a loud, drawn-out yawn, not bothering to cover his mouth. He leaned back against the dusty shelves of the local trading post, flipping a quarter into the air and catching it. Over and over. Toss, catch. Toss, catch. Miss. The coin rolled under a glass display case with a faint clatter. Groaning, Leo dropped to his hands and knees to retrieve it, his cheek pressed against the cold, unwashed floor. As he reached a hand into the narrow gap beneath the cabinet, he glanced up through the glass shelf above him. An intricate ruby ring sat on a velvet pillow. The unique halo of diamonds, the way the band curved—he knew it instantly. He sat up fast, bumping his head on the glass, staring directly at his grandmother’s long-lost engagement ring.

I counted the ceiling fans spinning lazily overhead. Three fans, four blades each. Twelve blades. I let out a long exhale, feeling the weight of the afternoon dragging me down. My cousin was debating the value of vintage comic books with the cashier, a conversation that had been looping in circles for twenty minutes. I dragged myself over to the nearest display case, resting my elbows heavily on the glass and letting my chin drop into my hands. I stared through the smudge marks at the velvet trays below, my mind totally blank. A chunky, outdated gold ring sat in the corner of the case. I stared at it for a full minute before my brain finally processed the familiar overlapping initials engraved on the face. It was my grandmother's engagement ring, pawned by my uncle a decade ago.

Sarah dragged her feet along the carpeted floor, tracing random patterns in the worn pile with the toe of her sneaker. She picked up a snow globe from a shelf, gave it a half-hearted shake, and set it down before the flakes even started to fall. The pawn shop was quiet, smelling of old paper and dust. She leaned her back against a glass case, crossing her arms and letting her head fall back to stare at the fluorescent lights. After a minute of counting the dead bugs in the light fixture, she turned around and slumped over the counter. She stared blankly at a tray of rings, not really seeing them, just passing the seconds. Then, an aquamarine stone set in a filigree band caught the light. Sarah gasped, recognizing her grandmother’s engagement ring instantly.

Elias sat cross-legged on the attic floor, watching a single dust mote lazily spiral in a shaft of weak afternoon light. He let out a slow exhale that fluttered the cobwebs on a nearby box. Downstairs, the grandfather clock chimed three, meaning only an hour had passed since he started organizing. He dragged a finger through the thick layer of powder on a cardboard lid, leaving a stark brown line, then opened the flaps with a sluggish heave. Resting his chin heavily on his palm, he pulled out a yellowed piece of paper. It was his mother's handwriting, dated 1982. "I can no longer tolerate this workplace," it began. Elias read the draft resignation twice, his eyes glazing over midway through the second pass. He dropped it back into the box, leaned his head against a rafter, and resumed watching the dust slowly drift through the stale air.

I spun the loose caster wheel of Dad’s old toolbox with my index finger, listening to the steady whir-click, whir-click until it stopped. Then I spun it again. The Sunday afternoon stretched out endlessly, an empty void of gray rain beating against the garage window. I dragged a rusty screwdriver back and forth across the workbench, tracing shallow figure-eights into the wood. Opening the top drawer, my eyes swept over random receipts without absorbing a single word. Near the back, I pulled out a folded piece of stationery. "To whom it may concern: I will be vacating my position," Dad had written in tight cursive. A resignation letter from thirty years ago. I stared at the faded blue ink for a long moment, tapped the paper against my knee three times, slipped it back under the receipts, and reached for the caster wheel to spin it once more.

Maya lay on her back across the basement carpet, staring at the popcorn ceiling. She counted the bumps—one hundred and four, one hundred and five—until she lost track and groaned, throwing her arm over her face. The silence in the house felt heavy, pressing down on her. She rolled onto her stomach, lazily reaching out to pull a stray file folder from a stack bound for the recycling bin. She flipped it open with a limp wrist. Inside was a typed letter signed by her father in 1994, informing a law firm of his immediate departure. She rested her cheek on the scratchy carpet, reading the formal declarations of irreconcilable differences. Her foot tapped a slow, rhythmic beat against the floorboards. She blew a stray curl out of her eyes, pushed the folder away, and rolled back onto her spine to begin counting again.

I had drawn fifty-two overlapping circles in the margins of my notebook before I finally dropped the pen. The ticking of the wall clock echoed in Mom’s old home office, each second stretching longer than the last. I slumped back in the leather chair, letting my head loll to the side. With a heavy sigh, I blindly tugged at the bottom desk drawer. It stuck at first, so I gave it a half-hearted kick until it rattled open. Amidst dried-up highlighters lay a crinkled letter. I unfolded it, my eyelids drooping. It was a draft from 1998: Mom quitting her management job due to "untenable expectations." I skimmed the paragraphs, rubbing my temples as the dense text blurred together. Letting the paper flutter down onto the desk, I picked up my pen, found a blank spot on my notebook, and began drawing circle number fifty-three.

Marcus leaned his elbows on the dining table, resting his chin in his hands. He let out a long, loud sigh that stretched his jaw to the limit, his eyes watering slightly. He stared at the mountain of old paperwork, picking up a single envelope, turning it over, and dropping it into a pile. Pick up, turn over, drop. The rhythm was hypnotic. He grabbed the next sheet—a yellow legal pad page filled with crossed-out sentences. "I must step down as foreman," his father had scrawled in the eighties. Marcus read the angry, scratched-out revisions, his gaze slipping off the page to the digital clock on the microwave. 2:14 PM. Only two minutes had passed since he last checked. He slumped forward, laying his forehead directly onto the stack of papers, and closed his eyes against the bright afternoon glare.

I lay upside down on my childhood bed, my head hanging off the edge so the blood rushed to my cheeks. I watched the ceiling fan blades slowly rotate—one, two, three, four. The silence of the house was absolute. Dragging my hand across the floorboards beneath the bed, my fingers brushed against a dusty shoebox. I pulled it out with minimal effort, knocking off the lid to reveal faded documents and a loose sheet of printer paper. Upside down, I read the lines: Dad’s typed 2002 resignation from the bank, citing a lack of upward mobility. I traced the signature with my thumb, then stared at the blank white space at the bottom of the page. After a few minutes of listening to my own steady breathing, I dropped the letter onto the carpet, crossed my arms over my chest, and went back to watching the fan blades.

Chloe rested her forehead against the cool glass of the study window, watching a snail slowly navigate the wet patio bricks outside. She traced its slimy path with her index finger, letting out an exaggerated groan that vibrated against the pane. Turning back to her mother’s old filing cabinet, she haphazardly grabbed a handful of manila folders and let them spill across the rug. One paper drifted to rest by her toe. It was dated September 1990. "Effective immediately, I am leaving the firm," it read, fraught with underlined words and exclamation points. Chloe propped her chin on her knees, staring blankly at the dramatic punctuation. She rubbed her eyes, feeling the heavy, sleepy pull of the afternoon. Pushing the letter away with her foot, she turned her head back to the window, hoping the snail had at least made it to the edge of the brick.

My legs felt like lead as I sat on the floor, surrounded by piles of forgotten clothes. I pulled a moth-eaten sweater over my head, covering my face, and sat in the dark woolly cave for a solid minute, doing absolutely nothing. When I finally yanked it off, I slumped forward, digging listlessly into the bottom of Mom's cedar trunk. My fingers brushed a stiff envelope. I opened it at a glacial pace, unfolding the thick parchment. It was a draft of a letter stepping down from her hospital residency in 1985, detailing severe exhaustion. I stared at her elegant handwriting, resting my heavy head on my palm. My eyes darted to the window, then back to the letter, then to a stray button on the floor. I folded the paper in half, then in quarters, then in eighths, until it was too thick to fold anymore.

Julian sat at the kitchen table, meticulously peeling the paper label off his empty water bottle. He managed to get a long strip before it tore, prompting a heavy sigh. He rested his cheek against the cool linoleum tabletop, his gaze drifting to the open box of his father’s old college and work keepsakes. Without lifting his head, he reached a limp arm out and dragged a crumpled, coffee-stained paper toward him. It was a handwritten draft from 1978, a fiery resignation from a local newspaper over editorial differences. Julian scanned the impassioned arguments, his eyes blinking slowly. The words blurred together. He tapped his fingernails rhythmically against the table—tap, tap, tap, tap. Tossing the historical artifact aside, he focused his attention back on the water bottle, determined to peel off the remaining adhesive in one perfectly continuous piece.

I had watched the DVD logo bounce around the black screen for twenty minutes, waiting to see if it would ever perfectly hit the corner. When it finally did, I felt nothing. I rolled off the sofa, landing on the plush rug with a soft thud. I dragged myself over to a stack of books Dad had asked me to sort. I opened a heavy encyclopedia and a folded paper fell out. "Please accept this as formal notice of my resignation," the 1991 document read. He had written extensively about the company culture. I lay flat on my back, holding the paper up to the ceiling light. The stillness of the room was deafening. I let the letter drop onto my chest. Crossing my arms behind my head, I stared past the paper at the television, watching the little blue logo resume its slow, agonizing journey across the screen.

Sam sat on the front porch steps, tossing a pebble into the air and catching it. Toss, catch. Toss, miss. He didn't bother leaning over to retrieve it. He grabbed a lock of his hair, twirling it around his finger while staring blankly at the overgrown lawn. Beside him sat his mother’s old milk crate of files. He reached in blindly and pulled out a faded pink sheet of paper. It was a drafted 1989 resignation from a bakery, detailing complaints about the early shifts. He read the cursive text, his jaw slack, eyes half-open. A dog barked three streets over. Sam rested his chin on his knees, holding the pink paper loosely in his hand. He folded it into a crude paper airplane, pulled his arm back with zero energy, and let it lazily nose-dive into a patch of weeds right at the base of the stairs.

I lay sprawled out on the bare floorboards of the empty living room, listening to my own breathing. The moving truck wasn't due for another three hours. I picked at a splinter in the wood, rolling over onto my side with a heavy groan. Tucked under the baseboard was a dusty piece of paper that had evidently slipped behind a bookshelf years ago. I dragged it toward me with one finger. It was Dad's draft resignation from the auto plant, dated 1976. He listed grievances about the assembly line and poor management. I propped my head up on my elbow, reading the faded ink, then looked over at the blank, white wall. I let out a long breath, puffing my cheeks out and letting the air escape with a slow sputter. Letting my head flop back onto the hard floor, I closed my eyes and waited for time to pass.

Mark clicked the remote thirty times in thirty seconds, watching fragments of infomercials and reality shows without registering a single word. He tossed the clicker onto the couch, letting his head loll back against the cushions to stare at a faint water stain on the ceiling. The rhythmic ticking of the wall clock seemed to stretch the afternoon into an endless void. Dragging his feet across the carpet, he pulled open the media console drawer, idly hoping to find a spare battery for the PlayStation controller. Instead, his fingers brushed against a folded piece of pink stationery. He picked it up, smoothing out the creases to reveal Sarah’s handwriting under the heading "Things to do before I die." Mark leaned his chin on his palm, his eyes slowly dragging across the bullet points of skydiving and learning Italian, barely registering the ink on the page.

The rain tapped against the window in a slow, repetitive rhythm that matched the heavy thrum of my pulse. I had already organized my sock drawer by color, rearranged the spices alphabetically, and scrolled to the bottom of my social media feed twice. With a long exhale, I slumped onto the bedroom floor, picking at a loose thread on the carpet. I reached blindly under the bed to retrieve a stray tennis ball, but my hand met a leather-bound notebook. I pulled it out, blowing off a thin layer of dust. Opening the cover, I saw Liam’s precise handwriting: "Ultimate Bucket List." I rested my head against the bedframe, my gaze drifting over entries about climbing Mount Fuji and running a marathon. I flipped the page with a slow, heavy finger, wondering if I should just take a nap until dinnertime.

Chloe stirred her lukewarm latte, watching the swirl of milk slowly dissolve into the brown liquid. She tapped her spoon against the ceramic mug—clink, clink, clink—until the barista shot her a warning glance. Resting her cheek on her fist, she watched the cars crawl by outside, counting the silver ones until she lost track at fourteen. David had left his satchel on the chair opposite hers while he took a phone call outside. Needing something, anything, to occupy her eyes, Chloe leaned over and pulled a crumpled receipt from the side pocket. It wasn't a receipt. It was a list titled "My Dreams." She read the words "swim with sharks" and "write a novel," blinking slowly. A loud yawn escaped her lips, and she slumped back into the booth, letting the paper flutter onto the table as she went back to staring at the street.

The white lines of the highway blurred into a continuous, unvarying streak. I rested my forehead against the cool glass of the passenger window, blowing out a breath that fogged up the pane. I drew a smiley face in the condensation, waited for it to fade, and drew it again. Next to me, Elena kept her eyes fixed on the endless stretch of asphalt. I fiddled with the air conditioning vent, clicking it left, then right, then left again. Desperate for a distraction, I popped open the glovebox, pushing aside old napkins. A folded yellow paper caught my eye. Unfolding it, I found a list in Elena’s scrawl: "Before Thirty." I read the bullet points—learning cello, visiting Paris—while resting my chin heavily in my hand. I stared at the paper, the words washing over me as the tires sang their endless humming song.

James let out a loud groan, his head rolling back against the stiff airport terminal chair. They had been at Gate 42 for three hours, and his phone battery had died forty minutes ago. He slouched lower in the seat, extending his legs and staring blankly at the tips of his sneakers. The overhead announcements had become a meaningless noise, blending with the hum of the vending machine nearby. When his wife went to buy a pretzel, James grabbed her denim jacket to use as a pillow. A small notebook slipped from the pocket and landed on the carpet. He picked it up, flipping the pages with a heavy thumb until he stopped at a page titled "Life Goals." He read about her desire to build a cabin and master archery, his eyelids drooping heavily as he tossed the book onto the empty seat beside him.

I sat on the cold concrete floor of the basement, my chin resting on my knees, watching the washing machine tumble its load. A red shirt appeared in the sudsy window, disappeared, and appeared again in an endless, rhythmic cycle. I caught myself counting the revolutions, reaching eighty-two before a heavy sigh escaped my lips. I shifted my weight, picking absently at the lint on my sweatpants. When the cycle finally beeped, I dragged myself up to transfer the clothes. Reaching into the pocket of Sam’s favorite jeans to check for loose change, my fingers brushed against a crumpled piece of paper. Smoothing it out on the lid of the dryer, I read "Sam's Bucket List" scribbled in blue ink. I skimmed the entries about deep-sea diving and writing poetry, propping my heavy head up with one arm as the dryer started its loud humming.

The power had been out for two hours, leaving the apartment bathed in the weak, flickering light of a single candle. Anita lay flat on her back on the living area rug, her arms splayed out wide. She watched a spider weave a web in the corner, feeling the agonizingly slow tick of the passing seconds. With a massive exhale, she rolled onto her side and pulled a random book from the bottom shelf, just to have something to hold. A folded piece of paper fluttered from between the pages. It was Tom’s handwriting, under the heading "Things I Must Do." She stared at his goals of backpacking through Europe and tasting exotic foods. Her eyes glazed over the enthusiastic punctuation. She let the paper drop to the floor, rolling onto her back again to simply stare up at the motionless shadows on the ceiling.

I swung my legs back and forth, letting my heels tap softly against the wooden legs of the waiting room chair. I had already leafed through a six-month-old home decor magazine, barely looking at the pictures of modern kitchens, before tossing it back onto the glass table. The receptionist typed on her keyboard with a steady, endless clack-clack-clack. I slumped down, sliding my hands into my pockets, pulling out lint. Marcus had left his planner on the seat next to me. With a heavy sigh, I flipped it open, scanning the pages until I hit a tab labeled "Bucket List." I traced the words "see the northern lights" with a slow index finger. Letting my head fall back against the beige wall, I closed my eyes, wishing the slow-moving clock hands would just spin a fraction faster.

Leo picked up another grey pebble from the dirt and tossed it lazily at the trunk of a nearby oak tree. It bounced off with a hollow thwack. He picked up another one, tossing it with the exact same motion, his chin propped heavily in his other hand. The park was deserted, the afternoon stretching out in a vast, grey expanse of nothingness. His boyfriend, Julian, had gone to the restroom, leaving his leather-bound sketchpad on the bench. Leo dragged the book onto his lap, flipping the pages with a slow, mechanical drag of his thumb. Near the back, he found a page filled entirely with text. "Life Bucket List," it read. Leo stared blankly at the words "bungee jumping" and "build a treehouse." He let out a long, vibrating breath through his lips, tossing one more pebble at the motionless tree while shifting his weight.

The speaker's voice dragged on in a relentless, flat rhythm that made my eyelids feel like they were lined with lead. I rested my cheek flat against the cold laminate of the folding table, using my pen to draw endless, meaningless spirals in the margins of the community newsletter. When I ran out of space, I lazily nudged Derek’s open notebook toward me. I expected to find notes on the proposed zoning laws, but instead, the page was topped with "My Bucket List." I read the bullet points—learning to scuba dive, running with the bulls in Pamplona. I blinked slowly, letting the pen slip from my fingers to clatter against the table. I rested my forehead on my crossed arms, staring at the list sideways as the speaker began reading aloud from a dense, endless slideshow about parking regulations.

Rachel traced the condensation on the sliding glass door with a limp finger, watching the fog roll over the beach. There was no internet, and she had already finished her only paperback. She flopped onto the sofa, throwing her legs over the armrest and staring upside down at the ceiling fan’s slow rotations. Letting out a loud, exaggerated groan, she slid off the cushions, dragging herself to the desk in the corner. She opened the top drawer, aimlessly sifting through dried-out pens and rusty paperclips. Beneath a pile of old takeout menus, she found a pink index card. It was written in Greg’s messy print: "Bucket List." She stared at his dreams of hiking Machu Picchu and riding a hot air balloon. Tapping her fingernails rhythmically against the wooden desk, she rested her heavy head on the drawer, closing her eyes against the ticking clock.

I kicked my foot against the desk, spinning the office chair in a slow circle. Once, twice, three times. The room was silent except for the squeak of the chair's wheels. I picked up the stapler, clicking it into the air just to hear the sharp metal snap. With a heavy sigh, I let my head thump softly onto the desk. Maya had left her bright yellow planner next to the computer monitor. I reached out a lazy hand and flipped the cover open, hoping to find a crossword puzzle or a doodle. Instead, there was a neatly bulleted list titled "Things to Do Before I Turn Forty." I scanned the entries about taking a pottery class and visiting the Grand Canyon. My eyes moved slowly over the words, unblinking, before I gave the chair another weak kick, starting my slow, squeaking rotation all over again.

Arthur clicked his retractable pen. Click, clack. Click, clack. The spreadsheet on his monitor had remained untouched for forty-five minutes. He minimized the window, leaning his cheek against his palm, and lazily scrolled through a literary forum. His eyelids drooped heavily as he skimmed threads about grammar. Then, a bolded headline caught his eye: 'E.R. Vance Steals Plots'. E.R. Vance was Arthur’s absolute favorite fantasy writer. He opened the thread, his chin still propped on his hand, and read the side-by-side text comparisons. Vance had ripped off a series of obscure blog posts verbatim. Arthur sighed, letting out a long, slow breath that ruffled the sticky notes on his desk. He dragged his cursor over the evidence, his eyes glazing over the identical paragraphs. He spun his rolling chair in a slow, squeaky half-circle, staring blankly at the gray fabric of his cubicle wall.

The digital counter at the front of the room flashed the number forty-two. I held ticket eighty-seven. I shifted my weight on the hard plastic chair, tracing the scuff marks on the linoleum floor with the toe of my sneaker. With a heavy exhale, I pulled out my phone and swiped downward with my thumb, over and over, letting the timeline blur. Half the posts were ads, the rest were complaints about the weather. Then, I stopped on a trending hashtag featuring my favorite mystery novelist. Someone had uploaded a video proving her latest bestseller was lifted entirely from a discontinued 90s television script. I watched the video on mute, watching the text overlays match the dialogue perfectly. The counter beeped loudly, displaying forty-three. I locked my phone screen, stared at the ceiling tiles, and began counting the little perforated dots above my head.

Rain drummed a monotonous rhythm against the bookstore window. Maya sat behind the register, blowing a stray lock of hair out of her face. She arranged the display of bookmarks into perfectly straight lines, then immediately messed them up just to straighten them again. With a heavy sigh, she picked up her phone and opened a literature gossip blog. A breaking expose sat at the top of the page. Silas Thorne, the author whose sci-fi trilogy she had read five times, was being sued. The article detailed how his entire universe was copy-pasted from an unpublished manuscript submitted to his former publishing house. Maya rested her head on the cool mahogany counter, lazily scrolling through the legal documents attached to the article. A customer walked in, the entry bell letting out a weak chime. Maya didn't lift her head, just kept swiping upward with a lethargic thumb.

The train clacked along the tracks in a steady, hypnotic rhythm. I rested my forehead against the cool, vibrating glass of the window, watching the endless stretch of gray suburbs blur past. There were still twelve stops until my station. I picked up my tablet, swiping through menus without clicking anything. Finally, I opened a newsletter I subscribed to, skimming the walls of text without really absorbing the words. Midway down, a paragraph highlighted a scandal involving Julian Hayes. The historical fiction author I admired had apparently stolen his award-winning prose from translated Russian diaries. I read the side-by-side excerpts, my eyes dragging slowly from left to right. It was a complete match. I set the tablet back down on my lap and slumped deeper into the scratchy upholstery of the train seat, watching a raindrop slowly trace a jagged path down the outside of the window.

Leo lay on his back on the living room rug, tossing a tennis ball at the ceiling and catching it. Thud, smack. Thud, smack. The summer heat pressed into the house, thick and heavy. He rolled onto his stomach, letting the ball roll away under the sofa, and dragged his laptop closer. He clicked refresh on his video feed for the fourth time in ten minutes. A new video popped up from a drama channel he followed. The thumbnail showed a red arrow pointing to the cover of his favorite fantasy novel. He clicked play, resting his chin on his crossed arms. The narrator's voice droned on, presenting undeniable proof that the author had stolen fanfiction from an old archive. Leo watched the evidence mount, his face resting flat against his forearms. He let out a long puff of air, closed the laptop lid, and stared out the window.

The soft, instrumental jazz playing through the waiting room speakers was looping for the third time. I flipped through an eighteen-month-old magazine, pausing to look at a recipe for a gelatin mold before letting the glossy pages flutter shut. I slumped sideways into the armrest, pulling out my phone. I swiped endlessly through my reading app's community forum. Someone had posted a link titled 'The Truth About Elena Vance'. I tapped it with a heavy thumb. The post revealed that the indie romance author I adored had been running her competitors' works through an AI rewriter and publishing them as her own. I scrolled through the massive wall of evidence, my eyes glazing slightly at the dense blocks of text. The receptionist cleared her throat, but didn't call my name. I locked my screen, crossed my arms, and began tapping my foot against the carpet.

Henry sat in his rocking chair, the porch floorboards creaking in a slow, rhythmic pattern. The Sunday paper lay open on his lap, though he had been staring at the same garden hose across the yard for the past twenty minutes. He let out a prolonged exhale, finally looking down at the arts and culture section. A prominent headline dominated the page. His favorite espionage writer, a man whose thrillers Henry had collected for decades, was exposed as a fraud. The article meticulously laid out how the author had plagiarized decommissioned intelligence memoirs word for word. Henry traced the black-and-white text with a sluggish finger, taking in the scandalous details. He folded the paper over, resting it on the side table, and leaned back, letting his eyes drift back to the coils of the green rubber garden hose baking in the afternoon sun.

The quarterly budget review had been going on for an hour and forty minutes. My manager's voice was a steady, unbroken drone coming through my headphones. I kept my camera angled just high enough to hide the fact that my chin was resting heavily in my palm. On my second monitor, I mindlessly clicked around a literary subreddit. A megathread sat at the top with thousands of comments. Apparently, the sci-fi author who wrote the only book series I actually cared about had been caught lifting entire chapters from obscure self-published novels. I clicked through the comparison links, scrolling down page after page of identical paragraphs. It was undeniable theft. I dragged my cursor in slow circles around the screen, letting out a quiet, prolonged breath. I minimized the window and went back to watching the little green sound bar bounce next to my manager's name.

Chloe twirled a yellow pencil around her thumb, watching it spin and drop onto her open biology textbook. She picked it up and spun it again, keeping her eyes fixed on the grain of the wooden library desk. The silence of the reading room felt thick and heavy. Seeking any distraction, she pulled her phone from her pocket and opened her favorite book reviewer's page. The reviewer had just posted a long thread exposing the acclaimed poet Chloe idolized. The poet had stolen her entire award-winning collection from translated works of a forgotten 19th-century author. Chloe read through the stolen stanzas, her face devoid of expression. She rested her cheek on the cool surface of the desk, letting her phone slip from her fingers. She stared at the dust motes dancing in the shaft of sunlight filtering through the tall library window.

The digital clock on the nightstand glared a neon 3:14 AM. I lay flat on my back, tracing the cracks in the ceiling plaster with my eyes. The house was dead quiet. With a heavy groan, I rolled over and grabbed my phone off the charger, the harsh blue light making me squint. I opened an entertainment news site, swiping idly past articles about celebrity diets and movie trailers. Then, a headline grabbed my attention. The historical biographer I admired had just confessed to plagiarizing the letters of the historical figures themselves, passing the original prose off as his own narrative styling. I read the author's lackluster apology statement, swiping my thumb down the glass in slow, lethargic motions. The article ended. I tossed the phone onto the empty pillow beside me, rolled onto my back again, and resumed my study of the ceiling cracks.

The lobby clock ticked loudly in the empty foyer. Marcus sat on the stool behind the front desk, his head propped on a stack of clean towels. He tapped his index finger against the marble counter, a slow, unending beat. He opened the web browser on the hotel's computer, navigating to a sci-fi fanzine. The front page was plastered in bold red text. The legendary author of his favorite space opera had been outed for plagiarizing cadet training manuals from the 1970s. Marcus clicked the link, his eyes tracking the side-by-side text comparisons that proved the devastating theft. He let out a long, whistling sigh that puffed his cheeks out, scrolling to the bottom of the page without reading the comments. He closed the tab, folded his arms over the marble counter, and rested his forehead against his sleeves.

I drummed my fingers against the steering wheel, watching the minutes tick by on the dashboard display. Sarah said she would only be five minutes, and that was twenty minutes ago. I slumped down in the driver’s seat, tilting my head back against the headrest, and pulled up a literary podcast on my phone. The hosts were discussing breaking news in the publishing world. The fantasy author who wrote my favorite childhood series was facing a massive lawsuit for copying the plot and world-building from a tabletop role-playing campaign. I listened to them read the verbatim similarities, my eyes fixed on a peeling sticker on the bumper of the car parked in front of me. I let out a long, heavy exhale, reached over to turn down the volume of the podcast, and went back to watching the dashboard clock.

Arthur clicked his ballpoint pen. In, out. In, out. The spreadsheet on his monitor had blurred into a gray grid of numbers an hour ago. He rested his chin in his palm, watching the second hand on the wall clock stutter past three-fifteen. His phone buzzed against the faux-wood laminate of his desk. He dragged his eyes downward. A notification glowed on the lock screen: Kevin Hodges sent you a friend request. Kevin. The same Kevin who used to shove Arthur’s head into the junior high lockers. Arthur stared at the tiny profile picture of a balding man holding a fish. He let out a long, slow breath that ruffled the corner of a sticky note, picked up his pen, and went back to clicking. In, out. In, out. The clock ticked to three-sixteen.

The laundromat smelled like cheap floral detergent and old lint. I sat on a hard plastic chair, my chin resting on my knuckles, watching my darks tumble in a hypnotic, endless circle. Thump, swoosh. Thump, swoosh. I pulled my phone from my pocket, unlocked it, swiped to the next screen, swiped back, and locked it again. A moment later, it vibrated. A social media alert. Amanda Vance wants to connect. I squinted at the thumbnail. Amanda. She had spent all of eighth grade making sure no one sat next to me at lunch. I looked up at the dryer. The darks were still tumbling. I swiped the notification away without opening the app, letting my head loll back against the cinderblock wall as I counted the cracked acoustic tiles on the ceiling. Twenty-four. Twenty-five.

Rain lashed against the bedroom window in a steady, drumming rhythm. Marcus lay flat on his back on the carpet, throwing a tennis ball at the ceiling and catching it. Thwack. Catch. Thwack. Catch. He had already scrolled through his entire feed twice and checked the fridge three times, hoping something new had materialized between the milk and the mustard. His tablet chimed from the nightstand. Rolling over with a heavy groan, he reached a limp arm up to grab it. Friend Request: Tommy Larson. Marcus blinked at the screen. Tommy had once thrown his science project into a muddy puddle. Marcus tossed the tablet onto the bed, picked up the tennis ball, and resumed his position on the floor. Thwack. Catch. Thwack. Catch. The rain kept falling.

The commuter train hadn't moved in twenty minutes. I rested my forehead against the cool glass of the window, tracing the path of a single condensation drip with my index finger. The guy next to me was breathing heavily through his nose. I unlocked my phone just to look at the battery percentage. Forty-two. A little bubble popped down from the top of the screen. Derek Stiles sent you a friend request. Derek. The kid who used to steal my sneakers during gym class and hide them in the showers. I stared at his name for a long time, the letters losing their shape the longer I looked. The train car hissed, but we didn’t move. I locked the screen, slid the phone back into my coat, and started counting the overhead lights.

Professor Higgins had been talking about the socioeconomic impacts of eighteenth-century agriculture for forty-five minutes. Chloe was coloring in the 'O's and 'P's in her notebook, her cheek squished flat against the cold surface of her desk. She stared blankly at the chalkboard, watching dust drift around the projector beam. A quiet buzz emanated from her backpack. She slowly unzipped the front pocket and slipped her phone out, desperate for any change in the room's atmosphere. Friend Request: Sarah Jenkins. Chloe stared at the name. Sarah, who used to mock her braces and call her 'metal-mouth' every morning by the bus stop. Chloe rubbed her eyes, let out a slow exhale through her nose, and shoved the phone back into the dark depths of her bag. She picked up her pen and found another 'O' to fill in.

I had already read the five-year-old issue of a dentistry magazine sitting on the glass table. I knew all about the advent of ceramic crowns. I leaned back in the vinyl waiting room chair, listening to the receptionist type on her keyboard. Click, clack, click. I tapped my foot to match her rhythm. My phone vibrated in my lap. Finally, a distraction. Friend request from Gregory Vance. I arched an eyebrow. Greg. The guy who tripped me in the cafeteria, sending my lunch flying across the linoleum. I looked at his profile picture, a poorly lit selfie in the driver's seat of a truck. The receptionist stopped typing. I sighed, tossed the phone back onto the table next to the magazines, and started reading a pamphlet about flossing for the third time.

The security booth smelled of stale coffee. Elias sat slumped in his ergonomic chair, staring at the grid of nine monitors. Monitor four showed an empty parking garage. Monitor seven showed an empty hallway. He picked up a paperclip, unbent it into a straight line, and then tried to bend it back into its original shape. His personal cell phone lit up on the console. Notification: Ricky Thorne wants to be your friend. Elias paused his paperclip bending. Ricky Thorne. The neighborhood terror who used to lock Elias in the community center shed. Elias looked back up at the monitors. The parking garage was still empty. The hallway was still empty. He tossed the mangled paperclip into the trash can, leaned his head back, and stared at the fluorescent light fixture above him.

The water in the pot was completely still. I leaned my hip against the kitchen counter, resting my chin in my hands, waiting for a single bubble to form. Nothing. I shifted my weight to the other leg. I picked up a piece of dry spaghetti and snapped it into tiny, half-inch pieces, lining them up on the granite. My phone chimed from across the room. I took my time walking over to it, dragging my fuzzy socks across the hardwood. New Friend Request: Jason Brody. Jason. The kid who used to corner me behind the bleachers and demand my pocket money. I stared at the notification, my face completely blank. I turned my head to look back at the stove. Still no bubbles. I left the phone on the table and went back to the dry pasta.

Summer break had stretched into a hazy, featureless void. Leo lay upside down on the living room sofa, his legs draped over the backrest, his head hovering inches from the floor. He watched a single dust mote float lazily through a shaft of afternoon sunlight. His phone slipped from his loose grip and thunked softly onto the rug, the screen flashing to life. Elena Rostova sent you a friend request. Leo blinked slowly at the glowing text. Elena. The girl who had made it her mission to spread rumors about him throughout all of sophomore year. He didn't bother to reach down and pick the device up. He just watched the screen dim, turn black, and return his reflection. He blew a puff of air upward, scattering the dust mote.

The DMV queue wrapped around three rows of plastic chairs. I was currently at position forty-two. The digital sign dinged and flashed seventeen. I slumped forward, resting my forehead on my knees. I had been refreshing my email inbox every two minutes just to see the little loading wheel spin. A banner dropped down from the top of my screen. Friend Request: Brad Miller. Brad had shoved me into the snowbank every morning of fifth grade. I stared at his smiling face in the tiny circle. The digital sign dinged again. Eighteen. I let out a long, slow breath, swiped Brad's face away, and opened my calculator app to see what forty-two divided by eighteen was. Anything to make the clock move faster.

Pacing from the fireplace to the bookshelf took exactly fourteen steps. Maya had counted five times. The house she was watching was dead silent, save for the grandfather clock ticking in the hall. Tick. Tock. Tick. Tock. She flopped onto the oversized armchair, draping her legs over one arm and her head over the other. Her pocket vibrated. She pulled the phone out, staring past the screen. Friend Request from Melissa Trent. Maya looked blankly at the words. Melissa had spent their entire senior year making sure Maya was excluded from every social event. Maya let her arm drop, the phone dangling limply from her fingers toward the floor. She stared at the ceiling molding, tracing the intricate floral patterns with her eyes, listening to the grandfather clock tick the seconds away.

It was past three in the morning. The ceiling fan spun in an endless, rhythmic blur. Click-whir, click-whir. I lay flat on my back, the blue light of my phone illuminating my face in the dark bedroom. My thumb moved on autopilot, swiping up, up, up through videos I wasn't really watching. A notification broke the stream. Oliver Quinn added you as a friend. I stopped swiping. Oliver. He was the reason I had a scar on my left eyebrow from a thrown rock in seventh grade. I looked at the notification, my expression unmoving in the pale glow. I didn't hit accept or decline. I just closed the app, set the phone face-down on the mattress, and went back to watching the ceiling fan go round and round.

Arthur counted the ceiling tiles for the third time this afternoon. Forty-eight intact, two chipped. The silence of the apartment felt thick, pressing against his eardrums. He dragged his thumb across his phone screen, swiping away notifications he didn't care to read, then tossed the device onto the sofa. The sudden, sharp knock at the door startled him. He dragged his feet across the carpet, turning the deadbolt to find a square cardboard box resting on the welcome mat. The shipping label read "To: Miranda Vance." Arthur stared at the name, realizing he hadn't spoken to another human being in three days. He picked up the package, turning it over in his hands, wondering if opening a stranger's mail was a federal offense or just the most exciting thing to happen to him all week.

I traced a slow figure-eight into the condensation on the windowpane, watching the drops merge and race down to the sill. The rain had been falling for hours, a steady, gray sheet that blurred the city skyline into a smudge. I let my head thump softly against the cold glass. Nothing but infomercials on television, and I had already rearranged my bookshelf alphabetically by author, then by spine color. A heavy thud from the hallway broke the drone of the rain. I padded to the front door, pulling it open. A small, brown parcel sat on the carpet. "Delivery for Gregson," I read aloud to the empty hallway. I’m not Gregson. Gregson moved out six months ago. I shook the box gently. Something inside rattled, sending a tiny spark of curiosity through the heavy afternoon.

Chloe sat at the kitchen island, meticulously peeling the paper label off her empty water bottle.
