She rolled the sticky scrap into a tight little ball and flicked it across the counter, watching it bounce off the toaster. The digital clock on the oven shifted from 2:14 to 2:15. She rested her chin in her palm, letting out a long, slow breath that fluttered her bangs. When the doorbell chimed, she didn't jump. She simply slid off the stool and shuffled toward the entryway, hoping it was someone selling magazines or asking for petitions. Anything at all. Instead, she found a bright yellow padded envelope addressed to Theodore Carmichael. Theodore was the guy who rented the place before her. Chloe squeezed the puffy envelope, wondering what kind of life Theodore had, and if it involved sitting around watching the clock.

Twelve silver sedans. That was my current tally for the last hour. I was sitting on the porch steps, tossing a single pebble from my left hand to my right, over and over again. The heat wave had trapped everyone indoors, leaving the neighborhood completely motionless. I closed my eyes and tried to guess the color of the next passing car by the sound of its tires. A delivery truck hissed to a stop at the curb, shattering my game. The driver jogged up my walkway, dropped a heavy crate at my feet, and vanished before I could speak. I looked down. The bold black letters spelled out Eleanor Rigby. Not really, but Eleanor something. The old tenant. I stared at the sealed wooden crate. I could take it inside, pry it open, and pretend I was a pirate uncovering lost treasure.

Elias stretched a rubber band between his thumbs, pulling it taut until it snapped against his skin. He winced, then did it again. The rhythmic sting was the only punctuation in a day that had stretched into an endless, shapeless void. He rolled onto his stomach, letting his arm dangle off the edge of the bed to trace patterns in the carpet fibers. Eventually, hunger forced him to his feet. Opening the door to grab his delivered takeout, his foot knocked against a small, velvet-wrapped box. It was addressed to Julianne, the woman who lived here a year ago. Elias picked it up, weighing it in his palm. It was surprisingly heavy. He walked back to his bed, ignoring his cold noodles, and spent the next twenty minutes imagining what Julianne had bought, grateful for the distraction.

I pushed off the edge of the desk, letting the wheeled office chair spin me around in slow circles. The ceiling fan blades chased each other above me. One, two, three, four. I dragged my shoe against the rug to stop the spinning, letting out a breath that ruffled my mustache. My computer screen showed an empty inbox. I refreshed the page. Still empty. A notification from the building concierge popped up on my phone, alerting me to a package at the front desk. I took the elevator down, counting the floors as they lit up. The doorman handed me a slender tube. I didn't bother looking at the label until I was back upstairs, spinning in my chair again. It belonged to Hector Ramirez. Hector was the guy who broke his lease last winter. I popped the plastic end cap off the tube.

Maya pinched a dead brown leaf off the potted ficus, crumbling it between her fingers. She dropped the dusty fragments over the balcony railing, watching them drift down to the street below. She leaned over, resting her chin on her crossed arms, observing a pigeon pecking at a discarded wrapper. The pigeon eventually flew away, leaving her to stare at the empty concrete. A loud knock echoed from her front door. She dragged herself inside, her bare feet slapping lazily against the hardwood. On the welcome mat sat a massive, cube-shaped box wrapped in international shipping tape. The customs form bore the name Sasha Petrov. Maya nudged the heavy cardboard with her toe. It didn't budge. She sat cross-legged on the floor right there in the entryway, tracing the strange foreign stamps with her index finger.

I checked the mailbox again, even though the carrier had already come and gone hours ago. Just an ad for a local pizzeria and a utility bill. I shuffled back down the hall, kicking a stray piece of lint ahead of me like a tiny, pathetic soccer ball. The hallway smelled of old cabbage and floor wax. When I reached my door, I almost tripped over a bundle wrapped in brown butcher paper. It was tied tightly with twine. I crouched down, squinting at the faded ink. It requested delivery to Beatrice Vance. Beatrice was the elderly lady who lived here before she moved into an assisted care facility. I plucked at the twine, letting it snap back against the paper. The knot was intricate. Unraveling it would probably take an hour, which sounded like a perfect way to spend the afternoon.

He clicked the remote, watching the screen flicker from a cooking show to a documentary about bees, then to a sitcom with a canned laugh track. Click. Click. Click. Liam tossed the remote onto the adjacent cushion and let his head loll back against the sofa. He stared at a water stain on the ceiling that looked vaguely like a map of Australia. The sharp buzz of the intercom made him jump. A distorted voice crackled out a delivery notification. Liam buzzed them up, standing in his open doorway as the driver handed him a sleek black box. Liam turned it over. The silver lettering read Marcus Thorne. Marcus was the previous tenant, a guy who supposedly moved to Europe. Liam sat back down on the couch, ignoring the television entirely, turning the smooth black box over and over in his hands.

I had taken to stacking my loose change into perfectly symmetrical towers on the coffee table. Four pennies, two dimes, a nickel. Repeat. I watched a fly buzz erratically against the window screen, bumping its head repeatedly in a futile attempt to escape. "I know how you feel, buddy," I muttered, flicking a stray penny off the table. It rolled across the floorboards and clinked against a padded mailer that someone must have shoved through the mail slot while I was making toast. I crawled over on my hands and knees to retrieve it. The name on the label was Jasmine DuBois. The former occupant. The envelope squished when I pressed it, feeling like it was full of gelatin or thick liquid. I spent the next ten minutes just squishing the plastic, wondering if it would ever pop.

Marcus lay in the backyard hammock, swaying gently as he tried to find shapes in the flat, gray overcast sky. There were no clouds to interpret, just a solid sheet of white noise above him. He picked a blade of grass and chewed on the bitter end, spitting it out when the taste faded. The squeak of the garden gate hinges made him lift his head. A parcel sat on the stone path, left by a courier who was already retreating down the alley. Marcus didn't hurry. He let his legs hang over the side of the hammock, eventually standing up to fetch the box. The shipping label was addressed to the family who owned the house three years ago. He shook the box, listening to the heavy thud of whatever was inside sliding back and forth.

I scrolled to the very bottom of my social media feed, reaching posts from three days ago that I had already liked. I refreshed the page. Nothing new. I locked the screen, stared at my dark reflection in the glass, and sighed. The silence in the apartment was deafening. I considered taking a nap, even though I had woken up only four hours ago. A knock at the door broke the quiet. I dragged myself upright, padding to the entrance in my socks. A tall, rectangular box leaned against the doorframe. The name printed on the side was Oscar Lin. Oscar was the guy who broke the lease before I moved in. I dragged the heavy box inside, letting it thud onto the carpet. I grabbed a pair of scissors, eager for an excuse to do absolutely anything else today.

Arthur watched the second hand of the wall clock tick with agonizing precision. Three-fourteen. Three-fifteen. He rearranged his paperclips into a neat little triangle, then pushed them into a square. When the mail cart squeaked down the aisle, he grabbed the lone envelope tossed into his tray just to have something for his hands to do. He sliced it open, staring at the cursive handwriting. It was from Claire, detailing her deepest regrets about the betrayal at the lake house ten years ago. Arthur rested his chin on his palm, scanning the tear-stained ink. He counted the number of times she used the word "sorry"—four times. He folded the thick parchment back into the envelope, dropped it into the recycling bin, and went back to rearranging his paperclips, this time aiming for a perfect hexagon.

I had already counted the water droplets racing down my living room window three times. The TV played a muted infomercial about a blender I didn't need, casting a pale blue light across the beige carpet. The postman had dropped a single thick envelope through the mail slot twenty minutes ago, and I finally trudged over to pick it up. Tearing the top off, I found a three-page letter from Marcus. He went on and on about the stolen inheritance, begging for my forgiveness after all these years. My eyes slid over the dramatic paragraphs. He used a rather dramatic font. I sighed, letting the pages drop onto the coffee table next to a half-empty mug of lukewarm tea. I flopped back onto the sofa, staring at the popcorn ceiling, wondering if I should try counting the little bumps above the ceiling fan instead.

The DMV waiting area smelled like old floor wax and damp wool. Maria slumped in her hard plastic chair, repeatedly clicking her retractable pen until the woman next to her shot a sharp glare. Maria stopped, exhaling a long breath, and dug through her purse for a distraction. She pulled out the envelope she’d fetched from her mailbox that morning. It was from her estranged father, pouring his heart out about abandoning them during her childhood, full of poetic apologies and promises to make amends. She traced the edge of the paper with her thumb, noting the expensive cardstock. "Ticket number A-42," the robotic voice crackled over the intercom. Maria looked at her ticket—A-89. She let her head fall back against the wall, resting the apology on her lap, and watched a fly buzz in lazy circles around the fluorescent light fixture.

The train clacked over the tracks with a rhythmic, unchanging thump. I stared at the blurry suburban houses sliding past, my cheek pressed against the cool, smudged glass. Having forgotten my headphones, the silence of the quiet car felt heavy. I dug into my coat pocket and pulled out the letter I had been carrying for two days. It was from Julia, desperately apologizing for sabotaging my college scholarship fifteen years ago. I skimmed the words 'devastated,' 'regret,' and 'cowardice' as the landscape continued its continuous blur. I flipped the page over, looking to see if the back was blank so I could sketch the sleeping man sitting across the aisle. It was covered in more cursive. I folded it back up, stuffed it deep into my pocket, and went back to watching the gray clouds hang motionless in the sky.

There were zero customers in the antique shop. Elias sat behind the counter, tracing the wood grain of the register stand with his index finger. He’d already dusted the porcelain figurines twice. Pulling a crumpled letter from his apron pocket, he flattened it out on the glass counter. It was from his ex-fiancée, a late plea for forgiveness regarding the wedding she walked out on eight years prior. She described her years of guilt in painstaking detail. Elias rested his chin in both hands, his heavy eyelids drooping as he read about her spiritual awakening in Peru. A grandfather clock chimed in the corner, slow and resonant. He let out a long breath, wishing someone, anyone, would walk through the door and ask him the price of a teapot, just so he could hear a voice other than the hum of the refrigerator.

The washing machine spun in endless, soapy circles. I sat on the cracked plastic bench, my legs stretched out in front of me, listening to the rhythmic slosh of water. I pulled the envelope from my back pocket just to have something to hold. Opening it, I recognized David's messy handwriting. It was a five-page apology for crashing my car and fleeing the scene a decade ago. I read the first paragraph, then skipped to the third, my eyes glazing over the emotional pleas and excuses. The fluorescent light above flickered, emitting a low, continuous buzz. I refolded the letter into a tiny paper airplane, resting it on my knee. There were still twenty-four minutes left on the wash cycle. I leaned my head against the cinderblock wall and watched the suds spin round and round, a hypnotic swirl of white and gray.

Sitting on the porch swing, Clara dragged her toe across the wooden floorboards, pushing herself back and forth in a slow, squeaky rhythm. Squeak. Creak. Squeak. Creak. The summer afternoon was thick and motionless. She opened the letter that had arrived in the morning post. It was from her former business partner, pouring out immense regret for the embezzlement that ruined their startup twelve years back. Clara scanned the tear-stained ink, her expression completely slack. A beetle crawled lazily across the railing. She watched it for a long moment, completely abandoning the letter on her lap. The confession of a lifetime lay ignored as she debated whether the beetle would turn left or right at the wooden post. It turned left. Clara let out a long exhale, rested her head against the swing chains, and continued to push. Squeak. Creak.

The parking lot of the grocery store was mostly empty. I drummed my fingers against the steering wheel to the beat of a song that wasn't playing on the radio. My sister had been inside for twenty minutes just to get milk. I reached into the passenger seat and picked up the letter from my high school bully. She had found a new path in life, sending three pages of deep, remorseful apologies for making my teenage years miserable. I stared at the words, resting my temple against the cold side window. The paper was slightly textured. I rubbed it between my thumb and forefinger, enjoying the tactile sensation far more than the heartfelt words written on it. A stray shopping cart slowly rolled across the asphalt, pushed by a gentle breeze. I watched it drift until it bumped into the curb.

Dust motes drifted through the shafts of sunlight cutting across the library's reading room. Julian sat at a massive oak table, his textbook open but unread. He propped his head up on one hand, his eyes heavy. He pulled an envelope out of his bag and broke the seal. Inside was an apology from his estranged brother, outlining his deep sorrow for ruining Julian's wedding day seven years earlier. Julian read the words, his face completely blank. He noticed a typo in the second paragraph. Then another in the fourth. He pulled a red pen from his pocket and slowly began circling the grammatical errors, fixing a misplaced comma and a dangling modifier. When he finished proofreading the agonizing confession, he placed it neatly to the side, let out a deep, echoing sigh, and stared blankly at the spines of the encyclopedias across the room.

I sat in the corner booth, swirling the ice in my empty water glass. The clinking sound was the most interesting thing happening in the entire café. I flattened out the letter on the sticky tabletop. It was from Sarah, confessing to stealing my portfolio designs in college and begging for my pardon all these years later. I read the paragraphs mechanically, noting how she looped her Y's. Outside, a pigeon pecked at a discarded french fry on the sidewalk. I watched it peck, hop, and peck again. The apology letter sat under my elbow, its profound revelations completely failing to hold my attention. I rested my chin on the table, my cheek smushing against my arm, and wondered if the waitress would ever come back with the check, or if I would be sitting in this booth until the end of time.

The hotel television played a documentary about the history of gravel. Chloe lay star-shaped on the uncomfortable bedspread, staring vacantly at the ceiling. The letter she had just opened lay beside her hip. It was a sprawling, emotional apology from her childhood best friend regarding a terrible lie told twenty years ago. Chloe picked it up, holding it above her face with a limp wrist. She let the paper flutter back down. She picked up the TV remote, flipping through channels. News. Soap opera. Fishing show. Back to the gravel documentary. She let her arm drop over the edge of the mattress, tracing the carpet pattern with her fingernails. The apology letter slid off the bed and landed on the floor with a soft papery sound. Chloe didn't move to pick it up, opting instead to close her eyes and listen to the droning narrator.

My shift at the front desk had started six hours ago, and the lobby had been deserted for five of them. I spun my chair in a slow circle, stopping to glance at the security monitors showing empty hallways. I picked up the letter I’d received that morning. It was from Captain Reynolds, formally apologizing for the friendly fire incident that ended my military career a decade ago. I read over the official letterhead, my eyes skimming the formal words of deep regret and sorrow. I reached for my stapler, opened it, and pressed it down onto a piece of scrap paper. Click. Click. Click. I looked back at the letter, folded it into thirds, and slid it under the wobbly leg of my desk chair. It leveled the chair perfectly. I let out a long breath and went back to watching monitor four.

Elias stared at the glossy cardstock that had slipped from the stack of bills. "Class of 2014, Ten Year Reunion," it declared in bright gold foil. He rested his chin in his palm, letting out a long, slow breath that ruffled the edge of the envelope. His eyes drifted from the invitation to the steady ticking of the wall clock, watching the second hand sweep its steady, unending circle. He picked at a loose thread on his sweatpants, wrapping it around his index finger until the tip turned purple, then unwrapping it again. The prospect of standing in a gym with watered-down punch and recounting his mid-level accounting job didn't even warrant a scoff. He nudged the heavy cardstock toward the edge of the kitchen island with his knuckle, letting it fall into the recycling bin before resting his forehead flat against the cool marble countertop.

The email subject line read: Westbridge High 15-Year Gathering! I didn't click it. I leaned back in my office chair, watching a gray pigeon peck at a cigarette butt on the window ledge outside. The screen saver on my monitor kicked in, a series of geometric shapes bouncing endlessly. I followed a blue square with my eyes, waiting for it to hit the exact corner. Bounce. Bounce. My phone buzzed with a group text from an old classmate, likely asking if I was attending. I spun my chair in a slow, lazy circle, listening to the faint squeak of the wheels. The pigeon abandoned the filter, flying off to find something else. I let out a long breath, letting my head loll back against the headrest, and began counting the tiny perforations in the acoustic ceiling tiles above me.

Maya held the thick envelope with two fingers, the return address instantly recognizable. Oak Creek High Alumni Association. She walked to the living room and collapsed onto the beige sofa, letting the mail drop onto the glass coffee table with a soft thud. The television was on, muted, playing an infomercial for a specialized garden hose. She watched the water spray in slow motion, her eyelids heavy and drooping. She picked up a glossy magazine from last month, flipped through the pages backward without focusing on a single image, and tossed it aside. The reunion invitation sat there, demanding a response. Maya stared at the beige wall behind the TV, tracing the faint outline of a spackled nail hole with her eyes. She let out a long exhale, rolled onto her side, and buried her face into the throw pillow, waiting for the afternoon to end.

My mother handed me the blue envelope over the kitchen table. "Looks like your ten-year is coming up," she said, tapping the crest. I took it, resting my elbow on the placemat and propping my heavy head in my hand. I traced the embossed lettering with my thumbnail, over and over, feeling the slight bumps of the paper. "Mhm," I murmured, my voice flat. Outside, a neighbor was mowing their lawn, the engine droning on in a steady, unending hum. I slid the invitation across the table until it touched the salt shaker, then pulled it back. Push, pull. Push, pull. "Are you going to RSVP?" she asked, wiping down the counters. I blinked slowly at the card, the vibrant blue doing nothing to stir my pulse. "Maybe," I said, suppressing a yawn and resting my forehead against the cool surface of the wooden table.

Arthur sat in his parked car, the engine off. The mail from his PO Box rested on the passenger seat, topped by a garish red flyer: Class of '84, Let's Relive the Glory Days! Arthur stared at the exclamation point. He drummed his fingers against the steering wheel in a slow rhythm. He watched a plastic grocery bag drift lazily across the asphalt until it snagged on a shopping cart wheel. He checked his watch. 2:14 PM. He looked away, counted to twenty in his head, and checked it again. Still 2:14 PM. The prospect of making small talk about his hardware store job with people from three decades ago felt like another chore. He leaned his head against the windowpane, staring blankly as the traffic light down the block cycled from green, to yellow, to red, over and over again.

The digital invitation popped up on my tablet while I was lying upside down on the couch, my legs dangling over the backrest. Lincoln High 20th Reunion. I let my arm drop to the floor, my knuckles grazing the carpet. A fly buzzed lazily around the ceiling fan, and I tracked its erratic flight paths for several minutes. Figure eight. Loop. Bump into the wall. I swiped away the notification with a heavy drag of my thumb. The house was quiet, save for the hum of the refrigerator. I blew a puff of air upward, watching my bangs flutter and settle back onto my forehead. Did I really want to put on pants, drive an hour, and stand by a buffet table eating stale pita chips? I closed my eyes, letting the tablet slip from my grasp and thud onto the rug beside my ear.

The golden-trimmed card announced the Roosevelt High five-year reunion. Chloe held it limply, her eyes half-closed as she slouched at her kitchen island. She rested her chin on the cool granite, squishing her cheeks together. With her free hand, she began peeling a clementine, methodically removing the tiniest strands of white pith. She lined the peels up in a perfectly straight row. The card boasted a DJ, an open bar, and a photo booth. Chloe exhaled loudly, a long rush of air that barely parted her lips. She poked at the fruit, not actually hungry. The steady drip-drip-drip of the faucet echoed in the quiet apartment. She watched a single drop form, swell, and fall into the stainless steel basin. She turned the invitation face down, resting her forehead on the back of the thick paper, waiting for the hours to pass.

I opened the mailbox and pulled out a stack of supermarket coupons, a credit card pre-approval, and a crisp white envelope from my old high school. Back inside, I dropped the pile onto my desk. Silver Anniversary Reunion. I sat down and picked up a ballpoint pen, clicking the top. Click-clack. Click-clack. I stared at the blank RSVP line. The silence in the room was absolute. I started doodling on the corner of the invitation, drawing tiny, overlapping circles until the glossy paper began to tear under the ink. Click-clack. I leaned back, letting my legs stretch out and cross at the ankles. I could picture the gymnasium, the limp balloons, the forced conversations about mortgages and cholesterol. I spun the pen around my thumb, dropped it, and watched it roll off the desk. I didn't bother leaning down to pick it up.

Marcus sat on the porch swing, pushing off the floorboards with one foot to maintain a slow, rocking momentum. In his lap sat a formal invitation to the Eastside High reunion. He traced the embossed eagle mascot with a lazy finger, feeling the ridges. A squirrel darted across the lawn, stopped, twitched its tail, and darted up an oak tree. Marcus watched it until it disappeared into the canopy. He let his head fall back against the wooden slats of the swing, staring up at the peeling white paint of the porch ceiling. The chains of the swing creaked with rhythmic predictability. Squeak, sway, squeak, sway. The invitation fluttered slightly in the breeze. He placed his phone over it to weigh it down, crossing his arms over his chest and letting out a long, slow sigh that dissolved into the quiet, stagnant afternoon air.

The thick envelope arrived via certified mail, which was incredibly dramatic for a ten-year high school reunion. I signed for it, walked into my living room, and collapsed back-first onto the mattress I still hadn't put a frame under. The ceiling was entirely blank. I held the invitation straight up in the air, right above my face, staring at the cursive font. If I dropped it, it would smack me right on the nose. I lowered my arm, letting the paper rest on my chest. I stared at the ceiling again. I tried to see shapes in the plaster texturing. That one looked like a cloud. That one looked like a slightly different cloud. My phone chimed with a reminder to buy groceries. I reached up and rubbed my eyes, letting my hands drag down my face, pulling the skin taut.

Sitting in the laundromat, Jenna watched her clothes tumble behind the thick glass door of the dryer. Round and round they went, an endless cycle of tumbling fabric. In her hand was a crumpled flyer pulled from her mail pile—an invite to her high school class reunion next month. She rested her elbows on her knees and her chin in her hands. The dryer hummed a low, vibrating note. Jenna kicked at a piece of lint on the scuffed floor, scooting it left, then right, then left again. Her eyes glazed over as a pair of blue jeans flopped over a gray towel inside the machine. The neon sign in the window buzzed intermittently. She folded the reunion flyer in half, then in quarters, then into a tiny, thick square, tossing it idly from one hand to the other while waiting for the timer to buzz.

I swiped past the Evite for the 'Class of 2012 Reunion Bash' on my phone. The attached video featured bouncing text and confetti, but I kept my device on mute. Sitting at a bus stop, waiting for the 414, I slouched deeply on the cold metal bench, letting my posture dissolve. I locked my eyes onto a crack in the pavement directly between my shoes. An ant was crawling out of it, carrying a microscopic white crumb. I tracked its incredibly slow journey toward a discarded gum wrapper. When it finally arrived, I looked up at the empty street. No bus in sight. The traffic light clicked green, but there were no cars to pass through. I unlocked my phone, opened the reunion invitation again, stared blankly at the RSVP options, and slowly locked the screen, letting my arm drop heavily against my leg.

Elias stared at the blinking cursor on his spreadsheet for the fourteenth consecutive minute. He picked a piece of lint off his gray slacks, flicked it onto the carpet, and rested his heavy chin in his palm. The rhythmic ticking of the wall clock echoed in the silent office. When the delivery guy dropped a massive bouquet of red roses on his desk, Elias merely blinked. There was no card tucked among the thorns. He rotated the glass vase exactly three degrees to the left, aligning it with the edge of his monitor, and sighed, a long exhale that disturbed a loose petal. He picked up his pen, clicked it open, clicked it shut, and then went back to watching the cursor blink against the glaring white screen, waiting for five o'clock to finally arrive.

I had already counted the water droplets racing down the living room window. Fifty-two drops had made it all the way to the sill. The television played an infomercial on mute, a man in a sweater enthusiastically chopping vegetables in a silent frenzy. A sharp knock at the door broke the quiet, and I dragged my feet across the carpet, hoping for a neighbor needing sugar or a misplaced package. A delivery woman shoved a bundle of yellow daisies into my arms and left. I rummaged through the damp cellophane, turning the stems over in my hands. Blank. Nothing. I tossed the crinkling wrapper into the trash bin and placed the flowers in a water glass on the counter. Slumping back onto the sofa, I picked up the remote, flipped through forty channels of static, and went back to watching the rain.

Martha spent her shift watching the dust motes drift through the beam of sunlight near the metal detector. She leaned back in her squeaky leather chair, tracing the familiar grooves on the edge of the security desk with a chipped thumbnail. When a courier abandoned a pristine arrangement of white lilies on her counter, she didn't even sit up straight. She poked at the waxy petals with the tip of her flashlight, searching for a note or a sender's name. Finding absolutely nothing, she pushed the ceramic pot to the far corner of the desk, right next to the stack of forgotten visitor badges. She let out a prolonged breath that puffed her bangs upward, folded her arms across her chest, and returned her gaze to the empty lobby doors, counting the alternating black and white tiles on the floor.

The ceiling fan rotated at a sluggish pace, the blades casting lazy shadows across my bedroom wall. I had scrolled through my entire social media feed twice, stopping only to watch a dog chase its tail for twenty seconds. The doorbell chimed. Shuffling downstairs in my mismatched socks, I opened the door to find a bouquet of purple orchids sitting on the welcome mat. I picked them up, inspecting the purple blooms. I shook the arrangement, but no hidden envelope fell to the porch. I carried the potted plant inside and set it on the dining table next to a pile of junk mail. I leaned my forehead against the cool granite of the kitchen island, tracing invisible circles on the surface with my index finger, listening to the hum of the refrigerator.

Julian lay flat on his back, observing a water stain on the ceiling that vaguely resembled a lopsided teapot. He pressed the button to raise his bed, lowered it, and raised it again, listening to the mechanical whirring of the mattress. A nurse bustled in, placed a crystal vase overflowing with pink carnations on the bedside tray, and vanished before he could speak. Julian peeled apart the green foliage, feeling around the wet stems for a tag. The plastic sticks were bare. He flopped his head back onto the stiff pillow, staring at the petals. He tapped his index fingers together, matching the rhythm of his heart monitor. Beep. Beep. Beep. He closed his eyes, wondering if he could fall asleep just to pass another hour, but his brain refused to power down in the sterile quiet.

Stirring my black coffee for the tenth time, I watched the liquid swirl into an infinite, dark funnel. The cafe was empty except for the barista polishing the espresso machine with agonizing slowness. I rested my chin on the sticky tabletop. Suddenly, a floral shop employee rushed in, slammed a sprawling arrangement of sunflowers onto my table, and bolted out the door into the wind. I dug through the bright yellow petals, turning the heavy vase around. No card. No explanation. I tore a napkin into tiny, perfectly even squares, arranging them in a grid around the base of the glass. The vibrant blooms towered over me, yet I felt entirely unmoved. I rested my face against the windowpane, letting out a heavy sigh that fogged the glass, and began drawing squiggles in the condensation.

Chloe threw her geometry textbook onto the rug, the thud completely muffled by the plush carpet. She rolled onto her back, dangling her head off the edge of the mattress so the world appeared upside down. Her mother walked in, set a bundle of blue hydrangeas wrapped in brown paper on her dresser, and shut the door. Chloe didn't bother sitting up. She lazily reached out a foot, using her toes to pull open a drawer, then pushed it shut. She finally slid off the bed and sifted through the rustling paper surrounding the flowers. No tag. She shrugged, grabbed a stray scrunchie, and tied it around the stems. She collapsed into her beanbag chair, grabbed a loose thread on her jeans, and began pulling it, watching the seam slowly unravel as the afternoon sun crept across the floorboards.

I sat in the dressing room, peeling a piece of chipped polish off my thumb. The play didn't start for another two hours. I had already organized my makeup brushes by height, then by thickness, and finally by color. A stagehand cracked the door open, thrust a bundle of baby's breath and crimson roses into my lap, and vanished down the corridor. I rummaged through the prickly stems, scratching my wrist in the process. There was no envelope nestled inside. I tossed the bouquet onto the vanity, next to my half-empty water bottle. Slouching in the velvet chair, I pulled up a solitaire game on my phone, mindlessly dragging red cards onto black cards until I lost. I locked the screen, letting my arms hang limp at my sides, and listened to the distant, muffled sound of footsteps.

The luxury boutique was completely devoid of customers. Vivienne leaned her elbows on the glass jewelry counter, puffing her cheeks out and blowing the air up to move a stray blonde curl from her forehead. A delivery boy pushed through the heavy glass doors, thrusting a massive bouquet of peonies into her arms before disappearing down the avenue. Vivienne carefully poked through the soft pink petals, her manicured fingers searching for a note. Finding the arrangement entirely anonymous, she walked it over to the register, setting it beside a stack of folded tissue paper. She let out a long, droning exhale, crossing her arms as she stared at the empty street outside. She began tapping her designer shoe against the marble floor, counting the seconds until the clock struck six and she could finally lock the doors.

The silence in the archives was so profound I could hear my own eyelashes brush against my skin when I blinked. I had alphabetized the returned periodicals three times. When a courier dropped a potted gardenia on the circulation desk, I didn't flinch. I slowly turned the pot in a full circle, scanning the soil and the waxy green leaves. Nothing. I pushed the heavy ceramic container to the edge of the desk. Resting my head on a stack of reference books, I stared at a fly buzzing erratically against the high windowpanes. It bumped the glass, backed up, and bumped it again. I watched its futile efforts for several minutes, my chin resting heavily in my palm, wishing a patron would come in and ask a question, even a stupid one, just to break the agonizing stillness.

Marcus stared at the seatback pocket in front of him, having already read the emergency evacuation card cover to cover. The plane had been grounded on the tarmac for an hour. A flight attendant walked down the aisle, inexplicably handing him a small bunch of wild daisies wrapped in a rubber band, offering no explanation before continuing her march. Marcus picked at the rubber band, snapping it against his wrist. He turned the daisies upside down, shaking them over his tray table, but no hidden message fluttered out. He shoved the stems into the empty cup holder, slumped down into his narrow seat, and crossed his arms over his chest. He spent the next twenty minutes watching the tiny, blinking red light on the wing through the scratched acrylic window, letting out a prolonged, heavy breath through his nose.

The documentary about the history of cardboard was doing nothing to keep me awake, but changing the channel required reaching the remote at the foot of the bed. I simply laid there, watching brown boxes move along a conveyor belt. The concierge knocked softly, letting himself in to place an extravagant arrangement of tropical lilies on the credenza. Once the door clicked shut, I dragged myself across the plush carpet to inspect them. I dug my fingers into the damp oasis foam at the base, searching for a tiny plastic card holder. Nothing at all. I left the flowers by the television and fell back onto the mattress. I stared at the stucco ceiling, tracing the bumpy patterns with my eyes, trying to find shapes in the plaster while the monotone narrator on the television explained the invention of the corrugated flap.

Arthur leaned against the hood of his sedan, tracking a lone ant crawling across the windshield wiper. The demolition crew had been setting up the wrecking ball for forty-five minutes. He checked his phone. No new messages. He locked it, unlocked it, swiped left, locked it again. Across the lawn, his sister dabbed her eyes with a tissue as the foreman shouted instructions. Arthur let out a long, slow exhale, puffing his cheeks out, before sinking down to crouch by the front tire. He picked up a stray pebble and tossed it at the curb, missing. He grabbed another pebble. Clink. The heavy machinery finally roared to life, drowning out the cicadas. Arthur checked his watch again, calculating if he could beat the lunch rush at the deli down the street once the roof finally caved in.

I dragged the toe of my sneaker through the gravel, drawing a crooked figure eight, then erasing it. Mom insisted we all come out to see the old farmhouse go down, but the bulldozer had blown a gasket or something. We had been standing in the July heat for over an hour. I swatted a fly away from my neck and stared at the peeling yellow paint of my old bedroom window. Nothing. I pulled a blade of grass, splitting it down the middle with my thumbnail. "How much longer?" I mumbled, shifting my weight to my left leg. Mom hushed me. I rolled my eyes, tilting my head back to watch a cloud shaped vaguely like a toaster drift across the sky. I wondered if I had set the DVR. I let out a heavy sigh and started drawing another gravel eight.

Maya sat on the concrete stoop across the street, resting her chin heavily in her palms. The excavator was tearing into the brick facade of her childhood townhouse, making a horrendous racket. She tapped her boots in a steady, monotonous rhythm against the curb. Tap, tap, tap. A brick tumbled down, shattering a windowpane on the first floor. Maya didn't blink. She pulled out a tube of lip balm, carefully unscrewing the cap, applying a thick layer, and screwing it back on. She read the tiny printed ingredients on the label: beeswax, coconut oil, peppermint. The foreman shouted over his radio. Maya leaned her head against the nearest lamppost, watching a pigeon peck at a discarded French fry in the gutter. It took the bird four tries to get the fry down. Maya checked her fingernails, making a mental note to schedule a manicure.

The sea breeze whipped around my jacket, but I was entirely focused on the loose thread hanging off my left cuff. I pulled it, watching the fabric pucker slightly, then snapped it off. Behind me, the roar of the tractor echoed as it ripped through the sunroom where I used to play with my toy boats. I leaned against the guardrail, letting my head loll to the side. The waves were washing up on the rocks in a steady, predictable loop. Crash, hiss, retreat. Crash, hiss, retreat. I pulled my phone from my pocket and started a game of solitaire, quickly moving a red seven onto a black eight. My brother patted my shoulder, whispering something about the end of an era. I nodded vacantly, my thumb hovering over the screen as I searched for a black five. "Yeah," I said, suppressing a yawn.

Elias kicked a pinecone. It skittered across the dirt road, bouncing into a ditch. He walked over, retrieved it, and kicked it again. The demolition crew had cordoned off the old A-frame cabin with bright yellow tape. Elias leaned his back against a massive oak, crossing his arms and sliding down until he was sitting in the dirt. He picked up a twig and started snapping it into perfectly even, one-inch pieces. Snap. Snap. Snap. A loud crack echoed as the backhoe took out the front porch. Elias didn't look up from his pile of twigs. He gathered the little wooden pieces and began arranging them into a perfectly symmetrical square on the ground. When the square was finished, he added a roof to make a little stick house. Then he swept his hand through it, destroying it, and started over.

I had already counted all the cacti within a fifty-foot radius. There were seventeen. Now I was counting the ridges on the plastic cap of my water bottle. The bulldozer's engine hummed in a low, constant drone as it chewed through the stucco walls of the old ranch house. Dust plumed into the air. I let out a long breath through my nose, crossing my arms over my chest and shifting my weight from one leg to the other. Aunt Helen was filming the entire thing on her tablet, completely engrossed. I stared blankly at the back of her head, tracking a single grey hair that stuck straight up from her scalp. I checked the time. 10:14 AM. I waited what felt like twenty minutes, looked again. 10:16 AM. I groaned softly, tilting my face toward the sun and closing my eyes.

Chloe sat in the passenger seat of her car with the window rolled down, blowing a giant pink bubble until it popped against her nose. She peeled the sticky gum off her skin while the wrecking crew smashed through the living room of her childhood split-level. The noise was deafening, but Chloe just cranked the radio volume up a few notches, drumming her fingers aimlessly against the steering wheel. She adjusted the rearview mirror, checking her teeth, then flipped the sun visor down and back up. Down, up. Down, up. A massive section of the roof collapsed in a cloud of drywall dust. Chloe let out a long, drawn-out puff of air, resting her cheek against the cool glass of the window. She watched a squirrel run along the telephone wire, tracking its progress until it disappeared into a cluster of oak leaves.

They were imploding the old housing project at noon. We stood on the observation deck three blocks away. I rested my elbows on the railing and rested my chin on my folded hands, staring out at the skyline. Someone had carved "J+K" into the metal rail. I traced the letters with my index finger, over and over, smoothing out the rough edges of the scratches. The mayor was giving a speech through a crackling megaphone about urban renewal and progress. I opened my mouth in a wide, jaw-cracking yawn, bringing a hand up to cover it a second too late. Sirens wailed, signaling the one-minute warning. I pulled my jacket tighter, watching a delivery truck navigate the traffic below. I tried to guess how many boxes were in the back of the truck based on how low the chassis sat on the tires.

Julian stood on the meticulously manicured lawn of the neighboring estate, twirling a silver pocket watch by its chain. The heavy steel ball swung through the air, crashing into the ornate turret of his grandfather’s Victorian home. Wood splintered. Glass shattered. Julian didn't flinch. He caught the watch in his palm, popped it open, watched the second hand tick a full circle, and snapped it shut. He repeated the motion. Open, watch, close. Open, watch, close. A stray dog wandered past the police barricade. Julian focused his entire attention on the animal, watching it sniff a fire hydrant, lift its leg, and trot away. He checked his phone, swiping through three pages of unread emails without opening a single one. He let out a low, whistling sigh, shifting his weight and leaning heavily on his umbrella as the second wall came down.

The operator ate a sandwich, taking his sweet time while the engine idled next to our old single-wide. I sat on my truck's hood, peeling a sticker off an apple. I scraped the gummy residue with my thumbnail, rolling it into a tiny ball. The metal siding groaned as the machine finally nudged it. I tossed the apple from my left hand to my right. Left, right, left, right. My cousin was crying beside me, gripping my sleeve. I offered her the apple. She shook her head. I took a bite, chewing slowly, staring at the faded plastic flamingo still stuck in the dirt out front. I wondered how many bites it would take to finish the fruit. I took another bite. Seven, maybe eight. I sighed, crossing my ankles.

Rain pattered against the umbrella Marcus held over his head. The bulldozer’s tracks churned up the muddy ground, slowly advancing on the stilted wooden bungalow. Marcus stared blankly at the mud. He began counting the raindrops dripping from the edge of his umbrella. One, two, three. He lost track and started over. One, two, three. He shifted the umbrella to his left hand, shoving his right deep into his pocket to jingle a handful of loose coins. Chink, chink. The heavy machinery roared, tearing through the porch where his father used to sit. Marcus tilted his head back, letting out a long puff of air that ruffled his lower lip. He stared at the grey sky, tracing the outline of a particularly dark raincloud. He pulled out his phone, checked the battery percentage, and shoved it back into his pocket.

The wrecking ball swung, completely missing the side of the stone townhouse. I let out a loud groan, dropping my head into my hands. We had been standing on the pavement for two hours. I started pacing the length of the barricade. Six steps to the left, turn, six steps to the right. My sister was taking photos with a vintage camera, adjusting the focus ring meticulously. I picked up a flattened soda can from the sidewalk and kicked it. It clattered against a lamppost. I walked over and kicked it again, chasing it down the gutter. The wrecking ball finally made contact with a dull thud, sending a shower of bricks onto the street. I didn't bother turning around. I pulled a receipt from my pocket, folding it in half, then in quarters, then into eighths, pressing the creases flat with my thumb.

I traced the peeling laminate on my sister’s kitchen table with my thumbnail, picking at a stubborn crumb. The clock above the stove ticked with an agonizing slowness, each second stretching like chewed bubblegum. Beside me, seven-year-old Lily narrated a rambling saga about her crayons that I tuned out ten minutes ago. "Mhmm, wow," I murmured, resting my heavy chin in my palm. My eyelids drooped as I watched her push a magenta wax stick across the construction paper. I let out a long, hollow exhale, wishing literally anything would happen to break the afternoon’s endless static. "And this is my secret friend, Barnaby," Lily announced. My eyes snapped open. I sat up straight, the heavy fog instantly vanishing from my brain. Staring back at me from the paper was a creature with three mismatched horns and a striped tail—my exact secret friend from twenty years ago.

Marcus slouched on the floral sofa, endlessly scrolling through a feed he’d refreshed four times already. The family reunion buzzed around him in a blur of small talk. He locked his phone screen, stared at his reflection, and let his head loll backward against the cushions. He counted the water stains on the ceiling—fourteen in total. At his feet, his five-year-old niece Chloe was sprawled on the rug, furiously scratching a marker against a sketchbook. Marcus let out a slow, rhythmic sigh, tapping his sneakers against the coffee table leg. "Look at Pip," Chloe chirped, holding up her pad. Marcus stopped tapping. The breath caught in his throat. Sketched in jagged blue ink was a floating top hat with a single googly eye, precisely as Marcus used to draw him.

I sat in the plastic waiting room chair, swinging my legs to make my heels softly thud against the base. The magazines on the table were all from three years ago. Every few minutes, I pulled my phone out just to check the time, groaning inwardly when I realized only two minutes had passed since my last check. Beside me, little Emma hummed a flat, repetitive tune while scribbling on a clinic notepad. I rested my forehead against the cool cinderblock wall, wishing for a fire alarm or anything to disrupt the absolute stillness of the afternoon. "Auntie, see my guardian?" she asked. I peeled one eye open, ready to offer a half-hearted nod. Instead, my heart hammered against my ribs. Pictured on the paper was a wolf with butterfly wings—the exact phantom protector I used to whisper to every night.

Elena rested her cheek against the dining table, watching a stray dust bunny drift across the floor. The ticking grandfather clock in the hallway felt like a hammer striking in a relentless, slow rhythm. She picked up a stray green colored pencil, balancing it on her index finger, watching it tip and fall. Pick up, balance, fall. Her niece, Maya, was quiet across the table, hunched over a sheet of printer paper. Elena exhaled a long stream of air that ruffled her bangs. She grabbed the pencil again, craving the end of the afternoon. "His name is Mr. Buttons," Maya said, sliding the paper across the polished wood. Elena lazily dragged her gaze downward, but her whole body suddenly went rigid. Staring back at her was a bear made entirely of patched burlap, wearing the identical lopsided bowtie Elena had invented in kindergarten.

I stirred the ice in my empty water glass with a plastic straw, watching the cubes melt into small puddles. The diner was empty except for a waitress wiping down the counter for the fifth time. I slouched deeper into the vinyl booth, tracing the sticky remnants of a syrup stain with my pinky. Across from me, my niece Sophie was fiercely occupied with a stack of paper placemats and a box of crayons. I rested my chin in both hands, staring blankly at the neon sign buzzing in the window, its red light flickering in a slow, hypnotic pulse. "Look at the star-man," Sophie murmured, pushing a grease-stained placemat toward me. I blinked heavily, dragging my focus from the window. The heavy fog lifted in an instant. Drawn in frantic yellow strokes was a figure with a star for a head, clutching a rusted umbrella. My star-man.

David lay flat on his back on the rug, tossing a tennis ball straight up into the air and catching it. Up and down. Up and down. The rhythmic thwack against his palm was the only sound in the house, aside from the light scratching of his niece’s pastels. He let the ball roll away, interlacing his fingers over his stomach while he stared blankly at the stucco ceiling. He tried to find shapes in the textured bumps, settling on one that vaguely resembled a lumpy potato. Time seemed to pool around him, thick and unmoving. "I drew a picture of Glimmer," his niece announced, blocking his view of the ceiling. David let out a heavy breath and focused on the paper held inches from his nose. He scrambled backward, heart pounding. There, perfectly rendered, was a girl with glowing silver hair and a cloak made of autumn leaves.

I slumped in the passenger seat of the parked car, watching rain streak down the windshield in fat, lazy drops. My sister had run into the grocery store twenty minutes ago. I drummed my fingers against the dashboard, leaning my head against the cold glass. From the backseat, my niece hummed, completely engrossed in her drawing tablet. I unbuckled my seatbelt, buckled it again, and let out a loud groan, wishing I was absolutely anywhere else. I closed my eyes, counting backward from one hundred just to give my brain a task. "Do you like him?" a small voice piped up from behind my headrest. I twisted around, eyes half-open, expecting a crude sketch of a house or a cat. Instead, the tablet screen glowed with an illustration of a tortoise wearing a miniature top hat and monocle—the exact friend I used to have tea parties with.

Sitting at the edge of the sandbox, Julian dragged a stick through the dry dirt, carving meaningless squiggles before erasing them with his shoe. He checked his watch, noting that only three minutes had passed since he last looked. He propped his heavy head in his hands, watching the neighborhood kids swing with a glazed expression. His niece pattered over, clutching a crumpled piece of paper she’d scavenged. Julian offered a slow, unenthusiastic nod as she shoved the paper into his lap. He didn't really look at it until a splash of violet caught his eye. He sat bolt upright, tossing the stick aside. The drawing depicted a shadowy figure with abnormally long, spindly fingers and a wide, stitched smile. It was Mr. Smiles, the creature Julian had whispered his secrets to in the dark.

I flicked the plastic tab on the juice box back and forth until it finally snapped off, then flicked the tiny piece across the patio. The afternoon sun beat down, making the air thick and heavy. I slouched in the canvas lawn chair, mindlessly picking at a loose thread on my shorts while my niece colored with watercolors at the picnic table. I sighed deeply, staring at the motionless leaves on the oak tree, feeling like the day had stretched into a decade. I laid my head back, closing my eyes and letting out a long, pathetic hum. "Look at my fishy," she said, tapping my knee. I dragged my heavy eyelids open, glancing down. The breath rushed out of my lungs. Painted on the damp paper was a massive koi fish, but instead of scales, it was covered in mechanical gears—my childhood imaginary invention, Sprocket.

Sarah lay face down on the guest room bed, her arms dangling loosely off the sides of the mattress. The sheer lack of activity in the house felt like a physical weight pressing her into the duvet. She lazily kicked her feet in the air, watching a moth bump repeatedly against the window pane. "Thud. Thud. Thud," she whispered, mimicking the insect's futile efforts. She rolled onto her back, staring at the blank ceiling, feeling her mind turn to mush. From the floor, her niece thrust a spiral-bound notebook upward. Sarah reached down with a limp arm, dragging the notebook onto her chest without lifting her head. She eventually forced her eyes to focus on the page. She gasped, suddenly wide awake. Sketched in charcoal was a towering tree with an old, bearded face etched into the bark—the exact guardian she used to talk to.

I dragged my sneakers across the airport carpet, leaving long trails in the fibrous material. Our flight had been delayed again, and I had officially run out of ways to entertain myself. I slumped against the departure gate counter, resting my forehead against the cool metal barrier, letting out an exasperated puff of air. My eight-year-old niece sat cross-legged beside my duffel bag, humming happily as she dragged a stylus across her tablet. I pulled my phone out, swiped between the home screens five times without opening an app, and shoved it back into my pocket. "Uncle, see the knight?" she asked, tugging my pant leg. I crouched down with a heavy sigh, peering at the screen. A jolt of electricity shot down my spine. Staring back at me was a warrior clad in violet armor, holding a shield shaped like a crescent moon. Sir Alaric.

Arthur sat on the porch steps, peeling a single blade of grass into thinner strips until it was just green mush on his fingers. The humid summer afternoon dragged on, thick and silent. He rested his chin on his fists, staring at a pebble on the driveway, willing it to move just so something would happen. Beside him, his niece Clara was aggressively applying chalk to the concrete patio. Arthur let out a long, low whistle, tapping his boot in a slow, monotonous rhythm. "Finished," Clara declared, stepping back with hands covered in pink dust. Arthur turned his head lazily, forcing a weak smile to his lips. The smile vanished instantly. Etched into the gray stone was a massive, floating jellyfish with glowing yellow eyes and a crown of daisies. He scrambled to his feet, staring at the exact phantom that used to float above his childhood bed.

As Mr. Henderson prattled on about the 'Director of Operations' vacancy, I meticulously shaded the thirty-second square on my graph paper. Beside me, Sarah sat ramrod straight, her pen hovering over her legal pad like a hawk ready to dive. She nodded at every buzzword—synergy, optimization, deliverables. I let out a long, slow breath, resting my chin heavily in my palm. The fluorescent light above emitted a faint, high-pitched hum that matched the exact frequency of my approaching migraine. "Who wants to spearhead the Q3 analysis?" Henderson asked, looking between us. Sarah’s hand shot up instantly. I traced my pen over a previously shaded square, pressing hard enough to tear the thin paper, watching the clock’s red second hand sweep with agonizing slowness toward five.

Liam rested the back of his head against the beige wall of the waiting area, tracking a solitary ant marching across the baseboard. Three feet away, Mark frantically flipped through a stack of flashcards, muttering corporate statistics under his breath. The promotion to Senior Analyst hung between them, a supposedly glittering prize. Liam let his eyes slide out of focus, his right leg jouncing rhythmically against the metal chair leg. Thump, thump, thump. He picked a piece of lint off his trousers, rolled it into a tiny ball, and flicked it onto the carpet. Mark shot him a glaring look, smoothing his perfectly ironed tie. Liam offered a weak, half-hearted shrug and tilted his head toward the ceiling, silently attempting to calculate exactly how many acoustic tiles covered the room. Only forty-seven minutes until his lunch break.

"If I get the Regional Manager spot, I’m overhauling the entire filing system," Greg said, his eyes practically vibrating with caffeine. I stared at the dark surface of my lukewarm coffee, swirling it around the paper cup just to watch the tiny bubbles pop. "That's great, Greg," I murmured, leaning against the breakroom counter. My gaze drifted to the vending machine, studying the coils holding the stale powdered donuts. Greg continued mapping out his grand vision, chopping the air with his hands. A heavy sigh escaped my lips, sinking my shoulders down an inch further. I blinked slowly, feeling a deep, leaden weight behind my eyes. The coffee tasted like copper and old water. I wondered, idly, if it would be socially acceptable to simply lay down on the linoleum floor and close my eyes until five o'clock rolled around.

The regional director’s face filled the primary screen, her mouth moving in a continuous loop of corporate jargon regarding the open Vice President role. David minimized the window until her face was the size of a postage stamp. In the gallery view, his rival, Chloe, nodded furiously, typing notes with aggressive enthusiasm. David clicked into a new tab, scrolling endlessly through pictures of vintage wristwatches. He rested his cheek against his fist, feeling the skin of his face squish upward. He clicked back to the meeting just long enough to paste a faint, polite smile on his face, unmuted his microphone to say, "Absolutely, Susan, great point," and instantly muted again. He turned his attention back to his browser, clicking onto a Wikipedia article about the history of the stapler. He had read three paragraphs before he realized he wasn't absorbing a single word.

The spreadsheet on my monitor blurred into a meaningless wall of gray and green cells. Tomorrow morning, both Jenkins and I would sit before the board to pitch ourselves for the Senior Developer role. Across the aisle, Jenkins was still hammering away at his keyboard, constructing elaborate PowerPoint transitions. I picked up a rubber band from my desk tray and stretched it between my thumb and index finger, plucking it like a tiny, out-of-tune guitar. Twang. Twang. I spun my chair in a slow, squeaky circle, staring at the ceiling tiles as they rotated above me. The silence of the empty office was deafening, broken only by Jenkins’ frantic typing. I slumped forward, resting my forehead against the cool, smooth surface of my desk. I closed my eyes, letting the hum of the hard drive wash over me like a lullaby.

Elena rested her elbow on the car window sill, her chin propped heavily in her hand as traffic crawled along the interstate. Today was the day management would announce whether she or Tom got the Lead Designer gig. She let out a long breath, fogging up the glass, and aimlessly drew a smiley face in the condensation with her index finger. The radio played a morning talk show, but the voices sounded like the drone of angry bees. She flicked the turn signal on, watching the green arrow blink rhythmically on her dashboard. Tick. Tick. Tick. She counted the seconds between each flash. Tom had likely been at the office for two hours already, kissing up to the art directors. Elena yawned, stretching her jaw wide, her eyes drifting to a plastic bag tumbling lazily across the asphalt in the morning breeze.

"Why do you believe you are the best fit for Head Chef?" the owner asked, steepled fingers resting on his mahogany desk. Julian, sitting to my left, launched into a passionate monologue about farm-to-table sourcing and culinary innovation. I stared at the second hand of the grandfather clock in the corner. Its loud tick echoed in my ears, completely drowning out Julian's ambitious menu proposals. I picked at a loose thread on my apron, wrapping it tightly around my finger until the tip turned purple, then slowly unwrapping it. "And you?" the owner asked, turning his gaze to me. I blinked, pulling myself back from a daydream about watching paint dry. "I make good food," I said, my voice flat. I shifted my weight, slumping slightly in the stiff-backed chair, and went back to watching the steady, agonizing march of the clock's brass hand.

The company mixer was ostensibly a celebration, but everyone knew it was the final proving ground for the Managing Partner vacancy. Marcus watched his colleague, Evelyn, glide through the room, laughing loudly at every joke the senior partners made. Marcus stood by the refreshment table, shifting his weight from his left foot to his right. He picked up a plastic sword from a platter of cheese cubes, using it to gently poke at a decorative ice sculpture. The ice yielded slightly. He poked it again. The jazz band in the corner played a soft, unending melody that seemed to melt into the background chatter, creating a wall of white noise. Marcus let out a heavy sigh, his eyes glazing over as he stared at the condensation dripping down a silver punch bowl. He checked his watch. He had been there for twelve minutes.

"It’s going to come down to the quarterly metrics, I just know it," Brian said, jabbing his fork into his salad for emphasis. We were competing for the Shift Supervisor role, and Brian hadn't stopped talking about it since Tuesday. I rested my cheek on my fist, stirring my soup with agonizing slowness. A solitary crouton spun in circles, trapped in the gentle whirlpool of broth. "Mm," I offered, not bothering to look up. I watched a pigeon waddle across the windowsill outside, pecking at an invisible crumb. Brian pulled out a printed spreadsheet, laying it over his placemat. "Look at the projected yields," he urged. I let my eyelids droop, fighting a massive yawn that threatened to crack my jaw. The scrape of his fork against the plastic bowl became the only sound in the world, stretching my sanity thin.

The entire sales floor gathered around the main podium. The branch manager cleared his throat, holding the envelope that contained the name of the new Team Lead. Beside him stood Arthur and Rachel. Rachel practically bounced on her heels, her hands clasped tightly under her chin. Arthur slouched against a nearby desk, his arms crossed limply over his chest. He spent the manager's introductory speech counting the individual perforations on the ceiling tiles. When he lost his place at seventy-two, he simply sighed and started over. The manager's voice rose to a crescendo, praising their hard work. Arthur dragged his gaze down to his shoes, noting a scuff mark on the left toe. He wondered if he had shoe polish at home. As the manager finally shouted Rachel's name, Arthur let out a long exhale, offering a slow, rhythmic golf clap.

The elevator chimed at the fourth floor, and Diane stepped in, her arms laden with presentation binders for the Creative Director pitch. "Big day," she chirped, vibrating with nervous energy. I leaned heavily against the polished steel wall of the cab, staring blankly at the digital floor indicator. "Yep," I replied, my voice devoid of inflection. The numbers ticked upward. Five. Six. Seven. I traced the faint outline of a smudge on the mirrored panel next to me, dragging my finger through the grease mark. Diane started reciting her opening hook, pacing in the confined space. I closed my eyes, letting the gentle, vibrating hum of the elevator car lull me into a momentary stupor. The ride felt like it was lasting an eternity. I mentally cataloged the contents of my refrigerator, trying to decide what I was going to eat for dinner.

The Chief Medical Officer position would be filled by morning. Dr. Aris sat at his desk, watching Dr. Lin across the hall as she frantically rearranged her medical journals, preparing her office for a potential upgrade. Aris rested his chin on his stacked hands, staring at a small potted succulent. He tapped his pen against the rim of the ceramic pot. Tap. Tap. Tap. The rhythm echoed hollowly in his quiet office. He picked up a paperclip, unbending it until it was a straight wire, then methodically bent it back into a perfect triangle. He let out a long, shuddering sigh, his eyes half-closed as the hospital intercom buzzed with overhead pages. None of the urgency reached him. He tossed the mangled paperclip into his trash can, rested his head back against his leather chair, and waited for the clock to strike five.

Mark leaned his head against the cold steel panel, his eyes tracing the tiny perforated holes of the intercom speaker for the seventh time. Forty-two holes in the outer ring, thirty-six in the next. He exhaled slowly, the breath whistling through his teeth. Across the small cube, Sarah was explaining the intricate details of her cat’s new dietary regimen. Mark nodded at what felt like appropriate intervals, though his gaze had drifted back to the digital floor indicator, permanently stuck on the number eight. He pulled out his phone, woke the screen, stared at the battery icon—down to fourteen percent—and put it back in his pocket without opening any apps. He picked at a loose thread on his left cuff. "So," Mark said, his voice flat as he watched a dust mote drift through the fluorescent light. "Does he like the chicken flavor, then?"

I’ve memorized the maximum capacity sign. 'Two thousand five hundred pounds, or roughly sixteen passengers.' Dave from Accounting and I hardly make up a fraction of that limit. For the past two hours and forty-seven minutes, Dave has been pacing a tight triangle. I’m sitting flat on the linoleum floor, tossing a crumpled gum wrapper up and catching it. Toss, catch. Toss, miss. It lands near Dave's polished oxfords. I don't bother picking it up. I stretch my legs out, staring at the scuff marks on the doors. "Do you think they forgot about us?" Dave asks again, wringing his hands. I let out a long, heavy exhale, tilting my head back against the mirror. I start mentally listing every state capital in alphabetical order just to give my brain something to chew on. Alabama, Montgomery. Alaska, Juneau. Arizona... what was Arizona again?

The instrumental version of 'The Girl from Ipanema' had looped through the overhead speakers exactly twenty-four times. Elena knew this because she had started making small scratches on the back of her leather notebook with a paperclip to keep track. Marcus sat in the opposite corner, arms crossed, eyes closed. Elena clicked her pen. Click-clack. Click-clack. Click-clack. Marcus shifted but didn't open his eyes. Elena sighed, a long deflation of air, and switched to tracing the faux-wood grain on the wall paneling with her index finger. The air was stale, smelling faintly of Marcus's morning coffee and ozone. She checked her wrist, watching the second hand sweep its agonizingly slow circle. It had been exactly three minutes since she last checked. She let her arm drop heavily to her side, leaning her forehead against the cool glass of the mirror.

Chloe keeps asking if we’re going to run out of oxygen. I stopped answering an hour ago, opting instead to give a noncommittal grunt while I play Snake on my phone. My thumb swipes the screen rhythmically. Up, left, down, right. The pixelated snake eats the square. I crash into the wall intentionally just to see the 'Game Over' screen, then hit restart. "Should we press the alarm button again?" Chloe asks. I drag my eyes away from the screen, blinking at the bright fluorescent lights overhead. I roll my shoulders, feeling an ache settling at the base of my neck. "They said they're working on it," I mumble, my voice flat. I shift my weight from my left foot to my right, staring blankly as the snake eats another pixel.

Greg had resorted to analyzing the elevator’s interior design. It was horribly outdated, a relic of the late nineties. He peeled a flake of dry paint from the handrail, rolling it between his thumb and forefinger until it crumbled into dust. Linda was sitting on her briefcase, reading a quarterly report by the dim emergency light. Greg paced two steps forward, turned on his heel, and took two steps back. He repeated this miniature patrol route six times before letting out a loud groan and sliding his back down the wall until he sat on the floor. He stretched his legs out, staring at the scuffed toes of his loafers. He pulled out a stray receipt from his pocket, folded it into a lopsided paper airplane, and tossed it weakly toward the doors. It nose-dived immediately. Greg rested his chin in his hand, watching it.

There’s a smudge on the brass handrail that looks vaguely like a poodle. I’ve been staring at it for so long that I’m starting to think it might be a terrier instead. Arthur is still talking about his lawn care routine. He’s been detailing the pros and cons of different fertilizers since minute forty-five. "And that's why you can't trust the big box store brands," he says, adjusting his tie. I nod slowly, letting my eyes glaze over. I pull a loose thread on the seam of my slacks, winding it tightly around my index finger until the tip turns purple, then unwinding it. I let my head loll back against the wall. The hum of the ventilation fan provides a steady, unchanging drone. I silently try to match my breathing to its mechanical rhythm, just to have a task to complete.

The silence between them had stretched so thin Jenna felt she could poke a hole through it. Todd was asleep in the corner, his head resting awkwardly against the control panel. Jenna sat cross-legged in the center of the car. She had taken a tube of red lipstick from her purse and drawn a crooked tic-tac-toe grid on the back of an old envelope. She played against herself. X in the center. O in the top right. X in the bottom left. She won every time, predictably. She capped the lipstick and tossed it back into her bag. She stared up at the ceiling hatch, wondering how difficult it would be to pry it open, not to escape, but just to see a different color besides the sterile beige of the walls. She checked her bare wrist, forgetting she hadn't worn a watch today.

Tap, tap, tap. The heel of my left shoe hits the linoleum. Simon shoots me a glaring look over the rim of his glasses. I stop tapping, but within ten seconds, my fingers take over, drumming a silent beat against my thigh. We’ve been trapped between the fourteenth and fifteenth floors long enough for me to memorize the exact pattern of the faux marble floor. Three gray veins, two black specks, one faint yellowish stain near the door. Simon sighs dramatically, wiping sweat from his forehead. I pull a hair tie off my wrist, stretch it out to its absolute limit, and let it snap back against my skin. The sharp sting is almost refreshing. I stretch it again. Snap. I gaze blankly at the emergency call button, entirely unmotivated to push it a fifth time just to hear the operator tell us to hold tight.

Liam had run out of complaints precisely two hours in. Now, he simply sat against the back wall, systematically popping the knuckles of each finger. Pop. Pop. Rachel lay flat on her back on the floor, staring directly at the fluorescent light fixture overhead. She tried to unfocus her eyes until the rectangular light split into two blurry shapes. When that lost its appeal, she started reciting the entirety of the Q3 marketing presentation in her head. Slide one: quarterly projections. Slide two: target demographics. She didn't even care about the presentation anymore. She just needed a sequence of words to drown out the mechanical hum of the stationary elevator. Liam shifted, his shoe squeaking against the floorboards. Rachel didn't move a muscle, letting out a long, heavy breath that ruffled the stray hairs falling across her face.

I’ve resorted to taking everything out of my wallet and putting it back in again. Loyalty cards, expired coupons, a receipt for a coffee I bought three weeks ago. I stack them neatly on my lap. Karen is leaning against the doors, her arms folded tightly. She hasn't said a word since the car jerked to a halt. I take out a slightly bent paperclip from my bag and begin straightening it. I bend it until it breaks into two jagged pieces. I drop the pieces onto my palm, rolling them around. The silence is thick, pressing into my ears. I look up at the digital display. Still stuck on floor 6. I look back down at the fragmented paperclip. I sort my credit cards by the expiration date, then shuffle them and sort them by color instead.

Tom sat with his knees pulled up to his chest, idly picking at the fraying hem of his jeans. Across from him, Angela was aggressively refreshing her email app, even though her phone clearly showed 'No Service' in the top corner. Tom rested his chin on his kneecaps. He started counting his own heartbeats, tapping his index finger against his ankle with every thud. He made it to two hundred and forty before losing track. He let out a long, shuddering sigh and let his head thunk softly against the elevator wall. He watched a single drop of condensation slowly slide down the chill metallic surface of the control panel. He traced its path with his eyes, mentally betting on whether it would hit the 'Door Open' button or the 'Close' button first. It hit the 'Open' button. The doors, naturally, remained sealed shut.

Jackson is pacing again. Four steps to the mirror, turn, four steps to the doors. I don't look up from the quarter I’m tossing into the air. It flips end over end, catching the dim emergency light, before landing with a dull smack in my palm. Heads. I toss it again. Tails. The metallic ringing is the only sound breaking the rhythmic thud of Jackson’s dress shoes. "Are you going to do that forever?" Jackson snaps, finally pausing in his march. I catch the coin one more time, closing my fist around it. I let out a slow, deflating breath and look up at him. "I don't know, Jackson. What else is there?" I lean my head against the cold steel of the wall, letting my eyes drift shut. The dull drone of the elevator shaft vibrates against my skull. I toss the coin again.

Mark dragged his spoon in slow, heavy circles through his lukewarm coffee, watching the brown liquid swirl in an endless, unchanging loop. The breakroom clock ticked, each second feeling like a physical weight pressing on his shoulders. He rested his chin in his palm, letting his eyelids droop as Sandra droned on about the new spreadsheet formatting. "And then I realized," she said, organizing the sugar packets by color, "that the lake in the background of my Zoom background is Lake Minnetonka. Camp Okoboji." Mark’s eyes dragged upward, focusing slightly. He blinked, the rhythmic tapping of his foot pausing. "Okoboji? I spent three Julys there," he muttered, finally straightening his spine a fraction of an inch as the unending grey of the afternoon cracked.

I had filled four entire Post-it notes with perfectly shaded microscopic squares. My spinning chair squeaked on the third rotation, and I kicked off the desk to start a fourth, staring blankly at the beige partition separating me from accounting. "Anyone else feel like the air conditioning is humming in B-flat?" I asked the ceiling. Over the partition, Greg’s head popped up, his chin resting heavily on his folded arms. "I was just counting the carpet stains," he replied, his voice flat. "Reminds me of the mess hall floor at Camp Whispering Pines." I stopped mid-spin, my foot planting firmly on the cheap carpet. "Whispering Pines? Cabin four?" I asked, my pen hovering over a fresh yellow square. "Cabin six," Greg said, suddenly standing up completely.

Sarah clicked her ballpoint pen—in, out, in, out—staring at the gallery of pixelated faces on her monitor. She inspected a slight chip in her thumbnail polish, tracing the jagged edge with her index finger while the quarterly compliance review stretched into its second hour. Muting her microphone, she let out a long, deflating exhale and typed into the private chat with Julian: *If he says 'synergy' again, I'm throwing my laptop out the window.* Julian replied: *It's worse than the endless morning announcements at Camp Timberwolf.* Sarah’s hand froze over her mouse. She leaned closer to the screen, reading the message twice. *Wait,* she typed back, her fingers moving with sudden, sharp purpose. *You know the Timberwolf chant?* The little typing bubbles appeared instantly.

The rhythmic shhh-clack, shhh-clack of the copy machine had become the entire soundtrack of my existence. I rested my forehead against the cool plastic of the document feeder, watching fifty copies of the revised employee handbook slide slowly into the tray. To my left, Maya was systematically clicking the caps on and off a row of dry-erase markers, her gaze fixed on the blank whiteboard. "Do you ever wonder how many copies it would take to build a bridge out of here?" she asked, her voice entirely devoid of inflection. "I built a bridge out of popsicle sticks once. Camp Hiawatha. Nineteen ninety-eight," I murmured, watching another paper slide out. Maya dropped the blue marker. It hit the linoleum with a sharp crack. "You were a Hiawatha kid?"

David sank deeper into the leather lobby chair, his posture dissolving until he was practically horizontal. He flipped a six-month-old issue of Dental Digest open, stared uncomprehendingly at a diagram of a molar, and let the glossy pages fall shut. Beside him, Chloe was meticulously peeling the label off her water bottle in tiny, exact strips. The receptionist hadn't moved in twenty minutes. "They’re going to find our skeletons here," David mumbled, tossing the magazine onto the glass table. "Just sitting here forever." Chloe didn't look up, continuing to scrape the adhesive with her thumbnail. "Feels like the timeout bench behind the mess hall at Camp Silverleaf." David sat up, the leather squeaking loudly in the silent room. "You got sent to the Silverleaf timeout bench too?"

I checked my watch. 2:14 PM. I could have sworn I last checked it an hour ago, but it had only been four minutes. I kicked a stray piece of cardboard across the concrete floor, watching it skid and stop in front of an endless aisle of identical brown boxes.
