Next to me, Liam was balancing a clipboard on his head, staring straight up at the fluorescent lights. "Box 402," I read, my voice echoing in the cavernous space. "Screws." Liam let the clipboard slide off his forehead, catching it limply. "Wow. Thrilling. Reminds me of sorting the arts and crafts beads at Camp Sunapee." I dropped my barcode scanner. It clattered loudly against the concrete. "Hold on," I said. "You survived the Sunapee bead sorting of '05?"

The brake lights ahead stretched out into a seemingly infinite sea of glowing red. Elena rested her cheek against the cool glass of the passenger window, letting out a breath that fogged the pane. Beside her, Tom drummed a slow, off-beat rhythm on the steering wheel, his eyes half-closed as the radio played the same pop song for the third time this afternoon. The car hadn't moved an inch in ten minutes. "We live here now," Elena stated softly, tracing a circle in the condensation on her window. "We are creatures of the highway." Tom stopped drumming and let his hands fall to his lap. "It's like the canoe traffic jam at Camp Waconda," he muttered. Elena's head snapped up from the glass. "You know about Waconda?"

I sat cross-legged on the damp grass, systematically pulling up individual blades and tearing them into microscopic green pieces. The facilitator, a guy in a polo shirt named Bryce, was talking about synergistic trust falls for what felt like the third consecutive century. I let out a long, slow breath, resting my heavy head in my hands. Beside me, Jenna was balancing an acorn on her knee, staring at it with intense, vacant focus. "If he makes us hold hands, I'm walking into the woods," she whispered, her voice totally flat. "The woods," I echoed softly. "Like the orientation hike at Camp Tall Trees." Jenna’s acorn tumbled into the grass. She turned to me, her eyes widening. "You went to Tall Trees? Did you have Counselor Dave?"

Arthur’s index finger moved in a mechanical rhythm on the keyboard, endlessly pasting values. He rubbed his tired eyes, feeling the grit behind his lids as row four thousand of the spreadsheet blurred into row four thousand and one. The office was suffocatingly quiet, save for the clicking of keys. Two desks down, Rita was leaning back so far in her chair she was almost parallel to the floor, balancing a yellow pencil precisely on her upper lip. "Row four thousand," Arthur announced to nobody, his tone hollow. Rita didn't drop the pencil. "It’s like counting the pinecones on the path to Cabin Seven at Camp Ockanickon," she mumbled around the wood. Arthur’s finger paused. He turned his head slowly. "Wait. You were at Ockanickon?"

Unfold the metal legs. Push down the seat. Place next to the previous chair. I had completed this sequence seventy-two times. The hotel ballroom stretched out in front of me, a vast expanse of patterned carpet that needed three hundred more chairs. I let my arms hang at my sides, my shoulders slumping under the weight of the endless afternoon. Chris was dragging two chairs across the floor, his sneakers squeaking loudly in the empty cavern. "Unfold. Place. Repeat," he mumbled, staring at the ceiling tiles. "It’s like setting up the folding benches for the talent show at Camp Kawanhee." I stopped mid-unfold, the metal clanking loudly as I let the seat drop. I stood up straight. "Kawanhee? You mean the one by the lake in Maine?"

The trade show floor had thinned out hours ago, leaving behind a humming silence of distant air conditioning. Marcus rested his elbows heavily on the draped table, meticulously building a house of cards using their company’s promotional flyers. Beside him, Lily was attempting to balance a branded stress ball on the tip of a promotional pen, her chin resting firmly on her other hand. "I think the carpet is actually growing," Marcus said quietly, watching his paper roof collapse into a flat pile. "It’s expanding." Lily sighed, letting the stress ball roll away. "It’s as endless as the archery field at Camp Arrowhead," she said, resting her forehead on the table. Marcus froze, leaving a flyer suspended in mid-air. "Arrowhead? Up in the Catskills?"

The digital clock glowed 3:14 AM. I watched the colon blink. On. Off. On. Off. The lobby was painfully silent. I slumped down in the ergonomic desk chair, letting my head loll to the side. At the other computer, Ben had made a line of six paperclips and was slowly pushing them forward with a ruler like a miniature army. "Do you think time has actually stopped?" I whispered, my voice sounding unnecessarily loud. "Maybe," Ben replied, not looking away from his paperclips. "It’s like the silent reading hour we had to endure every Sunday at Camp Blue Ridge." I slowly sat up, the blinking colon on the clock entirely forgotten. "Blue Ridge?" I stared at him. "Wait, did you have the bright orange bunk beds too?"

Mark practically vibrated beside me in the waiting area, muttering his elevator pitch under his breath for the twelfth time. "Do you think they'll ask about the supply chain metrics?" he whispered, gripping his pristine, linen-paper resume. I rested my chin heavily on my palm, tracing the geometric pattern of the carpet with the toe of my shoe. "Probably," I mumbled, letting my gaze drift to the ticking wall clock. The second hand seemed to stick slightly between the four and the five. It had taken exactly two hundred and forty-three ticks since we sat down. Mark started reciting his strengths and weaknesses again. I exhaled a long, flat breath, shifting my weight in the stiff chair to count the water stains on the acoustic ceiling tiles. There were seven.

Chloe scrolled frantically through the online portal, her eyes wide over the rim of her laptop. "I can't believe we're both going for the junior art director spot! This is going to be so intense!" she shrieked, tapping the keyboard with manic energy. Across the small café table, Sarah let her head loll back against the vinyl booth. She held a plastic stirrer, dragging it in slow, endless circles through her lukewarm latte. The milky foam had separated into tiny, sad islands ten minutes ago. "Yeah. Intense," Sarah said, her voice entirely flat. She watched a barista wipe down the espresso machine with agonizing slowness. Chloe launched into a detailed analysis of the company's recent color palettes. Sarah rested her cheek against the cool glass window, watching the gray traffic crawl down the damp street outside.

"Okay, section four. Have you ever been convicted of a felony?" Dave read aloud, leaning so close to my monitor his breath fogged the edge. We had decided to fill out the security firm applications together, but I was already clicking my pen. Click, clack. Click, clack. I balanced the plastic barrel on my index finger, watching it tip back and forth. "No," I said, my gaze wandering away from the glowing screen to the peeling paint on my bedroom windowsill. Dave aggressively typed his response. "What about the secondary references? Do you think Coach Miller is a better choice than Professor Hastings?" I rolled my eyes toward the ceiling, letting out a long, slow exhale that fluttered my bangs. I picked up a rubber band from the desk and began wrapping it around my thumb, waiting for this to end.

As soon as they stepped out of the corporate elevator, Julian grabbed Mateo’s arm. "Did you see the hiring manager's micro-expressions when I brought up the Q3 projections? Do you think I overstepped? What did you say when they asked about conflict resolution?" Julian’s words poured out in a frantic, unbroken stream. Mateo slouched against the polished marble wall of the lobby, letting his eyes un-focus until the chandelier above became a blurry smear of yellow light. He dug his hands deep into his pockets, kicking a microscopic pebble across the tile floor. "I just said I talk things out," Mateo replied, his jaw slack. He watched the lobby doors slide open and closed, the automated whoosh-thud anchoring him to the space. Julian started to replay his entire response. Mateo mentally alphabetized the groceries he needed to buy.

The notification pinged on both our phones simultaneously. Sitting on my living room rug, Jenny gasped, pressing her hands to her cheeks. "Oh my god, the museum sent the fellowship decisions! Open yours! Open yours!" she squealed. I swiped my thumb across the screen, barely registering the bright logo. My eyes skimmed the dense block of corporate text without absorbing the words. I rested my chin in my hand, tapping a completely out-of-tune rhythm on my knee. Jenny was hyperventilating, reading her email line by line. I tossed my phone face-down onto the couch. I stared at the dust motes floating through a shaft of afternoon sunlight, tracking a particularly large speck as it slowly drifted toward the floorboard. "Did you get it?" she demanded. I shrugged, letting out a heavy puff of air. "Don't know. Didn't finish reading it."

Liam slapped a stack of handwritten flashcards onto the library table. "We have to nail the technical questions. If we both get to the final round for the engineering role, we need to be flawless," he whispered fiercely. Emma sank lower in her wooden chair until her chin was nearly level with the tabletop. She poked at her cuticles with her thumbnail, ignoring the card Liam was waving in her face. "Come on, Emma. What's the standard deviation formula?" She blinked slowly, the fluorescent lights humming a steady, mind-numbing drone above them. She dragged her finger through the light layer of dust on the table, drawing a series of meaningless spirals. "Square root of the variance," she murmured in a monotone drawl. Liam flipped to the next card with a crisp snap. Emma rested her forehead against the cool wood, closing her eyes entirely.

Greg insisted we walk to the law firm together, claiming the crisp air would sharpen our minds. For the last six blocks, he had been practicing his handshake on the empty air, adjusting his tie, and reciting his opening statement. I dragged my feet, feeling the heavy, rhythmic thud of my loafers against the concrete. I started counting the cracks in the sidewalk. Every time I stepped on one, I imagined a tiny explosion. Step, boom. Step, boom. "Are you going to bring up the summer seminar?" Greg asked, turning to me with a sweat-beaded forehead. I stared at him blankly, a prolonged silence stretching between us until I finally offered a limp shrug. I looked away, watching a discarded plastic bag caught in an updraft, tumbling lazily over a rusted fence. I let out a long breath, wishing the walk would magically end.

The diner smelled of stale fry oil and cheap coffee. Marcus was passionately circling bullet points on the printed job description for the management trainee program. "Look at this requirement: 'Dynamic leadership in fast-paced environments.' We both have that from the retreat!" Marcus tapped the paper emphatically. Opposite him, Trey rested his heavy head on a folded arm. With his free hand, he used a fork to construct a tiny, fragile tower out of cold french fries. He nudged the bottom fry, watching the greasy structure collapse onto the ceramic plate. "Yeah. Dynamic," Trey said, not looking up. He started arranging the fallen fries by length. Marcus leaned in, his voice rising in excitement about the benefits package. Trey let out a massive yawn, failing to cover his mouth in time, his eyes watering from the sheer length of the exhale.

We stood in the menswear department for what felt like the third century. Derek held a navy blue blazer in his left hand and a charcoal gray one in his right. "The bakery manager position requires a clean, authoritative look. Navy says trustworthy, but charcoal says capable. What do you think?" I sat slumped on the tiny velvet fitting-room stool, my legs stretched far out into the aisle. I spun my phone around on my knee, catching it just before it fell, over and over. "They're both dark," I muttered, staring at a loose thread on the cuff of my jeans. I pulled it, watching it unravel another inch. Derek held the blazers up to his chest, examining himself in the trifold mirror. I leaned my head back against the wall, tracing the swirling pattern of the hideous wallpaper with my eyes until they crossed.

Rachel hit the refresh button on her browser again, leaning intensely into the monitor. "Still 'Under Review.' I swear, applying for this nursing residency is taking years off my life. Have you checked yours?" Across the cramped dorm room, Mia lay flat on her back on the rug, her limbs splayed like a starfish. She was staring fixedly at the ceiling fan, tracking one slightly wobbly blade as it spun in a slow, hypnotic circle. "I checked it Tuesday," Mia said, her voice a hollow echo against the floorboards. "It's Thursday," Rachel snapped, frantically refreshing the page once more. Mia didn't move her head. She slowly raised her right arm, letting it flop back down onto the carpet with a dull thud. She began softly humming a commercial jingle she had heard three days ago, letting the melody stretch into a slow, tuneless drone.

The hiring manager left us in the conference room for a "collaborative exercise." Chris immediately took charge, uncapping a whiteboard marker and drawing a massive, complex flowchart for the theoretical marketing campaign. "Okay, so if I handle the demographic breakdown, you can optimize the SEO keywords," he directed, pointing the marker at me. I was slouched completely sideways in the ergonomic swivel chair, slowly spinning myself half-circles left, then right. Squeak, swish. Squeak, swish. "Sure," I said, my voice entirely devoid of inflection. I picked at a chipped piece of polish on my thumbnail, peeling it off in one tiny flake. Chris kept talking, his voice bouncing off the glass walls. I leaned forward, resting my cheek directly on the cool, mahogany conference table, and watched a dust particle float slowly through the beam of the overhead projector.

The glow of two laptops illuminated the dim kitchen. Sam typed furiously, the clacking of keys filling the silence. "I think I should change 'assisted' to 'spearheaded' on my barista experience. It sounds more proactive for the logistics role." Across the table, Leo’s screen had gone dark, displaying only the bouncing corporate logo of a screensaver. Leo rested his chin heavily in his cupped hands, his eyelids drooping until they were mere slits. He watched a drop of condensation slide painstakingly down the side of his water glass. It took a full minute to reach the coaster. "Spearheaded," Leo repeated, the word sounding like a deflating balloon. He poked the water glass, sending a tiny ripple across the surface. Sam started reading his entire objective statement aloud. Leo let out a long, whistling sigh and began organizing a scattered pile of paperclips by size.

The group chat notifications buzzed against my thigh in rapid, relentless succession. First Liam demanding RSVPs for his rooftop bash, then Chloe immediately countering with an impassioned plea for her basement arcade night. Both were set for the 15th. I pulled my phone from my pocket, unlocked it, and watched the grey and blue bubbles fill the screen. I didn't read them. Instead, I focused on a small, jagged crack in the upper corner of my screen protector. I ran my thumbnail over it, feeling the tiny ridge, back and forth, back and forth. The phone buzzed twelve more times in a single minute. I placed it face down on the coffee table. The ceiling fan above me spun with a rhythmic, mechanical click. Click. Click. Click. I rested my chin in my palm, my eyes tracking a single wooden blade in its endless, unchanging circle.

"So if I do gold balloons, it completely ruins the aesthetic of my masquerade, right?" Maya asked, pacing the length of the living room. On the floor, Sam sat cross-legged, staring at a stray thread hanging from the hem of his jeans. He wrapped it around his index finger, letting it turn the tip slightly purple, then unwrapped it. "Right," he murmured flatly. Maya stopped and crossed her arms. "But Julian is already doing silver for his disco theme on the same night! I can't let him have the better metallic." Sam sighed, a long, slow exhale that ruffled his own bangs. He picked up his cold cup of coffee and swirled the mostly melted ice, watching the pale liquid slosh against the plastic sides. He checked the digital clock on the microwave. Only four minutes had passed since he last looked. "Totally," he said.

Two glossy invitations sat side-by-side on my desk. One was shaped like a cocktail glass for Sarah’s evening gala; the other was a neon pink rectangle for Mark’s retro bowl-a-thon. Saturday the 12th. Both at 8:00 PM. I picked up a paperclip and slowly bent the outer loop until the wire formed a straight line. Then, I unbent the inner loop. I pressed the straightened wire flat against the desk top, testing its rigidity. The ticking of the wall clock seemed exceptionally loud today. Tick. Pause. Tick. Pause. I nudged the cocktail glass invitation a quarter inch to the left, aligning its edge perfectly with the grain of the wood veneer. Then I nudged the neon pink card to match. I rested my forehead against the cool surface of the desk, listening to the muffled sound of a distant lawnmower drone on and on.

Elena stood in the party supply store's seventh aisle, surrounded by towering displays of disposable cutlery. A few feet away, Rachel was furiously texting David, arguing about who had the right to book the community hall for Saturday. Elena shifted her weight from her left foot to her right. She reached out and tapped a plastic fork package, then dragged her index finger along the edge of the shelf, collecting a thin layer of grey dust. She inspected the dust on her fingertip, wiped it on her jeans, and exhaled heavily through her nose. Rachel read a text aloud, her voice tight with indignation. "Can you believe he said that?" she asked. Elena gave a slow, mechanical nod, her gaze fixed on a flickering fluorescent tube near the ceiling. "Wow," Elena said, her voice entirely devoid of inflection. She began counting the ceiling tiles.

My phone was on speaker, resting in the center of the kitchen island. "I told you last month I was doing a dinner party on the 10th," Greg's voice crackled. "And I told you I already put down a deposit for the roller rink on the 10th!" Lisa fired back. I wandered away from the island and opened the refrigerator. I stared at a jar of pickles on the second shelf. The brine was slightly cloudy. I closed the door, walked over to the sink, and turned the tap on a slow trickle. I watched the water hit the stainless steel drain, mesmerized by the little vortex it created. "Who do you agree with?" Lisa yelled through the tiny speaker. I dragged a wet finger across the granite countertop, tracing an invisible figure eight. "I think you both make good points," I mumbled to the sink.

While Chris and Alex bickered over their overlapping birthday dinners, Jordan sat in the booth next to them, methodically peeling the label off a glass ketchup bottle. He used his thumbnail to scrape away a stubborn patch of adhesive, ensuring the glass underneath was perfectly smooth. Chris slammed a hand on the table. "I'm not moving my reservation! The steakhouse took weeks to book!" Alex scoffed loudly, "Well, the sushi place requires a minimum head count!" Jordan rested his chin in his hand, his eyes glazing over as he stared out the diner window. A plastic bag caught in the wind was tumbling lazily down the empty street. It caught on a fire hydrant, fluttered for a moment, and tore free. Jordan let out a soft, drawn-out sigh, his fingers mindlessly tapping a slow, unvarying rhythm against the edge of his water glass.

"So, my itinerary starts at 6 PM," Mia said, handing me a laminated sheet of paper. "But Derek’s escape room doesn't end until 6:30," she continued, her finger jabbing at the printed schedule. I laid the paper on my lap and slumped deeper into the armchair. I tilted my head back until I was looking at the ceiling upside down. There was a tiny spider weaving a web in the corner near the crown molding. It moved with methodical precision, anchoring a silk thread, dropping down, and climbing back up. I watched it for what felt like hours. "Are you even looking at the timeline?" Mia asked. I blinked, slowly bringing my head back down, and let out a long breath. "Yeah," I said, my voice completely flat. "Escape room. Six-thirty. Got it." I looked back up. The spider hadn't moved.

The argument in the living room had been going in circles for forty-five minutes. Emma wanted to host a pool party; Noah insisted on a formal dinner. Both adamantly claimed the 22nd. Sitting between them on the sofa, Leo picked up a throw pillow. He traced the geometric embroidered pattern with his index finger, following the yellow zigzag lines from one corner to the other. When he reached the end, he started over from the beginning. Emma pulled up a weather app to prove her point. Noah countered with an article about peak dining hours. Leo rested his face against his palm, his eyelids drooping heavily. He stared at the carpet, trying to find shapes in the crushed pile fibers. He found one that looked vaguely like a shoe, then lost it. He let out a loud, drawn-out yawn, not bothering to cover his mouth.

We were sitting in my car in the driveway, the engine turned off. In the passenger seat, Jenna was holding up two different mood boards on her tablet—one for her cottagecore picnic, the other for Ben’s industrial warehouse rave. Both on the same Saturday. I leaned my head against the driver's side window, feeling the cold glass against my temple. I started counting the dead bugs squashed against the windshield. One, two, three... there was a particularly large smudge near the wiper blade. "If you go to Ben's first, you won't have energy for my acoustic set," Jenna complained. I slowly rolled my head to face her, blinking heavily. "Mhm," I murmured. I turned the steering wheel a quarter inch to the left, then a quarter inch to the right. It locked with a dull click. I closed my eyes and sighed through my teeth.

To solve the overlap of their dual twenty-fifth birthdays, Kevin and Tyler insisted on presenting a joint PowerPoint presentation to their friend group. Marcus sat in the back row of the makeshift living-room theater. Tyler was enthusiastically pointing a laser pointer at a pie chart dividing their mutual friends' time. Marcus slumped downward, his tailbone sliding toward the edge of his chair. He pulled a pen from his pocket and began clicking it. Click-clack. Click-clack. Kevin glared at him. Marcus stopped, resting the pen on his thigh. He stared blankly at the bright projection screen, his vision blurring until the pie chart turned into a fuzzy, colorful circle. He checked his watch, calculating how many minutes had passed since Tyler started the slide on 'Commute Times Between Venues'. Three minutes. He let out a long breath and resumed clicking his pen inside his pocket.

Both GroupMe chats were going off simultaneously on my laptop. Ping. Ping. Ping. "Theme is glitter!" read one. "Theme is goth!" read the other. I sat at my desk, resting my chin on a stack of printer paper. I pulled a single sheet from the top and began folding it. A hot dog fold. A hamburger fold. I creased the edges sharply with my thumbnail, over and over, until the paper was soft and worn. "We need to coordinate carpools," a message popped up. I dragged my cursor around the desktop, highlighting a block of empty space, then releasing it, over and over again, drawing little blue selection squares. Ping. I rested my forehead on the cold, hard surface of my desk. I closed my eyes and listened to the steady, rhythmic hum of my laptop's cooling fan spinning into overdrive.

Sophie paced the kitchen, waving a spatula as she detailed her exact timeline for her birthday brunch, while ranting about how Claire scheduling a high tea on the same afternoon was a betrayal. Sitting at the island, Dan rested his chin in both hands. He watched a single drop of water gather at the lip of the kitchen faucet, swell, and eventually fall into the basin with a soft plink. He waited for the next drop to form. "And then she expects people to just skip my mimosa toast?" Sophie demanded, pausing for dramatic effect. Dan blinked slowly, keeping his eyes on the faucet. "Crazy," he said, his voice a low monotone. He picked up a stray breadcrumb from the counter, rolled it between his thumb and forefinger into a tiny, dense sphere, and flicked it across the granite surface. Plink went the faucet.

I rested my chin heavily on my palm, watching a lone housefly bump repeatedly against the coffee shop window. Across the small table, Mark was still gesturing wildly, knocking my spoon off its napkin. "And then the rain started pouring, right? Flooded the whole campsite!" he said, leaning in. I blinked slowly, tracking the fly's futile path up the glass. I distinctly remembered blistering sunburns and a dried-up creek on that trip, not a drop of rain in sight. "Right," I mumbled, my voice flat. I picked up a spare sugar packet, flicking it rhythmically against my thumb. Flick. Flick. Flick. The clock above the barista station ticked forward by exactly one minute. Mark launched into a detailed description of the imaginary mudslides. I slumped further down in my chair, staring blankly at the condensation pooling around the base of my iced tea.

Elias sat in the sterile glow of the laundromat, his eyes fixed on the hypnotic, endless tumbling of wet jeans in the dryer. Beside him, Julian was practically shouting over the hum of the machines. "Dude, when the lead singer stage-dived at that gig, the crowd parted like the Red Sea!" Julian laughed, slapping Elias on the shoulder. Elias let his head loll to the side, peeling a frayed sticker off the plastic chair. He knew for a fact the singer hadn't stage-dived; the guy had tripped over a monitor cable and face-planted. "Crazy," Elias offered in a monotone. He stretched his legs out, tracing the scuff marks on the linoleum floor with the toe of his sneaker. He watched a single gray sock slosh against the dryer glass, over and over, waiting for the cycle timer to drop from fourteen minutes to thirteen.

The train rattled along the tracks, a rhythmic clacking that matched the heavy thumping in my temples. I dragged my gaze from the blur of passing telephone poles to Chloe, who was animatedly recounting our high school prom. "I still can't believe Mr. Henderson caught us spiking the punch and chased us out to the parking lot," she said, eyes wide with residual adrenaline. I rested my forehead against the vibrating window. Henderson hadn't chased us anywhere; he’d just confiscated the bowl and told us to go back to the dance floor. "Yeah. Wild," I whispered, not looking away from the glass. I started counting the red barns we passed. One. Two. My eyelids drooped. Chloe moved on to describing the dress she wore, a dress I knew for a fact belonged to her sister. Three. Four barns. The horizon stretched on forever, unchanging.

In the breakroom, Marcus repeatedly clicked his pen. Click-clack. Click-clack. He stared at the sluggish drip of the coffee machine, watching a dark drop gather, swell, and eventually fall into the glass pot. Next to him, Greg was pacing the small room, reliving the corporate retreat. "Man, when our raft flipped on those rapids, I thought we were done for," Greg said, shadowboxing the air. Marcus rested his cheek against the cold refrigerator door. The raft hadn't flipped. They had gently bumped into a submerged rock and spun in a circle. "Terrifying," Marcus murmured, his tone devoid of inflection. He inspected a microscopic chip in his fingernail, turning his hand over under the harsh fluorescent lights. He watched the second hand on the wall clock sweep its slow, agonizing circle. Greg started demonstrating his supposedly heroic swimming technique, while Marcus let out a long, shuddering sigh.

The summer heat pressed down on the porch, thick and unmoving. I sat on the top step, dragging a stick through the loose dirt near my feet to draw endless, intersecting circles. Beside me, Leo was talking about the treehouse we built as kids. "Remember how we painted the whole thing bright blue? Took us three days," he said, taking a sip of his lemonade. I didn't look up from the dirt. We hadn't painted it at all; it was just bare, splintering pine that rotted after one winter. "Uh-huh," I said. I dropped the stick and began picking at the frayed hem of my denim shorts, pulling out one white thread at a time. A large green beetle crawled agonizingly slowly over the toe of my canvas sneaker. I rested my elbows on my knees, letting my face fall into my hands.

The library study room was suffocatingly quiet, save for the furious scratching of Clara’s highlighter. Opposite her, Maya leaned across the table, whispering fervently about their blind double-date last month. "And then the waiter just dumped the entire tray of red wine all over my lap!" Maya gasped, clutching her chest. Clara rested her chin heavily on her textbook, her eyes glazed over. She distinctly recalled Maya knocking the glasses over with her own purse while reaching for a breadstick. "Tragic," Clara whispered back, her voice hollow. She flipped her pencil end over end, watching the eraser tap the desk in a slow, monotonous rhythm. She began shading in all the letter 'O's on her printed syllabus, carefully filling each little circle with graphite, desperate for the hands on the digital clock to switch from 3:14 to 3:15.

I sat rigidly in the molded plastic chair, staring blankly at the red digital counter above the DMV desk. Now serving 42. The paper in my hand read 89. Next to me, Sam passionately dissected our Yosemite trip. "I’m telling you, that bear was easily eight feet tall, right outside our tent," he insisted, nudging my ribs. I let out a slow, breathy exhale, letting my head fall back against the cinderblock wall. It had been a mossy tree stump illuminated by a flashlight. "Huge," I muttered. I stretched my legs out, crossing and uncrossing my ankles. I began to count the ceiling tiles, making a mental grid. Now serving 43. Sam launched into a dramatic recreation of the growl he supposedly heard. I closed my eyes, heavily resting my cheek on my shoulder.

Traffic stretched for miles, a sea of unmoving red taillights glowing in the dusk. In the passenger seat, David rhythmically thumped his forehead against the cool glass of the window. Thump. Thump. Thump. Behind the wheel, Arthur was practically shouting his rendition of their college graduation prank. "When we released those three pigs into the dean's office, absolute chaos!" Arthur laughed, slapping the steering wheel. David stared blankly at the bumper sticker on the car ahead. It had been three chickens, not pigs, and they hadn't even made it past the lobby. "Yeah. Chaos," David replied, his voice completely flat. He picked up his phone, swiped to the next screen, swiped back, and locked it again. He sighed heavily, tracing the condensation on his window with a numb index finger, watching a single bead of water slowly carve a path to the door panel.

The video call had been going on for forty-seven minutes. I minimized Jenna’s face into a tiny square in the corner of my monitor and opened a game of solitaire, dragging black sevens onto red eights. Her voice crackled through my headset. "And Sarah was wearing this completely outrageous neon green dress at the wedding! Total eyesore," Jenna declared. I stared blankly at the digital cards. Sarah’s dress had been a muted navy blue; I had literally zipped her into it. "Totally," I murmured, mindlessly clicking the mouse. I began peeling a dried piece of tape off the edge of my desk, working it loose with my thumbnail. Jenna started describing the appetizers, an entire monologue about the shrimp cocktail. I leaned back in my ergonomic chair until the springs groaned, staring blankly up at the stucco texture of my bedroom ceiling.

The movie screen remained agonizingly dark. In the theater seat, Liam sat with his arms crossed, counting the rhythmic crunches coming from his right. Beside him, Theo was elbow-deep in a bucket of popcorn, enthusiastically reliving their middle school rivalry. "When I threw that first punch at Tommy behind the bleachers, the whole school gasped," Theo bragged, spraying a kernel. Liam let his eyes fall shut. He distinctly remembered Theo running away in tears before a single punch was ever thrown. "You really showed him," Liam mumbled into his chest. He pulled his phone out of his pocket, checked the blank lock screen, and shoved it back. He started meticulously separating the ice cubes in his soda cup with a plastic straw, pressing them down into the liquid and watching them bob back up, praying for the pre-show trailers to finally begin.

I sat on the cold metal park bench, watching a pigeon peck aimlessly at a discarded cigarette butt. Next to me, Sarah was waving her arms, finishing her epic tale about our European backpacking trip. "And we were totally stranded in Rome! Not a dime to our names, sleeping on the cobblestones," she cried dramatically. I traced the deep, splintered grain of the wooden bench with my thumb. We hadn't been stranded; she had just lost her debit card, and we spent the night in a perfectly fine hostel using my cash. "So rough," I said, my voice barely above a whisper. I slumped forward, resting my elbows on my knees and dangling my hands between my legs. I kicked a pebble across the pavement, watching it skitter to a halt. The pigeon flew away. I let out a long, hollow breath.

Inside the diner booth, Elena built a small, precarious tower out of pink sweetener packets. Across the sticky table, Nina was animatedly describing the time they supposedly fought a kitchen fire together. "The flames were licking the ceiling! We were basically firefighters," Nina declared, aggressively stabbing her hash browns with a fork. Elena slowly placed a blue packet on top of the pink ones. It had been a slightly burnt bagel that set off the smoke detector. "Heroes," Elena muttered, her tone entirely monotone. She rested her cheek in her palm, her eyes drifting upward to the ceiling fan. She watched one single wooden blade complete rotation after agonizingly slow rotation. Nina launched into a description of the imaginary smoke damage. Elena let out a long sigh, flicking her finger against the base of her packet tower and watching the whole thing scatter across the table.

I rested my chin heavily on my palm, tracing the rim of my lukewarm coffee cup for what felt like the hundredth time. Across the polished oak conference table, Mark was eagerly spreading out his schematics for the new municipal drainage system. "Look at this sub-pump layout," he said, tapping a blue line. I let my eyes slide over his diagrams. They were exactly the same as the ones sitting in my own portfolio, down to the millimeter. I blinked slowly, watching a single fly bump repeatedly against the glass of the window. "Oh," I muttered, my voice perfectly flat. "You used the alternating valve structure. Me too." Mark gasped, his eyes wide with the sheer impossibility of our cosmic coincidence. I just picked at a stray thread on my sleeve, wondering if it was too early to go down to the cafeteria for a stale muffin.

Elara dragged her finger through the dust on her mahogany workbench, watching the particles dance in the pale candlelight. Beside her, the visiting wizard, Galdor, threw off the velvet cloth covering his life’s work with a dramatic flourish. It was a perpetual motion sphere, humming softly with arcane energy. Elara let out a long, slow breath, her gaze drifting toward the cobwebs gathering in the corner of the ceiling. She nudged her own identical silver sphere with her elbow, causing it to clink against a beaker. Galdor stared at her invention, his jaw dropping as he realized they had spent three decades translating the exact same ancient runes. "By the gods, we are of one mind!" he whispered reverently. Elara rested her cheek on the cool wood of the table, idly rolling a piece of charcoal back and forth, counting the seconds until he would finally leave.

My foot tapped a relentless, hollow rhythm against the metal leg of the folding table. On the monitor to my left, the progress bar for my compiling code crept forward at a glacial pace. A guy from the adjacent booth leaned over, practically vibrating with caffeine and excitement. "Check out my predictive algorithm," he urged, shoving his laptop into my line of sight. I stared at the screen. The UI was identical to mine, and the core logic was line-for-line the exact script I had just pushed to the repository. "Wow," I said, leaning back in my chair and staring up at the flickering fluorescent lights. "That’s the exact same sentiment analysis tool I just built." He began babbling about neural networks and shared genius. I suppressed a yawn, tracing the grease stains on my discarded pizza box and wishing the clock read anything other than 3:14 AM.

Julian swirled the muddy brown water in his brush cup, resting his chin heavily on his knuckles. Next to him, Clara pulled the tarp off her marble block, beaming with pride at her newly chiseled sculpture. It was a winged lion caught in mid-roar. Julian let his heavy eyelids drift toward his own pedestal, where an identical winged lion sat, carved down to the exact curvature of the left pinion. Clara gasped, dropping her chisel on the concrete floor with a sharp clatter. "Julian! It's a miracle of synchronized inspiration!" she cried, rushing over to inspect his work. Julian offered a weak, tight-lipped smile, his gaze wandering away from the statues to the water stains on the exposed brick wall. He picked at a dry piece of clay on his thumb, wondering how long it would take for the afternoon rain to finally start.

I stirred the simmering reduction at a painfully slow pace, the wooden spoon scraping the bottom of the copper pot with a rhythmic, hollow sound. Two stations over, Chef Marcel tasted Henri’s dish and loudly praised the brilliant fusion of juniper and smoked cherry. I stared blankly at my own pan of juniper and smoked cherry reduction, the steam rising in slow spirals. Henri practically skipped over to my station, tasting spoon in hand. "Let me try yours!" he chirped, taking a sample. His eyes went wide. "Mon dieu, it is the exact same flavor profile! We are culinary twins!" I blinked heavily, shifting my weight from one foot to the other. "Yeah. Twins," I mumbled, leaning against the cold stainless steel counter. I watched a drop of water slowly slide down the front of the oven door, completely ignoring Henri’s continued raving about our synchronized palates.

Commander Vance stared blankly at the blinking green dot on the navigation console, his cheek smooshed against his palm. Dr. Aris rushed onto the bridge, clutching her datapad as if it held the secrets of the universe. "Vance, I've solved the hyperspace folding equation!" she announced, projecting her calculations onto the main viewing screen. Vance’s eyes slowly tracked the glowing numbers. He reached out with one languid finger and tapped his own console, bringing up the exact same sequence of equations he had formulated three hours prior. Aris froze, her mouth forming a perfect 'O' of shock. "You... you already did it?" she whispered, grappling with the astronomical odds. Vance let out a heavy sigh, his gaze drifting to the endless, unchanging void of stars outside the viewport. He slumped further down into his padded command chair, idly twirling a stylus between his fingers.

The afternoon sun beat down, but I couldn't bring myself to care. I sat on my overturned bucket, rhythmically tapping my trowel against a rock. Tap. Tap. Tap. Over by the trench, Sarah let out a piercing shriek of triumph. She scrambled up the dirt embankment, holding a clay tablet. "Look at this translation! I've decoded the agricultural ledgers!" she shouted, thrusting the parchment toward me. I gave it a glassy stare. The symbols matched the exact ledger I had translated in my tent yesterday morning. "Huh," I breathed out, my voice flat. "I got the same translation. Exactly the same." Sarah began pacing rapidly, theorizing about morphic resonance and shared consciousness. I rested my forehead on my dusty knees, watching a line of ants meticulously carry a single breadcrumb, calculating how many ants it would take to carry me away from this conversation.

Elias slouched on the piano bench, resting his forehead against the polished mahogany fallboard. The muffled sound of a cello drifted from the practice room next door. Suddenly, the door burst open and Leo rushed in, sheet music fluttering from his hands. "Elias! I've composed the perfect counter-melody for the sonata!" Leo exclaimed, slamming the pages onto the stand. Elias lifted his head at a glacial pace, his eyes half-closed. He stared at the notes, then slowly reached into his own folder, pulling out the exact same progression of chords, written in his own hand. Leo gasped, stepping back as if burned. "We... we wrote the identical piece!" he stammered. Elias let out a long breath that puffed his bangs up into the air. He gently poked the middle C key with his index finger, letting the single note fade into the heavy silence of the room.

I rested my head on the cool metal of the gymnasium bleachers, staring fixedly at a wad of dried gum stuck under the seat ahead of me. Down on the floor, Jeremy was violently waving his hands, trying to get my attention. I dragged my feet down the steps to his booth. "Look!" he practically vibrated, pointing to his homemade volcano powered by baking soda and a digitized pressure valve. I looked at it, then pointed a limp thumb over my shoulder to my own booth, where the exact same digitized pressure valve setup sat on a piece of cardboard. "Oh," I said in a deadpan drone. "Same valve." Jeremy started hyperventilating about the probability of simultaneous invention. I just crossed my arms, leaning all my weight against a basketball hoop pole, waiting for the ticking wall clock to finally strike three so I could go home.

Agent 47 sat in the dimly lit safehouse, tossing a brass coin in the air and letting it drop onto the table with a dull thud. Toss. Thud. Toss. Thud. The door flew open, and Agent 99 stormed in, pulling a thick dossier from her trench coat. "I've infiltrated the syndicate and mapped their entire supply chain," she declared proudly, spreading the documents. 47’s gaze slid slowly over the photographs. He steadily pulled open a desk drawer and produced an identical set of photographs, placing them side-by-side with hers. 99 stopped breathing, her eyes darting between the two identical dossiers. "We’ve been tracking the same ghost operation," she whispered in disbelief. 47 rested his chin on his fist, his expression completely blank. He looked away from the files, watching a moth flutter aimlessly around the single flickering overhead bulb, wishing the ceiling fan was on.

I sat on a wooden crate in the greenhouse, absentmindedly pulling the petals off a dead daisy one by one. Margaret bustled down the aisle, her face flushed with extreme excitement. "I've done it! I've cultivated the perfect cross-breed of the blue orchid and the nightshade!" she announced, presenting a pot containing a striking purple bloom. I slowly rotated my head toward her, then nudged my boot against the pot sitting by my feet. It held the exact same purple flower, right down to the silver streaked leaves. Margaret dropped her watering can, the water pooling around her shoes as she stared at my plant. "Goodness gracious, we engineered the identical hybrid!" she gasped. "Yeah," I muttered, resting my elbows on my knees and letting my chin drop into my hands. I watched the water slowly seep into the dirt floor, tuning out her endless chattering about cross-pollination.

Arthur slumped back in the plush armchair, staring blankly at the cursor blinking steadily on his laptop screen. Blinking. Blinking. Across the rustic cabin, Beatrice slammed her notebook shut with a victorious cry. "I've outlined the entire murder mystery! The killer is the clockmaker who uses the chimes to mask the gunshots!" she proclaimed. Arthur’s eyelids drooped. He reached out and slowly rotated his laptop so she could see the screen. The exact same plot outline, complete with the clockmaker twist, was typed in a bulleted list. Beatrice stood frozen, her hands flying to her mouth. "Great minds think exactly alike!" she whispered in awe. Arthur let out a long, heavy exhale through his nose. He slouched further into the chair, letting his arms dangle limply over the armrests, his eyes tracking a spider slowly making its way across the wooden beams of the ceiling.

I watched the ceiling fan make its slow, wobbly rotation. Thwump, thwump, thwump. Mark was pacing at the foot of the couch, waving his hands as he listed every reason a Golden Retriever would destroy our apartment. "They shed everywhere," he insisted, his voice a distant hum over the drone of the fan. "And the walks! Six AM in the snow!" I let my head roll to the side, my eyes tracing a water stain on the plaster that kind of looked like a walrus. I exhaled a long, heavy breath that fluttered my bangs. I didn't even want a dog that badly, to be honest. I just wanted something, anything, to break the endless stretch of identical Sunday afternoons. I reached down, found a stray piece of string on the carpet, and began twisting it around my index finger until the tip turned purple.

Sarah sorted the bowl of Skittles by color, sliding the purple ones to the left and the green ones to the right. Across the kitchen island, Chloe had opened a massive spreadsheet titled ‘Feline Financials.’ "You see," Chloe said, pointing a rigid finger at cell D4, "the cumulative cost of litter alone over a fifteen-year lifespan is staggering." Sarah rested her chin heavily in her palm. The refrigerator kicked on with a low hum, and she focused all her attention on the sound. She slowly pushed a yellow Skittle into the red pile, then pulled it back. "Are you even listening?" Chloe asked. Sarah blinked slowly, her gaze drifting toward the window where absolutely nothing was happening on the quiet street below. "Litter," Sarah repeated in a flat monotone, dragging out the syllables. "Right. So expensive." She popped a green Skittle into her mouth and chewed deliberately.

The tennis ball hit the drywall with a hollow thud, landed in my palm, and flew right back. Thud. Catch. Throw. "Reptiles carry salmonella," Greg announced from the armchair, aggressively scrolling through a WebMD article. "And they require heat lamps. Do you know what that will do to our electric bill?" I stared at a scuff mark near the baseboard. Thud. Catch. Throw. It was a Tuesday evening, and the silence in our living room usually felt thick enough to choke on. An iguana sounded like a disruption. A mess. A glorious, chaotic mess. "Salmonella," I echoed, letting my hand drop over the edge of the bed. The ball rolled away, disappearing under the nightstand. I didn't bother reaching for it. I just laid my head back against the pillow and started counting the little popcorn bumps on the ceiling texture. One, two, three.

Marcus tapped his pen against his knee in a rhythmic, unvarying tempo. Tap-tap-tap, pause, tap-tap-tap. Beside him, Leo was delivering an impassioned monologue on the sheer irresponsibility of adopting a ferret in a month-to-month rental. Marcus watched a single dust mote float through the shaft of afternoon sunlight cutting across the living room. It drifted upward, then spiraled lazily downward. He followed its journey with heavy eyes. "They steal things," Leo stressed, crossing his arms. "You’ll wake up and your keys will be inside the sofa." Marcus let his head loll against the back of the couch. He pulled out his phone, unlocked it, swiped right, swiped left, and locked it again without opening a single app. "Keys in the sofa," Marcus murmured, staring blankly at the dark television screen mirroring his reflection. "Imagine that. What a wild Tuesday that would be."

I peeled the label off my water bottle in microscopic, jagged strips, aiming to keep the entire strip intact. "A parrot?" Jenna shrieked, throwing her hands up. "Do you understand they live for eighty years? Eighty! It will outlive us!" I didn't look up, focusing entirely on a particularly stubborn patch of glue. I scraped at it with my thumbnail. Our apartment was dead quiet except for the hum of the AC unit. Every day was the same: wake up, go to work, come home, sit on this beige couch. I tossed a tiny shred of paper onto the coffee table. "We could teach it to sing," I offered, my voice entirely flat. I picked up a coaster and started flipping it over and over, watching the cork side alternate with the plastic side. Flip, flip, flip. "No birds," Jenna finalized. I sighed, slouching deeper.

David rested his forehead against the cool glass of the living room window. Outside, a plastic bag was caught in the branches of a barren oak tree, rustling faintly in the wind. He watched it flap. Behind him, Arthur was pacing the length of the worn rug, arguing against the logistics of a potbellied pig. "Zoning laws," Arthur practically yelled, waving a printout from the city council website. "We are in a residential zone, David! It’s classified as livestock!" David fogged up the windowpane with his breath, drew a tiny stick figure in the condensation, and watched it fade away. "Livestock," David repeated, his voice trailing off. He moved to the nearest armchair, slumped into the cushions, and began meticulously picking a stray thread off the hem of his sweater, pulling it millimeter by millimeter until it finally snapped.

"Fish are practically furniture," I mumbled, resting my cheek directly on the cold Formica countertop. "They don't even do anything." My roommate, Elena, slammed a brightly colored brochure for a 50-gallon saltwater aquarium onto the kitchen island. "They are a vibrant ecosystem!" she insisted, tapping the glossy paper. I watched a drop of water gather at the lip of the kitchen faucet. It swelled, stretched, and finally detached with a tiny plink against the stainless steel basin. I waited for the next one to form. I dragged my finger through a small spill of flour from last night's dinner, drawing a meaningless zigzag. The clock above the stove clicked over to 7:14 PM. Still three hours until it was acceptable to just go to sleep. "Vibrant," I sighed, watching the next water drop slowly begin to swell at the edge of the tap.

The metronome of the ticking wall clock seemed to amplify with every passing second. Tick. Tick. Tick. Maya sat cross-legged on the floor, stacking a tower of dominoes, while Sam launched into his third reason why a husky was a terrible idea. "The hair, Maya! Think of the shedding. We'd be eating fur!" Maya carefully placed a double-six on top of her trembling tower. Her eyes were glazed, fixated entirely on the black dots. She let out a long, slow exhale that ruffled her bangs. Without a word, she flicked the bottom piece. The entire structure collapsed into a chaotic clatter, scattering across the hardwood. She stared at the mess. Sam stopped mid-rant. "Did you hear me?" he asked. Maya flopped onto her back, staring straight up at the blank white ceiling, her arms spread wide like a starfish. "Yeah," she whispered softly. "Fur."

I swiveled my desk chair to the left, then used my toe to push myself in a slow circle to the right. "It's just a tarantula," I said to the ceiling as I spun. "It stays in a glass box." Across the dorm, Kyle was frantically Googling spider escape statistics on his laptop. "They can push the lids off! I saw a video!" he cried out, his voice cracking. I stopped my spin and dragged my eyes toward my open textbook. The black text blurred into meaningless shapes. I picked up a yellow highlighter, uncapped it, and meticulously colored in the center of every single 'O' on the page. By the time I finished the first paragraph, my eyelids felt like they were made of lead. I capped the highlighter, clicked my tongue against the roof of my mouth, and started on the 'P's.

Elias built a small pyramid out of sugar packets on the diner table, meticulously aligning the edges of the pink wrappers. Across the booth, Nathan was drawing a diagram on a napkin, aggressively explaining why two cats would create a territorial warzone in their tiny apartment. "It’s a fundamental issue of square footage," Nathan urged, tapping the pen against his drawing. Elias rested his chin on his fist. He watched the waitress wipe down a booth on the far side of the restaurant. He watched a car drive past the window. He watched a fly land on the salt shaker. With a heavy sigh, Elias reached out and flicked the center sugar packet. The pink pyramid slid into a messy pile. He instantly began rebuilding it, this time alternating pink and white packets, his gaze fixed on the paper squares.

"A chinchilla needs a dust bath, Claire. Dust! In the house!" Mindy threw her hands into the air, pacing the small kitchen. I sat at the table, balancing a spoon on my nose. I crossed my eyes to look at the shiny metal reflecting the overhead light. It slipped and clattered against the ceramic bowl. I picked it up and tried again, trying to beat my previous record of four seconds. "And they are nocturnal," Mindy pressed on, her voice a relentless drone. "We'd never sleep." I let the spoon fall to the table and rested my cheek on the cool wood. I stared at the woodgrain, tracing the dark, swirling lines with my thumbnail. "Yeah, dust," I mumbled into the table. I grabbed my phone, unlocked the screen, stared at the empty home page for a solid minute, and turned it off.

Julian stared at the television screen. It was turned off, and the black glass perfectly reflected the flat gray walls of their living room. In his periphery, Marcus was passionately reading a list of reasons why a hedgehog was a bad idea. "Number four," Marcus declared, his voice echoing in the sparse room. "Quill impalement." Julian blinked slowly, feeling the heaviness in his brow. He slumped deeper into the cushions, letting his legs stretch out until his heels rested on the coffee table. He picked up the TV remote, popped the back cover off, removed the AA batteries, and put them back in. He clicked the cover back into place. Then he did it again. Out, in, click. Out, in, click. "Are you even processing the danger of the quills?" Marcus demanded. Julian stared at his own dim reflection. "Quills," he murmured quietly.

I traced the grain of the mahogany table for the seventh time, noting how the swirl near the center looked vaguely like a squashed beetle. Beside me, my sister gasped as the attorney slid a polished brass key across the desk, claiming it opened a safe deposit box in Geneva. I propped my chin on my palm, my eyes drifting to the ticking clock above the door. Three-fifteen. It had been three-fourteen for an eternity. The lawyer pushed a frayed, mud-stained ledger toward me. "And for you," he droned. I let out a long breath, watching a speck of dust dance in a sunbeam. "Great," I muttered, not bothering to sit up straight. "A dirty notebook. Are we finished here? I have a load of laundry sitting in the washer that needs to go in the dryer."

Marcus lay flat on the dusty floorboards, tossing a tarnished coin in the air and catching it, over and over. "Look at this!" Leo exclaimed, holding up a shimmering, holographic deed to a lunar colony plot. Marcus caught the coin, letting his arm flop back onto the wood. "Neat," he said, staring blankly at a cobweb swaying gently near the rafters. He rolled his head to the side to look at his own inheritance: a rusted tin can filled with mismatched screws. Leo was practically vibrating, rambling about space travel and the future. Marcus let his eyes fall half-shut, his mind wandering to whether he should order pizza or tacos for dinner tonight. "Do you think there's oxygen up there?" Leo asked. Marcus let out a slow, heavy sigh. "I don't know, Leo. Can we just go downstairs now?"

I tapped my foot against the metal grate, keeping a steady, repetitive rhythm. Tap, tap, tap. Across the sterile white room, my brother held a glowing memory orb, weeping as generations of our family's digital history flowed directly into his neural port. The executor droid swiveled its optic sensor toward me and dispensed a physical, printed photograph onto the sterile table. It was a picture of a blurry tree. I rested my forehead on the cold edge of the table, letting my arms dangle limply at my sides. "Fascinating," I said in a completely flat voice. My brother was sobbing with profound ancestral joy. I closed my eyes, mentally counting backward from one hundred just to give my brain something to do. "Seventy-two, seventy-one," I whispered to myself, waiting for the droid to finally power down so I could leave.

Elara dragged her feet across the stone floor, her chin resting heavily in her palm as she leaned against a towering bookshelf. Her sister, Lyra, danced around the chamber, waving a wand that shot sparks of glittering sapphire into the air. "It chose me! The ancestral staff chose me!" Lyra squealed. Elara looked down at her hands, where a crumbling, gray stone sat entirely motionless. She poked it with her index finger. Nothing happened. She poked it again. Still nothing. Letting out a prolonged exhale, Elara watched a magical book fly past her head, feeling no urge to look up. "That's nice, Lyra," she mumbled, pulling a loose thread from the hem of her tunic. "Can we go back to the village now? The tavern has that stew I like, and standing here is making my legs fall asleep."

I clicked my tongue against the roof of my mouth, echoing the rhythmic dripping of water from the bunker's ceiling. My sister was on her knees, crying over a pristine map of safe zones our father had secretly encrypted for her. I picked up my item—a half-empty bottle of expired hot sauce—and rolled it back and forth across my lap. Forward. Backward. Forward. Backward. "We're saved," she whispered, tracing the blue lines. I slouched deeper into the uncomfortable folding chair, staring at the concrete wall. There were exactly forty-two cracks in the paint. I knew this because I had counted them three times since we sat down. "Sure," I said, my voice entirely devoid of inflection. I tossed the bottle of hot sauce into the air, caught it, and let out a long, loud yawn that echoed through the small room.

Julian sat on the edge of the stone fountain, rhythmically kicking his heel against the masonry. His brother, Arthur, stood in the center of the manicured lawn, clutching a binder detailing full ownership of the multi-million-dollar estate. Julian looked down at the rusty gardening trowel he had been handed. He dragged the metal tip through the dirt, drawing a series of meaningless squiggles, then erasing them with his shoe. Arthur was already on his cell phone, aggressively negotiating landscaping contracts and property taxes. Julian leaned his head back, watching a solitary cloud drift across the sky at an agonizingly slow pace. It looked a bit like a sheep. He checked his watch, noting that only two minutes had passed since he last looked. He let out a loud exhale, wondering how long Arthur was going to talk on the phone.

I kicked a loose bolt across the floor deck, watching it skitter into the dark corner of the cargo bay. Over by the main console, my sister was running her hands over the sleek controls of a fully operational star-fighter, her face glowing with the reflection of the ignition sequence. I looked down at the bulky, obsolete waste-recycler unit our mother had designated for me. I sat down heavily on top of it, resting my elbows on my knees and propping my face in both hands. My sister was crying about our mother's legacy. I peeled a tiny flake of dried paint off the recycler's casing, flicking it away. Then I found another flake. "Can we launch already?" I asked, my voice flat. "There's a holovision marathon starting in twenty minutes, and I really don't want to miss the beginning."

Sarah clicked her ballpoint pen. In. Out. In. Out. Across the worn kitchen table, her brother wept as he read the heartfelt, handwritten letter from their late grandfather, granting him the fertile north fields. Sarah stared at her own inheritance document: a legal notice making her the sole owner of a singular, elderly mule named Barnaby. She rested her cheek flat against the cool wood of the table, her eyes tracking a fly as it buzzed lazily around the sugar bowl. The fly landed, walked a few steps, and flew again. "This is so beautiful," her brother choked out, wiping his eyes. Sarah exhaled a long, heavy breath that fluttered a stray piece of paper. She didn't lift her head. "Yup," she mumbled, closing her eyes and wishing she was back in her apartment doing literally anything else.

I scooped up a handful of sand and let it sift slowly through my fingers, watching the grains pile up between my boots. A few feet away, my brother was losing his mind, hauling a massive chest of glittering gold doubloons out of the shallow water. I glanced down at the single wooden peg leg our pirate father had explicitly left to me. I tapped my knuckles against the hollow wood, listening to the dull thud. My brother was laughing, throwing coins into the air and letting them rain down on his shoulders. I sighed, slouching back against a palm tree and staring out at the completely empty, flat horizon. There wasn't a single ship in sight. I grabbed another handful of sand and started a second, smaller pile next to the first one, my eyelids drooping heavily in the afternoon sun.

Chloe leaned back in the plush leather chair, staring at the ceiling and slowly spinning herself in a circle. Her twin sister, Maya, stood at the floor-to-ceiling windows, hyperventilating as she signed the documents granting her fifty-one percent controlling shares of the tech conglomerate. Chloe stopped spinning, looked at her own document—a lifetime voucher for the company cafeteria—and pushed off the desk to start spinning the chair in the opposite direction. Maya was rapidly pacing, shouting into her earpiece about hostile takeovers and quarterly projections. Chloe let her chin drop to her chest, blowing a stray strand of hair out of her face. "Hey, Maya," she interrupted, her tone completely lifeless. "Does this voucher cover the premium smoothies, or just the regular fountain drinks? Actually, don't answer. I don't really care. Just tell me when we can leave."

I picked at the gold embroidery on the velvet chair, pulling a golden thread loose. My brother stood before the high altar, gasping as the high priest placed the jewel-encrusted Crown of the Ancients upon his head. The hall erupted in deafening cheers. I glanced down at the rusted iron horseshoe in my lap, supposedly an ancient relic meant just for me. I rested my chin in my hand, staring blankly at the back of a palace guard's helmet. The guard shifted his weight from his left foot to his right. Then back to his left. I let out a loud, prolonged yawn, not bothering to cover my mouth. The chanting continued endlessly. I slumped lower in my seat, hoping the royal banquet would at least serve cake.

Victor traced a figure-eight on the glass coffee table, over and over again, feeling the slight friction of the surface beneath his fingertip. His sister paced the gallery, crying tears of joy as the curator handed her the original, multi-million-dollar abstract canvas painted by their late mother. Victor looked down at his own inheritance: a blank, white piece of standard printer paper, signed in the bottom right corner. The curator was giving a passionate speech about the duality of nothingness. Victor leaned his head all the way back, staring up at the fluorescent lights until his vision started to swim. He let out a long, audible sigh, tapping his foot in a slow, steady rhythm. "So," Victor said, his voice flat and perfectly even, interrupting the curator's grand monologue. "Is there a coat check here, or should I just hold my jacket?"

My sister aggressively taped another cardboard box, her marker squeaking as she labeled it "Kitchen Crockery." I sat cross-legged on the faded floral carpet, staring at the ceiling fan. It completed exactly forty-two revolutions a minute. I know, because I counted. Thrice. I picked up a porcelain figurine of a shepherd boy, tracing its chipped ear with my thumb, then placed it exactly where I found it. "Are you going to help, or just breathe loudly?" Maya snapped, sliding a stack of doilies into a crate. I leaned my head back against the sofa, watching a lone dust speck drift through a shaft of afternoon sunlight. The grandfather clock in the hall ticked, each heavy pendulum swing stretching the silence into an endless, flat line. "I'll pack the spoons," I offered, making no move to stand up.

Leo rested his cheek against the cool mahogany dining table, tracing the woodgrain patterns with a bent paperclip. Across from him, Sarah reviewed the estate paperwork, her highlighter moving in sharp, decisive strokes. The inheritance of Gran's Victorian manor was meant to be a grand event, but the afternoon had stretched into a vast expanse of legalese. Leo flicked the paperclip. It spun, clattered against a teacup, and stopped. He sighed, adjusting his weight on the stiff-backed dining chair. He picked up the heavy velvet curtain tassel dangling near his elbow, braiding and unbraiding the gold threads. "Subsection 4b stipulates the garden maintenance," Sarah muttered. Leo let his eyes drift toward the window. The neighbor's sprinkler oscillated back and forth. Chk-chk-chk-chk. He synced his quiet tapping against the table to the water's rhythm, waiting for the sun to finally set.

We had been walking through the empty corridors for three hours, and I had long since stopped listening to Thomas appraise the crown molding. He knocked on a wall, murmuring about load-bearing beams. I dragged the toe of my sneaker along the skirting board, collecting a thick rim of dust. The house was massive, an endless labyrinth of beige wallpaper and sheet-covered furniture. I pulled my phone from my pocket, illuminated the blank lock screen, and shoved it back. Not even a spam notification. "Look at the craftsmanship of these banisters," Thomas said, his voice echoing in the hollow entryway. I rested my chin in my palm, staring at a cluster of dead flies trapped in the frosted glass of the chandelier. "Fascinating," I replied, my voice entirely flat. I began silently reciting the alphabet backwards just to give my brain something to chew on.

Dust motes danced lazily in the humid attic air. Chloe sat on an overturned milk crate, aimlessly opening and closing the brass latch of a steamer trunk. Click. Clack. Click. Clack. "Stop doing that, you're driving me crazy," her brother Elias muttered from the corner, where he was organizing their late grandmother’s collection of vintage photographs into chronological order. Chloe let her hand drop into her lap, exhaling a long, slow breath that ruffled her bangs. She picked at a loose thread on her jeans, pulling it until the denim puckered. The silence pressed heavily against her ears, interrupted only by the rustle of Elias’s photo paper. She stared at a stack of National Geographic magazines from 1982, reading the yellow spines over and over. "Do you think the paint on the walls downstairs will peel before we finish this?" she asked the ceiling.

Arthur dragged an armchair onto the wraparound porch, and I took the woven hammock. We had the keys to Nana's estate, a vast property miles away from the nearest town. He immediately opened his laptop to research property taxes. I lay back, pushing the hammock with one foot to create a slow, agonizingly predictable sway. Up, down. Up, down. The rhythmic creak of the rope against the hook became my entire universe. I watched a caterpillar inch its way across the wooden railing. It took five minutes to travel from one post to the next. I narrated its journey in my head, assigning it a dramatic backstory just to fill the void behind my eyes. Arthur’s keyboard clattered relentlessly. I let my arm dangle over the edge of the hammock, brushing my fingertips against the dry grass below, wondering if it was physically possible to melt into a puddle.

The garage smelled faintly of motor oil and mothballs. Jenny priced the endless boxes of ceramic thimbles, her pricing gun clicking rhythmically. Mark sat on a deflated air mattress in the corner, tossing a tennis ball against the drywall and catching it. Thump. Smack. Thump. Smack. "Could you be helpful?" Jenny asked without looking up. Mark caught the ball and held it. He looked around the dimly lit garage at the towers of Tupperware and ancient gardening tools. He picked up a rusted trowel, balanced it on his index finger, and watched it tip over and clatter to the concrete floor. He slouched forward, resting his elbows on his knees, and let out a loud, shuddering breath. "I'll manage the cash box," he offered, knowing full well the sale wouldn't start for another three days. He went back to tossing the ball, counting the bounces under his breath.

My brother scrubbed the grout with the zeal of a madman. I sat at the kitchen island, staring at the swirling linoleum pattern until the shapes began to blur into strange, mutated faces. Grandma’s house was ours now, but it felt like a museum where nothing ever happened. I took a sugar packet from the ceramic bowl in the center of the table and began carefully folding it into a tiny accordion. When that lost its appeal, I flattened it out and started over. "You missed a spot near the fridge," I pointed out, my voice lacking any real inflection. Jake grunted, scrubbing harder. I rested my cheek on the cool countertop, blowing a loose hair out of my eyes. A solitary ant marched past my nose. I placed my finger in its path, watched it turn around, and felt a tiny sliver of triumph at the distraction.

Mothballs and lavender perfumed the walk-in closet. Diane meticulously folded a series of pastel cardigans, her face a mask of fierce concentration. Beside her, Greg sat entirely motionless on a velvet ottoman. He had been holding the same beige scarf for twenty minutes. He stared at the wall, his jaw slack, eyes glazed over. Every few minutes, he shifted his weight, letting out a prolonged, airy sigh that fluttered his lips. He began to count the number of wooden hangers on the left rack. Fifty-two. He counted the plastic ones. Thirty-four. He tied the beige scarf into a thick knot, untied it, and then tied it into a double knot. "Do you think she kept all her shoes?" Greg mumbled, his chin resting heavily in his cupped hands. Diane didn't answer. Greg closed his eyes, mentally mapping the layout of his own ceiling at home.

The appraiser was three hours late. My sister, Clara, paced the length of the living room, nervously checking her wristwatch. I was slumped so far down in Gran’s floral recliner that my spine formed a perfect curve. I stared at the muted television screen, watching the reflection of the ceiling fan blades spin. I tapped my right heel against the carpet, creating a steady, muted drumbeat. Tap, tap, tap. "Stop that," Clara snapped. I stopped. I lifted my right hand and began drumming my fingers on the armrest instead. I examined my fingernails, mentally debating the pros and cons of clipping them now versus later. The antique grandfather clock ticked loudly in the hallway. I timed my breathing to its rhythm. Inhale on the tick, exhale on the tock. I wondered how many ticks it would take before I literally fused with the upholstery.

The sprawling backyard was severely overgrown. Patricia stood with her hands on her hips, detailing a grand vision for rose bushes and a gazebo. Simon sat on a rotting tree stump, staring intently at a blade of grass. He plucked it, split it down the middle with his thumbnail, and tossed the pieces into the wind. He grabbed another blade and repeated the process. Patricia’s voice droned on about soil acidity and pruning techniques, blending into a steady, meaningless hum in Simon’s ears. He leaned his head all the way back, watching a single cloud drift across the painfully blue sky. It looked vaguely like a shoe. Ten minutes later, it still looked like a shoe, just slightly stretched. He let his posture completely collapse, his shoulders rounding forward until he was hunched over his knees, endlessly peeling the bark off a dead twig.

The basement was cold and smelled of damp earth. While Nora examined the ancient furnace with a flashlight, I sat on the bottom step of the wooden stairs. I kicked my heel against the riser. Thud. I waited exactly five seconds. Thud. "I think the pilot light is completely rusted," Nora called out from the darkness. "Mm," I responded, not bothering to open my mouth. I pulled my phone out, swiped to the home screen, swiped to the second page of apps, swiped back, and locked it. I noticed a small spider weaving a web between the banister and the wall. I leaned in close, watching the tiny creature work. It was the most action I had seen all morning. I rested my chin on my knees, letting my eyes go out of focus until the web blurred into a hazy, vibrating gray blob.

The library smelled of decaying paper and old leather. Evelyn carefully removed each book from the mahogany shelves, dusting the covers with a microfiber cloth. Miles was tasked with carrying the boxes, but he had instead draped himself across the leather Chesterfield sofa. His legs hung off one armrest, his head off the other. He stared upside down at the bookshelves, watching Evelyn move in slow motion. He picked up a leather-bound dictionary, opened it to a random page, and read the definition for 'spoon.' He closed the book. He opened it again to the definition for 'lint.' He closed it. He blew a raspberry, the sound vibrating loudly in the quiet room. "Miles, please," Evelyn sighed, not turning around. Miles dropped the heavy book onto the carpet, let his arm hang limp towards the floor, and watched the dust settle in the sunlight.

I counted the ceiling tiles for the fourth time—forty-eight complete squares, twelve partials along the edges. The ticking of the wall clock felt like physical taps on my forehead. I slumped down in the vinyl chair, letting my chin rest heavily on my palm, watching dust motes drift through a sliver of sunlight. A woman sat across from me, mindlessly peeling the label off her water bottle. "Fibrodysplasia ossificans?" she asked suddenly, noticing the rigid brace on my arm. I blinked, pulling myself from a deep study of a scuff mark on the linoleum. "Yeah," I replied, shifting my weight to relieve the stiffness. "You too?" She nodded, pointing to her own locked shoulder joint. We sat back in the silence. It was a one-in-two-million genetic mutation, yet here we were, just two people waiting another agonizing forty minutes for Dr. Aris.

Julian dragged his sneakers along the carpeted floor of the pharmacy, advancing exactly three inches every two minutes. He let his head loll back, staring at the fluorescent lights until his vision blurred, then checked his watch. Only three minutes had passed since he last checked. He exhaled loudly, a long rush of air that puffed his cheeks, and leaned his entire body weight against the display of seasonal allergy medications. Beside him, a girl in a yellow sweater was systematically clicking and unclicking a ballpoint pen. Click-clack. Click-clack. Julian stared at her prescription slip, recognizing the impossible twelve-syllable name of the medication he was also here to pick up. "Kleine-Levin Syndrome?" he mumbled, his eyelids heavy. She stopped clicking her pen, staring at him. "You sleep for weeks at a time, too?" she asked. Julian just nodded slowly, resting his forehead against the metal shelving.

My thumb swiped up the phone screen. Swipe. Swipe. Swipe. Nothing new. Just endless photos of lattes and dogs. I rested my forehead against the cool glass of the cafe window, watching cars stop at the red light, go on green, stop on red. Over and over. I pulled up my obscure medical support group, scrolling past the same three posts from yesterday about Alice in Wonderland Syndrome. Someone named 'TeaDrinker99' had just posted: Sitting at the Beanery on 4th, everything looks tiny today. I paused my thumb. I was at the Beanery on 4th. I looked up. A guy two tables over was tracing the rim of his mug with a dead-eyed expression, occasionally holding up his hand and squinting at it. I walked over, dragging my feet. "Your hands feel like they're shrinking?" I asked. He looked up, his jaw dropping.

Maya folded the edge of her informational pamphlet, smoothed it out, folded it again, and tore off the tiny triangle of paper. She rested her cheek against her palm, letting her eyes glaze over as the speaker at the front droned on about dietary fiber. The folding chair dug into her lower back. She began counting the number of times the speaker said 'um.' Beside her, an older man was meticulously aligning and realigning a row of three mints on his knee. Maya glanced at the chart peeking out of his folder. "Foreign Accent Syndrome," it read. She sat up a fraction of an inch. "You woke up sounding like a 1920s British aristocrat, too?" she whispered, her thick, misplaced cockney accent bleeding through. The man turned, his eyes widening. "Indeed, I did," he whispered back in perfect, unearned Scottish brogue. Maya went back to tearing paper.

Six hours down, eight to go. I stared at the back of the seat in front of me, tracing the woven pattern of the grey fabric with my eyes. Up, over, down, across. My movie screen had frozen on a still frame of an explosion three hours ago. I sighed, letting my arms dangle uselessly over the armrests, tapping an erratic rhythm against the plastic casing. The guy next to me was doing the exact same thing, his chin buried in his chest. I noticed the thick, specialized compression gloves on his hands, identical to the ones hiding in my pockets. "Aquagenic urticaria?" I asked softly, my voice raspy from disuse. He stopped tapping, turning his head slowly toward me. "Water allergy," he confirmed. "I break out in hives if I sweat." I nodded. "Me too." We stared at the frozen screen together.

Arthur kicked a pebble across the pavement. It clattered against the metal leg of the bus shelter. He kicked it back. It took exactly three seconds to roll from his left shoe to his right. The bus was delayed. Again. He slumped onto the wooden bench, tilting his head back to watch a lone grey cloud inch its way across a washed-out sky. A young woman sat on the other end of the bench, blowing a massive bubblegum bubble until it popped, then reeling it back in to chew. As she stretched her legs, Arthur saw the distinctive, custom-molded orthopedic shoes she wore, designed specifically for Proteus syndrome. He glanced down at his own identical, clunky footwear. "Overgrowth of the bones?" he asked, not changing his slouched posture. She popped another bubble. "Left femur and right ribs," she mumbled. Arthur nodded, kicking the pebble again.
