I stirred the greyish soup with my plastic spoon, watching noodles swirl into a miniature whirlpool before settling into a stagnant puddle. Lift spoon, drop liquid, repeat. The cafeteria smelled of bleach and boiled carrots. I rested my chin on my free hand, letting my eyes drop half-shut. A woman slid her tray onto the table opposite me, her gaze fixed on an identical bowl. She began tearing her napkin into tiny, perfectly square pieces. I noticed the distinct yellow tint to her sclera and the tremor in her hands. "Wilson's disease?" I asked, my voice flat, barely carrying over the hum of the vending machines. She stopped tearing the napkin and looked at my hands, which were shaking in the exact same rhythm. "Too much copper in the system," she said. I offered a slow nod and went back to stirring.

Leo stared at the digital counter above the desk. Now serving: 42. He looked at his ticket. Number 89. He slid down in his plastic chair until his knees hit the seat in front of him, letting out a long, whistling exhale. He picked at a stray thread on his jeans, pulling it until it snapped. To his right, a teenager was mindlessly spinning a keychain around her finger. Round and round. She dropped her paperwork, and as Leo leaned over to hand it back, he saw the medical exemption form for Trimethylaminuria. He paused, looking at her. "Your body can't process TMA either?" he asked, recognizing the condition he was here to register for. She stopped spinning the keys. "Yeah," she said quietly. Leo handed the paper back, slumped down further into his chair, and watched the counter click to 43.

Floor 3. Floor 4. Floor 5. I watched the illuminated numbers change, leaning heavily against the brass handrail. The Muzak overhead was an instrumental version of a pop song from ten years ago. I tapped the toe of my shoe against the carpet, wishing the metal box would move faster. The only other person in the elevator was a woman staring blankly at the floor indicators, chewing slowly on a piece of gum. I noticed she was wearing the highly specialized tinted glasses I had in my purse. "Achromatopsia?" I asked into the quiet space, not bothering to lift my head. She glanced over, her eyes completely devoid of color cones, just like mine. "Total colorblindness, yeah," she muttered. Floor 8. Floor 9. "We're the one in thirty thousand," I said flatly. She popped a bubble. "Cool," she replied. The elevator music looped back to the chorus.

Sam rested his forehead against the vibrating glass of the train window. The landscape outside was a continuous, gray smear of concrete and power lines. He scrolled through his phone, closing apps immediately after opening them. He sighed, turning his phone over in his hands. Across the aisle, a man was meticulously peeling the label off an empty water bottle, strip by tiny strip. Sam noticed the man’s eyes—the distinct, star-shaped cataracts clouding both pupils. It was the exact complication of the rare genetic metabolic disorder Sam had. "Galactosemia?" Sam asked aloud, his voice devoid of inflection. The man stopped peeling, squinting through his clouded vision. "Since birth," the man answered. "Can't digest galactose." Sam tapped his phone against his knee. "Same," he said, turning back to the window to watch another row of power lines zip past into the gray distance.

I flipped the page of the textbook, read the first sentence, and promptly forgot it. I flipped back, read it again, and sighed. The library was suffocatingly quiet. I rested my chin on my crossed arms, staring at the dust particles dancing in the shaft of light on my desk. At the next table, a guy was balancing a pencil on his nose, letting it fall, and balancing it again. As he reached to catch it, his sleeve rode up, revealing a medical alert bracelet. I recognized the specific engraving for Pompe disease. I rolled up my own sleeve, exposing an identical metal band. He stopped balancing the pencil, his eyes dropping to my wrist. "Glycogen storage issue?" he asked. "Yeah," I mumbled, resting my heavy head back on the desk. "Muscles turn to mush." I went back to staring at the dust.

Elena traced the grain of the wooden park bench with her thumbnail, following a groove until it ended, then finding another. Pigeons pecked at the concrete nearby, but she didn't bother looking at them. The afternoon stretched out in front of her, vast and empty. Beside her, a stranger was tossing a crumpled receipt into the air and catching it. Over and over. When the receipt missed his hand, it landed on his lap, right next to his specialized auto-injector pen. Elena stopped tracing the wood. She pulled out an identical pen from her bag. "Mast Cell Activation Syndrome?" she asked, her voice dragging. The stranger caught his receipt, glancing at the pen in her hand. "Yeah," he said, slouching back. "Allergic to basically the whole world." Elena gave a slow nod, putting her pen away. The stranger tossed his receipt into the air again.

Elias stirred his lukewarm coffee for the twentieth time, watching the brown liquid swirl in slow, lazy circles. Across the table, the woman—Sarah, he thought her name was—was hyperventilating, thrusting her phone in his face to show him a text from Marcus. Elias didn't look at the screen. Instead, he studied a water stain on the ceiling tile above her head, noting how it looked vaguely like a tortoise. "So he's with both of us," Sarah gasped, tears welling in her eyes. "Can you believe it?" Elias let out a long, slow exhale, letting his chin rest heavily in his palm. "Yeah. Crazy," he mumbled, his voice entirely flat. He picked at a stray thread on his sleeve, pulling it until it snapped. He wondered if the bus was running on schedule today; he really didn't want to wait at the stop.

The guy cornered me near the abstract sculptures, his face flushed red as he held up a framed photo of my girlfriend, Chloe, kissing his cheek. He was breathless, launching into a timeline of their relationship that perfectly overlapped with mine. I nodded slowly, my eyes drifting away from his frantic gestures to count the scuff marks on the hardwood floor. One, two, three. "Did you hear me?" he demanded, his voice echoing slightly in the quiet gallery. "She's playing us." I suppressed a yawn, covering my mouth with the back of my hand. "Right," I said, shifting my weight from my left foot to my right. I checked my watch, noting that I still had forty-five minutes before the museum café opened. "So," I said, staring past him at a beige canvas, "do you think they serve decent pastries here, or is it just muffins?"

The hum of the washing machines drowned out most of what the crying stranger was saying, but Maya got the gist. David was cheating on them both. Maya sat rigidly on the plastic folding chair, her chin resting heavily on her fist. She stared blankly at the tumbling clothes in dryer number four. A single red sock flipped over and over, trapped in an endless, predictable loop. "We have to confront him," the woman urged, grabbing Maya’s limp arm. Maya let her arm be shaken, feeling like a ragdoll. She slowly blinked her heavy eyelids, letting out a prolonged, airy sigh. "Sure," Maya said, her tone devoid of any inflection. She checked her phone screen for the fifth time in three minutes—no new notifications. "Could we do it after my heavy delicates finish? There are still twenty-two minutes left on the cycle."

I tossed another piece of bread onto the cobblestones, watching the pigeons swarm. The woman next to me was still talking. She'd introduced herself as Mark's fiancée. I was Mark's girlfriend of two years. She was vibrating with rage, detailing his lies. I rested my chin on my palm, my gaze fixed on a pigeon with a missing toe. It hobbled around, pecking the dirt. "Aren't you furious?" she finally yelled, snapping her fingers in front of my face. I blinked, pulling my attention back to her with great effort. "Yeah," I said, my voice completely level. "Totally." I ripped another crust, rolling it between my thumb and forefinger into a tiny sphere. "Do you think birds can taste the difference between sourdough and rye, or is it all just the same to them?"

Oliver traced the geometric pattern of the lobby's carpet with the tip of his shoe, letting his mind drift as the man next to him spiraled. "I just saw her kiss you," the man stammered, pacing back and forth. "Elena. She told me she was working late." Oliver slumped deeper into the plush leather sofa, letting his head roll back against the cushion to stare at the fluorescent ceiling lights. They hummed with a low, static buzz. "She tells me that, too," Oliver replied, his voice a slow drawl. He tapped his fingers rhythmically against his thigh—one, two, three, four. The man stopped pacing, leaning in close. "We need a plan." Oliver let out a heavy breath, slowly bringing his head back down to look at the man's frantic face. "Can we plan it later?" Oliver muttered. "I've been sitting here for an hour."

The girl beside me on the bench was shaking, holding up a printout of my boyfriend's dating profile. "He matched with me three months ago," she whispered, a tear slipping down her cheek. I kept my eyes glued to the street. Seven red cars had passed since I sat down. I was hoping for an even ten. "Did you hear me?" she asked, her voice cracking. "He's playing both of us." I leaned my head against the cold glass of the bus shelter, exhaling slowly. The glass fogged up, and I lazily drew a smiley face in the condensation with my index finger. "Yeah, I heard you," I murmured, watching the smile slowly drip away. Another red car zoomed by. Eight. I checked the digital schedule above us. Twelve more minutes. I closed my eyes and let my head loll to the side.

The man with the shopping cart was practically in tears, clutching a box of cereal as he explained how he and Jessica had been engaged for six months. Julian stood beside him in the breakfast aisle, holding a jar of peanut butter. Julian’s eyes slowly scanned the nutritional information on the back of the label. Two hundred calories per serving. He wondered why anyone cared. "She's tearing my life apart!" the man cried, gesturing wildly. Julian let his shoulders slump, letting out a drawn-out puff of air that rustled his own bangs. He slowly placed the peanut butter back on the shelf, perfectly aligning it with the edge. "That's rough," Julian said in a flat monotone. He grabbed a different brand of peanut butter, spinning it lazily in his hand to read the ingredients. "Anyway, do you know if she prefers crunchy or smooth?"

He cornered me in the reference section, whispering fiercely about my husband's secret apartment downtown and the life they had built there. As he unloaded the betrayal, I flipped the pages of the encyclopedia in front of me. I wasn't reading the text. I just liked the soft, papery sound they made when they turned. Swish, swish. "Are you even listening?" he hissed, slamming his hand down on the table. I slowly raised my eyes, giving him a blank, heavy-lidded look. I propped my cheek on my fist. "Yes. Secret apartment. Got it," I mumbled softly. I picked up a pencil and began shading in the letter 'O' on a scrap piece of paper until it was a solid, dark circle. "I guess that explains his Tuesday nights," I added with a slow exhale, tapping the pencil's eraser repeatedly against the wooden desk.

The bartender had just dropped off their drinks when the woman next to Leo dropped the bomb. She was dating Sam, too. As she ranted about Sam’s lies, her voice rising in pitch, Leo stared fixedly at his beer bottle. With slow, methodical scrapes of his thumbnail, he worked on peeling the paper label off in one continuous strip. It tore halfway through. Leo gave a profound, heavy sigh. "This is a disaster," the woman wailed, covering her face with her hands. Leo rested his chin on the sticky mahogany counter, his half-closed eyes tracking a lone ant crawling near the coaster. "Yeah," Leo murmured, his voice lacking any trace of volume or energy. He flicked a soggy piece of the label across the bar. "Do you think they have any pretzels in this place? Or maybe just peanuts?"

She confronted me right after spin class, holding out her phone to show me the identical texts Greg had sent us both that morning. "He's a monster," she panted, still sweaty from the workout. I sat heavily on the wooden bench, staring down at my sneakers. I took an agonizingly long time undoing the double knot on my left shoe. Pulling the laces apart felt like an enormous chore. "I feel so used," she continued, her voice echoing off the metal lockers. I kicked off the shoe and stared at my gray sock, wiggling my big toe. "Mhm," I replied, a prolonged hum that vibrated in my throat. I let my back hit the lockers behind me with a dull thud, staring up at the acoustic ceiling tiles. "Hey, did the instructor say we're doing hills next week, or sprints? I totally tuned out."

Arthur sat on the splintering bench, his legs stretched out and crossed at the ankles. The young man standing over him was frantic, waving a flight itinerary. "She's taking me to Paris next week! She told you she was on a work trip!" the man shouted. Arthur slowly rubbed his temples, feeling the heavy drag of the afternoon sun. He watched a golden retriever completely ignore a thrown tennis ball, opting instead to sniff a fire hydrant. "Paris. Nice," Arthur said, his tone perfectly flat. He let out a long, gaping yawn, not bothering to cover his mouth. He dug his hands deep into his jacket pockets, slouching further down until his spine curved like a 'C'. "I wonder if I should get a dog," Arthur mumbled softly to himself, completely ignoring the irate man beside him. "Or maybe a turtle. Turtles are quiet."

We were both at the clinic to pick up Alex. When we realized we were both his boyfriends, the other guy lost his mind. He paced the waiting area, muttering angrily. I sat slumped in the plastic chair, my gaze locked onto the zipper of my jacket. I pulled it up. Zzzzip. I pulled it down. Zzzzip. "How could he do this to us?" the guy demanded, glaring at me. I offered a slow, loose-shouldered shrug, letting my chin sink into my collarbone. "Dunno," I dragged the word out, my voice flat. I leaned my head back against the wall, staring blankly at the ticking clock. The second hand seemed to freeze between the four and the five. I let out a heavy sigh, closing my eyes. "Do you think the vending machine down the hall takes card?" I asked the ceiling.
